articles.title: Italy fines Meta €805 million over a Facebook feature that scanned Android camera rolls
articles.text:
The Italian Fine: Meta keeps racking up huge fines for violating users' privacy across the globe. According to Italy's data protection authority, the Facebook parent was hit with the largest penalty the regulator has ever issued, in part because it did not fully cooperate with authorities during the investigation.
The Italian Data Protection Authority (GPDP) recently announced a new, massive fine against Meta. According to the announcement, the social network giant accessed photos and videos of millions of Italian Android users without asking for proper permission first. Meta has been ordered to comply within two months, or face an even worse punishment.
Italy's Garante Privacy is fining Meta €805 million, or around $887 million, over a Facebook feature called "Get camera roll suggestions when you're browsing Facebook." The feature has been available since 2023, suggesting photos and videos taken straight from Android's "camera roll" as ideas for new posts.
The GPDP began investigating Facebook in 2025, after receiving a complaint from a consumer protection organization called CTCU. The authority eventually concluded that Facebook's behavior was unlawful under Italy's privacy code, which implements Europe's ePrivacy Directive. Access to camera rolls was requested with a single, app-wide permission, with an unclear notice about the potential impact on a user's privacy.
Furthermore, the feature was enabled by default. Users were unknowingly giving Facebook broad access to their photos and other private content, which goes against Article 122 of the Italian Data Protection Code. Around 20 million Italian Android users were affected by the issue, and the breach is still ongoing for people who have not updated the Facebook app over the past few years.
The GPDP said Meta did not properly cooperate during the investigation, and that weighed on the size of the penalty, which amounts to roughly 0.47% of its global turnover. Furthermore, Facebook must disable the infringing feature within 60 days, asking Android users for a new permission regardless of previously confirmed requests.
Meta responded by confirming it is going to appeal. A company spokesperson called the fine disproportionate, and said the straightforward Android feature simply helps people post new content on their Facebook feeds. Permission is always required, the spokesperson said, and can be changed at any time through the app's settings.
Either way, Meta is facing growing, worldwide pressure over these allegedly "straightforward" attempts to access users' content whenever and however the company feels like. In October, a New Mexico judge ordered Facebook's parent company to pay $25 billion, after a jury found it had violated the state's consumer protection laws more than 43 million times.

articles.title: Microsoft outage explained: a three-month-old bug's global impact
articles.text:
Microsoft has finally explained what caused last week’s massive outage, which disrupted businesses and governments worldwide.
The Microsoft 365 outage, which started on Nov. 12 and continued until the morning of Nov. 14, was caused by a combination of issues, including a defect introduced in a July 2026 patch.
Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, took to Twitter/X to share the details behind the outage. First, Lamanna noted that “a latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions.” Notably, Lamanna said the defect was the “result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers” and didn’t impact broader Windows deployments.
The defect was introduced in July, but did not cause any issues until now. Moreover, Lamanna said the defect wasn’t detected by Microsoft’s internal tests, which focused on “weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.” The defect, however, was “worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware.”
The second issue Lamanna highlighted was a surge in load caused by a Teams issue that happened roughly 15 hours before the Microsoft 365 outage. Lamanna explained that Microsoft maintains multiple network gateway systems for its services so that if there’s an issue with one, there’s a fallback. The Teams issue caused it to move to the same gateway used for Exchange Online (which powers email services like Outlook), significantly increasing the load on that gateway.
Finally, Lamanna said that “nearly 14% of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service due to an unrelated issue from the previous day.”
Combined, these issues triggered the July defect, leading requests to build up until servers ultimately stopped responding in the midst of North America’s peak traffic window. Worse, Microsoft’s traffic management systems respond to outages like this by automatically routing traffic to healthy servers. But that caused the July bug to trigger again, resulting in multiple servers failing — at the worst point, over 80 per cent of the company’s servers were unresponsive.
Lamanna explained that recovery took longer than usual because as servers came back online, waiting traffic immediately overwhelmed them again, causing the July defect to trigger and make the servers unresponsive. And since the bug was several months old, Microsoft wasn’t able to quickly revert the change. Instead, the company had to patch the bug, restart the servers in batches, and slowly bring things back online.
Microsoft is expected to publish a final post-incident report on Nov. 20, which will likely include more details about the cause of this outage. Still, the fact that this outage happened is cause for concern, and yet another valid reason for getting off U.S. tech. At the very least, Microsoft should be held accountable for the mess this caused — perhaps a Canadian law firm will do just that.

articles.title: Cybersecurity AI startup Corma reaches $1B valuation in about 3 months | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.
The startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP, a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled.
Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

articles.title: Wie heiß wird’s? Auf der UN-Klimakonferenz stehen diese Themen auf der Tagesordnung
articles.text:
Klimaanpassungen, Finanzierung und fossile Brennstoffe: Was wird die UN-Klimakonferenz erreichen?
Alle Jahre wieder: Tausende Delegierte, Lobbyist:innen und Journalist:innen sind zu den UN-Klimaverhandlungen, diesmal in Antalya in der Türkei, zusammengekommen. Damit ist gerade die größte Bühne für den Beginn der Verhandlungen der weltweiten Klimapolitik eröffnet. Noch bis 20. November gehen die Diskussionen.
Auf diesem jährlichen Treffen kann man gut sehen, wo die Welt bei der Bewältigung der Klimakrise und der Anpassung daran steht. Und die diesjährigen Gespräche werden es sicherlich in sich haben. Zu erwarten ist viel Hin und Her in Bezug auf fossile Brennstoffe und die Klimafinanzierung. Daher solltest du das Folgende über die COP31 wissen:
Welche Vertreter nehmen in diesem Jahr an der Klimakonferenz teil?
In den letzten Jahren ist die Spannung immer groß, wenn die COP (Abkürzung für „Conference of the Parties“) ansteht. Doch dieses Jahr scheint die Lage besonders angespannt: Die Welt hat nach wie vor mit dem Krieg im Iran zu kämpfen, der den Nahen Osten erschüttert. Die wirtschaftlichen Schockwellen sind global durch den sprunghaften Anstieg der Energiepreise zu spüren.
Die diesjährige Weltklimakonferenz wird die zweite sein, an der keine offizielle Delegation aus den USA teilnimmt. Präsident Trump hat das Land Anfang des Jahres offiziell aus dem Pariser Abkommen zurückgezogen und ist dabei, auch aus dem UN-Rahmenübereinkommen über Klimaänderungen auszutreten. Das ist der Vertrag, der eine formelle Teilnahme an den Verhandlungen ermöglicht. Ein Blick nach Deutschland zeigt, dass ebenso Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz dem Treffen zur Klimapolitik fern bleibt.
Unterdessen sieht es nicht gut aus für das Pariser Abkommen, das vor elf Jahren bei den UN-Klimaverhandlungen geschlossen wurde. Damals legte es das Ziel fest, die Erwärmung auf 1,5 Grad Celsius gegenüber dem vorindustriellen Niveau zu begrenzen. In einem im September veröffentlichten Bericht räumte das UN-Umweltprogramm ein, dass die globale Erwärmung dieses 1,5-Grad-Ziel „wahrscheinlich in den nächsten Jahren“ überschreiten wird.
Kosten, um Emissionen zu senken: Jährlich sind 300 Milliarden US-Dollar nötig
Zu Beginn der Klimaverhandlungen stellt sich daher die offensichtliche und dringende Frage, wie die Emissionen schnell gesenkt werden können, um die Erwärmung zu begrenzen. Hinzu kommt die wichtige Frage, wie die Maßnahmen zur Emissionsminderung finanziert und wie einer sich erwärmenden Welt geholfen werden kann, die unvermeidbaren Schäden zu bewältigen.
Vor zwei Jahren endeten die Verhandlungen mit dem Ziel, bis 2035 jährlich 300 Milliarden US-Dollar zu mobilisieren, um die Kosten für die Emissionsminderung und die Anpassung an den Klimawandel zu decken. Die reichen Nationen stellten im Jahr 2024 136,7 Milliarden US-Dollar bereit, laut der Organisation für wirtschaftliche Zusammenarbeit und Entwicklung (OECD). Und im vergangenen Jahr enthielt das COP30-Abkommen das Ziel, die Mittel für Anpassungsmaßnahmen in diesem Zeitraum zu verdreifachen. (Diese Finanzmittel sind in den letzten Jahren weitgehend unverändert geblieben.)
Die Welt wurde Anfang dieses Jahres auf tragische Weise daran erinnert, wie hoch der Einsatz ist, als ein Gletschereinsturz verheerende Überschwemmungen im Himalaya verursachte. Die Flut forderte etwa 1.500 Todesopfer, über 5.000 Menschen werden noch vermisst, und es entstand ein Schaden von fast fünf Milliarden US-Dollar. Der UN-Fonds für Verluste und Schäden stellte 20 Millionen US-Dollar zur Unterstützung Nepals beim Wiederaufbau bereit (weniger als ein Prozent der geschätzten Gesamtkosten für das Land).
Was geschieht mit dem Thema „Ausstieg aus fossilen Brennstoffen“?
Ein weiterer wichtiger Trend, den es zu beobachten gilt, ist, wie das Thema fossile Brennstoffe in den formellen Verhandlungen behandelt wird. Vor drei Jahren forderte der endgültige Vertragstext ausdrücklich einen Ausstieg aus fossilen Brennstoffen. Doch es schien, als hätte es im letzten Jahr einen Rückschritt gegeben, als der Begriff „fossile Brennstoffe“ im endgültigen Abkommen kein einziges Mal erwähnt wurde.
Das wird eine interessante Diskussion werden, insbesondere da die beiden Gastgeberländer Türkei und Australien beide wegen ihrer Beziehungen zu diesen Brennstoffen in der Kritik stehen. Australien ist ein bedeutender Exporteur von Kohle und Erdgas, und das türkische Stromnetz ist stark von fossilen Brennstoffen, einschließlich Kohle, abhängig.
Außerhalb der formellen Verhandlungen treibt der Vorsitzende der COP31, Murat Kurum, der türkische Umweltminister, eine Nebenagenda voran. Sie beinhaltet zwei informelle Initiativen, die man im Auge behalten sollte. Diese würden zwar nicht Teil des offiziellen Abkommenstextes sein, aber die Länder könnten sich anschließen, um ihre Unterstützung zu signalisieren.
Lachhafte KI-Verpflichtung und mehr Stromverbrauch gefordert
Eine davon ist eine Verpflichtung, KI nachhaltiger zu gestalten. Das ist fast schon lächerlich vage, selbst für freiwillige COP-Verpflichtungen. Der Text enthält den ausdrücklichen Hinweis, dass dadurch keine neuen Verpflichtungen für die Länder entstehen – man sollte also keine Durchsetzungsmaßnahmen in dieser Hinsicht erwarten.
Die COP-Führung drängt zudem darauf, den Anteil von Strom am Energieverbrauch der Mitgliedsländer zu erhöhen. Derzeit werden weltweit nur etwa 23 Prozent der Energie in Form von Strom genutzt. Fossile Brennstoffe, wie Benzin in Fahrzeugen oder Erdgas zum Heizen, machen den Großteil des Rests aus. Eine Umstellung auf einen höheren Stromverbrauch und die Nutzung sauberer Quellen für diesen Strom könnten dazu beitragen, die Emissionen zu senken. Das Ziel der neuen Verpflichtung sieht vor, dass Strom bis 2035 35 Prozent des gesamten Energieverbrauchs ausmacht.
Da die Führung diese Klimakonferenz als „Umsetzungs-COP“ bezeichnet, wäre es großartig, echte, greifbare Fortschritte bei der Bewältigung der globalen Herausforderung des Klimawandels zu sehen. Aber erwartet nichts Bahnbrechendes.

articles.title: Overlocker uses vibecoded BIOS modification to target Intel's non-K overclocking restrictions — attempts to revive ASRock's discontinued SkyOC technology
articles.text:
Overlocker uses vibecoded BIOS modification to target Intel's non-K overclocking restrictions — attempts to revive ASRock's discontinued SkyOC technology
An old ASRock trick gets a second shot.
In an attempt to resurrect ASRock's discontinued SkyOC overclocking feature, an enthusiast has vibe-coded a motherboard BIOS using AI, potentially bringing non-K CPU overclocking to modern Intel CPUs. According to a post on X, Hardware 360º used Chat-GPT Astra to decompile and compare two versions of an ASRock BIOS, one released with SkyOC and another with the feature disabled. The AI reportedly identified the code responsible for enabling the overclocking workaround and modified it to create a BIOS ready for implementation on a compatible motherboard. Unfortunately, it remains to be seen whether the modified firmware can restore SkyOC on modern Intel platforms, as the workaround is yet to be fully tested.
For context, Intel offers multiplier-based overclocking only on its unlocked K-series processors like the Core i9-14900K and the newer Core Ultra 270K Plus. Non-K models have locked multipliers, which restrict users from pushing CPU frequencies. However, there’s another way to raise the speed of a processor by pushing the base clock itself. The base clock, or BCLK, typically runs at 100 MHz and works alongside the CPU multiplier to determine its operating frequency. For example, raising the base clock speed of a CPU to 105 MHz increases the clock speed by 5%. The only downside is that BCLK adjustments can also affect the entire motherboard, including memory and PCIe-based components, thereby potentially causing system instability.
ASRock's SkyOC technology, which was introduced for Intel's Skylake processors in 2016, allowed users to overclock locked non-K CPUs through BCLK adjustments. Certain motherboards also featured independent clock generators, allowing CPU clock adjustments without affecting the rest of the system. Intel was not particularly pleased with the workaround, and ASRock eventually had to remove SkyOC from its motherboards via BIOS updates. Additionally, Intel introduced microcode changes to prevent non-K overclocking.
The current experiment revisits that workaround by identifying the original BIOS code and adapting it for modern motherboards. Hardware 360º claims Intel's restrictions include a mechanism that triggers a shutdown when BCLK exceeds 103 MHz, and that SkyOC originally worked around this by tricking the processor with a false report of the actual BCLK value.
Finding the original code for SkyOC does not necessarily mean it can be successfully ported to a modern motherboard BIOS. Newer Intel processors use different firmware, microcode, and clock-management mechanisms, which would make adapting the workaround considerably more complicated. Flashing modified motherboard firmware also comes with its own set of risks, including the possibility of rendering the board completely unusable. Nevertheless, it is interesting to see how AI-assisted reverse engineering can help gain access to BIOS modifications that would otherwise require a considerable amount of effort.

articles.title: Goodbye, manual work: AI-native CRM platform Dreamteam raises $53M to automate enterprise sales - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Goodbye, manual work: AI-native CRM platform Dreamteam raises $53M to automate enterprise sales
Intelligent sales software startup Dreamteam AI Inc. said today it has raised $53 million in early-stage funding to try to flip the narrative around customer relationship management platforms, which often seem like more of a hindrance than a help, by actually getting work done for sales teams.
The funds come by way of a seed and Series A round led by Accel Partners with participation from Together Fund and Premji Invest.
CRM platforms such as Salesforce and Hubspot have served as vital cogs in the wheel sales-focused enterprises for more than a quarter of a century. But these days they often create just as much work as they save, says Dreamteam co-founder and Chief Executive Anand Venkatraman (pictured, center, alongside co-founders Ramesh Parthasarathy and Senthil Kanthaswamy). While organizations are striving to use artificial intelligence to automate more of their business processes, CRMs are holding them back, he believes.
The problem with legacy CRM platforms is that they’re totally reliant on manual data entry, Venkatraman explained. Because their architectures are built around structured data fields and rigid, hand-coded workflows, they create a tight bottleneck that makes it almost impossible for autonomous AI agents that feed primarily on semantic data to get anything done.
“When a sales prospect expresses price hesitation or mentions a competitor, a salesperson registers it immediately,” he said. “But a legacy CRM, starving for unstructured nuance, misses it entirely, leaving AI agents without the vital context needed to reason effectively.”
To provide this context, Dreamteam has rebuilt the CRM from the ground up around the idea of a “company brain,” or a living memory of the business that constantly updates itself by ingesting new information from meetings with clients, prospects and team members, emails and other connected tools. As with all AI-native platforms, there’s also a generous dose of automation in the shape of four AI agents, or teammates, which specialize in different tasks.
The agents include Rachel, which handles account research; Sally for meeting preparations and follow-ups; Raj, which monitors for pipeline risks; and Alex, which serves as the CRM administrator, keeping the platform ticking over without any human intervention.
Venkatraman said he and his co-founders designed Dreamteam’s architecture specifically to address the historic shortcomings of legacy CRM platforms, which struggle to dig up the most vital business intelligence, leaving teams flying blind. “When a CEO asks why the quarter’s three biggest deals were lost, RevOps spends two weeks building a partial answer from whatever the reps happened to type,” he said. “The richest signals from meetings, emails, and calls were never captured, so the answer is always incomplete and always late.”
Legacy CRMs also fail to capture institutional knowledge, which means that everything a senior sales representative knows about the clients they work with leaves when they depart the company. There’s also a heavy administrative tax, with users forced to waste valuable time entering data to keep the platform up to date.
“CRMs don’t have a shortage of features,” Venkatraman said. “But they have a shortage of context and trust, and they lack the ability to get actual work done.”
Dreamteam does things differently. By capturing the unspoken context around each deal an organization does, it says, its platform can help to prevent new leads from going stale. Monitoring everything that’s said and agreed to in meetings, via chats and emails and other tools, the platform can pick out the most important signals, such as pricing sensitivities, objections and stakeholder dynamics.
It remembers all of the fine details of each specific deal. That way, even if the main sales rep involved suddenly leaves, it will retain all of the context so whoever takes over the account knows what needs to be done next.
The platform also employs humanlike reasoning. “When a prospect says, ‘The board is pushing hard on costs,’ it knows the proposal should lead with ROI, not features,” Venkatraman explained. “The CRM was supposed to give companies a complete picture of their customers, yet the richest parts of that picture have always lived outside the CRM.”
The startup has already witnessed significant traction with its agentic, contextual approach: It’s used by hundreds of organizations across the AI, healthcare, manufacturing, consulting and online media sectors. Dreamteam has enabled those early adopters to transform the way they handle sales.
Because the CRM continuously self-updates its records following daily customer interactions, it means sales people have much more time to focus on actually selling rather than data entry. Senior leaders have more visibility into deal pipelines, and can immediately find out why deals are stalling or how their customer’s sentiments are shifting.
Scott Olechowski, chief product officer at the video streaming service Plex Inc., said he was especially taken with the tight level of integration with Dreamteam and the company’s existing information technology stack. “The combination of simplicity and power hits the sweet spot for us,” he said. “The ability to integrate with the AI tools we are using across our organization is a game-changer.”
Venkatraman believes Dreamteam can have an even greater impact in future by expanding its shared intelligence layer beyond sales operations. His ambition is to build a platform that spans the entire customer lifecycle, from onboarding to customer success, renewals and upselling, to ensure that organizations can squeeze the most value out of the deal context it captures.
“Much of what’s learned during sales is lost or fragmented when a customer moves into implementation or customer success,” he pointed out. “But the same company brain that knows why a customer bought should also help teams onboard them, spot risks and find ways to grow the relationship.”
One way Dreamteam intends to pursue this vision is through what it calls “Magic Apps,” which is a capability that lets users build custom dashboards and tailored CRM workflows using natural language prompts. “The apps live inside Dreamteam, inherit its data permissions and action-level authorizations, and stay connected to customer records, workflows and the Company Brain, so you can customize without rebuilding the foundation,” Venkatraman said.
Premji Invest’s Saravanan Nattanmai has already bought into this vision, stressing the need for CRM systems to become more than just a system of record. He characterizes what Dreamteam is building as a “system of intelligence.”
“Dreamteam sets out to intuitively understand user intent, build deep contextual intelligence and execute workflows seamlessly through autonomous AI teammates,” he said. “We believe the future of enterprise software lies in AI-native systems that don’t just augment existing workflows but fundamentally reimagine how work gets done.”

articles.title: Des circuits espions découverts dans des portefeuilles crypto Trezor, les phrases de récupération visées
articles.text:
Trois portefeuilles matériels Trezor Safe 5 ont été trafiqués pour dérober les secrets donnant accès aux cryptomonnaies de leurs propriétaires. Une découverte qui intervient alors que le fabricant a déjà engagé une refonte de son réseau de distribution, après une première affaire impliquant le même revendeur.
Sale temps pour l'écosystème des cryptomonnaies. Après les récents déboires de Binance, c'est au tour de Trezor de faire parler de lui, cette fois pour une affaire de portefeuilles matériels trafiqués. Le fabricant vient de confirmer la découverte de circuits espions dans plusieurs de ses appareils, capables d'intercepter les phrases de récupération des utilisateurs et de les transmettre à des pirates via le réseau mobile.
Un circuit espion glissé entre la carte mère et l'écran
L'affaire remonte à octobre dernier, lorsqu'un client découvre un composant électronique suspect à l'intérieur de son Trezor Safe 5, acheté auprès de CryptoBilis, un revendeur alors récemment écarté du réseau officiel du fabricant en Asie du Sud-Est. Alertée, l'entreprise ouvre dans la foulée une enquête et invite les autres clients du distributeur à faire vérifier leurs appareils. Au total, 48 clients prennent contact avec Trezor, qui confirme la présence d'implants dans trois Safe 5, le premier après un examen en laboratoire, les deux autres à partir de photographies transmises par leurs propriétaires. Tous ont été achetés entre le 20 août et le 23 septembre 2026.
L'examen du premier appareil et l'analyse du firmware de l'implant ont permis à Trezor de reconstituer son fonctionnement. Les pirates avaient intercalé un circuit supplémentaire entre la carte mère du portefeuille et son écran, lui permettant de surveiller les informations affichées et saisies sur l'appareil. Le tout sans modifier son firmware légitime ni toucher à son composant sécurisé, chargé de protéger les clés cryptographiques.
Le dispositif était programmé pour reconnaître les mots composant la phrase de récupération du portefeuille, aussi bien lors de sa création que pendant la restauration d'une sauvegarde. Une information particulièrement sensible, puisqu'elle permet de reconstituer les clés donnant accès aux cryptomonnaies, même sans posséder l'appareil d'origine. L'implant pouvait également intercepter les phrases de passe lorsqu'elles apparaissaient à l'écran.
Une fois collectées, les données étaient chiffrées puis envoyées vers un serveur contrôlé par les attaquants, via le réseau mobile. En cas d’échec de connexion, le circuit stockait les informations en mémoire pour réessayer jusqu'à leur transmission.
Un correctif logiciel, mais des secrets potentiellement déjà compromis
Pour neutraliser ces dispositifs, Trezor a publié le 11 novembre une mise à jour de son firmware, numérotée 2.13.1. Selon le fabricant, elle empêche les implants identifiés au cours de l'enquête de récupérer les informations sensibles, sans qu'il soit nécessaire de retirer physiquement les composants malveillants.
La mise à jour présente malgré tout une limite importante : elle ne peut rien contre les phrases de récupération qui auraient déjà été interceptées. Trezor a donc recommandé aux acheteurs concernés de transférer leurs cryptomonnaies vers un nouveau portefeuille, doté d'une nouvelle phrase de récupération. Le fabricant a également annoncé le remplacement des appareils achetés auprès de CryptoBilis depuis mars 2026, même sans preuve de compromission.
Cette découverte vient conforter un durcissement de la politique de distribution de Trezor, engagé dès octobre après la découverte de circuits espions similaires dans des portefeuilles Ledger vendus par CryptoBilis, ayant conduit à des vols de cryptomonnaies. Le fabricant indique avoir depuis réduit d'environ 80 % son réseau mondial de revendeurs, les partenaires conservés étant désormais soumis à des exigences plus strictes concernant l'approvisionnement, le stockage et l'accès aux appareils.
A noter enfin que les investigations n'ont, pour l'heure, révélé aucun autre appareil compromis en dehors de ceux vendus par CryptoBilis, et qu’aucun des trois propriétaires de Trezor Safe 5 trafiqués n'a signalé de perte de fonds.

articles.title: Este es el valor de la criptomoneda Bitcoin este 16 de noviembre
articles.text:
El bitcoin fue la primera criptomoneda que salió al mercado. Ideada por Satoshi Nakamoto en 2008, esta divisa digital promovía un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales luego de la crisis financiera mundial que se vivió ese año.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Valor de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
La cotización de bitcoin para este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) es de 64273.85 dólares, lo que significa que la criptomoneda sufrió un cambio de -1.81% en las últimas 24 horas.
Por otro lado, registró un cambio de 0.0% con respecto a su valor hace una hora. En cuanto a su popularidad, se ubica en la posición #1.
Bitcoin alcanzó su máximo histórico
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.

articles.title: Black-out du 17 novembre : pourquoi la rumeur qui affole les réseaux sociaux ne tient pas debout
articles.text:
À l’approche du 17 novembre, les vidéos alarmistes se multiplient sur TikTok, X ou Facebook, certaines dépassant les dix millions de vues. Selon les versions, la France ou le monde entier serait privé de courant et d’internet pendant deux jours, 72 heures, voire trois mois, à cause d’une cyberattaque géante. Plusieurs médias ont déjà remonté le fil de cette infox, qui ne repose sur rien de concret.
Un simple test d’alerte américain
La date vient pourtant d’un exercice bien réel qui aura lieu de l’autre côté de l’Atlantique. L’agence américaine de gestion des urgences (FEMA) et le régulateur des télécommunications (FCC) mèneront un test national du système d’alerte. Il aura lieu vers 20h20 en France (14h20 heure local), et sera diffusé « uniquement à la radio et à la télévision, sans être envoyé sur les téléphones mobiles », précise la FEMA. Cette dernière ajoute qu’ « aucune action n’est nécessaire de la part du public ». Aucune coupure de courant n’est évidemment prévue, ni aux États-Unis ni ailleurs.
Des comptes spécialisés dans les cryptomonnaies y ont pourtant vu, sans la moindre preuve, l’annonce d’une cyberattaque massive. La rumeur s’est ensuite nourrie d’éléments sortis de leur contexte, comme la recommandation de la Commission européenne de préparer un kit d’urgence pour tenir 72 heures, ou un vieil épisode des Simpson évoquant une panne un 17 novembre. Des comptes russophones auraient aussi contribué à amplifier la rumeur en Europe, selon les Vérificateurs de TF1-LCI.
Un black-out ne se programme pas
Le black-out n’est pas une invention des réseaux sociaux et il fait bel et bien référence à une coupure d’électricité à très grande échelle. Le problème est qu’il ne s’annonce jamais à l’avance, puisqu’il s’agit par définition d’un accident, comme peut nous avons pu le voir l’an dernier dans la péninsule Ibérique.
Le 28 avril 2025, les réseaux espagnol et portugais se sont ainsi effondrés en moins de 90 secondes, à cause d’une cascade de surtensions accentuée par une réaction en chaîne avec des déconnexions de plusieurs sites de production d’électricité. Personne ne l’avait vu venir, et le courant est revenu en 12 à 16 heures.
En France, parmi les coupures liées à un manque d’électricité, la seule qui puisse être anticipée est le délestage. Il s’agit de coupures volontaires, maîtrisées et tournantes de deux heures maximum, organisées en dernier recours lors d’un déséquilibre entre la production et la consommation (souvent en cas de grand froid) et précédées d’alertes publiques. Rien à voir donc avec une panne nationale de plusieurs jours.
Le Secrétariat général de la défense et de la sécurité nationale (SGDSN) prépare bien un exercice de black-out généralisé pour 2027, mais il s’agira d’un « exercice sur table », sans aucune coupure pour la population,.
Gare aux arnaques
Le vrai risque de cette rumeur se trouve plutôt du côté de votre portefeuille. Plusieurs comptes à l’origine de la panique conseillent de vider ses comptes bancaires ou de placer ses économies dans des cryptomonnaies pour les « protéger ». Ils surfent sur un contexte bien réel, alors qu’une banque française a récemment été piratée, mais le procédé est celui des escrocs. Il joue sur la peur pour pousser à agir dans l’urgence.
Aucune banque ni aucune autorité ne demande de déplacer son argent en prévision d’une panne, et tout message en ce sens doit être considéré comme une tentative d’arnaque, sur le modèle des escroqueries au faux conseiller bancaire.
Le seul conseil raisonnable reste celui des autorités, sans aucun lien avec le 17 novembre. Il consiste à garder chez soi de quoi tenir quelques jours en cas de crise, avec de l’eau, de la nourriture, une lampe et une radio à piles.

articles.title: SpaceX ha hecho historia con el vuelo 14 y 15 de Starship: ahora espera repetir la hazaña con el vuelo 16
articles.text:
El vuelo 14 de Starship fue un éxito, con su inserción en órbita por primera vez para depositar una carga útil. Solo la mitad del vuelo 15 ha sido exitoso, pero ha sido justamente la mitad más importante, así que hay un gran revuelo al respecto. Ahora toca pensar en qué será lo siguiente. ¿Habrá un vuelo 16? ¿Qué hará SpaceX con la nave que han recuperado? ¿Cómo se investigará lo sucedido con la primera etapa? Vayamos por partes.
Vuelo 16 a la vista (pero no mucho). Lógicamente, habrá un vuelo 16. Sin embargo, de momento no hay información oficial al respecto. Algunos medios de comunicación hablan de una fecha tentativa en torno al mes que viene (diciembre de 2026). No obstante, se trata de datos citados en prensa a partir de material de planificación de la Administración Federal de Aviación de Estados Unidos, por lo que no proceden directamente de SpaceX.
Tampoco hay mucha información sobre el desarrollo de dicho vuelo. Se ha mencionado que podría ir cargado con el lote 30-1 de Starlink y que sería el primer vuelo de Starship en lanzarse desde Florida, aunque se seguirán haciendo lanzamientos desde Starbase (Texas). Sea como sea, hay que tener en cuenta que, incluso si SpaceX contaba de verdad con lanzar en diciembre, esta fecha podría experimentar retrasos, ya que debe quedar claro qué es lo que falló con la recuperación de la primera etapa en el vuelo 15 antes de programar definitivamente el siguiente.
Después del vuelo 15. Tras el vuelo 15 ha llegado el momento de que SpaceX demuestre que puede reutilizar de forma rápida cualquiera de las dos etapas. El propulsor Super Heavy se ha reutilizado en dos ocasiones, pero con meses de diferencia, y la segunda etapa nunca ha volado dos veces. No se pudo recuperar el Super Heavy con el vuelo 15, pero sí la Ship que compone la segunda etapa, por lo que la siguiente fase será prepararla para su reutilización. Aunque en un principio se habló de usarla en el vuelo 16, desde NASA Space Flight señalan que lo más probable es que dicha prueba se lleve a cabo sin esperar a que la Ship del vuelo 15 esté lista.
Más reutilización, más vuelos. Elon Musk ha manifestado en varias ocasiones que su objetivo es llevar a cabo 10.000 lanzamientos por año de Starship en 2030. Eso sería más de un lanzamiento por hora. Lógicamente, para que sea viable económicamente y, de paso, no abarrote aún más la órbita terrestre de basura espacial, lo ideal sería reutilizar tanto la primera como la segunda etapa de la misma. Lo logrado con el vuelo 15 demuestra que es una posibilidad. Ahora hay que trabajar en ella.
Destino: la Luna. Si todo va bien, la Ship de Starship, esa segunda etapa que se ha logrado recuperar, se convertirá en uno de los módulos de aterrizaje de los que dispondrá la NASA para alunizar durante las misiones Artemis. Por eso, además de seguir demostrando su viabilidad para colocar cargas útiles en órbita, se debe seguir trabajando en la instalación de una cabina y un sistema de soporte vital. Así, podrá albergar a los tripulantes elegidos para alunizar, mientras el resto siguen en la cápsula Orión de la NASA.
SpaceX ya está trabajando en un prototipo de tierra, llamado Cabin 1, que debe estar listo para finales de 2026. Además, para que la Ship pueda llegar a la Luna necesita más combustible del que puede acarrear desde la Tierra, por lo que tendrá que repostar directamente en órbita. Esto se hará gracias a dos tipos de Ship: una que actuará como camión cisterna y otra que hará de depósito y permanecerá siempre en órbita. El objetivo es que las Ships cisterna viajen regularmente a llenar el depósito, al que se tendrá que acoplar la Ship que debe repostar para el alunizaje. Todo esto también se debe perfeccionar para que Starship esté lista para Artemis IV, cuando finalmente, si todo va bien, los humanos vuelvan a caminar sobre la Luna. No es poco todo lo que le queda por delante a SpaceX después del gran logro de su décimo quinto vuelo.

articles.title: Papa John's wants your pizza photos for AI quality checks, with free pizza as the reward
articles.text:
Why it matters: Combining Papa John's pizzas with AI sounds like another use of the technology that will make people cringe, but the company claims it's all about making its pizzas better. The fast-food giant is asking customers to help develop its AI quality-control system by sending in a picture of their orders. There's a free pizza on offer in return, which sounds like a good deal, although there are a few conditions.
Papa John's said asking customers to send in a photo of their pizza, along with some feedback, is part of an AI-based quality-control campaign to help make sure each of its pizzas is properly cooked and cut.
CEO Todd Penegor told Reuters the promotion would help improve pizza quality across the chain's franchised restaurants, tackling inconsistencies he described as the brand's "Achilles' heel."
According to the company's announcement, customers must have a Papa Rewards account, opt into text messages, and place an order worth at least $15 through its app or website. They then receive a text inviting them to upload an unedited photo and feedback. Once the photo is confirmed, they unlock a free large one-topping pizza, but redeeming it requires spending at least $5 on their next order.
Penegor said the goal is to replicate what the chain's in-store quality-control cameras already do. Those systems use AI to check for burned cheese, make sure pepperoni slices are cut smoothly, and confirm that the outer crust resembles "a beautiful breadstick."
The problem is that only a few hundred of the chain's roughly 6,000 locations worldwide have those cameras. Photos submitted by customers could give the company a much cheaper way to check pizza quality across more restaurants, though they aren't yet as accurate as the in-store systems.
The company collects the images and customer feedback on what Penegor described as a "huge dashboard." The promotion brought in thousands of photos within days of launching on November 9 and will run until November 20.
According to Penegor, the technology was relatively cheap to build in-house, taking advantage of AI tools the company had already developed with Google Cloud. He said the feedback would help identify which fixes to prioritize and show franchisees where their restaurants are falling short.
This isn't the first non-traditional use of technology in the pizza-delivering business. In 2025, Domino's tested using Boston Dynamics' quadrupedal robot, Spot, to deliver pizzas to customers on a beach and protect the food from seagulls.

articles.title: Ten Years On, Google Updates the SRE Book for the AI Era
articles.text:
Google has announced a completely rewritten second edition of their seminal book Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems, ten years after the original book was first published. The book updates thinking on site reliability engineering (SRE) to encompass modern cloud architectures, platform engineering and AI workloads, whilst keeping the original emphasis on applying good software engineering techniques to operations work.
Announced by Google's SRE programme manager Betsy Beyer and software engineer David Huska, the new edition is positioned as a response to a production environment that has changed substantially since 2016, when the first edition appeared. The authors argue that the central problem is no longer adopting cloud infrastructure, but maintaining reliability as systems become more distributed, interdependent and continuously changing.
"Modern production environments operate under constant change. System boundaries are more complex, dependencies are deep, and failure modes are more complex and damaging than ever before."
Betsy Beyer and David Huska, Google Cloud Blog
The original SRE book became influential because it gave a public account of how Google operated large-scale services. It described practices such as service level objectives (SLOs), error budgets, toil reduction, incident management and postmortems. InfoQ's 2016 review noted that the book presented SRE as the application of software engineering to an operations function, with engineers expected to automate repetitive operational work rather than simply respond to it.
The second edition does not present SRE as a fixed set of practices. Instead, it describes how those practices have changed as organisations have moved from early cloud migration and monolithic applications towards microservices, multi-cloud deployments, serverless systems and internal developer platforms.
One of the clearest changes over the years concerns SLOs and error budgets. Google says that teams once relied on basic availability metrics and manually applied error-budget policies. The revised guidance describes user-centred, multi-tiered SLOs, dynamic burn-rate alerting and automated policy enforcement. Reliability practice itself has evolved away from infrastructure uptime alone and towards measures that describe the effect of failures on users.
Observability has also evolved, and the book's new edition talks this through. The first edition's world of static dashboards, basic logs and manual alert triage has given way, in Google's account, to OpenTelemetry, distributed tracing and automated anomaly correlation. The aim is not merely to collect more telemetry, but to reduce the time between an alert and a credible explanation of what has failed.
Automation is the third major area of revision. Google describes a movement from custom scripts addressing isolated tasks towards declarative infrastructure as code, internal developer platforms and self-healing systems. This aligns with the platform-engineering model now common in larger organisations: reliability capabilities are built once into a platform and consumed by product teams, rather than being reimplemented by every team.
Reliability testing has also changed. Google contrasts scheduled game days and synthetic load tests with continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing and live production canary verification. The practical implication is that resilience becomes part of the delivery pipeline rather than an occasional exercise performed before a major release.
"Rather than relying solely on scheduled game days and synthetic load tests, modern engineering embeds continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing, and live production canary verification."
Betsy Beyer and David Huska, Google Cloud Blog
Capacity management is another area where the book has been updated. Google says that manual provisioning and static forecasting have been replaced by dynamic auto-scaling, cloud FinOps alignment and optimisation for GPU and TPU clusters. This matters because AI training and inference workloads can concentrate demand on scarce accelerated computing resources, making capacity planning, networking and cost control more operationally significant.
Generative AI inevitably appears in the second edition, in two facets. First, SRE is presented as a discipline needed to operate AI infrastructure. The book covers the reliability of large GPU and TPU clusters, network topologies, non-deterministic model outputs, latency behaviour and the pipelines used for training, fine-tuning and data processing. These are different operational problems from those posed by a conventional stateless web service.
Second, AI is presented as a tool for reliability engineers. The post welcomes generative AI support for incident triage and postmortem writing, natural-language queries over telemetry, and predictive models that identify resource bottlenecks before they cause an outage. The examples in the announcement mostly place AI in a supporting role, gathering and organising evidence for engineers, rather than claiming that AI can replace operational judgement. Recent industry activity appears to support this, with InfoQ reporting in October 2026 that Datadog had released Scout, a specialist model intended to investigate production problems inside its Bits AI SRE product. Other vendors are exploring similar territory, including Honeycomb's Canvas Agent, Splunk AI SRE and New Relic's SRE Agent. InfoQ also reported in February 2026 on Google Cloud SREs using the Gemini CLI during real outages; using AI to help engineers work through incidents, rather than as an autonomous replacement for on-call staff.
The announcement also revises the organisational side of SRE. Google describes a move beyond dedicated SRE teams attached to particular applications, towards hybrid models, platform-engineering integration and reliability champions embedded in product teams. This has come about because many organisations cannot staff a central SRE team for every service, so reliability expertise has to be distributed more widely.
Despite the technological updates, Google argues that the underlying culture has not changed. The authors restate the importance of reliability-focused culture and expand the book's coverage of the human aspects of systems engineering. David Blank-Edelman made a related point in a presentation, You Are Asking the Wrong Questions (about Reliability and SRE), delivered at InfoQ Dev Summit Boston in 2025. He argued that reliability work should start from the customer's perspective rather than the component's perspective, and described SRE as fundamentally collaborative. He also challenged the conventional focus on a single root cause, favouring an examination of the contributing factors behind a failure.
The second edition is available in physical format through Google Books and in digital format from O'Reilly. For teams already practising SRE, its value is likely to lie less in introducing familiar concepts than in showing how those concepts have been adapted for platforms, distributed systems and AI-heavy infrastructure. For organisations earlier in their reliability journey, it remains a substantial reference on how to make operations a software-engineering problem rather than a collection of manual tasks.

articles.title: How to watch Young, British and Tradwife from anywhere – it's *FREE*
articles.text:
How to watch Young, British and Tradwife from anywhere – it's *FREE*
Filmmaker Poppy Jay investigates why young British women are turning to traditional gender roles
- Watch Young, British and Tradwife free on BBC iPlayer (UK only)
- Use NordVPN to watch when traveling abroad
- Premieres Monday, November 16 on BBC One

articles.title: Shareholders sue Intel, its CEO, and CFO after stock drops 28.6 percent in one day
articles.text:
Intel is being sued by shareholders, who are accusing the chipmaker of misleading them about the impact of the PC sales slump that contributed to a drop of 28.6 percent in the price of Intel’s stock on October 30.
The lawsuit (PDF), filed on Friday in the San Jose, California, federal court, is seeking class-action certification and lists the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System and “all others similarly situated” as plaintiffs. In addition to Intel, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Intel’s EVP and CFO David Zinsner are listed as defendants.
The plaintiffs claim that Intel made “materially false and misleading statements and omissions” between July 23 and October 29. They are seeking unspecified compensatory damages, plus legal and other associated fees, for shareholders during that period.
In the complaint, the shareholders argue that Intel misled them by failing to disclose: the full impact that the PC market sales slump would have on Intel’s third quarter and beyond; the impact of increasing PC component prices on PC sales for Intel’s OEM and distribution partners; that Intel was dealing with substrate supply constraints that would limit its ability to meet data center CPU demand; and “that any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset” by the PC sales slump.

articles.title: Palo Alto Networks report finds organizations struggle to track and secure AI agents in the cloud - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Palo Alto Networks report finds organizations struggle to track and secure AI agents in the cloud
A new report out today from cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks Inc. finds that artificial intelligence agents have quickly become a fixture in software development, but many organizations can’t properly track or secure what those agents are doing in the cloud.
Now in its sixth year, the State of Cloud Security Report 2026 is based on a survey of 2,800 security executives and practitioners in 10 countries. Along with how AI is being used to build and deploy software, the report looks at how quickly organizations are able to respond when something goes wrong.
The use of AI agents was found to be close to universal, with 99% of respondents saying they use agents for autonomous or semiautonomous actions in their development pipelines. Some 73% said the agents are allowed to modify code, pipeline configurations or production environments, and agents are even doing security testing at 44% of organizations.
The amount of change is going up as a result. Some 82% said AI-driven development has increased the volume of infrastructure updates reaching their cloud, yet organizations on average enforce fewer than three of the eight predeployment security checks measured in the survey. AI is also being used to generate infrastructure-as-code templates at 42% of organizations, but only 34% scan that code before production.
Not surprisingly, problems are getting through. Respondents said that on average, 19% of high and critical application security issues reached production over a 90-day period. It takes an average of 18.4 days to get a fix for a security issue found in code into production.
When respondents were asked what was stopping them from fixing issues before deployment, the most common answer was business pressure to release quickly at 39%. Unclear risk acceptance policies came second at 30%.
Accountability is also an issue when it comes to agents. Two in five organizations said they are unable to reconstruct what an AI agent did, a share that rises to 46% in financial services, while 53% said agent activity is logged under a developer’s identity or personal access token. That means when something goes wrong, investigators first have to figure out which actions were taken by a person and which were taken by an agent before they can work out what was affected.
Removing access once something does go wrong is also slow. Some 60% of organizations still need manual intervention to revoke access for nonhuman identities, and it takes an average of 2.5 days to revoke or rotate compromised developer credentials, API keys or pipeline secrets.
Data governance has its own issues. Nearly all organizations, 99%, said they had found ungoverned AI in their environment in the past year, yet only 9% are able to automatically discover and classify it. Some 40% said governed data had been copied into ungoverned AI tools, and 39% had seen sensitive or regulated data used to train or fine-tune models without authorization.
Despite the gaps, confidence is high. Almost every respondent, 97%, said they are at least somewhat confident they can secure their AI supply chain and applications, though only 36% can monitor AI behavior in production and just 30% can detect prompt injection.
The final section of the report looks at the threat from frontier AI models that can find and exploit software vulnerabilities on their own. Nearly all respondents, 98%, said they are concerned about it, and 65% said it poses a significant or severe threat to global critical infrastructure and financial systems over the next 12 to 18 months. Utilities were the most likely of any sector to rate the threat as significant or severe at 79%, compared with 48% in telecommunications.
Interestingly, though the report refers to “frontier AI-powered capabilities,” the survey questions at the back of it call them “Mythos-grade” threats, a reference to Anthropic PBC’s Claude Mythos models. Palo Alto Networks was one of the launch partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, which gave defenders early access to Claude Mythos Preview in April.
The report argues that against attackers working at machine speed, an 18.4-day fix cycle leaves organizations exposed for more than 17 days after a vulnerability can be discovered. Part of the problem, according to the report, is fragmented tooling, with only 19% of organizations saying they operate with unified telemetry and workflows across code, cloud, identity and runtime. Nearly half of organizations, 47%, still do the work of correlating application vulnerabilities with runtime threats by hand, a number that’s even higher in the U.S. at 55%.
The report ends with a series of recommendations for organizations to secure their cloud environments as AI agents take on more work. Agents should be given their own identities with a clear owner and only the permissions they need to do their job. Security teams are also advised to automate the fixing of recurring issues, though only after rollback procedures have been put in place.

articles.title: Gemini Notebooks: So werden aus deinen Notizen jetzt interaktive Webseiten
articles.text:
Gemini Notebooks: So werden aus deinen Notizen jetzt interaktive Webseiten
Seit einigen Monaten trägt das einstige NotebookLM einen neuen Namen. Da Google das Recherchetool immer enger mit der hauseigenen KI verzahnt, wurde kurzerhand aus dem Dienst Gemini Notebook. Dieser Wechsel macht sich nicht nur auf dem Papier bemerkbar. Denn Google ist darauf bedacht, dem Tool immer wieder neue Funktionen zu spendieren, die von Gemini-Modellen getragen werden. So auch bei einem jetzt angekündigten Feature für Gemini Notebook.
Gemini Notebook: Wie aus Notizen Webseiten werden
In einem Blog-Beitrag zeigt Google, dass Gemini Notebook jetzt in der Lage ist, recherchierte Inhalte und Notizen umzuwandeln. Die KI nimmt dabei alle Inhalte samt Quellen auf und verarbeitet sie zu einer interaktiven Webseite. Alles, was User:innen dafür machen müssen, ist, die KI per Prompt anzuweisen. Laut Google reicht dabei ein einfaches „Erstelle mir eine Website“ aus, um erste Ergebnisse zu erzielen.
Allerdings solltest du Gemini Notebook mit weiteren Informationen füttern, welche Ansprüche du an die Seite hast. Nur so kann das Tool etwas bauen, das dir auch tatsächlich nützt. In einem Beispiel zeigt Google etwa, wie Notizen und Quellen aus der Chemie genutzt werden, um eine interaktive Lernseite zu erstellen. Die Userin spezifiziert dabei, dass sich die Inhalte um das Periodensystem drehen sollen und Gemini Notebook am Ende ein Quiz hinzufügen soll, um das Gelernte abzufragen.
Laut Google richtet sich die neue Funktion deshalb unter anderem an Studierende, die sich auf Prüfungen vorbereiten wollen. Zudem soll sich das Feature von Gemini Notebook zur anschaulicheren Analyse von Daten, etwa von Sales-Berichten, oder beim Projektmanagement als interaktiver Tracker für alle Beteiligten eignen. Dementsprechend lassen sich einmal geöffnete Webseiten auch einfach mit anderen User:innen teilen.
Das neue Webseiten-Feature für Gemini Notebook wird ab sofort global ausgerollt. Wie Google betont, steht die Funktion allen User:innen zur Verfügung, die über 18 Jahre alt sind. Dazu zählen auch alle, die ihren Zugang über ein Abo von Google Workspace beziehen. Bislang ist das Feature nur über das Web verfügbar. Die Mobile-App soll zu einem späteren Zeitpunkt nachziehen.

articles.title: Cyber giant Infoblox confirms security incident after hackers access 'company information' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Cybersecurity and automation giant Infoblox has confirmed a cybersecurity incident, during which hackers accessed company information through one of its technology vendors.
Infoblox is a privately held cyber giant that provides companies cybersecurity and networking services, such as domain name resolution and identity and user access management.
In a statement, a spokesperson for Infoblox told TechCrunch that the company is “investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor.”
“We immediately activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident and are working with leading outside cybersecurity experts to investigate the facts, understand the scope and address any confirmed risks.”
TechCrunch has learned that the data breach involves a vendor that provides SharePoint data migration services, according to a notification sent by Infoblox about the breach, two people with knowledge of the incident told TechCrunch.
One of the people said sensitive customer data was taken in the breach.
According to public internet records seen by TechCrunch, Infoblox hosts much of its files, emails, and infrastructure with Microsoft, including a SharePoint server, which TechCrunch confirmed is accessible through Infoblox’s single sign-on provider. SharePoint is web-based software that companies use to share and host internal files and documents.
Infoblox has not named the third-party migration vendor that was hacked, but one person with knowledge of the incident said that Infoblox has terminated its work with the vendor.
The company’s spokesperson did not comment on this, but added that the company has “no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved” in the breach.
Infoblox would not say how many customers were affected by the incident, or if the company is aware at this time. The company also did not say, when asked, if it had been contacted by the hackers and if they had made any demands.

articles.title: Lenovo Googlebook Duet 13 : une date de lancement fuite pour la première tablette GooglebookOS
articles.text:
Évoquée pour la première fois en août mais finalement reportée, la première tablette Googlebook à clavier détachable arriverait chez Lenovo en janvier prochain. C’est ce qu’indique cette semaine le leaker Evan Blass, souvent bien renseigné, qui en profite d’ailleurs pour nous partager quelques visuels de l’ardoise en question.
Nous vous parlions début novembre de celle qui pourrait bien être la toute première tablette Googlebook à clavier détachable. Cette ardoise voit désormais sa date de sortie se préciser un peu plus, pour janvier en l’occurrence. C’est ce que nous dit cette semaine le leaker Evan Blass sur X. Souvent bien informé, l’intéressé assortit cette estimation de quelques visuels de la tablette en question, tout en nous renseignant sur son probable nom définitif : appelez-la la Lenovo Googlebook Duet 13.
Vers un positionnement milieu de gamme ?
Les visuels partagés par Evan Blass nous montrent une tablette sobre, équipée semble-t-il d’un seul et unique port USB-C. Son clavier détachable comporte bien les touches propres à l’environnement Googlebook OS et s’accompagne d’un pied dépliable conçu pour s’aimanter au dos de l’ardoise. Le voyant RGB spécifique à la gamme Googlebook est quant à lui logé à proximité immédiate du capteur photo arrière de la tablette.
On ignore pour l’instant le détail de sa fiche technique, Evan Blass reste d’ailleurs silencieux sur ce point dans son dernier post, mais de précédentes fuites nous éclairent quand même en partie. Comme le rappelle Android Authority, cette Lenovo Googlebook Duet 13 serait équipée d'un écran de 13 pouces et d'un processeur MediaTek Dimensity CX C10 Max couplé à 16 Go de mémoire vive.
Cette puce lancée en septembre avait pour objectif de faire baisser le tarif (souvent jugé trop élevé) des premiers modèles de Googlebook. On peut donc imaginer un positionnement milieu de gamme pour cette Lenovo Googlebook Duet 13, même si nous ne serons fixés qu’en début d’année prochaine… Aucun prix précis n’ayant pour l’instant fuité.
Coup d’envoi pressenti pour janvier
Au-delà de la fiabilité habituelle d’Evan Blass, dont les leaks s’avèrent souvent justes, le créneau de janvier évoqué nous paraît crédible pour au moins deux raisons : il correspond à la période du CES, propice aux annonces et aux lancements en tous genres ; et il colle par ailleurs aux dernières déclarations de Google, qui promettait, lors de son dernier Android Dev Summit (organisé fin octobre), le lancement prochain d’une première tablette Googlebook à clavier détachable. Janvier serait donc une période toute désignée.
Reste maintenant à savoir si l’arrivée de cette nouvelle tablette permettra de relancer un peu l’intérêt pour les Googlebook, qui s’est rapidement essoufflé suite aux premiers pas décevants de la plateforme de Google sur le marché. Réponse dans deux mois ?
Source : Android Authority

articles.title: Elastic{ON} Mumbai: Why context, not the model, is the real AI advantage
articles.text:
Elastic
View Brand Publisher
Elastic{ON} Mumbai: Why context, not the model, is the real AI advantage
At Elastic{ON} Mumbai, CEO Ash Kulkarni argued that every business already owns what AI models lack. The rest of the day showed what it takes to put that context to work.
As AI models become available to everyone, the advantage for enterprises is shifting to something no model providers can supply: the context that makes AI useful to a specific business. Elastic{ON} Mumbai took on that challenge, bringing together the people building and running AI in India’s enterprises to work out how to make their data count.
The Elastic{ON} Tour 2026/2027 stopped in Mumbai on September 30, bringing developers, SREs, IT and security leaders and practitioners to JW Marriott Mumbai Sahar under the theme ‘Forge the Future’. Across keynotes, live demos, customer and partner sessions, and a hackathon awards ceremony, one idea kept returning: context is what turns a widely available model into a lasting business advantage.
Context is your moat
Ash Kulkarni, CEO of Elastic, who grew up a short distance away in Vile Parle, opened by tying the company’s name to the city. “Mumbai has stretched, it has evolved, it has transformed. It has never broken,” he said.
That adaptability matters, he argued, because AI is moving faster than any earlier technology shift, and the models driving it share a blind spot. “None of these models have any understanding of your business. They don’t understand your data,” Kulkarni said. “The bottleneck is the context.”
Every industry now faces startups trading human capital for token capital. What they cannot copy, Kulkarni said, is a company’s accumulated learnings, experience, and data on how best to serve its customers and partners. “That context is your moat.”
The challenge is that context is scattered. Customer information alone sits across CRM, entitlement, and ticketing systems. Kulkarni’s answer is a bridge that connects it all, securely and with privacy built in, to any model. The result, he said, is “actual intelligence”: the reasoning power of the model combined with the context of the business. Delivering that has meant evolving Elastic’s core engine.
Making context affordable
Ajay Nair, GM, Elasticsearch and Platform, Elastic, picked up the thread. “The model’s only half the equation,” he said. An agent that does not know a customer has raised ten support tickets might still send them a renewal pitch, and that will not go well.
Nair said most teams make their models rebuild context from scratch every time a question is asked, an approach he called “top-down” context that burns tokens on every query. The more efficient pattern is “bottom-up”: deriving relationships, metadata, and risk factors once, keeping them fresh, and handing models a ready-made picture.
That is the idea behind the Elastic Context Engine, which Nair announced on stage and which is now in private preview.
Context at work in operations and security
The same foundation runs through Elastic’s observability and security solutions. Vinay Chandrasekhar, Director of Product Management, Observability, Elastic, demonstrated Elastic nightshift AI SRE, an AI agent that surfaces problems no alert was set up to catch, tests several root-cause hypotheses in parallel, and shows every step of its reasoning. Kulkarni noted that it gets better at investigating “within the context of your environment”, adding: “It’s not generic.” Elastic has since announced nightshift in private preview on Elastic Observability Serverless.
James Spiteri, Senior Director of Product Management, Elastic, argued that “the SIEM has never mattered more”. He previewed what has since launched as AlertZero, the agentic layer built into Elastic Security. Specialised groups of agents, called Watches, triage alerts, hunt for threats, and investigate incidents, learning from how a team already works, while analysts decide which actions need their approval. AlertZero is now available in technical preview across Elastic Cloud, self-managed, and air-gapped environments.
A day built with the community
Beyond the keynotes, customers carried much of the program. On the morning panel, moderated by Ravindra Ramnani, Head of Field Engineering at Elastic India, leaders from Axis Bank, Standard Chartered Bank, and Easebuzz debated whether enterprises can observe, audit, and explain what their AI agents do. Nykaa joined AWS to describe how its SREs now investigate incidents by querying logs conversationally with Elastic AI Assistant. Afternoon breakouts featured Network18 on AI governance, Qualys on closing the SOC loop with agentic AI, and Standard Chartered Bank on standardising observability across 40 countries, alongside community sessions from Iron Mountain, Jolera, and Sprinklr.
Partners showed how they ground AI in enterprise context. Google Cloud explained how its agent tooling and Gemini models work with Elastic retrieval to turn sensitive enterprise data into trusted context without moving it. Microsoft and Elastic walked through OverflowAI, Stack Overflow’s retrieval-first architecture, in which Elasticsearch hybrid retrieval grounds Azure OpenAI in the community’s validated answers.
The community also had its moment on the main stage, as the Forge the Future Hackathon awards recognised the top teams from the Grand Finale held in Bengaluru on September 18 and 19. Frustrated Engineers took first place, followed by Sandboxed in second and Defcon in third. Powered by Elastic and AWS, the hackathon challenged teams to build explainable, production-ready AI agents across search, observability, and security.
Models will change. Context stays.
Kulkarni closed with commitments that put a customer’s context, not any single model, at the centre. Elastic will stay model agnostic, he said, because “there is no winner yet, and there will likely never be a single winner.” It will also run wherever customers do, in the cloud or self-managed.
Models will keep getting better. The context that makes them useful belongs to the business, and Elastic{ON} Mumbai made the case that connecting the two is where the lasting advantage lies.

To know more, visit Make all your data an AI advantage at Elastic{ON}

articles.title: Criptomonedas: el costo de ethereum para este lunes
articles.text:
Ethereum es una plataforma digital que adopta la tecnología de cadena de bloques (blockchain) y expande su uso a una gran variedad de aplicaciones, mientras que ether es su criptomoneda nativa. En el mundo de las finanzas digitales es común que la criptomoneda sea llamada como la red, aunque en realidad no son lo mismo.
La plataforma ethereum, creada en el 2015 por el programador Vitalik Buterin, buscaba ser un instrumento para aplicaciones descentralizadas y colaborativas sobre las que se pueden hacer contratos inteligentes (dAPPs)
Al igual que el bitcoin, el valor de ether se disparó en un corto periodo de tiempo. En enero de 2016, ether cotizaba alrededor de un dólar y actualmente tiene un máximo histórico de 4.953,73 dólares.
La cotización de ethereum para este día a las 14:05 horas (UTC) es de 1801.83 dólares, lo que significa que la criptomoneda tuvo un cambio de -1.47 % en el último día.
Por otro lado, registró un cambio de 0.0 % con respecto a su valor hace una hora. En cuanto a su popularidad, se ubica en la posición #2.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Ethereum
Ethereum y su última actualización
Tras varios meses de retraso y con el temor de que ya nunca pasaría, finalmente el 15 de septiembre de 2022 Ethereum llevó a cabo su tan ansiada fusión o actualización al nuevo nivel 2.0 con la promesa de mejorar la experiencia de los usuarios de esta criptomoneda.
“The Merge”, inglés para “La Fusión”, es una transformación en la forma en que Ethereum procesa las transacciones y en cómo se crean nuevos tokens de Ether.
Esta fusión se trata de la combinación de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum con una nueva cadena de bloques separada conocido como proof-of-stake, el cual reduce el consumo de energía de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum en un 99,9 %, según sus propios desarrolladores, lo que la vuelve más “amigable” con el ambiente al tiempo que las transacciones serían más baratas.
Sus defensores creen que la fusión hará que Ethereum resulte favorecido con respecto al máximo rival, Bitcoin, pues podría aumentar su uso.
En el proceso Proof Stake los propietarios de Ether bloquearán cantidades establecidas de sus criptomonedas para verificar nuevos registros en la cadena de bloques, ganando nuevas monedas además de su criptografía “participada”.

articles.title: Le chercheur en guerre contre Microsoft dévoile une 16ᵉ faille Windows, elle peut désactiver votre antivirus
articles.text:
NightmareEclipse a encore frappé. Quelques heures après le Patch Tuesday du 10 novembre, le chercheur Abdelhamid Naceri a mis en ligne une nouvelle faille zero day dans Windows. Baptisée SignDrop, elle permet à un simple utilisateur d’obtenir les droits « SYSTEM », c’est-à-dire les pleins pouvoirs sur l’ordinateur. Comme à son habitude, le chercheur a publié le code d’exploitation sur GitHub, sans prévenir Microsoft en amont, dans le but de mettre la pression sur l’éditeur.
À lire aussi : deux failles de BitLocker permettent de lire les fichiers protégés sur Windows
Une protection de Windows retournée contre lui
Cette fois, le chercheur s’attaque à une protection conçue par Microsoft. La faille se situe dans le CLFS (Common Log File System), un composant clé de Windows qui gère les fichiers journaux du système. Devenu une cible de choix pour les pirates, le composant a eu droit à un mécanisme de protection. L’an dernier, Microsoft a ajouté un système d’authentification, taillé pour signer les fichiers afin de détecter toute modification suspecte.
C’est dans ce système que se trouve la faille SignDrop. Dans les détails, la vulnérabilité pousse Microsoft Defender, l’antivirus par défaut intégré à Windows, à ouvrir un fichier journal (« log ») piégé. Comme Defender dispose des droits les plus élevés du système, Windows crée alors un fichier de signature avec ces mêmes droits, à un emplacement choisi par le pirate. Il n’a plus qu’à y glisser son propre code.
« Si tout est enchaîné correctement, de façon amusante, cette mesure de sécurité légitime peut être utilisée contre elle-même et permettre une élévation de privilèges. Tout est fait correctement par Microsoft ici, mais la logique permet un abus », explique Abdelhamid Naceri.
« Désactiver n’importe quel antivirus »
Le chercheur va plus loin dans son rapport. Selon lui, la technique fonctionne pour « désactiver n’importe quel antivirus
». La demande de création de fichier frauduleuse semble en effet venir du logiciel de sécurité lui-même, ce qui peut berner n’importe quel outil de sécurité. Après avoir testé la faille sur plusieurs versions du système d’exploitation, le chercheur estime que 80 % des installations Windows sont vulnérables. « Si votre installation de Windows a plus de 90 jours », vous êtes vraisemblablement vulnérable, avance Abdelhamid Naceri.
Les chercheurs de Cyderes ont réussi à reproduire l’attaque pour prendre le contrôle d’un ordinateur. Les experts jugent toutefois qu’il est peu probable que 80 % des machines Windows soient vraiment vulnérables. Pour les chercheurs, « la défense est la vulnérabilité ».
Une nouvelle faille signée NightmareEclipse
Le chercheur n’en est pas à son coup d’essai. Également connu sous les pseudonymes de Chaotic Eclipse ou MSNightmare, cet ancien employé de Microsoft enchaîne les révélations depuis le mois d’avril 2026. Parmi ces faits d’arme, on trouve BlueHammer, RedSun, YellowKey, RoguePlanet, ShieldBreak ou encore BigDiskBuster. C’est la seizième faille en un peu plus de sept mois, soit environ une toutes les deux semaines.
Le plus souvent, l’expert attend que Microsoft dévoile son Patch Tuesday avant de dégainer ses découvertes. Pour rappel, le chercheur reproche au géant de Redmond de l’avoir licencié sans bonne raison. En mai dernier, Microsoft avait évoqué la perspective d’une action en justice contre le chercheur, sans mettre ses menaces à exécution jusqu’à maintenant.
À lire aussi : Windows vient de battre un nouveau record monstrueux
Microsoft enquête sur la faille
Microsoft assure avoir pris des mesures à la suite de la découverte d’Abdelhamid Naceri. L’éditeur explique enquêter « activement sur la vulnérabilité signalée » et s’engage à « prendre les mesures nécessaires pour mettre à jour les produits concernés dès que possible ». Microsoft ajoute que Defender « détecte et bloque l’exploitation de cette vulnérabilité », qui n’a pas encore été exploitée par des hackers.
