articles.title: Intel sued by shareholders for misleading investors after stock plunges 29% — class action claims the company downplayed the severity of PC market headwinds
articles.text:
Intel sued by shareholders for misleading investors after stock plunges 29% — class action claims the company downplayed the severity of PC market headwinds
Time to re-install mid-quarter updates at Intel?
Intel has been sued by shareholders who accuse the company of misleading investors about the severity of the PC market downturn and its impact on the company's financial performance before its shares plunged by nearly 29% in late October, reports Reuters.
The proposed class action lawsuit led by the Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System pension fund was filed on Friday in a federal court in San Jose, California. The lawsuit alleges that Intel failed to inform investors in a timely manner about the extent to which slow demand for consumer processors and excessive inventories would affect its sales. In particular, the plaintiffs argue that the negative impact of the PC market downturn on Intel's business was greater than the benefits the company enjoyed from the unprecedented buildout of AI data center infrastructure and other AI-related opportunities.
"Intel made statements that were materially false and/or misleading when made because they failed to disclose the following adverse facts pertaining to Intel’s business," the lawsuit reads.
While Intel, like many other major technology companies, has invested heavily in its manufacturing capabilities, supply constraints have prevented the chipmaker from fully capitalizing on strong demand for data center processors. Meanwhile, a severe shortage of memory has driven up DRAM prices and, consequently, the cost of PCs, which has affected demand for consumer systems. As a result, Intel could not sell enough CPUs in the third quarter, which dramatically affected the company's stock price in October.
Intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan expressed disappointment with the supply constraints, the extraordinary situation in the memory market, and the subsequent weakness of the PC business during the company's earnings call. Yet, the plaintiff believes that the company should have warned about the turmoil situation on the client PC market earlier. In fact, back in the early 2000s, when Intel was led by Craig Barrett, the company routinely issued mid-quarter business updates to inform investors about changes in its financial outlook. In fact, in September 2004, Intel used such an update to cut its third-quarter revenue and gross margin projections due to weaker-than-expected demand for its processors and inventory adjustments by its customers, which were very similar circumstances that the company faced in the third quarter of 2026.
A similar update could have alerted Intel's shareholders to the challenges the chipmaker faced well ahead of its quarterly earnings release. Unfortunately, Intel abandoned the practice of mid-quarter updates in January 2006 under Paul Otellini, though it occasionally revised its guidance between quarterly earnings releases thereafter, particularly during the global financial crisis of 2008 – 2010.
Intel's shareholders also allege that the company had a financial incentive to withhold information about the state of its business as it raised $23 billion through a stock offering at $95 per share in mid-August, roughly halfway through its third quarter. Intel secured the additional capital as it planned to expand its semiconductor production capacity.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Intel’s stock price dropped by 28.6% on October 30, erasing around $140 billion of the company's market capitalization, after the chipmaker issued Q4 revenue and earnings projections that fell short of expectations and warned that the PC market downturn would persist. Meanwhile, despite the massive sell-off, Intel's shares have gained 62% since the beginning of the year.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages on behalf of Intel investors who purchased the company's shares between July 23 and October 29, 2026. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and CFO David Zinsner are also named as defendants.

articles.title: Apple to add Face Unlock to iPhone Duo in future software update - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Apple is adding facial unlock for the new iPhone Duo in the next iOS 27.3 update which will use the front-facing camera when the device is in the closed position.
Many iPhone Duo customers were surprised to find out the device did not have Face ID but instead used Touch ID for security.
We know many customers, most coming from a previous iPhone, found it jarring not to have the instant unlock that Face ID provides.
READ TECH GUIDE’S iPHONE DUO REVIEW HERE
Apple has responded to these reactions and decided to remedy the situation with this new facial unlock feature which is only available on the lock screen.
Facial unlock will still require Touch ID to authenticate.
Touch ID will be required again after 45 minutes of inactivity.
The new feature needs to be enabled in the settings under Touch ID and Passcode.
Touch ID will still be required to authorise Apple Pay and access your passwords folder.
Apple has also added Close To Lock feature, which, as its name suggests locks the iPhone Duo when you close it.
Closing the iPhone Duo without this setting just transfer what you’re viewing to the front screen.
This feature can be activated in the Display & Brightness settings.
These features have just been released to developers in the beta for the iOS 27.3 software update.
Customers can expect the update to be available in early December.

articles.title: Affaire Nvidia : Elon Musk et 157 000 personnes réclament le retour de Jensen Huang
articles.text:
Le 12 novembre dernier, Jensen Huang a démissionné de son poste de PDG de Nvidia, après des révélations sur ses relations extraconjugales, dont l’une impliquerait Alice Huang, suspectée par Washington d’être une espionne au service de la Chine. En attendant que le conseil d’administration de Nvidia trouve un remplaçant, c’est Colette Kress qui occupe la plus haute fonction de l’entreprise par intérim. Mais Jensen Huang pourrait-il récupérer son poste ? En tout cas, différentes actions sont mises en place pour que cela arrive un jour.
Une lettre ouverte réclame le retour de Jensen Huang chez Nvidia
Nous vous en parlions récemment, une partie des employés de Nvidia réclame le retour de Jensen Huang. Quelques jours plus tard, nous avons appris qu’une cellule de crise, composée de dirigeants d’entreprises tech, se serait formée autour de l’homme d’affaires. L’objectif de cette cellule de crise : faire pression sur le conseil d’administration pour remettre Jensen Huang à la tête de Nvidia.
Mais cela n’est pas tout puisqu’une lettre ouverte, réclamant le retour de Jensen Huang à la tête de Nvidia et comptant plus de 157 000 signataires, vient d’être dévoilée. Parmi les signataires, nous retrouvons sans surprise Elon Musk, qui s’était dit prêt à l’embaucher chez SpaceXSI (anciennement SpaceXAI), mais aussi Garry Tan (président de Y Combinator) et Tim Sweeney (PDG d’Epic Games), qui a appelé sur le réseau social X à « Sauver Jensen ». Nous retrouvons aussi parmi les signataires, 8 000 personnes se déclarant salariées de Nvidia, soit environ 18 % des effectifs du groupe.
Cette lettre ouverte demande au conseil d’administration de Nvidia de « ramener Jensen pendant qu’une enquête indépendante établit les faits ». Et si cela n’est pas effectué, le conseil d’administration doit fournir « des preuves convaincantes que son éviction est dans l’intérêt de Nvidia ». Il est ensuite indiqué que « Jensen mérite une procédure équitable, pas un tribunal populaire ». De son côté, Travis Kalanick, fondateur d’Uber, a déclaré : « Il a commis des erreurs, oui – l’erreur est humaine -, mais je ne crois pas que quoi que ce soit de ce qu’il a fait justifie de l’écarter de son entreprise ». À noter que les organisateurs de cette lettre ouverte assurent être indépendants de Nvidia et de Jensen Huang.
Le ministre américain des Finances demande un remaniement chez Nvidia
En fin de compte, les affaires de relations extraconjugales de Jensen Huang, y compris celle qu’il aurait entretenue avec Alice Huang, suspectée d’être une espionne chinoise, risquent de ne plus être son principal problème. En effet, Nvidia, sous la direction de Jensen Huang, est soupçonnée d’avoir laissé passer jusqu’à 1,5 million de puces interdites vers la Chine. En d’autres termes, il serait question de contrebande.
Scott Bessent, le ministre américain des Finances, a déclaré sur la chaîne Fox News : « Ce qui importe davantage, c’est d’examiner si Nvidia avait une culture de conformité aux restrictions américaines à l’exportation ». Il a ajouté ensuite que la direction de Nvidia a besoin d’un « remaniement en profondeur » et a invité l’entreprise à trouver son nouveau dirigeant « à l’extérieur ». Rappelons que Washington envisage d’ores et déjà de nouvelles restrictions contre la Chine concernant l’exportation de puces Nvidia.
Donald Trump et Jensen Huang ont souvent affiché une certaine complicité, mais il n’est pas sûr que celle-ci résiste à cette affaire de contrebande de puces, si elle est avérée.

articles.title: Microsoft explica "apagão" que derrubou o Outlook (não foi hacker) • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Microsoft explica “apagão” que derrubou o Outlook (não foi hacker)
Microsoft informou que o "apagão" recente no Outlook e em outros serviços foi causado por uma falha em uma atualização de software aplicada em julho.
O “apagão” que a Microsoft sofreu na última semana, que manteve o Outlook e vários serviços da companhia inacessíveis ou instáveis por horas, deixou algumas dúvidas no ar, entre elas, “a companhia teria sido alvo de hackers?”. Bom, de acordo com a própria empresa, o problema foi causado por falha em uma atualização de software.
Chega a ser irônico, pois atualizações de software visam corrigir falhas, não causá-las. Mas foi o que aconteceu aqui. Em um relatório preliminar sobre o caso, a companhia explica que o problema começou em uma atualização aplicada em julho deste ano em servidores de “gateway de rede” ligados ao Microsoft 365.
Esses servidores controlam o acesso aos serviços da empresa (embora não respondam pela autenticação de usuários), recebendo solicitações dos usuários e as encaminhando para os sistemas que devem lidar com elas. Se essa dinâmica falha, os tais serviços deixam de ser acessados.
A tal atualização de software visava corrigir um problema anterior. Depois que o procedimento foi realizado, nenhuma anormalidade foi percebida. Testes de carga de trabalho chegaram a ser executados, mas nenhum deles apontou falhas ou sinais de impactos operacionais negativos. Mas o problema estava lá.
A própria Microsoft reconheceu que os testes pós-atualização não foram executados corretamente. Eles foram baseados em computadores mais antigos, com menos núcleos de processamento. Porém, o problema se manifestava com hardware mais recente e, portanto, com mais núcleos.
Eis que, no último dia 12, uma sequência de acontecimentos criou o cenário perfeito para que a falha, até então desconhecida, ganhasse forma.
Cerca de 15 horas antes da interrupção, o Microsoft Teams passou por um procedimento de failover, que transferiu seu tráfego para o gateway principal, também utilizado pelo Exchange Online.
Esse tipo de transferência de carga não é incomum ou inesperado. O problema é que, na ocasião, 14% da capacidade dos servidores de gateway estava indisponível devido a outro problema. Embora a infraestrutura da empresa ainda tivesse capacidade para absorver essa transferência isoladamente, a combinação com a demanda do Microsoft Teams fez a falha se manifestar.
A consequência foi esta: o Outlook e outros serviços ficaram indisponíveis por horas. A normalização nos sistemas da Microsoft só ocorreu no dia seguinte (13/11).
Tamanha demora se deve à dificuldade que a companhia teve para identificar a origem do problema e aplicar uma atualização para reverter a correção que estava no centro do caos. A Microsoft chegou a ativar uma capacidade extra nos servidores de gateway, mas nem isso foi suficiente. A solução só se mostrou efetiva com a reversão.
Quem acha que o Outlook foi o serviço mais afetado, achou certo. Isso aconteceu porque o Outlook depende do Exchange Online. Enquanto serviços como Teams, OneDrive e SharePoint conseguiram recorrer a caminhos alternativos, por assim dizer, o Exchange Online não teve essa possibilidade em escala suficiente para manter a sua operação.
Vale destacar que este é um posicionamento preliminar. A Microsoft deve publicar um relatório mais detalhado sobre o “apagão” no próximo dia 20.

articles.title: Agentische KI: Wer Kontrolle für eine Bremse hält, hat Automatisierung nicht zu Ende gedacht
articles.text:
Agentische KI: Wer Kontrolle für eine Bremse hält, hat Automatisierung nicht zu Ende gedacht
Im Juli 2026 ließ OpenAI für eine Sicherheitsevaluation Tausende Agenten auf Schwachstellen los. Einige fanden einen Weg aus der abgeschotteten Testumgebung, nutzten fremde Zugangsdaten und drangen in Systeme von Hugging Face ein. Zwei Monate später legte OpenAI den Vorfall offen. Man kann dem Unternehmen durchaus vorwerfen, dass das so lange dauerte. Andererseits darf man ihm zugutehalten, dass sie es überhaupt offengelegt haben. Sonst wüssten wir unter Umständen gar nicht, wie sich ein Agent verhält, wenn er ein Ziel hat – und ein Hindernis.
Seitdem gibt es zwei Lager. Das eine sieht einen falsch konfigurierten Container und offen herumliegende Schlüssel. Das andere sieht Software, die sich eigene Wege sucht, und ruft nach dem Notausschalter. Satya Nadella hat beim All-In Summit im September beide Lesarten sortiert: Das Banale sei klassisches DevOps-Versagen, das Neue sei Reward Hacking durch dauerhaft laufende Agenten, ein neues Insider-Risiko für jedes Unternehmen. Seine Antwort: aggressives Monitoring, lückenlose Nachvollziehbarkeit, und wenn ein Showstopper auftaucht, „stop the show“.
Ich halte das grundsätzlich für richtig. Und zugleich für unvollständig.
Ein Protokoll erklärt den Schaden, es verhindert ihn aber nicht
Natürlich müssen wir nachvollziehen können, was ein Agent getan hat und warum. Dafür gibt es den Audit-Trail, das lückenlose Protokoll, wer wann was mit welchen Daten getan hat. Nur hilft mir dieses Protokoll wenig, wenn das Geld bereits überwiesen, der Versicherungsantrag abgelehnt oder die falsche Buchung ausgelöst ist. Kontrolle muss daher früher beginnen. Bevor ein Agent handeln darf, müssen drei Fragen beantwortet sein: Welche Entscheidungen darf er treffen? Auf welcher Grundlage? Und in welchen Situationen muss er die Kontrolle abgeben?
Die übliche Antwort darauf heißt Human in the Loop. Ein Mensch schaut immer wieder drauf, egal wie wichtig der Schritt gerade ist. Das klingt nach Sicherheit und ist in der Praxis ein Stempelkissen. Wer tausendmal am Tag auf einen grünen Haken klickt, prüft nichts mehr, er bestätigt. Ich bevorzuge daher Human in the Lead. Ein Mensch mit Kompetenz und Erfahrung wird genau dort gebraucht, wo eine Entscheidung Folgen hat, und er bekommt dort genau die Informationen, die er für sein Urteil braucht. Das ist der Unterschied zwischen beobachtbarer und beherrschbarer KI.
Die Pflicht trifft jeden, der ein Sprachmodell einsetzt
Ob der Hugging-Face-Fall ein Sicherheitsproblem oder ein KI-Problem war, finde ich müßig. Testumgebungen von produktiven Systemen zu trennen, gehört zum Handwerkszeug. Aber ein Agent hat eigenständig Wege gefunden, Grenzen zu überwinden, die ihm gesetzt waren. Das ist die neue Qualität: Software, die selbstständig nach Wegen zum Ziel sucht, auch nach solchen, die niemand vorgesehen hat. Deshalb überzeugt mich der Einwand nicht, es sei ja nur ein Test gewesen. Wenn ein Test reale Auswirkungen auf fremde Systeme hat, dann war die Grenze einfach nicht abgesichert.
Das ist der Vorwurf an OpenAI. Die Verpflichtung dahinter trifft jeden Anbieter eines Sprachmodells und jedes Unternehmen, das darauf eine Anwendung baut: Verlasst euch nicht darauf, dass ein Agent eure Absichten schon richtig interpretiert. Die technischen Möglichkeiten von Agentic AI müssen enger begrenzt sein als die Fähigkeit, Lösungen zu finden.
Die Grenze liegt dort, wo aus Information eine Handlung wird
In den dokumentenbasierten Prozessen, mit denen ich täglich zu tun habe, ist diese Grenze gut erkennbar. Ein Agent liest eine Arztrechnung, ordnet die Leistungen zu und gleicht sie mit den Versicherungsbedingungen ab. Bis hierhin ist das Informationsverarbeitung. Lehnt er anschließend eine Leistung ab oder löst eine Auszahlung aus, hat das unmittelbare Folgen für einen Menschen. Trotzdem muss nicht jede Auszahlung manuell freigegeben werden. Ein geprüfter Standardfall mit eindeutiger Deckung, plausiblen Daten und einem Betrag innerhalb vereinbarter Grenzen darf automatisch durchlaufen.
Anders bei widersprüchlichen Daten. Ein Agent bereitet eine Rechnung zur Zahlung vor und stellt fest, dass die Bankverbindung von den Stammdaten abweicht. Hier hält er an, dokumentiert die Abweichung und übergibt an eine zuständige Person. Die braucht keine zwanzigseitige Dokumentation seiner Überlegungen, sondern drei Dinge: welche Daten sich widersprechen, woher sie stammen und was der Agent vorhatte. Und das Stoppen muss technisch durchgesetzt sein. Eine gesperrte Auszahlung darf nicht über einen anderen Prozessweg doch noch ausgelöst werden.
Wer Kontrolle für eine Bremse hält, hat Automatisierung nicht zu Ende gedacht
Ein immer wiederkehrender Einwand lautet: Kontrolle vorab bremst. Wer vor dem Start alles klärt, startet später als der Wettbewerb. Das stimmt, solange jeder einzelne Vorgang eine Freigabe braucht. Wer aber einmal sauber definiert, welche Fälle automatisch bearbeitet werden dürfen, verarbeitet anschließend Tausende Vorgänge ohne manuellen Eingriff. Kontrolle vorab ist eine Investition in Geschwindigkeit. Banken und Versicherungen haben hier einen Vorteil, den sie selten als solchen wahrnehmen: Berechtigungskonzepte, Risikoklassen, Vier-Augen-Prinzip und Freigabegrenzen sind hier seit Jahrzehnten Alltag und lassen sich auf Agenten übertragen. Ich glaube deshalb, dass regulierte Unternehmen KI-Agenten langfristig schneller produktiv einsetzen als Unternehmen, die zunächst alles erlauben und später feststellen, dass ihre Systeme nicht mehr beherrschbar sind.
Unabhängigkeit muss sich ein Agent verdienen
Nadella hat recht: Wer einen Showstopper sieht, soll die Show stoppen. Nur setzt das voraus, dass vorher jemand festgelegt hat, wo der Schalter sitzt, wer ihn drücken darf und dass er überhaupt existiert. OpenAI hat zwei Monate gebraucht, um zu sagen, was passiert ist. Ein Unternehmen, dessen Agent eine falsche Auszahlung auslöst, hat diese Zeit nicht. Wer die Kontrollfrage heute nicht beantworten kann, muss kein Projekt stoppen. Er überträgt dem Agenten weniger Verantwortung. Erst analysieren und vorschlagen, dann klar definierte, reversible Aktionen, dann mehr. Ein Agent muss nicht alles dürfen, nur weil er vieles kann. Wir sollten mit der Verantwortung beginnen, die wir sicher beherrschen. Und sie dann systematisch ausbauen.
Was ist das eigentlich für eine Entwicklung? Wir hatten klassische Computerprogramme, die auf dem eigenen System laufen und einfach das tun, was sie sollen.
Stattdessen wollen jetzt alle wechseln zu „KI“ Agenten, die manchmal das tun, was sie sollen, extra Software (oder sogar weitere „KI“ Agenten“) zur Kontrolle brauchen und dabei so massiv Resourcen brauchen, dass sie eigentlich nur gut in nem Rechenzentrum laufen.
Was ist der Vorteil? Dass man mit natürlicher Sprache sagen kann, was das System tun soll und keine Entwickler mehr braucht, die Software entwickeln? Dafür Abhängigkeiten zu Großkonzernen und Ungewissheit hat, ob man das bekommt, was man will? Toller Plan.

articles.title: Una jueza dejó avanzar la demanda contra Samsung, SK Hynix y Micron por el precio de la memoria RAM
articles.text:
La jueza federal Noël Wise rechazó el 14 de noviembre el pedido de Samsung, SK Hynix y Micron para frenar una demanda colectiva que los acusa de restringir de manera coordinada la oferta de memoria DRAM, la que usan las computadoras y los teléfonos. La decisión no establece que hubo un acuerdo ilegal: solo permite que el caso siga.
Los demandantes son 17 consumidores y pequeñas empresas de cinco estados, según la orden judicial. Medios surcoreanos como Seoul Economic Daily precisan que son 14 consumidores y tres ensambladoras y distribuidoras de computadoras, y que presentaron la demanda en junio.
Sostienen que los tres fabricantes recortaron la producción al mismo tiempo, coordinaron el giro hacia la memoria de alto ancho de banda (HBM, el tipo que necesitan los chips de inteligencia artificial) y abandonaron los formatos DDR3 y DDR4. Según la demanda, la oferta de memoria convencional quedó bloqueada mientras los precios subían casi 700%.
La orden recoge otro dato de la demanda: al tercer trimestre de 2025, las tres empresas concentraban más del 91% de los ingresos mundiales de DRAM. SK Hynix tenía el 33,2%, Samsung el 32,6% y Micron el 25,7%. En su pedido de rechazo, las propias compañías admitieron que el sector es un oligopolio, dominado por pocos actores.
Por qué la jueza no vio una repetición de 2018
Las empresas argumentaron que el caso repetía otro, presentado en 2018, sobre el alza de precios de 2016 a 2018, cuyo rechazo confirmó en 2022 un tribunal de apelaciones. Wise respondió que no es así. Los demandantes, escribió, no buscan volver a discutir aquel episodio y describen conductas distintas.
Entre ellas figuran recortes de producción simultáneos, una reasignación coordinada de la capacidad, la salida paralela de productos, el retiro de equipos usados por parte de Samsung y SK Hynix y controles casi idénticos que cada empresa aplicó a sus clientes. Cada compañía sostuvo que sus decisiones fueron racionales y respondieron a su interés propio.
Para la jueza, el cuadro cambia por los detalles: SK Hynix y Micron iniciaron los recortes más arriesgados, no un único líder del mercado, y las decisiones eran difíciles de revertir si los demás no las seguían. Las empresas tampoco aprovecharon, al menos hasta la demanda, un alza cercana al 700%. Eso distingue este caso del anterior, concluyó.
Los demandados habían citado una frase del juez Posner: en los mercados concentrados, los competidores se vigilan “como halcones”. Wise respondió que lo alegado va más allá de que se vigilen entre sí. Se parece más a halcones que vuelan en formación, escribió, “una actividad que los halcones normalmente no hacen”.
También pesó el historial. Según la demanda que cita la orden, una investigación del Departamento de Justicia llevó a que cuatro empresas se declararan culpables de fijar precios de DRAM, entre ellas Hynix (multa de USD 185 millones) y Samsung (USD 300 millones). Micron participó, pero obtuvo inmunidad por colaborar. Para Wise, esos antecedentes respaldan a los demandantes.
Un fallo preliminar que no declara culpables
La resolución corresponde a la etapa inicial del proceso. Wise precisó que, para avanzar, los demandantes no necesitan demostrar que se descarta toda conducta independiente y lícita: les basta con exponer hechos más compatibles con una acción coordinada que con decisiones separadas. Las empresas pueden seguir defendiéndose y la jueza no resolvió si hubo colusión.
El telón de fondo, según la propia orden, es la caída de la demanda de memoria a fines de 2022 y el auge posterior de la inteligencia artificial, que llevó a los compradores a adquirir memoria en volúmenes que la industria no había visto. La demanda alega que los fabricantes respondieron a ese salto con restricciones de oferta.
Las tres compañías deben presentar su respuesta formal a la demanda antes del 7 de diciembre de 2026. La primera audiencia de gestión del caso quedó fijada para el 12 de enero de 2027, según la orden de la jueza.

articles.title: Governed Autonomous Intelligence for Mission-Critical Utility
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- In a regulated utility environment, an agentic operations platform keeps reasoning separate from execution: agents correlate signals, assess business impact, and propose remediation, but every production action crosses a deterministic policy boundary that the model cannot override.
- That boundary is defined outside the model. Each proposed action maps to a risk class and approval requirement in a predefined, versioned action catalog, which keeps approval decisions predictable, testable, and reviewable before deployment.
- A governed tool gateway enforces the boundary as the only path from an agent proposal to a production change, with least privilege, independent authorization, approval verification, and complete action evidence attached to that single door.
- Because every action passes through one governed path, the platform produces the evidence needed to support the regulatory and governance requirements of each system, without claiming that the platform itself creates compliance.
- Autonomy is earned rather than assumed: the platform starts read-only and expands one action class at a time, guided by recommendation quality, operator acceptance, execution outcomes, and rollback safety, and that autonomy can be revoked as easily as it is granted.
Introduction
Utility operations teams - the IT and platform teams responsible for supporting enterprise applications, integrations, and infrastructure already have more monitoring data than they can comfortably consume.
Application logs, infrastructure metrics, API telemetry, security events, job failures, service-management tickets, and business alerts all describe pieces of the same operating environment. The hard problem is not collecting another signal. It is connecting those signals quickly enough to understand what is happening, what it may affect, and what should happen next.
Agentic AI is attractive because it can reason across that fragmented evidence, retrieve operational knowledge, call tools, and coordinate multi-step work. But a utility organization cannot treat an agent the same way it treats a conversational assistant. A wrong summary is inconvenient. A wrong production action can affect a customer-facing service, a safety-related workflow, regulatory reporting, or a system that participates in reliable energy delivery.
This article describes the architecture pattern we used for an agentic operations platform in a regulated utility environment. The reference implementation uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock, retrieval over enterprise runbooks and incident history, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool interfaces.
The model can propose anything. It can execute only what the policy gate authorizes, through the governed tool path, with human approval wherever policy requires it. Authority never lives inside the model.
Some capabilities, especially prediction and autonomous remediation, are intentionally enabled incrementally rather than all at once. That is not a limitation to hide. In a regulated environment, the ability to expand autonomy gradually and revoke it quickly is part of the architecture.
Why Utility Operations Need a Different Agentic Pattern
A large utility estate spans custom applications, SaaS products, cloud platforms, integration layers, databases, observability tools, field and operational systems, and third-party services. Each domain can be monitored well in isolation while the end-to-end service remains difficult to reason about.
The recurring operational gaps are familiar. Related signals appear in separate tools and are correlated manually. Technical severity is visible, but the business consequence is not. Runbooks and lessons learned exist, but they are spread across wikis, ticket histories, shared drives, and the memory of experienced engineers. Thresholds tell teams when a known condition has already occurred; weaker precursors across dependent systems are easy to miss. When action is finally taken, the evidence tying the change to its rationale, authorization, approver, and outcome may be assembled after the fact.
This is especially important in utilities because the governing context is not uniform. Regulatory requirements vary across utility sectors, operational environments, and jurisdictions. For example, North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) requirements apply to the Bulk Electric System (BES) and defined in-scope BES Cyber Systems. At the same time, customer-facing services, billing, field operations, and other utility programs may be subject to applicable industry-specific, federal, state, or local regulatory requirements.
The architecture therefore has to do more than produce a better dashboard. It must correlate across domains, reason with trusted operational knowledge, map technical events to business impact, support prediction without pretending prediction is certain, and preserve an execution model that security, compliance, operators, and auditors can understand.
Figure 1. Fragmented observability leaves operations teams to correlate application, infrastructure, integration, security, and service-management signals manually (Image source: created by the author)
The Control-Plane Pattern: Separate Reasoning from Execution
The organizing idea is an AI control plane. The term is borrowed deliberately from networking and cloud infrastructure, where the control plane decides what should happen and a separate plane carries it out. The separation is useful here for the same reasons: safety, auditability, and blast-radius containment.
Figure 2. The AI control plane separates reasoning authority from execution authority. The model can propose broadly; only policy-authorized actions can cross into the execution plane. (Image source: created by the author)
In the reasoning plane, the orchestrator and domain agents can analyze events, retrieve context, compare an incident with historical patterns, estimate business impact, predict likely failure modes, and propose remediation. None of those components holds authority to change a production system directly.
A proposed action crosses into the execution plane only through a deterministic policy gate and a governed tool gateway. The gate decides whether the action is permitted and what approval is required. The gateway enforces the final authorization, obtains narrowly scoped credentials, invokes the target system, records the result, and performs or requests post-action validation.
This distinction matters when the model is wrong. A hallucinated root cause in a conventional autonomous design can become a bad action. In this design, it becomes a bad proposal. Policy can reject the proposal, a human can review it, or the gateway can deny authorization. The model’s error still matters, but its cost is limited by construction.
Reference Implementation on AWS
The reference implementation runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore supplies managed agent runtime, memory, gateway, identity, and observability integrations with Amazon Bedrock for model access and Bedrock Knowledge Bases for retrieval over enterprise knowledge. AgentCore Policy, generally available since March 2026, covers the boundary this pattern relies on: rules authored in natural language or policy-as-code are compiled to Cedar, AWS’s open-source authorization policy language, and attached to an AgentCore Gateway, which evaluates every agent-tool request before allowing or denying it. That is deterministic, action-level authorization enforced at the gateway rather than inside agent logic, and teams starting today should evaluate it before building an equivalent. In this design, AgentCore Gateway is the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. AgentCore Evaluations supports continuous and on-demand evaluation of agent behavior.
MCP is used at the tool boundary to standardize how tools are described and invoked. A schema-defined tool boundary gives the platform one place to constrain operations, validate arguments, enforce policy, and record evidence.
The "one place" property is important. A tool gateway is only a governance boundary if agents cannot bypass it. In our design, that means no target-system credentials in the reasoning runtime, deny-by-default identity policies, tightly restricted network paths, and credentials exposed only to the tool implementation that needs them. The principle is simple: one door to production, with every control attached to that door.
Figure 3. The pattern mapped onto AWS services. Everything in the reasoning plane can only propose; requests cross the dashed boundary solely through the policy gate and AgentCore Gateway, the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. (Image source: created by the author)
Equivalent Services on Other Platforms
The pattern is not tied to AWS. It needs a managed agent runtime, a retrieval layer, and a policy-enforcing tool gateway that agents cannot bypass. On Microsoft Azure, Microsoft Foundry Agent Service provides the runtime, Microsoft Entra supplies agent identities, and Azure AI Search handles retrieval, with Azure API Management serving as the tool gateway and an AI gateway for model and MCP traffic (some of these governance features are still in preview). On Google Cloud, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform provides Agent Runtime and Agent Identity, with Agent Gateway as the tool gateway, enforcing IAM access policies and Model Armor screening for prompt injection.
End-to-End Responsibilities
The boundary that matters sits between the agentic layer and the tool gateway; everything above it reasons, and nothing above it can act.
| Layer | Responsibility | 
| Source | Alerts, logs, events, and telemetry from applications, infrastructure, cloud, monitoring, and security systems. | 
| Integration | Ingests and normalizes signals through APIs, webhooks, and streaming into a common schema. | 
| Queue | Buffers events for asynchronous processing and absorbs spikes without loss. | 
| Orchestrator | Receives events, determines analysis needs, routes to domain agents, and assembles findings. | 
| Agentic layer | Bounded agents for correlation, root-cause analysis, business impact, prediction, and remediation proposals. | 
| Knowledge base | Runbooks, SOPs, architecture documents, incident history, and dependency maps for trusted context. | 
| Model access | Reasoning, interpretation, and recommendations grounded in enterprise knowledge. | 
| Policy gate | Maps proposed actions to risk classes and approval requirements outside the model. | 
| Tool gateway (MCP; AgentCore Gateway on AWS) | Single governed production path enforcing authorization, approvals, scoped credentials, schema validation, and evidence capture. | 
| Target systems | Applications, cloud services, databases, networks, ITSM, and observability platforms receiving remediation. | 
| Human approval | Operator or owner review with recorded decision, identity, and timestamp. | 
| Operations view | Health, predictions, business impact, approvals, remediation status, and validated outcomes. | 
Table 1. End-to-end responsibilities across the governed pipeline, from signal ingestion to the operations view
Multi-Agent Reasoning Grounded in Operational Knowledge
The reasoning plane uses a hierarchical multi-agent structure rather than one large agent with broad access. A narrow agent with a bounded responsibility is easier to test, constrain, evaluate, and explain than a monolithic agent that knows every domain and can call every tool.
The Orchestrator Agent is the entry point for normalized operational events. It determines the analysis required, routes work to the appropriate domain agents, and assembles their findings. It coordinates but does not execute.
The Application Reliability Agent analyzes application failures and degradations against known patterns and recent history. The Platform Intelligence Agent looks at API and interface failures, latency, partial degradation, and upstream/downstream dependencies. The Business Impact Agent translates technical state into business consequences — for example, a risk to customer service, billing, a safety-related program, a reliability commitment, or a reporting deadline. The Remediation Agent is the only reasoning component allowed to propose a production-touching action, and its proposal still has no authority until it passes the policy and approval path.
Figure 4. The orchestrator decomposes each event and routes analysis to bounded domain agents; only the Remediation Agent proposes production actions, and those proposals still pass through policy and the tool gateway (Image source: created by the author)
All agents use shared operational context retrieved from enterprise knowledge. The useful corpus is the organization’s runbooks, SOPs, architecture documentation, incident history, business rules, dependency maps, and known recovery procedures. Grounding a recommendation in the documented procedure for this environment produces a very different artifact from a plausible answer based only on general model training.
The quality of this layer depends heavily on knowledge hygiene. If a runbook is outdated, contradictory, or missing a rollback step, RAG will faithfully retrieve an outdated, contradictory, or incomplete instruction. Curation, ownership, versioning, and source traceability are therefore part of the operational design, not a content-management side project.
In practice, every runbook carries a named owner and a last-review date, and retrieval returns both with each passage. Runbooks past their review interval are flagged to the owner, and operator rejections citing a faulty runbook are routed to the runbook’s owner for correction.
A common event contract is just as important as the knowledge base. We normalize incoming signals into a small operational schema that includes the affected service or component, environment, event type, timestamp, source, technical severity, dependency identifiers, correlation keys, business-service mapping, and a reference back to the original evidence. The raw payload is preserved, but deterministic parsing and source adapters, not the LLM, establish basic facts such as which system emitted the event and whether two identifiers refer to the same service. A model can help interpret an unfamiliar log message, but those foundational facts are too important to leave to probabilistic extraction.
The simplified example below shows a normalized event from the walkthrough scenario. The business-service mapping is looked up from the service catalog, not inferred by the model.
{
  "event_id": "evt-000193",
  "timestamp": "2026-04-12T14:03:27Z",
  "source": "apm",
  "source_event_ref": "apm://alerts/88213",
  "service": "customer-payments-api",
  "environment": "prod",
  "event_type": "latency_degradation",
  "technical_severity": "warning",
  "dependency_ids": ["billing-integration", "payments-queue"],
  "correlation_keys": ["chain:bill-payment-flow"],
  "business_service": {
    "name": "Customer bill payment",
    "criticality": "high",
    "mapping_source": "service-catalog"
  }
}
Walking Through a Governed Event
Consider a common integration-operations pattern. An API has not failed, but its latency begins to rise. At roughly the same time, a downstream integration starts retrying more frequently, and a processing queue grows. Each signal on its own may still be below a page-worthy threshold. Together they suggest that a customer-facing workflow could degrade if the pattern continues.
The ingestion layer normalizes the three signals and preserves their source evidence. The orchestrator recognizes that the affected components share a dependency chain and asks the Platform Intelligence Agent to analyze the interface behavior. The Application Reliability Agent checks whether the application has shown a similar resource or connection pattern in prior incidents. The Business Impact Agent maps the dependency to the business service that relies on it.
Retrieval then pulls the current runbook for this failure class and the most relevant historical incidents. The agents don't merely summarize alerts; they produce a structured operational hypothesis: the likely failure mode, supporting evidence, dependent services that may be affected, and documented remediation options. If the evidence is weak or contradictory, that uncertainty is carried forward rather than hidden.
Suppose the runbook permits two next steps: gather additional diagnostics and, if a specific condition is confirmed, restart a stateless component. The action catalog may classify the diagnostic tool as low risk and allow it to run automatically. In this deployment, the catalog maps the restart to a human-approval rule. The Remediation Agent can propose it, but it cannot decide to downgrade its risk because the model is confident.
When an operator approves the restart, the tool gateway verifies the approval reference and policy, obtains the scoped execution identity, invokes only the permitted operation, and captures the response. The workflow then checks the signals that motivated the action: latency, retry behavior, queue trend, and service health. If those conditions do not recover, the workflow does not mark the remediation successful simply because the restart command completed.
The architecture removes manual correlation and runbook hunting from a familiar operational problem while preserving the same controls an experienced engineer would expect before touching production.
Prediction Without Granting Prediction Authority
Prediction is where the platform moves beyond faster incident summarization. The goal is to identify combinations of weak signals that historically precede a failure: rising latency, queue growth, retry behavior, resource saturation, repeated warning patterns, or anomalies that become meaningful only when correlated across a dependency chain.
The prediction layer can use historical incidents, time-series trends, dependency information, and semantic analysis of unstructured logs to produce a forward-looking statement: what may fail, on what horizon, through which mechanism, with what confidence, and with what likely business consequence.
The important design decision is what prediction is not allowed to do. A confidence score is not an authorization token. Predictions enter the same governed path as observed incidents. They carry evidence, confidence, and business-weighted risk so operators can decide how to respond.
False positives are expected. They should be measured, reviewed, and reduced over time. Overselling prediction is one of the fastest ways to lose operator trust.
Governed Remediation: Deterministic Risk and Human Approval
Human control should not be a sentence in a governance document. It should sit directly on the execution path.
The platform maps every candidate action to a predefined risk class outside the model. An approved action catalog drives that classification, not the model deciding whether its own proposal is dangerous. The catalog can consider the operation, target environment, blast radius, reversibility, data impact, and dependency sensitivity, but the resulting policy is fixed, versioned, testable, and reviewable.
| Risk class | Examples | Governance | 
| Low | Read-only diagnostics, health checks, additional telemetry | May auto-execute; fully logged | 
| Medium | Reversible changes, such as approved stateless service restarts or scaling within limits | Approval per policy | 
| High | Production configuration changes, failover, sensitive data operations, or broad-impact changes | Explicit approval; dual control where policy requires it | 
Table 2. Action risk classification and governance requirements
This is intentionally conservative. In the early stages of deployment, even some low-risk actions may remain approval-only until the team has enough evidence to allow automatic execution.
The policy record should be concrete enough to test without an LLM. For each permitted operation, we keep the tool identifier, target environment, allowed scope, risk class, required approval type, execution timeout, key preconditions, and expected postconditions, plus a link to the rollback procedure where rollback is meaningful. The agent may supply parameters such as a service name or requested capacity, but policy decides whether they fall inside the authorized envelope. The risk-driving facts should come from controlled configuration, inventory, or independently verified context, because asking the model to label its own proposal low, medium, or high leaves the authority decision with the model.
Figure 5. Deterministic policy maps each proposed action to a risk class and approval requirement before the governed tool gateway can execute it (Image source: created by the author)
Post-action validation is easy to underestimate. "API returned 200" is not the same as "the system is healthy," so a remediation workflow should validate the outcome it was meant to produce and escalate if the expected state is not restored.
The gateway also provides defense in depth. It scopes least-privilege credentials to specific tools, authorizes each agent-and-action combination independently, and rechecks required approvals at execution time instead of trusting an upstream component’s claim that they happened. It also validates tool arguments against their schemas. Every invocation records the requesting identity, policy decision, approval reference, inputs, result, and post-action health status.
Typed tools constrain what a manipulated agent can request, but they do not make prompt injection disappear, because an agent can still misuse an operation within its allowed scope. The control therefore comes from layers: treating ingested content as untrusted data, narrow tools, argument validation, least privilege, policy enforcement, approval requirements, network constraints, and post-action validation.
Content inspection adds one more layer at the same boundary; since June 2026, AgentCore Policy can evaluate Bedrock Guardrails to screen tool gateway inputs and outputs for prompt injection and sensitive-data exposure (initially in a subset of AWS Regions). Treat that as one more control on the door rather than a solution to injection, and keep the bounded-authority layers regardless of how good the detection gets.
Security, Auditability, and Compliance
For regulated operations, governance is not a section added after the architecture. It is why the architecture has this shape.
Teams should manage model and agent changes with the same discipline as other production software: version-controlled prompts and agent definitions, reviewed changes, evaluation before promotion, and rollback capability. Historical incidents and adversarial cases provide useful regression tests. Teams should sample production traces and evaluate them for task completion, tool selection, groundedness, safety, and policy adherence. They should also monitor confidence and recommendation quality for drift after deployment.
Teams should also minimize operational data. Logs and tickets can contain customer, employee, or security-sensitive information irrelevant to the reasoning task. Before broad ingestion, teams should establish data classification, domain isolation, encryption in transit and at rest, and retention rules. OWASP’s Top 10 for LLM Applications identifies prompt injection and excessive agency as distinct risks, and its agentic security guidance extends that thinking to goal hijacking, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, and multi-agent interactions.
Audit evidence should answer more than "what did the system do?" For every consequential action, the organization should be able to reconstruct the originating signal, retrieved evidence, recommendation, applicable policy, human decision if required, executed operation, identity used, and validated result. Whether you can call that record immutable depends on the actual storage control; at minimum, it should be durable, access-controlled, tamper-evident, or otherwise protected according to enterprise evidence requirements.
The compliance mapping must be equally precise. NERC CIP does not apply to every application operated by an electric utility. For in-scope BES Cyber Systems, CIP-010-4 addresses configuration change management and vulnerability assessments; CIP-004-7 includes personnel and access-management requirements; CIP-011-3 addresses protection of BES Cyber System Information; and CIP-008-6 covers cyber-security incident reporting and response planning. An agentic platform can support the evidence needed for applicable requirements, but the platform itself does not create compliance.
For customer-facing and regulated programs, evidence and reporting obligations may vary based on applicable jurisdictional requirements. Corporate applications outside CIP scope may instead fall under internal change controls, privacy requirements, or financial controls. The practical rule is to map evidence to the regime governing the specific system rather than labeling the entire utility estate "CIP compliant".
Frameworks such as NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 can organize the broader AI governance program, but they complement rather than replace industry-specific requirements.
Measure Value and Earn Autonomy
In regulated environments, organizations should measure agentic AI value against operational baselines, not unsupported improvement percentages. The signals we tracked included detection time from the earliest useful signal to an actionable alert; response time to validated resolution; prediction precision, false-positive rate, lead time, and operator-rated usefulness; engineering effort spent on manual correlation, after-hours paging, and repeated analysis; and governance measures such as approval latency, policy denials, blocked unauthorized actions, evidence completeness, and audit reconstruction time.
We expanded autonomy in phases, one action class at a time. No action class moved forward on model confidence alone. Each step required agreement from the system owner and change-management reviewers, based on the evidence below.
| Phase | Action class | Execution mode | Evidence required to move on | 
| 1 | All actions | Read-only: observe, correlate, retrieve, predict, and recommend | Operators consistently accepted recommendations, and rejection reasons were reviewed and addressed | 
| 2 | Read-only diagnostics and health checks | Approval-only → automatic | No diagnostic ran outside its authorized scope; evidence records were complete | 
| 3 | Reversible changes, such as stateless service restarts | Introduced as approval-only | Post-action validation confirmed recovery; rollback procedures were tested | 
| 4 | Selected low-impact reversible changes, such as restarting an approved stateless service or scaling within predefined limits | Approval-only → automatic, within defined scope and time windows | Approved consistently without modification; post-action validation confirmed recovery; rollback succeeded when tested; no policy denials or out-of-scope requests | 
| 5 | High-risk changes, such as configuration changes and failover | Always explicit approval | Not eligible for automatic execution | 
Table 3. Phased autonomy progression and evidence requirements
Conclusion: Lessons for Teams Adopting This Pattern
Agentic AI can correlate operational signals, assess business impact, and recommend remediation, but in mission-critical environments its value depends on how well its authority is governed. For teams adopting this pattern, a few recommendations stand out:
- Establish governance first: Build the governed execution path, enforce least privilege, and define the action catalog before introducing agents.
- Enforce deterministic policies: Manage risk classification and approval requirements through versioned configuration, not model prompts.
- Validate outcomes: Confirm service recovery rather than relying on successful command execution.
- Earn autonomy gradually: Enable one action class at a time, with the ability to revoke authorization when needed.
The goal is not maximum autonomy, but evidence-based autonomy that can be safely governed and revoked.

articles.title: Meet the new James Bond: Robert Pattinson
articles.text:
The Internet has been abuzz for months about which actor would replace Daniel Craig as British agent 007 James Bond in the franchise. We finally have the answer: Robert Pattinson, who built on his 2005 role as the doomed Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire into an illustrious career mixing roles in franchises and Hollywood blockbusters with daring arthouse fare.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”
The choice will reunite Pattinson with Denis Villeneuve, who recently worked with him on the forthcoming Dune: Part III and will direct the next (as yet untitled) Bond installment. “I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey,” Villeneuve said in a statement. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”
Not everyone is happy with the casting choice; some have never forgiven Pattinson for the Twilight franchise, despite the actor’s impressive recent films. Pattinson has played darker roles in recent years, often as a villain. And at 40, Pattinson is a bit older than the actors he beat out, most notably Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden (Slow Horses), Josh O’Connor (Wake Up, Dead Man), and Callum Turner (Fantastic Beasts).

articles.title: Telus ditches Westbank's two Vancouver AI data centre projects
articles.text:
Telus is no longer a partner with local developer Westbank to build two artificial intelligence (AI) data centres within Vancouver, but the developer says both projects will continue under a new partnership.
The pivot comes about six months after both companies formally announced their plans for major new AI data centre facilities at 150 West Georgia St. (on Beatty Street, immediately next to BC Place Stadium) in Downtown Vancouver, and within the existing M3 office building at 111 East 5th Ave. (near Main Street) in the Mount Pleasant Industrial Area.
In response to inquiries from Daily Hive Urbanized yesterday, both companies confirmed that Telus is no longer involved in the two Vancouver projects, which are under Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Enabling Large-Scale Sovereign AI Data Centres initiative.
“TELUS has decided not to proceed with co-developing two previously announced Vancouver data centres with Westbank,” said a Telus spokesperson.
Westbank separately confirmed the telecommunications company’s departure while maintaining that it fully intends to move ahead with a different partner that has yet to be publicly announced.
“We can confirm that Telus is no longer a partner on the two Vancouver projects but we are proceeding with a new partnership,” said a Westbank spokesperson.
Telus noted that it is advancing other plans to expand Canadian AI computing infrastructure, including an expansion of its existing Kamloops facility.
“TELUS remains committed to advancing Canada’s digital sovereignty to build the secure, sustainable, high-performance compute infrastructure our country needs to lead in the global AI economy,” continued the Telus spokesperson.
The telecommunications company is expanding the Kamloops facility to 20 megawatts (MW) by the end of 2028. Data centre capacity is typically measured in MW because available electrical power and cooling capacity largely determine how much computing equipment a facility can operate.
Telus is also considering development partners and locations for further expansion of its AI data centre infrastructure elsewhere in B.C.
Telus is working with the provincial and federal governments and aligning its plans with the federal AI data centre initiative. The Telus spokesperson attributes the expansion to growing demand at its existing facilities and says the company will release more details about its strategy in the coming months.
The original Telus-Westbank partnership announcement in May 2026 formally revealed the two Vancouver projects and the Kamloops expansion as a three-site network intended to provide Canadian-controlled computing infrastructure for businesses, post-secondary institutions, researchers, public institutions, and governments. The federal government has determined a need for such “sovereign” facilities for national security reasons — a strategy to keep AI computing infrastructure and sensitive data in Canada and under Canadian control, reducing the reliance on foreign providers.
At the time, Telus said it had secured an initial 85 MW of electricity from BC Hydro for the network, with combined capacity expected to exceed 150 MW by 2032. Both Vancouver projects were expected to be ready before the end of this decade.
The change in strategy also comes after the departure of longtime Telus CEO Darren Entwistle at the end of June 2026. He was replaced by Victor Dodig, a former CEO of CIBC.
The two Vancouver projects involve substantially different approaches.
At 111 East 5th Ave. in Mount Pleasant, Westbank wants to convert M3 — the existing six-storey office building within its Main Alley campus that previously housed part of Hootsuite’s headquarters — into a data centre.
The rezoning application would allow data storage uses throughout the office floors and convert underground parking levels for supporting equipment and other facilities. A restaurant would be added at ground level. No increase in the building’s overall size is proposed. Westbank’s project website describes M3 as a 26 MW facility.
But this Mount Pleasant proposal remains subject to further public consultation. On July 21, the previous Vancouver City Council returned the rezoning application’s referral report to City of Vancouver staff, removing it from the July 23 public hearing agenda and requesting that additional public consultation be performed after the October civic election.
The municipal government has since announced another formal public consultation period for the M3 application, running from Dec. 2 to 15, 2026.
Existing Condition:
Future condition:
At 150 West Georgia St., a new 10-storey AI data centre building is planned for a site previously set for a major new office building. A rezoning application is not needed, as data centre uses are already permitted for the site; a 2023-approved rezoning text amendment permits bulk data storage on this property.
This Downtown Vancouver project’s specific location is highly strategic for environmental reasons, as it would be fully integrated with Creative Energy’s steam plant below the data centre on the same site. Major construction work is currently ongoing for an expanded and electrified steam plant — transitioning away from its decades-long use of natural gas boilers — with its below-grade structure on Expo Boulevard forming a part of the foundations for the planned data centre building above Beatty Street.
Through its bulk steam heat and extensive network of underground pipes, this Creative Energy facility already provides spatial heating and hot water for over 200 buildings — totalling about 50 million sq. ft. of building floor area — across the Downtown Vancouver peninsula. Extensive heat recovered from the data centre would be used to help produce the steam to heat these buildings, effectively greatly reducing the energy — electricity and/or natural gas — required to produce the steam heat.
The May 2026 announcement also noted the possibility of connecting the M3 data centre facility to the City’s Neighbourhood Energy Utility.
Existing condition:
Future Condition:
Both Vancouver data centre projects have prompted protests and rallies over the past half year. Opponents have raised concerns about electricity and water consumption, noise, the use of centrally-located urban land, and whether the facilities would provide enough lasting local jobs and public benefits. Critics have also linked their opposition to broader economic concerns about AI replacing workers.
Moving forward, data centre projects also face the prospect of closer scrutiny under Vancouver’s newly elected City Council.
On Nov. 18, City Council is scheduled to consider a member motion from Vancouver city councillor Lucy Maloney seeking stronger oversight of data centres. Her proposal would explore requiring applicants to commission third-party independent assessments of potential water use, emissions, noise, heat, and employment impacts before rezoning or permitting.
It would also examine a dedicated business licence requiring annual public disclosure of water and electricity consumption and noise levels, along with possible fees or contributions to secure public benefits. The motion requests further policy work by City staff; it would not itself immediately enact those requirements.
Westbank and TELUS have had a longstanding successful relationship for over a decade. While our Vancouver projects will be proceeding under a new partnership, we look forward to continuing our working relationship with TELUS in other capacities and will be sharing more details in the near future,” said a spokesperson representing the two Vancouver data centre projects.
“We are supportive of Councillor Lucy Maloney’s motion to study compute infrastructure and how it can be implemented thoughtfully, because we share her objective of helping Vancouver demonstrate leadership in highly sustainable net positive compute. There will be more to follow on our initiative to create sovereign net positive compute infrastructure for Canada.”

articles.title: Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen promises to fix one of the most annoying things about AI — having to ask it the same thing over and over again — I tried it and I’m impressed
articles.text:
Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen promises to fix one of the most annoying things about AI — having to ask it the same thing over and over again — I tried it and I’m impressed
Gemini 4 Hydrogen is now a personal project collaborator, not just an assistant
Google's new Gemini 4 Hydrogen, the new default model in the Gemini app, promises to cut out the forgetfulness usually associated with AI and keep you on task. It also promises to respond faster and more accurately than 3.8 Flash.
One of the most annoying things I’ve found about using AI on the day-to-day, is having to remind it of my specific preferences and rules when I write prompts. We’ve all tried to give AI a set of guidelines in a prompt, such as a word count or specific inclusions, only to find that the final result is completely lacking them. Or sometimes, Gemini Flash would just make up an answer.
As someone who has frequently had to enter a prompting battle to get an acceptable result out of AI, I was curious to put Gemini 4 Hydrogen to the test to see if it could do better — and I was pleasantly surprised.
No more blank slate
To put Gemini 4 Hydrogen to the test against its predecessor, 3.8 Flash, I decided to continue a project I started during the height of the summer heatwave. I’ve long been considering installing some kind of solar panel setup to subsidize my energy bills, and given how much sun the UK actually got this year, and how much money I spent running an air conditioner, it really seems like a no-brainer.
Back then, I used Gemini 3.8 Flash to try and figure out the best cost-to-panel-efficiency while trying to stick within my budget and quickly ran into trouble trying to work out an estimated cost.
Flash 3.8 frequently fluctuated its estimates between chats and struggled to remember the local safety regulations and price quotes for things like scaffolding and labor that I had included in previous prompts. Out of frustration, the whole idea went on hold.
On the weekend just past, I revisited the project with the help of Gemini 4 Hydrogen to see if I could get an accurate answer.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
To start, it was time to test Hydrogen's ability to recall previous conversations. I told Gemini I wanted to pick up where I had left off in my previous conversations about solar panels, and gave it several key pieces of key information to test it's long term continuity and memory; I have an outdoor power socket; my garden is southeast facing; I have a budget of £600; and I’d like to be able to subsidize the power consumption of a 0.9 kWh air conditioner.
After a couple seconds of waiting, Gemini provided me with a concise summary of my previous conversations with 3.8 Flash, followed by a complete breakdown of three plug-in solar panel kits that fit within my budget and requirements with the exact price points of each solar panel from each retailer.
Compared to 3.8 Flash, which would give an estimated range of prices within a set of budgets, Hydrogen's ability to provide specific pricing from UK retailers adds a mark against Google's promise of more accurate and helpful responses.
When one of the suggestions fell slightly below my budget, Hydrogen also helpfully suggested spending the excess on ballast for the floor-mounted panels or a longer cable if the sunniest spot in my garden exceeds the default 5 meter plug length.
When 3.8 Flash tried to answer the same question, it focused purely on the math and did not account for other problems I could solve with any left over budget. Hydrogen on the other hand was able to identify potential friction points in the project — things I hadn't even thought of — and offered a solution, adding more value in response to a single question.
I then asked Gemini to estimate the expected annual savings for its top suggestion alongside the estimated monthly power generation from the kit based on my postcode, to which Gemini generated a graph that not only laid out exactly what I asked for, but also included a savings range based on how much power I’d actually use.
3.8 Fable really struggled with complex data sets and comparing calculations. Being able to give highly accurate local context and performing more accurately in complex calculations is a significant step up for Hydrogen.
Seeing the annual savings I could achieve, I then asked Gemini if increasing my initial budget would lead to a higher savings amount and a shorter payback period. After an initial breakdown of where my budget sat in relation to the return on investment for the solar panels it had suggested, Gemini also generated an impressive interactive model to see exactly how much I would save over a 15-year lifespan.
In comparison to 3.8 Flash, Hydrogen drastically changes how it displays information. Rather than having to scroll through a text-dense wall of information and do the math myself (or submit individual prompts for each calculation), I instead have a much more visual and easier to understand projection that can be quickly adjusted within the chat.
As a stickler for the rules, I also wanted to make sure I hadn’t missed any new or revised regulations that may have changed since my conversations with 3.8 Flash. I asked Gemini for a full checklist for one of the plug-in solar kits it had suggested. At this point, I was expecting a wall of text typical of Gemini 4 Hydrogen’s predecessor, but once again I was pleasantly surprised.
Gemini generated an interactive checklist that allowed me to tick off exactly how my outdoor electrical socket was compliant, while also ensuring I would be compliant with my local planning permission guidelines for plug in solar panel installation — especially if I wanted to mount the panels to the roof of my shed. The only time I had previously mentioned mounting the panels to my shed was in a previous chat with 3.8 Flash, so color me impressed.
Overall, there was one thing I noticed in my testing of Gemini 4 Hydrogen over 3.8 Flash: a huge boost to workflow speed. Sure, I would have eventually squeezed out a similar amount of information from Flash, but it would have taken significantly more prompts, more time, and more frustration.
Hydrogen added additional relevant context, identified other problems that could be solved, provided highly accurate statistics and figures, and made the information much easier to digest without the need to spend time making follow-up corrections.
My interaction with Hydrogen has done a lot to change my perspective on the helpfulness of AI. Not once did I have to remind it of my requirements or which specific solar kit I wanted to use, as was the case with 3.8 Flash.
The biggest take away from my weekend of solar panel planning is that Hydrogen feels more like a collaborator than an assistant. There is no more short-term memory loss and it's actually made me want to use it for future projects without that sinking feeling in the back of my mind that I may have to enter a prompting battle to get exactly what I want in the way I want it.

articles.title: Jensen Huang could be plotting return as Nvidia CEO, report claims — allies have formed a ‘war room’ to drive reinstatement days after resignation scandal
articles.text:
Jensen Huang could be plotting return as Nvidia CEO, report claims — allies have formed a ‘war room’ to drive reinstatement days after resignation scandal
SpaceX's Elon Musk and Epic Games' Tim Sweeney are two of Huang's biggest cheerleaders in an attempt to get him his job back.
Just days after he left the company under a cloud of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang might be on his way back to the company he founded. That's after a number of his allies rallied in support for Huang, including influential SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and outspoken Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. The pair are just two of those demanding that Nvidia's board has a rethink, hoping that it will choose to "Bring Jensen Back" to the company. Huang is now discussing that possibility, according to a Financial Times report.
"Huang has discussed with confidantes the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter," the report claimed, adding that allies were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley figures to try and lobby for his return.
Huang's resignation from his Nvidia post came after he released a statement confirming his affair, one which could have repercussions far beyond Nvidia itself. U.S. intelligence was reported to believe that the woman involved in an affair with Jensen Huang, Alice Huang (no relation), is a spy working for the Chinese Ministry of State Security, or MSS. Ms. Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, an AI company accused of smuggling $2 billion worth of AI chips into China via a subsidiary called Speedmatrix. Since Jensen Huang admitted to his adultery, it was further alleged that he had a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. That alone would potentially constitute a violation of Nvidia's own code of conduct. But the affair with an alleged Chinese spy is likely to be the most troublesome for the former-but-potentially-returning CEO.
Now, an open letter sent to Nvidia's board by Huang's allies has urged them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” The open letter was penned by Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker, both shareholders.
However, Nvidia has already started looking elsewhere. After placing chief financial officer Colette Kress in charge on an interim basis, it's believed the company has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a potential Huang successor. Haas spent around seven years at Nvidia before leaving in 2013, but no official confirmation has been announced, nor is it likely to be until a decision is made.
It's possible that Huang can expect a vote of confidence from U.S. President Donald Trump, with the pair having a good relationship to date. But Trump recently called for former Apple CEO Tim Cook to take over at Nvidia.
Outside of the White House, Huang has other concerns to deal with. Congress has summoned him to appear before a Select Committee over his affair with the suspected Chinese spy, threatening to subpoena him if necessary.
