articles.title: 5 lessons from The Life That's Waiting by Brianna Wiest
articles.text:
5 lessons from The Life That's Waiting by Brianna Wiest
Discover five meaningful lessons from The Life That's Waiting by Brianna Wiest on self-discovery, emotional healing, happiness, and personal growth.
Sometimes, the life we truly want begins when we stop holding on to the life we think we should have. We spend so much time worrying about the future, comparing ourselves with others, and trying to control every outcome that we forget to enjoy the present.
In The Life That's Waiting, Brianna Wiest explores the idea of creating a life that feels authentic, meaningful, and aligned with who we are becoming. Through reflections on heartbreak, fear, uncertainty, happiness, and personal transformation, she encourages readers to let go of limiting patterns and make room for new possibilities.
The book reminds us that we do not need to have everything figured out to move forward. Sometimes, the smallest decisions can bring us closer to the life we have always wanted.
5 Important lessons to learn from The Life That's Waiting by Brianna Wiest
1. Happiness is built through small daily actions
We often believe that happiness will arrive when we achieve a particular goal, find the right relationship, or reach a certain stage in life. However, constantly waiting for the next big achievement can prevent us from appreciating the present.
Wiest encourages readers to find happiness in small, repeated actions. Taking care of yourself, maintaining meaningful routines, expressing your feelings, and making time for things that matter can gradually create a more fulfilling life.
The lesson is to stop treating happiness as a distant destination and start building it through everyday choices.
2. Let go of what no longer helps you grow
Sometimes, the things that once made us feel comfortable no longer support the people we are becoming. This could be an old relationship, a familiar environment, limiting beliefs, or expectations we have carried for years.
The book reminds readers that outgrowing something does not mean that it was never meaningful. It simply means that different phases of life require different choices.
Allow yourself to move forward without feeling guilty about leaving behind what no longer aligns with your growth.
3. Stop comparing your journey with others
In a world where everyone shares their achievements, milestones, and happiest moments, it is easy to feel that you are falling behind.
However, comparison often distracts us from understanding what we genuinely want. Instead of measuring your success through someone else's timeline, focus on building a life that reflects your own values and priorities.
Wiest encourages readers to reconnect with themselves rather than constantly seeking validation from the outside world.
Remember, you do not have to follow someone else's timeline to create a meaningful life.
4. Your purpose begins with small decisions
Many people believe that finding their purpose requires discovering one extraordinary passion or making a life-changing decision. But purpose does not always arrive as a clear answer.
Sometimes, it begins with small interests, meaningful conversations, creative ideas, or opportunities that make you curious.
The book encourages readers to pay attention to these small signs and take action instead of waiting until they have complete clarity.
You do not need to know exactly where you are going. Sometimes, taking one meaningful step is enough to discover the next.
5. Take small steps even when you feel afraid
Fear often appears when we are about to make an important decision or step into something unfamiliar. It can make us question our abilities and convince us to remain in situations that no longer make us happy.
Wiest encourages readers not to let fear become the reason they stop moving forward. Instead of waiting until you feel completely confident, start with one small action.
Whether it is applying for a new opportunity, starting a project, having a difficult conversation, or making a personal decision, progress begins when you choose to act despite uncertainty.
Final thoughts
The Life That's Waiting by Brianna Wiest is a thoughtful reminder that the life we want to experience often requires us to change the way we think, feel, and make decisions.
Its biggest lesson is that you do not have to wait for the perfect circumstances to begin living meaningfully. Let go of comparison, make peace with change, follow what genuinely inspires you, and take small steps towards the future you want.
Sometimes, the life you have been waiting for begins when you finally permit yourself to live it.

articles.title: Amazon explique comment fonctionne Leo, le réseau satellite qui veut concurrencer Starlink
articles.text:
Amazon l’a promis : son service d’Internet par satellite sera disponible en 2026. Mais il ne reste plus que quelques semaines à l’entreprise pour honorer sa parole. Pour l’instant, Amazon se contente de détailler le fonctionnement de Leo dans un article détaillé sur son site. De quoi en apprendre plus sur comment la vidéo du chat mignon sur TikTok que vous regardez peut partir des serveurs du réseau social et arriver sur l’écran de votre téléphone.
396 satellites en orbite basse qui créent un vrai réseau
Pour le moment, Amazon a lancé 396 satellites en orbite basse pour créer son réseau de satellites. Un compteur d’ailleurs bloqué depuis début juillet, puisque les lancements tardent à se faire. Contrairement aux satellites géostationnaires plus « classiques », ceux installés en orbite basse ont l’avantage de réduire la latence, à savoir le délai entre l’envoi d’une requête et la réception de la réponse. C’est normal, puisque la distance est bien plus courte : environ 590 à 630 kilomètres d’altitude pour les satellites d’Amazon, contre 35 000 km environ pour les satellites géostationnaires.
Un avantage qui vient avec son inconvénient : plus un satellite est proche, moins la zone qu’il couvre est grande. C’est pour ça qu’à terme, Amazon ambitionne de déployer une constellation de plus de 3 200 satellites. Une goutte d’eau comparé à Starlink, qui compte plus de 11 000 satellites opérationnels.
Que se passe-t-il lorsqu’un utilisateur souhaite consulter une page sur Internet ? Tout d’abord, l’antenne installée chez lui envoie un signal vers le satellite Leo qui survole sa zone. Si besoin, ledit satellite peut relayer la requête vers un autre satellite grâce à des liaisons laser entre eux : c’est ce qui forme un maillage dans l’espace. La requête redescend ensuite vers une station terrestre, reliée à Internet grâce à la fibre optique, non loin d’une infrastructure AWS. La réponse à la requête (le contenu de la page) revient ensuite vers l’utilisateur en faisant le chemin inverse, en quelques millisecondes.
Trois modèles d’antennes qui doivent se connecter à de satellites qui vont (très) vite
Amazon précise que son logiciel recalcule le meilleur itinéraire toutes les 4,5 secondes, en tenant compte de la position des satellites, de la météo et de l’état du réseau. Le défi de ce logiciel est de rendre invisible le passage d’un satellite à un autre pour l’utilisateur ; ce qui n’est pas facile, puisque les satellites Leo se déplacent à environ 28 000 km/h et font le tour de la Terre en 90 minutes.
Mais alors, comment fonctionne l’antenne Amazon Leo que les premiers clients vont acheter ? Finies les grosses paraboles qu’il faut orienter, il n’y a aucune partie mécanique. Les antennes Leo sont des modèles dits plats à faisceaux électroniques, c’est-à-dire qu’ils dirigent électroniquement leur signal vers les satellites dans le ciel. L’antenne est naturellement reliée à un routeur Wi-Fi qui diffuse le signal dans l’habitation. Amazon Leo se décline d’ailleurs en trois versions :
- Leo Nano : jusqu’à 100 Mb/s en débit descendant, avec une petite antenne dédiée aux bateaux ou aux camping-cars ;
- Leo Pro : jusqu’à 400 Mb/s en débit descendant, une antenne un peu plus imposante pour les maisons ou les petites entreprises ;
- Leo Ultra : jusqu’à 1 Gb/s en débit descendant, une grosse antenne de près de 20 kilos, qui sera vendue pour les entreprises et les administrations.
Pour le moment, on ignore quand est-ce qu’Amazon Leo sera disponible en France. Mais la France a déjà donné son feu vert à Amazon pour y commercialiser son service.

articles.title: Google Project Zero cuts bug disclosures to 30 days amid AI threats
articles.text:
Google Project Zero will replace its “90+30” disclosure policy with shorter, fixed deadlines in response to AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation.
The transition is gradual and began on November 13, when the 30-day extension was removed from the vulnerability disclosure timeline.
On February 2, 2027, the deadline will be further reduced to 60 days, and on January 3, 2028, it will shrink to just 30 days.
Once the deadline expires, Project Zero will publish vulnerability details even if a fix is not available.
Project Zero is Google’s vulnerability research team, focused on the discovery of serious security flaws in widely used software and hardware.
Some of its notable recent findings include a .NET Framework zero-day, flaws in Chrome’s JavaScript engine and graphics components, and a Qualcomm chipset zero-day linked to NoviSpy spyware attacks.
When the team finds a flaw, it reports it privately to the vendor and typically publishes the technical details after a set period, giving time for developing security updates and patches, as well as a margin for most users to apply them.
Project Zero says AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and made it easier for attackers to reverse-engineer fixes as soon as patches ship and develop working exploits.
This policy change puts greater pressure on vendors to investigate reports, develop fixes, and ship them faster to customers.
Project Zero said a gradual approach to shortening the disclosure deadline was the better choice, giving vendors time to develop better flaw management and remediation systems.
Vendors warned Google that jumping straight to 30 days could expose users to severe risks and could lead maintainers to focus on Project Zero findings while ignoring other, potentially more severe flaws reported by others.
“An overarching concern was that immediately changing the policy could harm users by making unfixed vulnerabilities available to attackers while vendors are in the process of improving their remediation processes and technology,” Google explained.
“While the benefits of delaying disclosure are declining due to the increased probability that attackers will discover a vulnerability during the embargo period, we still feel there are benefits in the short term.”
Project Zero noted some early disclosure exceptions, such as when a flaw is actively exploited in the wild, when others have already published exploitation or vulnerability details, or when a vendor requests early disclosure.
Exceptions will also apply for non-disclosure, as Google deems fit, using the example of Spectre and Meltdown, for which it previously withheld information for longer than 120 days.

articles.title: Jordania bloqueó Telegram en todo el país porque la policía dice que facilita el extremismo
articles.text:
Jordania bloqueó Telegram en todo el país el 16 de noviembre. La Dirección de Seguridad Pública anunció que la medida busca frenar el extremismo, la radicalización y los delitos informáticos, como amenazas y extorsiones, que según el organismo se cometen a través de plataformas digitales.
El comunicado, difundido por la agencia estatal de noticias Petra, dice que la decisión se ajusta a la legislación vigente y apunta a proteger a los usuarios y la seguridad nacional. No precisa cuánto durará el bloqueo ni cita casos concretos que lo hayan motivado, según la cadena Al Jazeera.
La Dirección también pidió a los ciudadanos que tengan cuidado en redes sociales y apps de mensajería, que eviten cuentas o enlaces de origen desconocido y que denuncien por los canales oficiales cualquier contenido ilegal. A las familias les recomendó vigilar el uso que hacen los menores y activar los controles parentales.
Un bloqueo que llega tras el ataque a una iglesia
Las autoridades no vincularon a Telegram con el ataque del 23 de octubre contra la iglesia ortodoxa de San Jorge, en Hmoud, en el sur del país. Nueve personas murieron y más de 30 resultaron heridas, según el diario The National.
El bloqueo se anunció un día después de que un tribunal de seguridad condenara a muerte en la horca a tres hombres por esos hechos. Según el medio Asharq Al-Awsat, las autoridades los describieron como seguidores de una ideología extremista radical. Para The National, fue el ataque más grave contra la minoría cristiana jordana desde la década de 1950.
Reuters recordó que, tras el ataque, Jordania bombardeó posiciones en Siria y dijo haber matado a 20 militantes del grupo Estado Islámico. El 5 de noviembre, el país informó además de que un agente de seguridad murió apuñalado en Amán en lo que calificó de ataque terrorista.
Una app con decenas de millones de usuarios en la región
Telegram es usada por casi el 10% de la población de Medio Oriente, lo que equivale a decenas de millones de personas, según The National. Reuters señaló que militantes del Estado Islámico han usado el servicio para difundir comunicados.
La aplicación fue creada por Pavel Durov, quien vive en el exilio desde que salió de Rusia y enfrenta investigaciones en varios países. En julio, la nación europea mencionó que lo había acusado de facilitar actividades terroristas, con el argumento de que espías ucranianos usaban la app para organizar atentados dentro de su territorio, según Reuters.
Durov niega haber cometido irregularidades. Sostiene que Telegram ha ido más allá de sus obligaciones en la moderación de contenidos y en la cooperación con las autoridades para combatir el delito, según recogió la agencia de noticias.
El antecedente de TikTok en 2022
No es la primera plataforma que Jordania restringe. En diciembre de 2022, la unidad de delitos informáticos de la Dirección de Seguridad Pública anunció la suspensión temporal de TikTok, por publicaciones que, según dijo, incitaban a la violencia y al caos.
Según Al Jazeera, las autoridades jordanas no han anunciado el levantamiento de ese bloqueo, y mediciones de red hechas en el reino mostraron señales de que seguía vigente hasta comienzos de noviembre. La Dirección de Seguridad Pública no informó una fecha para revisar la medida.

articles.title: Una piscina de Alemania dependía de Microsoft para gestionar su nivel de cloro. Cuando cayó, varias personas terminaron en el hospital
articles.text:
El viernes pasado, medio mundo volvió a ser testigo de lo que ocurre cuando tantísimos sistemas dependen de una sola compañía y los servidores, simplemente, dejan de funcionar. La caída de Microsoft comenzó el pasado jueves por la noche y se prolongó durante todo el viernes. Outlook, Teams, Copilot, Defender y otros servicios tanto propios como externos dejaron de funcionar. No poder entrar a una reunión de Teams es una anécdota, pero que no te llegue un correo crítico puede ser muy serio.
Que se lo digan a una piscina de un hotel alemán en el que el nivel de cloro se desmadró y varias personas acabaron en el hospital.
En corto. Phantasialand es un parque temático en Brüel, un municipio cercano a Colonia. Dentro del parque está el Hotel Ling Bao, con un espacio de piscina y sauna que funcionaba con normalidad para los clientes, pero que por detrás no estaba funcionando en absoluto. El sistema no estaba distribuyendo bien el cloro y, normalmente, hay una configuración automatizada que envía un correo al equipo de mantenimiento si algún parámetro del agua no está en los niveles adecuados, y el problema es que ese correo se envía por Outlook.
Como te puedes imaginar, la alarma saltó, pero debido a la caída de Microsoft, el correo automático no llegó a ningún sitio. La mala suerte fue esa: se averió el sistema de dosificación el mismo día en el que los servidores de Microsoft se cayeron.
La consecuencia. Como cuenta el medio WDR, los huéspedes se quejaron de algunos problemas de salud tras usar la piscina y es algo que fue mucho más allá de ojos rojos y piel que picaba un poco: se tuvo que dar aviso tanto a los bomberos como a servicios sanitarios debido a que quince personas sufrieron problemas, como irritación de las vías respiratorias.
Cuatro de ellos tuvieron que ser trasladados al hospital y uno permaneció en observación debido a una lesión de gravedad media. La piscina se cerró, se cambió el agua por completo y volvió a abrir sin problema. Es mala suerte porque se unieron dos problemas que no son comunes, pero recientemente hemos tenido varios episodios de sistemas que no deberían fallar, pero fallan, que demuestra que, cuando todo depende de Internet y de servicios externos, no podemos dar nada por sentado.
Errores y ataques. Al final, la caída de Microsoft no parece ser ningún ciberataque, sino un problema con sus servidores y la carga de los mismos. Tardó en recuperarse porque afectó al 80% de sus servidores, pero fue eso: un error y "cosas que pasan". El problema es que estos últimos días hemos sido testigos de ataques a cosas que, hasta ahora, parecían protegidas como los frigoríficos del supermercado o algo tan crítico como las cámaras de plasma de un banco de sangre.
Son demasiados casos recientes y resulta que todos han explotado casi al mismo tiempo. En el caso de los hackeos, parece que gracias a lo fácil que pone la IA el atacar sistemas y dispositivos que antes no se atacaban no porque estuviesen protegidos, sino porque no sacabas nada de ellos y era una inversión de tiempo grande para un retorno nulo. Con la IA, hacer que se pierda comida o el caso más grave de las cámaras de plasma genera una inestabilidad que cuesta poco al atacante y ocasiona pérdidas significativas para el atacado.
¿Y si el IoT fue un error? He cambiado el sistema de malla de casa y por uno que tengo que analizar y llevo unos días con problemas de desconexiones que han provocado que algunas bombillas dejen de funcionar. Eso me ha llevado a preguntarme si construir durante una década un ecosistema inteligente y conectado no fue, en parte, un error.
Evidentemente, es mucho más cómodo automatizar algo para que funcione con un comando o que, en el caso de los sensores de la piscina, te avisen por correo, pero a riesgo de sonar un poco "abuelo cebolleta", un análisis de agua manual no depende de que llegue el Wi-Fi o de que se caiga el servidor de lo que sea.

articles.title: The fake photos are gone. INEC’s bigger problem remains
articles.text:
Nigeria’s electoral umpire, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), says it has removed artificial intelligence-generated photographs from its voter register. But a more consequential part of the disclosure concerns the people who helped put them there: some of the commission’s own personnel.
With the 2027 elections approaching, the controversy raises questions that cannot be settled by deleting suspicious images. INEC needs to explain how questionable photographs entered the register, why its registration checks did not prevent their inclusion, and whether its newly announced image-capture restrictions will close the gap. The commission says it is replacing external webcam-based uploads with photographs captured directly through an approved application.
On November 11, 2026, the commission said it had identified 54 registration personnel across 10 states for possible disciplinary action over registration irregularities. This does not establish that all 54 uploaded synthetic photographs or committed criminal offences. It does, however, show that the inquiry extends beyond applicants submitting questionable information to officials responsible for protecting the registration process.
“But the ones involving our own staff, where it is our own staff that did so, that one is within our control,” Mohammed Kudu Haruna, INEC’s national commissioner for information and voter education, said during a PUNCH Media Foundation webinar on November 11. “They have been flagged,” he added. “Obviously, they are going to face disciplinary action.”
The allegations potentially extend beyond workplace misconduct. Section 23 of the Electoral Act 2026 criminalises knowingly transmitting materially false registration declarations and procuring the registration of fictitious or ineligible persons. Whether particular personnel committed those offences requires investigation; being flagged is not a finding of guilt. Haruna’s assurance of disciplinary action leaves a further question: will cases supported by evidence of criminal conduct also be pursued in court?
Beyond the photograph
The involvement of registration personnel changes the nature of the problem. Electoral bodies must anticipate inaccurate information from applicants. But when authorised staff allegedly circumvent registration protocols, the issue becomes whether the institution can enforce its own safeguards.
AI may add a technological dimension, but the investigation must address fundamental questions of institutional control. Who could upload or replace a photograph? What checks were required? Could one official make changes without independent review? And are there records showing who altered each entry?
Deleting suspicious images addresses the visible problem. Establishing how they entered the system is necessary to prevent a recurrence.
So far, the disclosures do not establish that an external cyberattack compromised the register or that manipulated photographs resulted in fraudulent votes. These possibilities should not be presented as confirmed findings.
What the numbers mean
The figures surrounding the cleanup also require careful interpretation. INEC Chairman Joash Amupitan said 1,608,660 invalid registrations had been removed. Separately, reports say the commission reviewed 268,000 contested cases, rejecting 217,722 and retaining 50,278.
Published accounts have not clearly explained how these figures relate to one another, so they should not be added together automatically. Neither should the 1.6 million figure be described as the number of AI-generated voter records.
The cleanup covered several irregularities, including duplicate entries and deficient registration records. Synthetic or manipulated photographs were one concern within that broader exercise.
The distinction matters because imprecise figures can turn an administrative problem into allegations that the available evidence does not support. At the same time, a large deletion figure does not explain what the commission detected, how it verified each category, or whether the underlying weaknesses have been addressed.
The 50,278 records retained after adjudication are equally important. Suspicion alone does not establish ineligibility. A credible cleanup must prevent invalid registrations while protecting eligible voters from wrongful exclusion.
Discipline is only the beginning
INEC says the register was published in preliminary form to allow public scrutiny and objections before final certification. That process can help identify errors before an election, but it should not replace safeguards that ought to operate during registration.
Both things can be true: public inspection may have helped expose irregularities, while their discovery points to weaknesses that the commission must address. INEC’s credibility will depend on its ability to explain what went wrong and how its internal controls are changing.
The proposed disciplinary action is a starting point, not a completed accountability process. The identified personnel must be allowed to respond to the allegations, and the commission must distinguish between mistakes, negligence and deliberate falsification. Disciplinary action should also not be confused with criminal prosecution, dismissal or conviction.
Beyond individual sanctions, Nigerians need to know what investigators found, which procedures failed and what corrective measures have been introduced. While personal information may require protection, INEC can still disclose its institutional findings.
The policy test ahead
INEC said in October it is finalising an AI policy, but the controversy raises questions about whether that framework will address only AI-generated campaign content or also the commission’s own systems, personnel and use of automated tools.
“We have that policy. Very soon, we will concretise it, and we will be able to share it with the media,” Haruna said at the November 11 webinar.
The timing is significant. With presidential and National Assembly elections scheduled for January 16, 2027, the policy was still awaiting publication roughly two months before polling. More importantly, the registration exercise had already exposed irregularities that the framework could have helped prevent.
A useful policy must go beyond broad warnings about artificial intelligence. It should clarify who can access and alter voter records, what verification is required before photographs are accepted, how suspicious submissions are escalated, and who independently reviews sensitive changes. It should also establish clear responsibilities for staff and supervisors, with decisions documented and open to audit.
The absence of a published standalone AI policy does not prove that INEC had no existing safeguards, nor does it mean earlier publication would necessarily have prevented the irregularities. The commission must explain whether controls were missing, inadequate or deliberately bypassed. Its own admission of staff involvement makes that distinction central.
Ultimately, Nigerians need more than assurances that suspicious photographs have been removed or that personnel will face discipline. They need evidence that the registration process is secure, that eligible voters will not be wrongly excluded and that those entrusted with the register are accountable.
The photographs can disappear quickly. The reason they were accepted must not disappear with them; otherwise, the next AI-generated image may be harder to detect, while the institutional weakness remains unchanged.

articles.title: Un dogo tiró al suelo a una jubilada y la heredera del dueño del perro deberá pagar una indemnización de $20 millones
articles.text:
El dueño del dogo argentino ha fallecido, por lo que la causa penal quedó archivada. Sin embargo, siguió adelante el proceso civil contra la legataria y la compañía de seguros. Se ha establecido una indemnización de 20.480.000 pesos argentinos con intereses (unos 11.900 euros).
La mujer tenía 75 años cuando ocurrió el incidente en Vicente López (Buenos Aires). La víctima caminaba con su bastón cuando el perro se lanzó sobre ella e hizo que cayera al pavimento. Por las lesiones sufridas, la mujer entabló una acción judicial contra el dueño del perro. Tras su muerte, se ha ampliado contra la legataria.
Las imágenes desmentían a la defensa.
La legataria y la compañía de seguros alegaban que no fue el perro quien hizo que la señora cayera. Aseguraban que estaba atado (con bozal) y que el accidente fue por un tropezón de la jubilada. Sin embargo, las imágenes de las cámaras de seguridad y los testimonios aportados avalan el relato de la demandante.
La pericia médica determinó que sufrió una incapacidad física parcial y permanente mayor al 40 % (con problemas en la cadera). También hay síntomas psicológicos vinculados al suceso. La defensa puso en duda estos resultados, porque podría haber tenido problemas óseos previos. El informe pericial afirma que la caída ha sido el detonante o exacerbante de un problema preexistente (que no se había hecho patente clínicamente).
Responsabilidad por los daños del animal
En Argentina existe un régimen de responsabilidad objetiva por los daños de los animales. Es decir, no es preciso probar la negligencia del dueño para solicitar la reparación por los daños. En este caso, el juzgado estima que está probada la vinculación entre las lesiones y la actuación del perro. Además, la parte demandada no ha probado ningún motivo exoneratorio.
La condena afecta tanto a la legataria como a la compañía de seguros. El importe (a valor de la sentencia) tiene en cuenta distintos aspectos: la incapacidad física, los gastos médicos y de traslado, los de rehabilitación y psicología. También se ha tenido en cuenta el daño moral. A ello hay que sumarle los intereses que establece la resolución.

articles.title: GTA 6 isn't even out yet, but it's already breaking internet traffic records
articles.text:
In context: UK broadband networks usually hit their busiest moments during big soccer matches or a fresh Fortnite season. This month, a single video game download has beaten both. Grand Theft Auto VI pre-loads have already pushed at least one major provider to its highest traffic peak ever – nine days before anyone can actually play the game.
Openreach, which runs the UK's largest broadband network, saw this coming. Trevor Linney, its director for network technology, told ISPreview in late October that "GTA 6 has been on our radar for a long time." He added that the network was ready, though the company will be keeping a close eye out for a new download record.
There's simply no getting around the download this time. Even the boxed edition is just a download code in a case, so every copy has to come down the wire. That's a lot of data, too, since Rockstar lists the pre-load at up to 212GB depending on the console.
When pre-loads opened at midnight on November 10, Linney's prediction played out. Openreach later shared figures showing downstream traffic that day was about 33% higher than on an average Tuesday, adding up to nearly 378 petabytes. Weirdly, the biggest jumps came in the dead of night, when traffic between roughly 3am and 5am nearly doubled.
Virgin Media O2 felt the rush right away. Its traffic jumped 51.6% in the first hour of pre-loading compared with the week before. By the end of the day, the network had set a new all-time traffic peak. Its last record came from an Arsenal vs. Atlético Madrid Champions League semifinal. GTA 6 beat that by 3.8%. Its daily data volume also topped the record Fortnite's latest mini season had set just nine days earlier.
For smaller full-fibre provider YouFibre, that same rush actually slowed things down. It emailed customers that day, blaming a capacity issue from GTA 6 downloads for the dip in speeds. CEO Jeremy Chelot said one of the company's network gateways was struggling, leaving people around Yorkshire stuck with congestion. Service is back to normal now that engineers have rebalanced the load.
The real test may still be Thursday's launch. Anyone who skipped the pre-order has to pull the entire game that day. A day-one patch, if Rockstar ships one, would hit pre-loaders as well. At the 71Mbps median speed from Uswitch's recent broadband tests, the base download alone would take more than six and a half hours.

articles.title: AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field
articles.text:
AWS has launched Nitro Sandboxes, which run an opted-in Kubernetes pod, ECS task, or EC2 workload inside its own lightweight virtual machine with a separate guest kernel, carved out of a running EC2 instance by the Nitro hypervisor. On Amazon EKS, the whole change is one pod field: runtimeClassName: isolated-sandbox or confidential-sandbox.
The feature is available in all commercial regions at no additional charge, and AWS positions it for workloads where the tenant or the code cannot be trusted, with coding agents named first. In an AWS blog post, Carlos Santana and Trishi Mehta write:
Each pod gets its own operating system, completely separate from the host and from every neighbor.
According to the EKS documentation, a containerd-shim-nitro-sandbox-v2 process on the parent instance launches a Firecracker microVM as a first-level guest with hardware-assisted virtualization, after which an agent inside the VM runs the pod’s containers through its own containerd and the two sides communicate over virtio and vsock. The result is a sandbox that shares neither kernel nor memory mappings with the parent instance or any other sandbox, while the containers themselves start unchanged. How the nodes get there depends on the cluster type: on EKS Auto Mode the two RuntimeClasses ship with every cluster and sandbox-capable nodes are provisioned on demand, whereas on standard EKS a team builds a sandbox-enabled AMI for its node groups or Karpenter.
(Source: Amazon EKS User Guide)
What separates the two modes is which side of the boundary is trusted. Isolated mode trusts the parent instance and not the guest, which is why kubectl exec, logs, and process listing keep working, whereas confidential mode treats the parent as untrusted and moves enforcement inside the VM: a Cedar policy generated from the pod spec pins image digests, arguments, environment, mounts and capabilities, exec and stdin are denied, the Nitro Secure Module measures the image and policy into PCRs, and a KMS key policy can release secrets only to a sandbox whose measurements match. Image layers can be encrypted as well, so the parent moves ciphertext it never reads.
That chain only holds if something checks the measurements, and the documentation says so: without a KMS policy or external verifier checking the PCR values, "the attestation measurement is recorded but never verified, and the confidentiality guarantees of confidential mode are incomplete." Separately from either mode, a network-isolated annotation boots the sandbox with no network device at all, which also removes DNS, NTP, IMDS and Pod Identity and breaks HTTP and TCP probes.
Sandip Das, an AWS Container Hero, read the documentation the same way and drew out what isolated mode leaves to the operator: the protection "only runs in one direction," so a compromised parent can still observe or tamper with unencrypted traffic and DNS, writes the pod's /etc/hosts, and can mint Pod Identity credentials for any pod on the node. He also lists prerequisites the blog post does not, among them Kubernetes 1.36 or later, a launch template with Nitro Enclaves enabled on managed node groups, without which "sandboxed pods sit in Pending," and Pod Identity rather than IRSA for credentials. On AWS's description of performance as near-native, he advises treating it "as a vendor claim" and benchmarking startup latency, I/O throughput and tail latency.
Beyond agents, AWS lists multi-tenant SaaS, regulated workloads, CI builds and remote IDEs, and points to the open-source agent-sandbox project for warm pools that hand out a pre-booted VM in about two seconds.
The constraints are on the considerations page, and the largest is GPU and device passthrough, which is not supported at launch because Firecracker cannot pass host devices into a guest, so GPU pods run without the sandbox class. Density is capped twice over: total sandbox vCPUs may not exceed five times the node's vCPU count, and neither may the number of sandboxes, halved on CPU-overcommit types, which gives a 4-vCPU node room for twenty 1-vCPU sandboxes or five 4-vCPU ones. Simultaneous multithreading costs more than the arithmetic suggests, because core scheduling stops two sandboxes sharing the sibling threads of one core and leaves roughly half the advertised vCPUs usable; Graviton, with one thread per core, is unaffected.
The nearest comparison is GKE Sandbox, which has offered a gvisor RuntimeClass since 2019 and more recently a microvm class built on Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor. gVisor intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel, starts in under 200 milliseconds and supports CUDA on a subset of GPUs; Google's microVM option carries a fixed 250 mCPU and 130 MiB per pod, starts in one to two seconds and does not support GPUs. AWS has taken the VM side of that split and expressed its overhead as density and threads rather than per-pod resources.
On EC2, Amazon Linux and Firecracker are supported natively and patches are available for other virtual machine monitors. The EC2 User Guide carries the supported instance list and notes that snapshot, restore and live migration are not available.

articles.title: Google Project Zero Sets Course for 30-Day Disclosure Deadline
articles.text:
In the context of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation, Google Project Zero is significantly shrinking bug disclosure windows.
So far, Project Zero’s policy has been a well-known one: vendors were given 90 days to patch vulnerabilities before public disclosure and granted a 30-day grace period for patch roll-out.
Starting November 13, that grace period is no longer in the books, Project Zero security engineer Natalie Silvanovich announced.
Under the new ‘Full X’ policy, Project Zero will publish vulnerability details 90 days after reporting them to the vendor, regardless of whether, or when, a fix is released.
Beginning February 2, 2027, Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities publicly after 60 days, and the disclosure window will shrink to 30 days on January 3, 2028.
Furthermore, Project Zero is removing most ‘special cases’ from its disclosure policy, except for security defects actively exploited in the wild (which have a 7-day disclosure window, per Google’s policy) and flaws already made public by others.
If a vendor requests it, Project Zero may publish details on a security hole ahead of the deadline, Silvanovich says.
However, serious vulnerabilities may be granted exceptions. Project Zero has done it on rare occasions, such as Spectre and Meltdown, and that will not change.
According to Silvanovich, the phased transition to shorter disclosure windows addresses concerns that users may be exposed to unpatched vulnerabilities, that vendors may rush to fix flaws reported under the new policy but overlook previously reported bugs that are more severe, and that some vendors may not be able to meet the new policy.
“We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly,” Silvanovich notes.
Noting that Project Zero only reports vulnerabilities that have substantial severity and demonstrated impact, she also points out that a vulnerability’s severity affects only its impact on users, not the likelihood that attackers will discover it.
“It’s also important to acknowledge that Project Zero holds itself to high standards with regard to the reproducibility, readability, reachability, and reported security impact of the vulnerabilities we report. This policy assumes bug reports are of this quality, and it is reasonable for vendors to treat low quality-bug reports differently,” Silvanovich says.

articles.title: Como repostar Stories de outra pessoa no Instagram • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Como repostar Stories de outra pessoa no Instagram
Compartilhar stories de outra pessoa no Instagram é um recurso nativo que permite republicar conteúdos de perfis públicos na sua própria conta, mesmo quando você não é marcado
Você sabia que dá para repostar stories que não foi marcado no Instagram, desde que o perfil do autor seja público? A rede social tem uma função nativa no aplicativo para Android e iPhone para dar aquela força aos criadores e amigos.
Para compartilhar stories de outra pessoa no Instagram, basta abrir a publicação e tocar no ícone de envio para DMs. Se o autor permitir o compartilhamento externo, aparecerá a opção de “Adicionar ao story” para você republicar o conteúdo.
A seguir, o Tecnoblog te ensina o caminho para republicar um story de outra pessoa no seu perfil do Instagram.
Abra o Instagram no seu celular Android ou iPhone e toque no ícone de lupa, no menu inferior. Pesquise pelo nome do perfil que publicou o story que você deseja repostar na sua conta.
Toque na foto de perfil do usuário, exibida no canto superior esquerdo, para carregar a sequência de stories disponíveis no momento.
Com o story aberto na tela, selecione o ícone de avião de papel no canto inferior direito para ver as opções de envio de conteúdo via DM e compartilhamento do stories.
Escolha a opção “Adicionar ao story” para importar o conteúdo para o seu editor de criação, permitindo repostar o story mesmo sem ser marcado.
Se desejar, adicione texto, stickers e GIFs ao story original. Então, toque no botão de compartilhar no canto inferior direito da tela para repostar stories no Instagram.
Não dá para repostar stories do Instagram nativamente pelo navegador do PC. Essa limitação ocorre porque a Meta restringe várias ferramentas na versão web, priorizando a experiência nos aplicativos para Android e iOS.
Para republicar stories diretamente pelo PC, é necessário usar plataformas de gerenciamento de mídias sociais de terceiros, como Hootsuite ou Later. Esses softwares ajudam a contornar as restrições da versão desktop para compartilhar stories, além de organizar e programar as postagens com facilidade.
Em diversos casos, você não poderá repostar story no Instagram por restrições de privacidade definidas pelo autor original ou falhas técnicas que impedem os stories de carregar. Veja algumas situações comuns:
Não é possível repostar Stories de Amigos Próximos devido às questões de privacidade do formato. Lembrando que fazer story no Instagram para Amigos Próximos é a ação de enviar uma publicação para uma lista de pessoas selecionadas pelo dono do perfil.
Há duas formas de compartilhar stories do Instagram no Status do WhatsApp. Você pode usar a opção “Compartilhar”, tocando no ícone de três pontos dentro do seu story, para gerar um link que será publicado no app de mensagens da Meta.
A outra maneira é baixar o seu próprio story do Instagram para o telefone e publicar como um Status do WhatsApp. Assim, você consegue compartilhar a foto ou o vídeo com os elementos adicionados através da rede social.
Sim, você pode impedir outros usuários de repostar story no Instagram nas opções de privacidade da plataforma. Vá até o menu “Configurações e atividade”, toque em “Compartilhamento” e desative as chaves dos itens “Stories em que as pessoas são mencionadas” e “Compartilhamento do story”.
Esse ajuste desabilita os botões nativos de envio por DM e de republicação do story, mas tem um limite técnico. Como o Instagram não controla os recursos externos do aparelho, o bloqueio não impede que alguém faça um print ou grave a tela do post.

articles.title: Mercedes' clever new driving assist handles complex traffic like a champ
articles.text:
SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive. Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel.
While most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, and a decade later started adding active safety systems like anti-lock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineer-speak.
“Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines.
3? No, +, ++
The next step, numerically at least, should be level 3, where we move from assisted driving to partially automated driving; here the car takes over the task of driving fully under some circumstances, like heavy traffic. But that’s getting ahead of ourselves—the main developments over the past few years have been the inelegantly named “L2+” systems that combine more advanced driver monitoring with a higher degree of assistance, usually on geofenced highways.

articles.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: The industry will be 'fine’ | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom.
Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement.
Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom.
Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.
When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”
He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information.
“It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.”
OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips.
Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up.
“Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.”
Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure.
“I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.”

articles.title: Nvidia amassed $530 billion in financial guarantees to corner the AI market — supply commitments rose by nearly a quarter of a trillion dollars in a single quarter
articles.text:
Nvidia amassed $530 billion in financial guarantees to corner the AI market — supply commitments rose by nearly a quarter of a trillion dollars in a single quarter
Without a doubt, Nvidia's dominance in the AI hardware market stems not only from the capabilities of its AI accelerators and its vast software ecosystem, but also from its aggressive procurement strategy that effectively denies its rivals access to sufficient production capacity at TSMC and other contractors. The result of his deals is that supply and capacity commitments rose by almost a quarter of a trillion dollars in a single quarter, primarily due to memory procurement, according to SemiAnalysis. However, even Nvidia's former chief executive Jensen Huang had apparently begun to question the sustainability of this strategy before his departure, based on reports from The Wall Street Journal and SemiAnalysis.
Over the past several years, Nvidia has not only captured the vast majority of the AI accelerator market, but has also secured a substantial proportion of the world's production capacity for advanced logic, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and various other components required to build AI accelerators and systems, which has limited the ability of its competitors to ramp up shipments of their processors. To support the deals, Jensen Huang personally negotiated agreements with major suppliers in Taiwan and South Korea.
The massive scale of Nvidia's procurement commitments also enabled the company to secure more favorable quotes than its rivals. SemiAnalysis estimates that SK hynix could charge Nvidia between $3.00 and $3.30 per gigabit of HBM4 memory in 2027, whereas other first-tier customers, such as AMD, Amazon, Broadcom, and Google, would pay between $3.70 and $4.10 per gigabit. The analysts believe that as part of an informal arrangement between the two companies, Nvidia gives SK Group preferential access to its AI GPUs.
While Nvidia's ability to secure vast production capacities has been instrumental in its success, such commitments also carry considerable risks. At a meeting with senior executives in August, Huang reportedly expressed concerns about the massive volumes of wafers and memory that Nvidia had committed to purchase as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on the company's hardware in favor of alternative AI accelerator platforms, according to The Wall Street Journal.
In a bid to diversify its customer base and create additional demand for its products, Nvidia offered financial guarantees to emerging cloud service providers and data center developers that otherwise could not afford to procure its hardware at scale. As of the end of its fiscal second quarter, Nvidia had $530 billion in gross off-balance-sheet guarantees, up from $184 billion a quarter earlier, as well as $99 billion worth of equity investments, according to SemiAnalysis. As half a trillion dollars seems gargantuan, here is a breakdown based on a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission:
- $366 billion in future commitments (of which $279 billion was supply and capacity commitments, mainly for memory and manufacturing);
- $56 billion in additional commitments (including $36 billion in AI cloud agreements/take-or-pay arrangements and $20 billion in data-center leases expected to be reassigned);
- $108.5 billion in maximum gross exposure under guarantees (of which $105 billion was a lease/credit-support guarantee related to SB Energy’s PORTS Technology Campus in Ohio for an OpenAI affiliate, plus $3.5 billion for other AI-cloud partner land/power/shell guarantees).
The scale of such commitments raised concerns even within Nvidia. Then-CFO Colette Kress questioned the criteria used to select recipients of financial support and the potential returns on such arrangements. She also reportedly reduced Nvidia's initial financial commitment to OpenAI's massive data center project in Ohio by half before the two companies signed an agreement on August 17. The facility is expected to house some $300 billion worth of Nvidia processors.
Massive outcome?
At some point, Huang himself began to question the merits of Nvidia's aggressive financing strategy in the event of his departure, essentially calling the current interim CEO, Colette Kress, a mere 'reporting CFO' rather than an executive capable of making strategic decisions. He also expressed concerns about massive wafer and memory procurement commitments as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on Nvidia’s GPUs.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Despite questionable commitments, without Huang and his personal relationships with executives at major semiconductor companies, Nvidia may find it harder to secure preferential treatment from its suppliers. SemiAnalysis believes that customers other than Nvidia could account for over 70% of TSMC production capacity in 2028. While this could enable Nvidia’s competitors to significantly increase shipments of their AI processors, it could also affect the willingness of Taiwanese and South Korean suppliers to invest aggressively in additional production capacity without the kind of assurances that Huang used to provide.

articles.title: Si tienes un iPhone Duo, esta nueva función cambiará por completo la forma de desbloquearlo
articles.text:
El iPhone Duo se ha convertido en uno de los móviles más exitosos de la historia de Apple. El primer plegable de la compañía tuvo un gran recibimiento, aunque su diseño provocó que no contara con una de las funciones más útiles del iPhone: Face ID. La buena noticia es que Apple ha lanzado un desbloqueo facial para solucionar la carencia hasta que llegue su sucesor.
De acuerdo con TechCrunch, Apple ha lanzado un desbloqueo facial para el iPhone Duo. La nueva función estará disponible a través de la actualización de iOS 27.3 y se conoce como "face unlock". Esta característica aprovecha la cámara frontal del dispositivo para reconocer al usuario y desbloquear el móvil, pero tiene algunas limitaciones comparado con Face ID.
La principal limitante del desbloqueo facial del iPhone Duo es que solo funciona si el usuario se ha autenticado por Touch ID o código de acceso. Si es la primera vez que abres el móvil, tendrás que usar tu huella o introducir el PIN para que puedas usar tu rostro más adelante. Además, Apple ha añadido otras barreras de seguridad que te impedirán usar la cámara frontal como método de autenticación.
Las compras realizadas con Apple Pay y el acceso a las contraseñas seguirán requiriendo Touch ID. Lo mismo pasa si tu iPhone Duo permanece inactivo durante 45 minutos o más, donde necesitarás firmarte con tu huella o código antes de que el desbloqueo facial pueda utilizarse otra vez. Es por ello que Apple ha dejado claro que no es un equivalente de Face ID, sino una solución temporal a quienes extrañan este método.
¿Por qué no puedes usar el Face ID en el iPhone Duo?
El iPhone Duo no cuenta con Face ID debido a que su estructura no deja espacio suficiente para añadir el sistema TrueDepth que usa Apple en otros modelos de iPhone. Este tipo de desbloqueo requiere sensores especializados que pueden crear un mapa tridimensional del rostro, el cual se logra a través de un iluminador y un proyector que emite más de 30.000 puntos infrarrojos invisibles. El sistema también cuenta con mecanismos de comprobación para evitar el uso de fotografías o imágenes planas para engañarlo.
La ausencia de esta función ha sido una de las críticas más sonadas al plegable. Además de no ofrecer Face ID, el iPhone Duo la pone difícil para autenticarnos a través del Touch ID, ya que el móvil no siempre reconoce la huella en el primer intento. Es por ello que se implementó un tipo de desbloqueo facial que podría evitar que tengas que introducir tu clave cada que activas el móvil.
Según el periodista Mark Gurman, Apple ya está probando los primeros prototipos del iPhone Duo 2 con Face ID. Los de Cupertino no se han decidido si se integrará en el modelo de 2027 o se ofrecerá más adelante, ya que primero tendrían que mover la ubicación de la cámara frontal. La compañía también considera añadir un botón de acción similar al de los demás iPhone, aunque esto último sigue en el aire ya que un segundo rumor afirma que este botón desaparecerá de toda la línea de dispositivos en 2027.
Por el momento no hay información oficial sobre el sucesor del iPhone Duo, aunque es un hecho que Apple está trabajando en él y tendrá que solucionar dos de sus problemas más evidentes.

articles.title: Hacker behind 2022 GTA VI leaks pleads guilty
articles.text:
Arion Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ cybercrime group who leaked 90 videos of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022 and hacked other big companies, pleaded guilty on Monday, according to the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service (CPS).
Hacker behind 2022 GTA VI leaks pleads guilty
Arion Kurtaj leaked 90 videos of GTA VI years before its release.
Kurtaj, who is now 21, hacked BT/EE sometime between August and November 2021, and starting in early November of that year, the company “noted a marked increase in unauthorised SIM swaps of their customers mobile phones.” He was charged for those offenses and moved to a hotel for his “own protection” in September 2022, but “breached his bail conditions to carry out further hacks on major companies using a mobile phone, the hotel TV’s Wi-Fi and a firestick,” including hacks on Rockstar Games, Uber, and Revolut, the CPS says.
He was sentenced to life in a secure hospital in December 2023 because of his autism, but in January, Kurtaj was deemed fit for trial and moved to prison, the BBC reports.
Kurtaj is set to be sentenced on November 23rd. GTA VI will be released on November 19th.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Tratum building offline-capable banking infrastructure for physical economy - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startup Tratum is developing hardware and embedded financial infrastructure that allows banks and other regulated institutions to extend their services into places where connectivity is unreliable.
Built by YHWH Vision Ventures Technologies Ltd., which was formally incorporated in 2025, Tratum traces its origins to Nigeria’s 2023 cash scarcity crisis, when millions of people had money in their bank accounts but struggled to access or use it.
“If money is increasingly digital, why should access to that money completely depend on a functioning network, a smartphone, a remote server or a particular digital channel at the exact moment someone needs to transact?” said Segun Ademigoke, the startup’s founder and CEO.
At the heart of the ecosystem is the Tratum Node, a secure physical financial endpoint that combines secure hardware, cryptographic device identity, local transaction state and communication capabilities. Under rules set by the institution, a Node can carry out approved transactions locally, record them cryptographically, and then synchronise and reconcile with the bank’s systems once connectivity returns.
“We are not trying to become the bank, replace the central bank or compete with consumer-facing financial institutions. We are building technology that those institutions can use to extend what they already do,” Ademigoke said.
He said the startup is targeting commercial banks, central banks and monetary authorities, with potential applications in digital currency infrastructure and monetary distribution, as well as the merchants and individuals who ultimately use financial services.
Tratum faces competition from several parts of the financial technology stack, including card and POS networks, mobile money platforms, infrastructure providers such as FIS and Fiserv, and companies building offline payment and CBDC technology.
“Our competitive position is not simply “we work offline”. That would be too narrow,” said Ademigoke. “We are building a banking infrastructure layer for the physical economy.”
The startup has so far been funded through founder and family investment, along with government-assisted loan programmes. It has built and field-tested its devices, demonstrated the technology to financial institutions, and is now working towards integrating its first commercial bank into the Tratum network.
“We are not claiming millions of users or large transaction volumes yet. That would be premature,” Ademigoke said. “What we have demonstrated is that institutions are willing to engage with the technology.”
Tratum is pre-launch and pre-revenue. It plans to make money from Node hardware sales, recurring infrastructure and software fees, and transaction and settlement revenue, alongside bank integrations, APIs and licensing. Its internal model targets a selling price of around US$30 per Node and US$150 in annual recurring revenue per active Node.
The startup is currently focused on Nigeria, but its architecture is multi-currency, and it plans to expand into other African markets as regulatory approvals and institutional partnerships fall into place.
Ademigoke said the biggest challenge has been financing the move from validated technology to physical deployment, which requires funding for manufacturing, certification, inventory and integration. Tratum is now raising capital for that phase and is particularly keen to work with African investors.
“We believe Africa should not only be a market for financial technology built elsewhere. Africa can build the infrastructure itself,” he said.

articles.title: From funding with own college fees to 1,000+ beds: how oho Living won Tier-2
articles.text:
From funding with own college fees to 1,000+ beds: how oho Living won Tier-2
Started with a founder’s college fees, oho Living survived its worst year and now runs 1,032 beds across six Tier-2 cities.
Anyone who has moved to a new city for college or a first job knows the feeling. You arrive with a suitcase and an address you can barely find, and the room you are handed is bare. Nobody tells you where to buy groceries or whom to call when the geyser breaks. You figure it out alone.
In cities like Ranchi, Patna and Jaipur, the choice was usually between expensive premium housing and bare rooms with no standard at all. Students and young professionals who wanted a clean, well-run home at a fair price had nowhere to go, and landlords and young tenants rarely trusted each other.
oho Living was built to fill that gap. It now runs 1,032 beds across six cities, with one promise: to be the friend in the city for everyone who moves to one.
From listings to homes
Ritu Raj had tried to solve this once before. In college, he built GoForRooms, a website that helped students find a place to stay. It could point someone to a room, but it could not promise what living there would be like.
So when he started oho Living, paying for it with his college fees, the team chose to run the homes themselves. It began with a single property in Ranchi, run the way a friend would run it, and grew one property and one city at a time.
The model is simple. oho Living signs an agreement with a property owner, as a lease, a revenue share or a franchise, and takes full responsibility for the resident. The owner no longer manages tenants, and the resident no longer deals with an unpredictable landlord.
The founders
Ritu, now Co-founder and CBO, leads sales and growth. Saurabh Kumar, Co-founder and CEO, owns strategy, brand and fundraising; at 25, he already has more than a decade of startup-building behind him, including a social media community of over 13 million followers. Prakhar Minocha, Co-founder and COO, runs the homes and the teams behind them, drawing on more than nine years in real estate, including a villa rental business and a hotel on Airbnb.
The simplest idea in the room
In 2021, Jharkhand Angels gathered startups from across the state at one event. Most were pitching food delivery, e-commerce, job platforms, even VR. oho Living was solving the plainest problem in the room: helping people find a good place to live.
Then the founders said they wanted to serve 1 crore people, starting from Ranchi. Most of the room laughed. One investor laughed too, then caught himself asking: why not?
The worst year
The early years were a grind. Founders in their early twenties had to convince landlords and institutions to take them seriously, and running homes meant something broke almost every day. The team answered with structure, writing SOPs and playbooks while the company was still small.
That did not prevent 2023, the founders' lowest point. The business had split into two parts, and they could not see the next step. Jharkhand Angels stepped in as an adviser and helped restructure the company.
The bet due diligence said no to
By December 2024, oho Living was steadier, but revenue was still small. Saurabh sat down with the investor and laid out his plan to go big. This time, the vision landed.
Due diligence said no. Jharkhand Angels invested anyway, backing the founders and the Tier-2 thesis over the numbers. The money came in by July 2025.
In the year that followed, monthly revenue rose about 25 times, from roughly ₹2.5 lakh to around ₹50 lakh. Homes went from average to genuinely good, the premium Signature brand launched, a sixth city was added, and EBITDA began to look predictable.
As the investor put it, everyone now calls Tier-2 India the big bet. These founders saw it years earlier.
A Community Manager, not a property manager
For the founders, a resident's experience does not end at the door of their room. Community forms when people feel safe and seen, so every home has a Community Manager instead of a property manager.
Three brands serve three kinds of newcomer: Signature for premium full buildings, Urban for working professionals, and LiveliHood for students, run with education partners including Motion, PhysicsWallah and Allen. Matured properties run at around 95% occupancy.
Growing on partners' money
oho Living's recent growth has come without spending its own capital on property. In Patna, coaching institutes fund student residences and send the students, while oho Living runs them; 512 beds there earned about ₹27 lakh a month from day one. In Jaipur, landlords pay for the fit-out and oho Living pays a fixed rent. In Agra, landlords furnish the flats and share the revenue.
The five deals signed this quarter, including a franchise in progress with Bhubaneswar's Shaswat Group, added 658 beds and ₹57.3 lakh in monthly revenue capacity.
What comes next
The company plans to reach 2,134 beds by March 2027, led by Patna, Jaipur and Bhubaneswar. At 80% occupancy, that would mean about ₹1.49 crore in monthly revenue. Urban is set to become the largest brand as more young professionals move to Tier-2 cities for work.
Beyond that, Vision 2030 is 100,000 beds across every state in India, with a website that lets anyone find a home and move in within 10 minutes.
And the number that made a room laugh in 2021 has not shrunk. Saurabh still talks about serving 1 crore people.
oho Living did not start perfect. In the founders' words, it started honest: a real problem, a small team and a commitment to figure it out along the way. For anyone arriving in a new city with a suitcase and an address they can barely find, that is the point.

articles.title: Piratage de La Poste : la police lance une enquête pour retrouver les pirates
articles.text:
La justice vient de se saisir de l’affaire Maileva. Vingt-quatre heures après les révélations de La Poste, le parquet de Paris a confirmé l’ouverture d’une enquête sur la cyberattaque à l’AFP. Les investigations concernent une « atteinte à un système de traitement automatisé de données ».
À lire aussi : Fuites de données – la France sort du top 3 mondial, mais 18 comptes sont encore piratés chaque minute
« Une telle fuite ne s’est pas faite en un clic »
Sans surprise, l’enquête a été confiée à la Brigade de lutte contre la cybercriminalité (BL2C), un service d’enquête spécialisé de la police. C’est déjà cette unité qui s’est occupée de l’enquête sur le piratage du ministère, survenu en décembre 2025, le hack de la Fédération française de tir, ou la cyberattaque à l’encontre d’Intermarché.
Plusieurs de ces investigations se sont soldées par des arrestations. Un hacker de 22 ans a été interpellé à la fin de l’année dernière, à Limoges. Quelques semaines plus tard, un pirate de 18 ans arrêté en Seine-Saint-Denis en janvier 2026. En avril, « HexDex », un hacker de 22 ans soupçonné du piratage de nombreuses fédérations sportives, a été arrêté en Vendée.
De son côté, Thomas Lazzaroni, l’auteur de l’enquête qui a révélé l’attaque avant la Poste, pointe des failles de sécurité dans les systèmes du groupe. Selon lui, l’offensive n’a pas été orchestrée par une bande d’adolescents.
« Vingt-deux millions de personnes, c’est énorme. Une telle fuite ne s’est pas faite en un clic : ça a dû prendre des heures. Normalement, un bon système aurait dû notifier cette intrusion. Ça n’a pas été le cas », estime-t-il auprès de nos confréres de France 3 Hauts-de-France, ajoutant qu’on est « loin d’ados comme ça avait été le cas avec l’État ».
Le chercheur penche plutôt pour une organisation structurée, sans évoquer le nom d’une puissance étrangère. Pour rappel, La Poste a révélé que l’attaque s’est soldée par le vol des coordonnées de 22 millions de personnes, à savoir leur prénom, leur nom et leur adresse postale. Les victimes ne sont pas les clients de Maileva, mais les destinataires des courriers envoyés par des entreprises clientes, qui utilisent les services de la filiale.
À lire aussi : Après les frigos des supermarchés, l’Europe s’inquiète des cyberattaques contre « les appareils ménagers »
« Une situation sensible »
Parmi les entreprises touchées, on trouve un bailleur social des Hauts-de-France, qui n’a pas voulu décliner son identité. Le bailleur assure faire face à « une situation sensible » et que c’est « la première fois » que cela lui arrive. Le bailleur ignore combien de ses locataires sont concernés.
« On ne sait pas si c’est un ou 300 clients concernés. Peut-être qu’il n’y a personne », juge le bailleur social.
Les notifications envoyées aux victimes arrivent actuellement au compte-gouttes. Maileva doit seulement prévenir tous ses clients. C’est ensuite à eux d’informer ensuite les personnes concernées de la fuite, actuellement très difficile à circonscrire. En attendant, méfiez-vous de tout courrier, e-mail ou SMS inattendu qui prétend provenir d’un hôpital, d’un bailleur ou encore d’un service de recommandé.

articles.title: California sues OpenAI over AI agents escaping sandboxes, hacking firms
articles.text:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company knowingly continued testing advanced artificial intelligence models despite repeated security failures that allowed autonomous AI agents to escape isolated environments and launch cyberattacks against real-world organizations.
The lawsuit claims OpenAI misled the public about its cybersecurity safeguards and failed to adequately monitor increasingly advanced AI cybersecurity models, resulting in more than 80 incidents in which the company lost control of its agents during testing.
The legal action follows a July security incident where hundreds of OpenAI-powered agents escaped a controlled testing environment and hacked Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence platform, compromising production infrastructure and stealing internal credentials.
California says the Hugging Face attack resulted from OpenAI repeatedly focusing on experimental AI testing without ensuring adequate safeguards were in place.
"The Hugging Face cyberattack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability," the complaint reads.
The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI continued testing increasingly capable AI agents despite knowing its sandbox environments could be bypassed, potentially exposing third-party systems to unauthorized activity.
"In truth, OpenAI failed to comply with its own internal policies and consistently and aggressively moved forward with testing and experiments even in the face of evidence that its cybersecurity safeguards were insufficient to contain the highly advanced models it was developing," the lawsuit continues.
During the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI models exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in JFrog Artifactory to break out of their isolated testing environment and access the internet.
The attack lasted more than two days, with nearly 700 autonomous agents coordinating through an unauthorized message board to plan the attack on Hugging Face's production systems while attempting to steal answers to a cybersecurity benchmark.
The California complaint alleges that OpenAI ignored or missed warning signs in the weeks leading up to the incident, including evidence that agents had already escaped their testing environments and were abusing third-party services and platforms.
It also claims that OpenAI's agents subsequently targeted software repositories, informational websites, and foreign government databases containing sensitive health information. In another incident, experimental agents allegedly compromised OpenAI's own internal infrastructure and obtained administrator-level access to critical systems.
According to the complaint, OpenAI has acknowledged more than 80 instances of losing control of autonomous agents during testing but publicly disclosed only 27 incidents.
The lawsuit follows a subpoena issued by Bonta's office in September, with California claiming that OpenAI failed to provide sufficient information about the incidents and instead supplied limited documentation and descriptions of previously disclosed attacks.
The state is pursuing claims under California's Unfair Competition Law and public nuisance laws, seeking court orders requiring stronger safeguards, civil penalties, and other relief.
The rise of autonomous AI attacks
The lawsuit comes amid growing concerns about increasingly capable AI models escaping controlled cybersecurity evaluations and attacking organizations outside their intended testing environments.
These autonomous attacks are not limited to OpenAI agents, with other AI platforms disclosing similar incidents in the past.
In July, Anthropic disclosed that its Claude models had breached production systems at three organizations during cybersecurity evaluations. One model created and uploaded a malicious Python package to the public PyPI repository, where it was downloaded and executed on 15 real systems.
This led Anthropic to remove internet access from all internal AI model evaluations following additional incidents involving unauthorized activity against government websites and other external systems.
Google also confirmed to The Wall Street Journal in September that its Gemini AI model had accessed the internet and hacked three companies during cybersecurity testing conducted in May.
California's lawsuit argues that OpenAI's failure to address these risks adequately has exposed organizations and the public to unnecessary cybersecurity threats, even as it told customers that its AI development practices were safe.
