articles.title: Delivery drones are coming. For some with PTSD, that's a terrifying prospect.
articles.text:
In August, Amazon announced plans to expand its Prime Air delivery drone program to “nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026.” Combined with similar uncrewed aerial delivery programs from DoorDash and Zipline (in partnership with Uber and Walmart), the expansion suggests that flying robots dropping their payloads onto suburban lawns will soon be commonplace.
For many people, delivery drones will be little more than a novelty, occasionally good for a laugh when one does something ridiculous. For others, though, their growing use could be a nightmare. As the instant delivery industry clears the last FAA hurdles to rapid deliveries beyond an operator’s line of sight, an increasing number of people worldwide are living with post-traumatic stress disorder or other anxiety-related disorders triggered by drones.
The use of all manner of weaponized drones in the ongoing war in Ukraine and in Israeli attacks on Lebanon and Gaza has already produced an epidemic of what some mental health professionals have dubbed “dronophobia.” And while relatively few US troops have been targeted by drones flown by Iran, ISIS, and Iran-backed militias throughout the Middle East, even those who have not directly been attacked may experience anxiety simply because of the ample video footage of attacks circulating in news and social media.
Combined with broader anxiety about surveillance technologies, artificial intelligence, and things generally falling from the sky, the resulting hypervigilance could result in some unintended deliveries from those Prime Air flying robots.
Heralds of destruction
The aftermath of an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City on October 9, 2023, leaving widespread destruction in the Rimal area.
The aftermath of an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City on October 9, 2023, leaving widespread destruction in the Rimal area.
Credit:
CC BY-SA 3.0
Drones have been a part of the battlefield in some form since the late 1980s, when the Israeli Defense Forces began using them. From the beginning, they have had a psychological impact on both those in the sights of drone operators and the operators themselves.
The first military use of drones was for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. I witnessed the development of naval drone operations aboard USS Iowa in 1986 and 1987, and for many on the ship at the time, the drones were a curiosity—or, at worst, an annoyance. Our crews spent hours standing by a boat, ready to retrieve crashed drones from the water. But we were helping develop a capability that would eventually lead to Iraqi troops surrendering to the USS Wisconsin‘s drone during the Gulf War. Back then, drones were merely heralds of destruction, acting as forward observers for the Air Force ordnance fired or launched from elsewhere.
Iraqi troops on Faylaka Island associated the Pioneer RPV with the bombardment they had just experienced from the USS Missouri. When the Wisconsin’s drone flew in to assess the damage, their morale was broken.
Over southern Lebanon, the same kinds of drones were part of what amounted, for some residents, to sonic psychological warfare—the hum of lawnmower-like engines overhead was a reminder of constant surveillance and the ever-present threat of artillery or air strikes. The resulting anxiety intensified as drones began carrying their own weapons and “loitering munitions,” one-way drones designed to fly into targets and explode.
Dronophobia
Israel’s continued fight against Hezbollah in Lebanon, along with the US wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, accelerated the evolution of drone warfare and expanded the population experiencing its psychological effects. A Stanford Law study in 2012 of the impact of US drones in Pakistan (PDF) highlighted how drones were destroying the fabric of communities in northwest Pakistan:
Drones hover twenty-four hours a day over communities in northwest Pakistan, striking homes, vehicles, and public spaces without warning. Their presence terrorizes men, women, and children, giving rise to anxiety and psychological trauma among civilian communities. Those living under drones have to face the constant worry that a deadly strike may be fired at any moment and the knowledge that they are powerless to protect themselves.
That experience has been repeated and amplified in current conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Ukraine. A team of US and Ukrainian psychiatrists has reported that Ukrainian military personnel and civilians who have experienced a drone attack, particularly those injured in one, “are at heightened risk for developing persistent psychological symptoms, a vulnerability intensified by the ongoing threat of repeated attacks.”
Those symptoms—a “unique hypervigilance behavior with corresponding hyperarousal and avoidance behaviors”—are now referred to by some Ukrainian doctors as “dronophobia.”
“The distinct hum of an approaching drone, often likened to the swarming of hornets, has itself become a psychological weapon,” noted the team led by Dr. Joseph L. Bonvie of Massachusetts General Hospital. “The escalating pitch as a drone draws near elicits fear and helplessness even before an attack.”
Similar symptoms have been reported in women and children in Gaza, where Israeli drone strikes have been persistent. In consultations with 19 patients in Gaza, “all patients reported an intense phobic reaction to the acoustic signature of drones (the ‘zannana’), associated with imminent bombing and death, manifesting as full-blown panic attacks,” wrote Dr. Mohammad Abu Slaih, a Jordanian psychiatrist, in an article for European Psychiatry. “Three children developed a specific fear of looking at the sky. “
The Iranian drone attacks on Gulf states, while hardly comparable to what Gaza has endured, have had a broad impact on civilians in the United Arab Emirates and other countries in the region, disrupting sleep, causing fatigue, and fueling anticipatory anxiety as people wait for the next drone to strike.
That anxiety is common across populations exposed to drone warfare. The US Army Training and Doctrine Command (TRADOC) has compared drones’ potential to induce PTSD to the “shell shock” of World War I and the “battle fatigue” of World War II, noting that the “fear and stress from (the sound of) near-persistent drone presence creates anticipatory anxiety… Fears can persist beyond the drone’s presence, enhancing a soldier’s anxiety even when out of harm’s way.”
An RQ-2 Pioneer UAV, developed jointly by AAI Corporation and Israel Aircraft Industries.
An RQ-2 Pioneer UAV, developed jointly by AAI Corporation and Israel Aircraft Industries.
Credit:
US Navy
The use of drone video by both Russia and Ukraine as a psychological warfare tool extends the impact of drones beyond those who experience attacks firsthand. Footage of attacks on individual soldiers has been posted on social media to spread anxiety among opposing forces, sometimes going viral and exposing thousands of other people to the attacks. Ukrainian military units often publish first-person-view videos of drones chasing down Russian soldiers, complete with horror-film-styled soundtracks.
According to Neda Gould, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, that aspect sets drone-induced PTSD apart from other types of the disorder. In an interview with Psychiatry Online, Gould said social media could amplify trauma because “not only does the soldier have to grapple with the PTSD-related consequences of the attack itself, but they may also relive the experience in a way that is completely out of their control,” especially when social media comments express support for the attacks.
Reversal of misfortune
The US military has grappled with drone-induced PTSD and other mental health symptoms over the past 15 years. The first signs of stress for American troops, however, came from drone operators themselves.
In 2014, a team of researchers led by a US Air Force psychologist found that 4.3 percent of Air Force drone operators displayed “a pattern of symptoms of moderate to extreme level of severity” associated with PTSD. More recent studies have found that drone operators are just as likely to experience PTSD symptoms as members of aircrews deployed to war zones. Differences in how crews operate between manned combat aircraft and unmanned systems crews may even put drone operators at greater risk of psychological impact.
According to the latter study:
Drone missions generally involve days or weeks of surveillance of targets before launching strikes
Operators have a constant feed of imagery and radio communications from the area of operations for long periods, including imagery of their targets
Operators do not have transit time to and from the area of operation and may not experience “the adrenaline rush or thrill of accomplishing the mission”
Since operators have more time to study their targets, errors are not as easily shrugged off
Unlike their counterparts sitting in a pilot seat aboard a warplane, drone operators continue observation after the strikes to assess the extent of damage and are more likely to be exposed to disturbing imagery of the death and destruction resulting from their handwork
The dual psychological impact of drone warfare was aptly demonstrated by Killbox, a video artwork and “game” that presents two perspectives: those of a drone operator and a child on the ground. Playing it leaves many people deeply saddened, offering a glimpse of the moral injury some drone operators have experienced after their missions.
US troops are no longer just the ones behind the screens, however. Beginning with operations against ISIS, US troops have faced increasingly sophisticated drone warfare, starting with grenades dropped by ISIS-operated consumer quadcopter drones in 2017. Since then, Iranian-built drones, some based on reverse-engineered technology from downed US drones, have been used against US troops and ships by Iran and Iranian-backed militias in Yemen and Iraq. Among these is the Shahed, a long-range attack drone that Iran has sold in large numbers to Russia for its war on Ukraine.
Remains of a Shahed 136 drone at an exhibition showing missiles and drones Russia used to attack Kyiv, Ukraine.
Remains of a Shahed 136 drone at an exhibition showing missiles and drones Russia used to attack Kyiv, Ukraine.
Credit:
Oleksii Samsonov/Global Images Ukraine/Getty Images
The US Army TRADOC report also recognized that the psychological effects of drone attacks can reach further than those wounded in attacks, and even beyond the units that encounter them, saying:
Drones amplify the uncertainties of war because rear areas are less secure as long-range drones extend danger zones beyond that of artillery and rockets. The feeling of nowhere being safe exacerbates anxiety even when drones are not present.
While little public data is available on drone-induced PTSD among US veterans, evidence suggests that drones could also affect people with PTSD stemming from other kinds of trauma. The sound of a drone, its shadow, a glimpse of one in peripheral vision, or other stimuli from drones could trigger hypervigilance because of their unexpectedness, their similarity to other triggering stimuli, or a range of other factors.
Even for those who have not experienced drone attacks, the presence of an uncrewed aircraft can cause anxiety. Drones purportedly operated by the Department of Homeland Security in Minneapolis earlier this year appeared to be used not just for surveillance of targets of Immigration and Customs Enforcement but also to intimidate individuals who had been tracking ICE activity.
The expanding use of drones by law enforcement organizations in the US as part of “drone first responder” programs has exposed an increasing number of Americans to drone surveillance, with over 1,000 agencies applying for FAA waivers for drone operations as of February 2026, based on data from the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Combined with news reports about drone attacks and foreign governments’ use of drones, the disquiet of drone propeller noises and blinking lights in the sky has already created a War of the Worldslevel of dronophobia.
Drones and rumors of drones
Over the past two years, several drone incidents have been linked, or suspected of being linked, to state-actor espionage, with a surge in reports in November and December of 2024. Three occurred in Southern California, including a drone flyover of Vandenberg Air Force Base as a National Reconnaissance Office payload was being loaded ont0 a SpaceX rocket. A Chinese national was charged in the case and arrested while attempting to leave the country. Other cases in the US were officially downplayed as posing no security threat.
In November 2024, incidents in the UK centered on multiple air bases used by the US, including incursions near RAF Fairford, the base recently allegedly targeted in a plot that the British government attributed to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Similar incursions occurred in Germany.
Many of these sightings turned out to be crewed aircraft or helicopters, toy drones, or, in very few cases, authorized commercial drone flights. Former Maryland Governor Larry Hogan even reported seeing dozens of large drones above his house, only for others to quickly point out that the objects were actually the constellation Orion.
The unfriendly skies
PTSD is a treatable condition, and coping strategies can help people manage triggers. But severe PTSD can be extremely debilitating, and research into the effects of drones on PTSD remains limited. It’s still unclear how well survivors of drone attacks will be able to process the fears and traumatic memories associated with drones, especially if the aircraft become a pervasive part of daily life.
I, for one, won’t be placing any Prime Air orders anytime soon.

articles.title: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab
articles.text:
At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers.
The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems, each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks.
A Supercomputing Lab on Any Desk
The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work.
It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up.
At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 20TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1.
With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises.
The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems.
The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures.
Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control.
What Researchers Can Do With It
The kit opens up new possibilities for researchers.
Researchers can explore agent-assisted workflows that prepare simulation inputs, launch runs and summarize results, while the scientists validate the setup and conclusions.
Researchers can also train AI models that approximate slow simulations, then use them to refine wing designs toward minimum drag.
Before committing supercomputer time, a team can narrow a 10-million-cell simulation to the 50-500 dimensions that matter.
- Kvantify is using NVIDIA cuQuantum, and reports running tensor-network simulations of quantum-chemistry circuits with up to 70 qubits and 975 gates on a single DGX Spark, benchmarking circuits generated for penicillin ground-state energy calculations.
- CYRAN AI, an IIT Delhi spin-out, uses DGX Spark and its PixelFlux library to accelerate JPEG 2000 decoding for large satellite images, supporting local geospatial analysis.
- OpenFold shows how researchers can fine-tune OpenFold3 on NVIDIA DGX Spark to improve protein-ligand structure predictions for drug discovery.
- The Rubin Lab at IGI at University of California, Berkeley is using a DGX Spark and NVIDIA Evo 2 model to predict bacterial traits directly from genome sequences by comparing embeddings from genomic and protein language models against the classical baselines. With no 11-hour cluster queue times, results arrived 15x sooner on DGX Spark.
- The Hartwig Group at UC Berkeley is using a DGX Spark to perform LoRA fine-tuning on the Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B model for chemistry machine learning, training a prediction head on experimental values. By running locally on the Spark using NVFP4 quantization, the lab successfully fit a 120B-class model on a single device and bypassed multi-day cluster queue times, allowing them to run continuous eight- to 24-hour training fits back-to-back.
Where to Find the Kit
The developer kit is on display at SC26 and available for sale. DGX Spark products and cables can be purchased from top OEM partners and are also available through NVIDIA Marketplace.
Partners include Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, H3C, HP, Lenovo, MSI and xFusion.
An NVIDIA playbook for building and running the NVIDIA HPC SDK, a software development kit for scientific computing, is coming soon. Once available, it will give scientists and researchers a local platform to develop multi-node GPU applications, explore FP32 and mixed-precision algorithms and run molecular dynamics and materials simulations using LAMMPS with Kokkos before scaling to data center systems.
Learn more about NVIDIA DGX Spark.
Subscribe to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter. Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook.
See notice regarding software product information.

articles.title: FBI says Artex AI open source hacking tool used to breach networks in 'under three hours' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.
In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory, the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.
Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that make it far more difficult for human defenders to keep up.
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”
The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.
Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.
The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.
The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.
The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.
A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim.
Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.
“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer, Arve Kjoelen.
A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.
After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.
It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.
Updated with response from Barracuda.

articles.title: Elon Musk quer fundir Tesla e SpaceX, mas as empresas já trabalham juntas
articles.text:
A possível fusão entre Tesla e SpaceX pode formalizar relação que já existe há anos. As empresas de Elon Musk compartilham engenheiros, executivos, tecnologias e projetos estratégicos, em integração que aproxima os negócios de carros elétricos, foguetes, inteligência artificial (IA) e infraestrutura de computação.
Uma reportagem do The New York Times, baseada em entrevistas com mais de uma dúzia de funcionários atuais e antigos, descreve como Musk vem movimentando profissionais entre as companhias e incentivando iniciativas conjuntas. Os relatos indicam que a colaboração vai muito além de contratos comerciais e já envolve equipes e operações das duas empresas.
O bilionário agora pretende unir os negócios em um conglomerado que poderia ultrapassar US$ 3 trilhões (cerca de R$ 16 trilhões) em valor de mercado. A operação, porém, ainda depende da aprovação de comitês independentes e dos acionistas das duas companhias.
Tesla e SpaceX já compartilham funcionários e projetos
- Um dos exemplos mais curiosos dessa aproximação é o desenvolvimento de um carro esportivo capaz de realizar manobras aéreas. Há quase dez anos, Musk pediu à equipe de design da Tesla que desenvolvesse um veículo voador. Para ajudar no projeto, engenheiros da SpaceX foram deslocados temporariamente para trabalhar no automóvel;
- Liderado por Bill Riley, executivo da empresa de foguetes, o grupo adaptou um Tesla Roadster com propulsores de gás frio, tecnologia normalmente utilizada em espaçonaves. Neste ano, o veículo passou por testes nas instalações de lançamento e testes de foguetes da SpaceX, no Texas (EUA);
- Em outubro, um Roadster sem motorista realizou um salto mortal no ar depois de ser lançado de uma rampa com mais de 18 metros de altura. Durante a demonstração, Musk exaltou a colaboração entre o que chamou de as duas melhores empresas do mundo em seus respectivos setores;
- O compartilhamento de profissionais também acontece em cargos estratégicos. Charlie Kuehmann, por exemplo, ocupa a vice-presidência de engenharia de materiais das duas companhias desde 2015;
- Outro caso é o de Ashok Elluswamy, vice-presidente de IA da Tesla e responsável por áreas, como o software de direção autônoma e a robótica humanoide. Neste ano, ele também passou a trabalhar com a unidade de IA da SpaceX, segundo pessoas familiarizadas com suas atividades;
- Dados da empresa de inteligência Live Data Technologies mostram que aproximadamente um em cada 22 funcionários da SpaceX trabalhou anteriormente na Tesla. A fabricante de veículos elétricos é a maior fonte de novas contratações da companhia de foguetes, e o ritmo de recrutamento de profissionais vindos da Tesla mais que dobrou neste ano.
Engenheiros da Tesla ajudaram a construir data center da xAI
A integração também alcançou os negócios de IA de Musk. Em 2023, o empresário fundou a xAI para competir com empresas, como a OpenAI. Pouco depois, a startup transformou uma antiga fábrica em Memphis (EUA), em enorme data center chamado Colossus, destinado a sustentar o chatbot Grok.
Engenheiros da Tesla ajudaram a construir a instalação em apenas 122 dias. Parte dos profissionais veio da equipe responsável pelo data center de IA da fabricante no Texas, utilizado para desenvolver tecnologias de direção autônoma. Outros trabalhavam no Dojo, supercomputador da Tesla criado para competir com soluções da Nvidia.
Documentos internos consultados pelo Times também mostram que, na primavera de 2025, dois engenheiros da equipe Dojo trabalhavam simultaneamente para a Tesla e a xAI. Um deles, Dan Rowland, chegou a liderar a equipe de data centers da startup antes de deixar a empresa, em agosto.
As instalações construídas pela xAI posteriormente responderam por US$ 506 milhões (cerca de R$ 2,7 bilhões) em compras de baterias da Tesla.
Neste ano, Musk também transferiu para a equipe de Autopilot da Tesla um projeto da xAI voltado ao desenvolvimento de um agente de IA capaz de substituir parte das atividades de trabalhadores de escritório. A ferramenta, inicialmente chamada Digital Optimus, recebeu profissionais da startup e passou a integrar os projetos da fabricante de veículos.
Musk afirmou que a iniciativa faz parte da parceria de US$ 2 bilhões (aproximadamente R$ 10,7 bilhões) entre Tesla e xAI, posteriormente rebatizada de SpaceXSI.
Leia mais:
- Musk apostou (quase) meio bilhão e perdeu: o que vem agora para Tesla e SpaceX
- SpaceX pode anunciar fusão com a Tesla em dezembro, diz reportagem
- Elon Musk revela planos para versão do Starship ainda maior
Empresas também compartilham tecnologias e investimentos
A aproximação não se limita ao intercâmbio de funcionários. A Tesla incorporou produtos e serviços ligados ao universo de Musk, como o chatbot Grok em seus veículos e a integração planejada do serviço de internet via satélite Starlink.
Em janeiro, a fabricante anunciou investimento de US$ 2 bilhões (cerca de R$ 10,7 bilhões) na xAI, como parte de parceria mais ampla entre as empresas.
Já o prospecto da abertura de capital da SpaceX revelou que a companhia comprou aproximadamente US$ 890 milhões (cerca de R$ 4,8 bilhões) em produtos da Tesla desde 2023. Entre os itens estão picapes Cybertruck e baterias Megapack, utilizadas para fornecer energia aos data centers.
As companhias também compartilham jatos particulares. Além disso, em março, Tesla e SpaceX anunciaram um plano de investimento conjunto de US$ 16,8 bilhões (aproximadamente R$ 90 bilhões) em fábrica de semicondutores no Texas (EUA).
A instalação deverá produzir chips para os sistemas de IA da SpaceX e para os projetos de robótica e veículos autônomos da Tesla. Desde o anúncio, dezenas de engenheiros da empresa espacial passaram a aparecer nos organogramas internos da fabricante de automóveis.
Fusão ainda não é certeza, diz Musk
A consolidação dos negócios de Musk ganhou velocidade nos últimos anos. Em fevereiro, a xAI foi incorporada à SpaceX, levando engenheiros da companhia espacial para projetos da startup, incluindo a expansão de data centers e uma reorganização interna. Antes disso, a empresa de IA já havia sido fundida com o X.
A SpaceX, que abriu capital em junho, está avaliada em US$ 1,89 trilhão (cerca de R$ 10,1 trilhões). A Tesla, por sua vez, tem valor de mercado estimado em US$ 1,54 trilhão (aproximadamente R$ 8,2 trilhões).
Uma união entre as duas companhias concentraria em única estrutura negócios de veículos elétricos, energia solar, foguetes, satélites, IA e data centers. O conglomerado também reuniria uma fabricante de automóveis e uma empresa com contratos governamentais e planos ambiciosos de levar astronautas a Marte.
Apesar de defender que as atividades das companhias têm sinergias e que a fusão seria uma boa ideia, Musk evita tratar o negócio como certo. Em conversa com investidores no mês passado, ele afirmou que seria exagerado considerar a operação uma certeza.
O empresário também disse que não participará das discussões dos comitês especiais responsáveis por avaliar a transação, comparando a decisão a “dançar sapateado em um campo minado”.
A fusão precisará passar pela análise de comitês independentes de cada empresa e receber o aval dos acionistas. Representantes da Tesla e da SpaceX não responderam aos pedidos de comentário do NYT.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Los Samsung Galaxy S28 podrían recuperar una función de cámara que el iPhone 18 Pro volvió a poner de moda
articles.text:
Los Samsung Galaxy S27 todavía no se lanzaron, pero los rumores sobre sus sucesores no se están haciendo esperar. De acuerdo con un conocido filtrador, el fabricante coreano planea un importante cambio en la cámara de los Galaxy S28 Pro y Ultra. Esto implicaría la reintroducción de una tecnología con la que la compañía ya ha experimentado, pero que en el último tiempo se ha vuelto a poner de modo. Nos referimos a la apertura variable, por supuesto.
El leaker Yogesh Brar, quien suele publicar información confiable sobre móviles que todavía no se lanzaron, indicó que Samsung estaría analizando la posibilidad de dotar a los Galaxy S28 Pro y S28 Ultra de apertura variable. El susodicho no ha brindado más detalles respecto de este tema, aunque el dato no es descabellado si consideramos que Apple hizo bastante alarde de esta característica con su implementación en los iPhone 18 Pro y Pro Max.
Brar incluso menciona que los Galaxy S28 más premium no serían los únicos que adoptarían la apertura variable. Pese a no hacer menciones puntuales, es lógico pensar que es una referencia a los fabricantes chinos. Después de todo, es bastante normal que los móviles que llegan desde el gigante asiático copien las características de diseño y las funciones que más destacan de los iPhone de última generación.
Samsung reintroduciría la apertura variable en los Galaxy S28 Pro y Ultra
Si te preguntas por qué la apertura variable podría llegar con los Galaxy S28 Pro y Ultra, y no con los Galaxy S27 que se presentarán el próximo año, habría varias explicaciones. En agosto pasado, antes de que se anunciaran los iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max, SamMobile publicó que los buques insignia coreanos de 2027 no traerían esta característica. Esto se debería a que los componentes actuales ocuparían más espacio, serían más caros y no darían una mejora sustancial en la calidad de imagen.
Con un año más para desarrollar esta característica, Samsung podría lograr avances suficientes para reducir los costes y lograr que sea una actualización que merezca la pena y no un simple gimmick. Ya veremos si esto es realmente así, considerando que los Galaxy S28 llegarán recién en la primera parte de 2028. Claro que a la firma coreana ya se le hizo costumbre que sus dispositivos se filtren con bastante antelación, así que no habría que extrañarse si lo mismo sucede con estos. De ocurrir, seguro nos enteraremos de la adopción o no de la apertura variable con anticipación.
Samsung usó apertura variable en sus móviles en los Galaxy S9 y S10 que se lanzaron en 2018 y 2019, respectivamente. La compañía introdujo un sistema que permitía seleccionar entre dos aperturas fijas mediante un sistema mecánico. Y si bien fue una implementación bastante rudimentaria en comparación con la que ha llegado ahora con los iPhone 18 Pro, fue todo un avance para la época.

articles.title: Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him
articles.text:
Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO.
Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him
David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other big names in tech are raising questions about the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation.
At the center of this theory is the reporting from The New York Times that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy. US agencies haven’t confirmed whether this is the case, and President Donald Trump claims he was unaware of any spy allegations. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang set off the events that led to his resignation; subsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees at Nvidia, including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were funneling chips to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based company, according to Bloomberg.
David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The New York Times’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN, which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying: “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.”
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney said, “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.”
SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole.
More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter, calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”

articles.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
articles.text:
The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
Supporters are signing a petition to reinstate Huang. But findings on Nvidia chips in China and a new Commerce rule are threatening open-source AI’s reputation and progress regardless.
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.
These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).
Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.
But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.
On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.
It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.
But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.
It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.
What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.
But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.
The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

articles.title: NASA-Mission Voyager 1: Das Warten auf ein Signal aus der Unendlichkeit
articles.text:
Voyager 1 ist bald einen Lichttag von der Erde entfernt: So läuft die Kommunikation mit der Nasa-Sonde
Seit 49 Jahren schwebt die Raumsonde Voyager 1 durchs Weltall. Trotz ihrer alten Tage ist die Sonde noch teilweise funktionsfähig. Und schon bald wird sie einen Meilenstein erreichen, den zuvor noch kein anderes menschengemachtes Objekt im Weltall erreichen konnte.
Voyager 1 erreicht historische Lichttag-Distanz
Die Raumsonde wird als erstes einen Lichttag von der Erde entfernt sein. Dies entspricht etwa 25,9 Milliarden Kilometern. Wie das Wort „Lichttag“ schon sagt: Das Licht, das von einem Objekt in dieser Distanz ausgestrahlt wird, benötigt 24 Stunden, um die Erde zu erreichen. Die Nasa hat den Moment, an dem Voyager 1 einen Lichttag von der Erde entfernt sein wird, schon exakt berechnet. Demnach ist es am 18. November um 5:16 Uhr US-Ostküstenzeit so weit. Zu diesem Zeitpunkt wird die Distanz der Sonde zur Erde exakt 25.902.068.356 Kilometer betragen.
Ein Radiosignal, das die Kontrollstation auf der Erde in Richtung Voyager abschickt, ist dann ebenfalls einen ganzen Tag unterwegs. Das sorgt für massive Delays in der Kommunikation. „Wenn man ‚Voyager ‚Hallo‘ sagen will, schickt man seine Nachricht ab, geht nach Hause und wartet zwei Tage, bis man endlich eine Antwort bekommt“, sagte Suzanne Dodd vom Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) der Nasa in der Mitteilung.
Voyager 1 reagierte zweimal nicht auf Kontaktversuche
Erst kürzlich kam es zu einem Zwischenfall, der den Meilenstein fast verhindert hätte. Das Funk- und Kommunikationsnetzwerk der Nasa hatte am 18. und 19. Oktober Voyager 1 kontaktiert. Doch die Raumsonde blieb bei beiden Kontaktversuchen stumm. Wie die US-Raumfahrtbehörde kürzlich bekannt gab, löste sich das Problem aber von selbst. Am 20. Oktober meldete sich Voyager zurück. Seitdem ist die Kommunikation stabil.
Mittlerweile haben Nasa-Ingenieur:innen auch die Ursache herausgefunden. Eine Gruppe von Triebwerken der Voyager 1 ging unerwartet offline. Das System schaltete dann automatisch eine Backup-Gruppe hinzu. Um diesen Wechsel fehlerfrei durchzuführen, begibt sich das System in eine Art abgesicherten Modus und pausiert bis zur Umsetzung alle anderen Funktionen.
Fast 50 Jahre im All: Voyager 1 trotzt dem Zahn der Zeit
Voyager 1 startete am 5. September 1977 von Cape Canaveral aus. Seitdem bewegt sie sich mit einer Geschwindigkeit von über 60.000 Kilometern pro Stunde durchs All. Die Nasa-Sonde erforschte zunächst Jupiter und Saturn. Im Sommer 2012 trat sie als erstes von Menschen geschaffenes Objekt in den interstellaren Raum ein.
Doch ein Jahr vor ihrem 50. Geburtstag nagt der Zahn der Zeit an der Sonde. Deswegen musste die Nasa im Frühjahr 2026 ein weiteres Instrument abschalten, den Teilchenmesser LECP. (Low-energy Charged Particles). Die Abschaltung spart Energie, die der Sonde ein Jahr weiterer Lebensdauer verschaffen soll. Von ursprünglich elf Instrumenten an Bord der Voyager 1 sind damit nur noch zwei aktiv.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 05.11.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Interessant! Aber… die NASA Kontaktiert am 18.10. und die Sonde blieb still…
2 Tage auf eine Antwort warten, dann am 20.10. eine Antwort.
also, nicht still geblieben, oder? Aber genug für einen spannenden Artikel… denke ich!
!!! Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: SA e-health startup Alignd raises Knife Capital funding to expand into maternity, kidney care - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African value-based care startup Alignd has raised an undisclosed amount of funding from Knife Capital to fund its expansion beyond palliative care into maternity and kidney care.
Founded in 2018, Alignd designs value-based care programmes that align the interests of patients, healthcare providers and medical schemes. Instead of paying for volume, its model ties payment to the outcomes that matter to patients. It coordinates care across clinical teams and, where appropriate, brings care into the home.
The startup started with palliative care. Medical schemes there have traditionally covered costly in-hospital end-of-life care but not home-based support. Alignd has built a network of more than 500 providers delivering home-based, person-centred care, working with seven medical schemes. Its palliative programme reaches more than 3.3 million lives.
It has also launched two newer programmes – a maternity programme that links parents, providers and schemes in a coordinated ecosystem, with support tailored to each family; and a kidney care programme, which coordinates care for patients with chronic kidney disease, helping them preserve kidney function for as long as possible while helping schemes manage long-term costs.
To scale those programmes, Aligned has raised an undisclosed amount of funding from Knife Capital, via Knife Fund III.
“South Africa’s private healthcare system largely pays for activity rather than outcomes, and patients and their families often carry the cost of that misalignment,” said Dr Lungi Nyathi, CEO of Alignd.
“In palliative care, we’ve shown that when patients, providers, and schemes pull in the same direction, the quality of care goes up and unnecessary spend comes down. Knife Capital’s backing, and their experience in scaling businesses locally and abroad, gives us the support to take that model into maternity and kidney care, where the need is just as urgent.”
Knife Capital partner Catherine Young said Alignd stood out as a women-founded team that had taken on a difficult healthcare problem and proven there was a better way to deliver care.
“The outcomes they are achieving are meaningful for the patients, providers, and medical schemes. It is exactly the kind of business we want to back, and it further strengthens the health-tech vertical we are building at Knife Capital,” she said.

articles.title: Beyond payments: Where venture capital will flow across Indian fintech over the next 24 months
articles.text:
Beyond payments: Where venture capital will flow across Indian fintech over the next 24 months
India's fintech decade was built on distribution. The next one will be built on infrastructure, advice and intelligence—and capital is already repricing accordingly.
India spent the last ten years solving for reach. UPI, Aadhaar-based onboarding, and the Jan Dhan push put a payment instrument in almost every adult hand, and a generation of companies was built on that distribution. That problem is now largely solved. The harder question—how to serve those hundreds of millions of customers profitably, with products that measurably improve their financial lives—is where the next cycle of venture capital will go.
The funding data already reflects the shift. Indian fintech attracted $3.5 billion across 216 disclosed deals in 2024, and $2.9 billion across 156 deals in 2025 roughly 10% less capital across 27% fewer transactions, according to Fintech Global. This fits fewer, larger cheques into a narrower set of theses. Yet fintech remained the largest sector by funding in 2025 at 22% of all Indian startup capital, and close to 26% in the first half of 2026. Capital is not leaving the sector; it is becoming far more selective about where to park itself.
Three themes stand out as most likely to absorb that capital over the next 24 months.
Financial infrastructure: Rebuilding the core
India's financial institutions are running a modern distribution business on decades-old plumbing. Core banking, lending and policy administration systems at most banks, NBFCs and insurers were built for a branch-led world of batch processing and overnight reconciliation—not for real-time payments at population scale, continuous underwriting, or products assembled on the fly from a dozen data sources. Every new capability gets bolted onto that base, and each addition costs more than the last as the architecture ages.
India’s financial institutions need to upgrade their technology, creating one of the largest infrastructure opportunities in the sector. Most legacy systems were not built for the speed and flexibility institutions now need. The next generation of technology will be cloud-based, modular and API-first, making it easier for different systems to work together. Banks and financial institutions want to launch products in weeks, adjust pricing quickly, and add new data sources or distribution partners without rebuilding their core systems. Much of their existing technology cannot support this.
The opportunity extends beyond core banking systems. Financial institutions also need better tools for compliance, managing AI models and their risks, preventing fraud and money laundering, and protecting against cyber threats. They also need infrastructure that allows non-financial businesses to offer financial products, such as loans, cards and escrow accounts. These capabilities are essential to delivering new financial products while meeting regulatory requirements.
Regulation is making these investments more urgent. Since February 2025, Sebi has held regulated intermediaries responsible for the outputs of AI and machine learning tools they use, including those provided by third parties. In August 2025, the RBI’s FREE-AI committee issued 26 recommendations, followed by draft guidance on model risk management and data governance. Meanwhile, the substantive obligations under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, covering consent, notices and individuals’ data rights, are scheduled to take effect in May 2027. Financial institutions will need to demonstrate that their AI systems and data practices meet these requirements. For many, buying proven technology will be more practical than building it themselves.
For venture investors, this creates an attractive opportunity: businesses can generate recurring revenue from financial institutions, with customer relationships that become harder to replace as their software becomes embedded in day-to-day operations. Investors can also benefit from the growth of financial services technology without needing to predict which consumer-facing brand will win.
A less obvious opportunity lies in India’s Account Aggregator ecosystem. Between March 2025 and May 2026, the number of institutions consuming financial data grew by roughly 66%, crossing 1,000, while the number supplying data remained broadly flat at around 176. Demand for consent-based financial data is growing much faster than supply. Building the infrastructure needed to close this gap could become an important opportunity in its own right.
Wealthtech: The distribution is built, the advice is not
The structural tailwinds are no longer in question.
Mutual fund AUM reached Rs 85.76 lakh crore in July 2026, up from Rs 46.4 lakh crore three years earlier, according to ICRA Analytics.
Sebi’s annual report unique notes that mutual fund investors crossed 6.1 crore, growing 13% in a single financial year, with Tier III cities now accounting for more than half the investor base. Unique demat accounts stand at 12.18 crore, against 3.3 crore in April 2020. Households are visibly rotating: net financial savings rose from 27% of household savings in FY23 to 33% in FY25, and household flows into securities markets more than doubled as a share of GDP, from 0.99% to 2.17%.
But the gap between having an investment account and receiving investment advice is stark, and that is where the opportunity lies. In FY2025-26, 7.2 crore new SIPs were registered and 6.8 crore were discontinued or matured, as per Sebi data.
That is near-total churn. It is not a distribution failure because distribution worked. Rather, it is an advice failure.
The supply side explains why. India has roughly 1,042 Sebi-registered investment adviser entities against nearly 1.99 lakh AMFI-registered mutual fund distributors—about 191 commission-earning distributors for every fee-based adviser, and one adviser for every 58,500 mutual fund investors. Human advice at this ratio cannot reach the mass market, because the unit economics of servicing a Rs 5 lakh portfolio with a human adviser have never worked anywhere.
This is where the account aggregator (AA) framework and AI intersect to make something newly plausible. India’s AA rails had cumulatively fulfilled 493.5 million consents across 314.5 million linked accounts by June 2026, roughly tripling in fifteen months, and now span 16 categories of financial information, including deposits, mutual funds, equities, insurance, pension and GST filings. For the first time, a platform can obtain a consented, machine-readable, near-complete picture of a household's finances. Layer AI over that, and the marginal cost of producing a genuinely personalised recommendation—the kind previously reserved for private banking clients—falls by an order of magnitude.
AI: From feature to franchise
The third theme is the broadest, and the one where discipline matters the most. Almost every fintech firm now claims AI. The distinction worth drawing is between AI as a feature—a chatbot bolted onto an existing product—and AI as the reason the business model works at all.
Three variants look durable. First, consumer financial co-pilots that consolidate saving, investing, borrowing and insurance decisions into one interface. Their viability rests entirely on the AA-plus-AI combination above; without consented data, a co-pilot is a search engine with a friendly tone.
Second, enterprise workflow redesign inside financial institutions. Underwriting, collections, KYC remediation, claims processing, and internal audit are high-volume, rules-dense functions where agentic automation has clear economics and buyers have measurable cost lines to attack.
Third, and perhaps the most underrated, India as a delivery centre for AI-enabled professional services to the world. The IT industry was built on labour arbitrage in software; the same institutional muscle—managed delivery, compliance discipline, client trust at scale—can be pointed at legal review, audit, fund administration and healthcare operations, with AI compressing the cost base rather than headcount expanding it. Given India's incumbent position in global services, this may prove the largest of the three.
What all this adds up to
Payments proved Indians would adopt digital finance. The next 24 months will test whether the ecosystem can make that adoption profitable, well-advised and defensible, which makes a strong case for backing the layers rather than the surfaces: better technology for financial institutions, accessible financial advice for households, and AI that makes both economically possible.
The author is Principal, Flourish Ventures.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: Un encapuchado sube a un panel de tráfico sobre la A-92, en uno de los accesos a Sevilla, prende fuego a un radar y huye
articles.text:
Hay un aparato en España que tiene más enemigos que Batman, si bien solo cumplen una función informativa: el radar de tramo. Y es que ayer mismo alguien encapuchado se subió a la estructura de un panel informativo sobre los carriles de la A-92 (es decir, a la entrada de Sevilla) y le prendió fuego. Corre por la pasarela, se baja por una escalera lateral y se marcha. Y parece que el vídeo viral ha dado pie a otros, así que conviene separar los veraces de toda la imaginería que ha venido después, porque algunos contenidos incluso puede que estén hechos con IA.
El primer vídeo. Lo publicó el perfil de Instagram @lasevillaenfurecida. Según la prensa local, el radar está en la entrada a Sevilla desde Alcalá de Guadaíra, a la altura del Centro Zoosanitario municipal. Las versiones difieren en un punto. Unas dicen que el material ardiendo cae sobre el firme de la autovía. Otras, que las llamas alcanzan la zona bajo el dispositivo, junto a la calzada. No hubo avisos ni consta ningún accidente.
Un ataque más. El vídeo es parte de una serie de tres. En la SE-30, frente al mural del grupo SFDK, varios individuos cortan el poste de un radar con una herramienta de grandes dimensiones, lo cargan en un coche y lo queman. En Alcalá de Guadaíra, otro radar se ata a un vehículo, que lo arranca de cuajo, tirándo de él al estilo Mad Max, recurriendo quizá a una soga o cinchas.
El de la Ronda Urbana Norte. Aunque el vídeo se ha difundido ahora, ese ataque ocurrió a principios de mayo de 2026. Era uno de los cinco radares fijos que el Ayuntamiento instaló el otoño pasado en vías de 50 km/h. Los autores se llevaron la caja y el cableado, y el equipo apareció quemado en un descampado junto al aeropuerto de San Pablo. Según fuentes del caso, las pinzas hidráulicas se habrían sustraído antes de un parque de bomberos de la provincia. El Ayuntamiento sabía de la desaparición desde el 4 de mayo y a finales de junio solo quedaba el poste cortado.
Qué se sabe de la investigación. La unidad de investigación del Sector de Tráfico de Andalucía de la Guardia Civil (UNIS) ha abierto diligencias. No se ha comunicado oficialmente cuántos radares han resultado dañados ni quiénes son los implicados. Tampoco se conocen las fechas exactas de los ataques de la A-92 y de Alcalá. Una plataforma de verificación recoge el caso como abierto y aún sin investigar. Y aunque los vandalizados son los más visibles, la miniaturización de radares ha llevado a que cada vez estén mejor ocultos (el de Velolaser apenas mide 50 cm y mide 3kg).
Quién está detrás. La cuenta que difunde los vídeos atribuye las acciones a un "justiciero". Curiosamente, similar al grupo de jóvenes que se presentaba hace seis años como 'Payasos Justicieros', en referencia a los revolucionarios del bloque en la serie de comedia 'La Que Se Avecina'. Dice que actúan contra radares que consideran recaudatorios. La cuenta también los relaciona con otros vídeos ajenos a los radares, si bien no hay confirmación policial de ese vínculo.
Qué dice la ley. La DGT ya se pronunció en 2025, tras la vandalización de siete radares en otras comunidades. Lo considera un delito de daños, recogido en los artículos 263 a 267 del Código Penal. El tipo agravado, que se aplica cuando el daño busca impedir el ejercicio de la autoridad, prevé cárcel de 1 a 3 años y multa de 12 a 24 meses. La investigación dirá si procede aquí. Además, los autores deben responder por el coste del aparato, unos 67.000 euros por radar fijo según la DGT. Desde entonces, Tráfico ha instalado cámaras de vigilancia en esos puntos, conectadas a sus centros de gestión.
Por qué el radar. Los radares de la DGT recaudaron 246,8 millones de euros en 2025, un 14% más respecto al curso anterior, según Automovilistas Europeos Asociados. La velocidad ya supone el 41,5% de la recaudación por multas, sin contar País Vasco ni Cataluña. Solo 50 dispositivos concentraron 1,3 millones de denuncias. Sevilla fue la sexta provincia por recaudación total de multas de tráfico, con 26,3 millones.
La asociación sostiene que muchos son “meros instrumentos de recaudación”. La DGT replica con otro dato: según el Observatorio Europeo de Seguridad Vial, la velocidad excesiva está detrás del 10-15% de los accidentes y del 30% de los mortales. Su director, Pere Navarro, defiende los radares como la única vía eficaz para bajar la velocidad.
El precedente. En Francia, durante las protestas de los chalecos amarillos de 2018 quedaron inutilizados cientos de radares. En una radio se llegó a hablar de hasta el 60% de todos los radares automáticos del país. Se interpretó como un ataque al símbolo de un Gobierno que, según los manifestantes, les "usurpaba" demasiado dinero. Allí había un movimiento detrás y se sospecha que esté pasando lo mismo en Sevilla.
¿Más radares? El Ayuntamiento de Sevilla prevé más radares en vías como la Ronda Urbana Norte y la avenida de la Palmera. Forman parte de su plan contra el ruido, de unos diez millones de euros, que culminará en 2029. Después del vídeo

articles.title: Galaxy S27 Pro et Ultra : cette image montre-t-elle leur vrai design ?
articles.text:
À quelques mois de leur commercialisation prévue pour le début de l’année 2027, les futurs smartphones haut de gamme de Samsung font l’objet de nouvelles indiscrétions. Après l’apparition de modèles factices en ligne, Ice Universe, un leaker bien connu, affirme détenir le véritable design des appareils et partage un croquis technique détaillant le bloc caméra des futurs téléphones premium de la marque coréenne.
Trois capteurs et pas un de plus
Partagé sur X, ce visuel contredit les récentes maquettes aperçues en ligne la semaine dernière qui affichaient quatre caméras. Ice Universe affirme que ce quatrième capteur n’existe pas. Il n’hésite pas à utiliser les termes « 100 % confirmé » concernant le design et la présence de seulement trois capteurs pour les Galaxy S27 Pro et S27 Ultra.
Comme nous l’avons évoqué la semaine dernière, le Galaxy S27 Pro embarquerait ainsi un capteur principal de 200 mégapixels (un Samsung ISOCELL HP6), épaulé par un ultra grand-angle de 50 mégapixels et un téléobjectif de 10 mégapixels offrant un zoom optique 3x. De son côté, le S27 Ultra conserverait une optique principale de 200 mégapixels et un ultra grand-angle de 50 mégapixels, tout en musclant sa partie zoom avec un capteur de 50 mégapixels doté d’un zoom optique 5x.
Des changements stratégiques pour Samsung
Oui, le Galaxy S26 Ultra a bien quatre capteurs photo, et c’est d’ailleurs une de ses forces, comme nous l’avons souligné dans notre test, alors pourquoi Samsung reculerait sur ce point pour son Galaxy S27 Ultra ? Il semble que la marque miserait gros sur cette nouvelle génération, en prévoyant de concentrer plus de 70 % de la production de ses S27 sur les modèles Pro et Ultra. Ajoutez à cela la hausse du coût des composants, et l’on peut supposer que Samsung devra faire des choix stratégiques pour préserver sa marge sans pour autant faire exploser les prix.
À lire : Le Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra s’inspirerait en partie de l’iPhone 18 Pro
Reste que ces informations proviennent d’une fuite et demandent donc d’être prises avec des pincettes en attendant une officialisation par Samsung. À quelques mois du lancement des Galaxy S27, les rumeurs et fuites en tout genre devraient s’intensifier, apportant un éclairage de plus en plus précis sur les futurs S27.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.

articles.title: Alemania excluyó a Palantir, empresa estadounidense de software, de la lista de opciones de IA para su ejército
articles.text:
Alemania dejó a Palantir fuera de la lista de soluciones que evalúa para la plataforma de inteligencia artificial que quiere desplegar en su ejército desde el próximo año, según informó la agencia Reuters. Francia y Países Bajos también buscan proveedores europeos para reducir la dependencia de la tecnología de Estados Unidos.
La agencia citó a una persona al tanto del asunto, que explicó que el Gobierno alemán redujo las opciones a un puñado de soluciones. Ninguna igualaría las capacidades de Palantir, pero serían suficientes, garantizarían la soberanía sobre los datos nacionales y podrían cubrir cerca del 80% de lo necesario en un año.
Palantir es una empresa estadounidense de software que analiza grandes volúmenes de datos. Su sistema Maven Smart System es el programa central del Pentágono y fue muy usado por Ucrania en la guerra contra Rusia. El cuartel general militar de la OTAN lo adoptó el año pasado y en junio lo declaró listo para uso operativo en toda la alianza.
Según Reuters, algunos funcionarios y militares reconocen que Europa no tiene hoy un equivalente exacto en tamaño, despliegue y experiencia. Los ejércitos enfrentan así un dilema: apostar por sistemas propios, con más autonomía pero menos maduros, o usar una plataforma probada pese al riesgo de dependencia estratégica.
Francia desarrolla una plataforma militar soberana con IA llamada Arcadia. Alexandre Lahousse, subdirector de la agencia francesa de compras de defensa, dijo a Reuters que incluirá a varios proveedores. La agencia prevé adjudicar al menos algunos contratos antes de que termine el año y tener una versión operativa para el campo de batalla a mediados de 2027.
Países Bajos usa hoy parte del software de Palantir, pero quiere una alternativa europea en dos años. El ministro neerlandés de Compras de Armamento, Derk Boswijk, explicó a la agencia que su ejército se reúne con posibles proveedores y probablemente combinará empresas neerlandesas y de otros países europeos. “Tenemos mucho conocimiento en Europa sobre IA y toma de decisiones. Pero está muy fragmentado, y ese es el problema”, afirmó Boswijk.
Una empresa alemana presentó una alternativa europea
El 11 de noviembre, la empresa alemana Helsing presentó Clarity, un programa de inteligencia militar que, según la compañía, usa cientos de agentes de IA (asistentes que ejecutan tareas por su cuenta) para analizar imágenes de satélite, video de drones y partes escritas. Identifica posibles objetivos y prepara datos para los sistemas de armas, con aprobación humana de cada uno, según Helsing.
“Una capacidad tan crítica debe ser soberana”, dijo el cofundador y codirector ejecutivo de Helsing, Gundbert Scherf, en el comunicado de la compañía, citado por Kyiv Independent. Helsing aseguró a Reuters que podría entregar una versión inicial en pocos meses a la brigada alemana desplegada en Lituania.
Reuters mencionó otros fabricantes europeos de software militar: la danesa Systematic, cuyo producto SitaWare usan el ejército alemán y partes de la OTAN, las francesas Thales y Safran, y la startup parisina Comand AI.
Palantir intenta tranquilizar a los europeos. Su director internacional, Louis Mosley, dijo a la agencia de noticias que el sistema usado por la OTAN no tiene un “interruptor de apagado”, que sigue habiendo demanda en Europa, incluido el Reino Unido, donde el Ministerio de Defensa firmó el año pasado un acuerdo de tres años, y que espera convencer a Alemania.
El jefe del ejército alemán, el teniente general Christian Freuding, señaló en una conferencia en Berlín que persisten dudas sobre seguridad de los datos, entrenamiento de los sistemas y compatibilidad entre plataformas. Francia prevé adjudicar los primeros contratos de Arcadia antes de que termine 2026.

Points forts
- Performances en rastérisation et Ray tracing.
- Ventilateurs à l'arrêt quand la carte est au repos.
- Sortie vidéo HDMI 2.1a et DisplayPort 2.1.
- Système de refroidissement efficace.
- Silence de fonctionnement.
Points faibles
- Nombre de jeux FSR4 limités.
- Consommation de notre modèle OC.
L'AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT marque le retour en force d'AMD sur le segment milieu de gamme, offrant d'excellentes performances en 1440p et 4K grâce à l'architecture RDNA 4 et au FSR 4. Bien que consommant un peu plus que la concurrence et avec une adoption limitée du FSR 4, elle séduit par son efficacité en rastérisation et en raytracing. Le refroidissement performant et le silence de notre modèle de test imposent la Radeon RX 9070 XT comme un choix solide pour les joueurs en quête d'un rapport qualité-prix avantageux.
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).

articles.title: Surveiller entrée et jardin sans câble : le pack Blink à -83% pour le Black Friday
articles.text:
Le pack de surveillance Blink repasse à 24,99 € chez Amazon en plein Black Friday, soit le tarif que nous avions déjà relevé le 29 septembre. La caméra Outdoor 4, la sonnette vidéo 2K+ et le module de synchronisation sont affichés au lieu de 149,98 €, mais sans abonnement, aucune vidéo n’est enregistrée.
Blink, la marque de sécurité connectée d’Amazon, réunit ici deux appareils sans fil : la caméra extérieure Outdoor 4 et une sonnette vidéo 2K+, reliées par un module de synchronisation fourni. Amazon propose ce pack à 24,99 € au lieu de 149,98 €, soit 124,99 € d’économie et 83 % de remise sur le plus bas prix des 30 derniers jours affiché sur sa fiche.
Ce n’est pas un prix inédit : nous relayions déjà ce pack à 24,99 € le 29 septembre, après un passage à 39,99 € en août. L’offre parle surtout aux occupants d’une maison qui veulent équiper leur entrée et leur jardin sans faire venir d’électricien.
Le pack Blink Outdoor 4 et sonnette vidéo 2K+ est à 24,99 € au lieu de 149,98 € chez Amazon.
Pourquoi choisir le pack Blink Outdoor 4 et sonnette 2K+ ?
- Aucun câble à tirer : La caméra fonctionne avec deux piles AA lithium et la sonnette avec trois, pour une autonomie annoncée jusqu’à deux ans. Les kits de montage sont fournis, et vous posez le tout là où il n’y a pas de prise.
- Une sonnette qui voit jusqu’au sol : Son image carrée cadre le visiteur de la tête aux pieds, colis posé devant la porte compris. L’audio bidirectionnel permet de répondre sans ouvrir, et la vision infrarouge sert la nuit.
- Une seule application, avec Alexa : Caméra et sonnette se pilotent depuis l’appli Blink. Reliés à Alexa, ils peuvent afficher le direct, accueillir vos visiteurs ou s’activer à la voix.
De l’entrée au fond du jardin, ce que le pack surveille vraiment
La caméra Outdoor 4 filme en 1080p avec un champ de vision de 143°, contre 110° pour la génération précédente, comme nous le relevions dans notre article sur son arrivée en France. Un seul appareil suffit donc pour couvrir une allée ou une terrasse. Sa détection de mouvement à deux zones vous alerte quand quelqu’un remonte l’allée ou s’approche d’une fenêtre, tandis que la sonnette s’occupe de la porte, de jour comme de nuit.
Le pack convient aux foyers qui veulent s’équiper sans chantier, et à ceux qui possèdent déjà des enceintes Echo. Le module de synchronisation accepte jusqu’à dix caméras, ce qui laisse de la marge pour surveiller un garage plus tard. En appartement, l’intérêt baisse nettement, puisque l’ensemble vise une porte d’entrée et un extérieur. Vérifiez aussi votre box : les deux appareils ne se connectent qu’au Wi-Fi 2,4 GHz.
Blink face aux caméras sans abonnement
Le vrai point de comparaison n’est pas le prix de départ, mais le coût d’usage. Dans notre comparatif des meilleures caméras de surveillance, la Xiaomi CW300, une caméra extérieure filaire autour de 50 €, enregistre sur carte microSD sans abonnement obligatoire, et la Ring Spotlight Cam Pro, retenue pour l’écosystème Amazon, en réclame un pour l’historique. À notre dernier relevé, Blink facturait 3 € par mois et par appareil avec Blink Basic, ou 10 € par mois avec Blink Plus. Le pack coûte donc moins cher que la Xiaomi à l’achat, mais ses vidéos enregistrées ont un coût mensuel.
✅ Les points forts
- Caméra, sonnette et module de synchronisation pour 24,99 €
- Installation sans fil, autonomie annoncée jusqu’à deux ans
- Sonnette 2K+ qui cadre de la tête aux pieds
- Caméra à 143° de champ de vision
- Compatible Alexa, une seule application
❌ Les limites
- Aucune vidéo enregistrée sans abonnement Blink
- Notifications de personnes réservées aux abonnés
- Wi-Fi 2,4 GHz uniquement
- Même prix que le 29 septembre, pas un nouveau plancher
Amazon n’affichait plus que 5 exemplaires de ce pack à 24,99 € au moment de notre relevé du 16 novembre.
À 24,99 €, l’achat se résume à du matériel sans fil correct sur le papier : 1080p et 143° pour la caméra, une sonnette qui cadre de la tête aux pieds, une installation sans chantier. Ce n’est pourtant pas un tarif inédit, puisque nous l’avions déjà relevé le 29 septembre, et la remise ne règle pas la question de l’enregistrement des vidéos. Sans abonnement, vous gardez le direct et les alertes de mouvement, rien de plus.
Le pack s’adresse à ceux qui veulent surtout voir et répondre en direct depuis leur téléphone, ou qui comptent de toute façon s’abonner à Blink. L’essai gratuit de 30 jours de l’abonnement, inclus à l’achat, permet de tester l’enregistrement avant de payer. Si vous voulez conserver vos vidéos sans frais mensuels, une caméra à stockage microSD comme celles de notre comparatif sera plus adaptée. Dans tous les cas, ajoutez le coût de l’abonnement à votre calcul avant de commander.
Comment profiter des offres exclusives du Black Friday ?

Retrouvez tous les bons plans du Black Friday 2026 sur la page dédiée à l'événement.

articles.title: Entre Orange en octobre et SFR en novembre, la 2G disparaît de France en quelques semaines
articles.text:
Lancé en France à l’été 1992, le réseau mobile 2G vit ses dernières semaines. Orange a commencé au printemps en coupant la 2G dans ses premières villes du Sud-Ouest, puis a éteint son réseau dans les 43 derniers départements le 20 octobre. SFR suit désormais le mouvement.
Dans un communiqué publié ce lundi 16 novembre, l’opérateur au carré rouge confirme que l’arrêt définitif de sa 2G a commencé dimanche 15 novembre dans les grandes agglomérations. Cette première phase dure jusqu’au 30 novembre, avant le reste de la métropole du 1er au 15 décembre.
Les téléphones qui ne captent que la 2G ne marcheront plus sur son réseau, et les alarmes, systèmes de télésurveillance ou ascenseurs reposant sur cette génération devront être mis à niveau ou remplacés, si ce n’est pas déjà fait. Fin 2025, il restait encore 5,6 millions de cartes SIM dépendantes de la 2G. Quelques mois auparavant, le gouvernement avait mis en garde ceux qui s’en servent encore.
SFR avait annoncé la fin de ses réseaux 2G et 3G dès janvier 2023, et le calendrier de chaque opérateur est public depuis. Pour justifier l’arrêt, SFR met d’abord en avant la sécurité, puisque la 2G repose sur des protections dépassées qui exposent ses utilisateurs à la fraude et à l’interception des communications.
La 2G et la 3G pesaient aussi, en 2023, entre 21 et 33 % de l’électricité consommée par les antennes mobiles, alors qu’on ne s’en sert presque plus. Ces chiffres viennent d’une étude publiée par l’Arcep, le régulateur des télécoms. La migration vers la 4G et la 5G vise donc à répondre à plusieurs besoins. Pourtant, la transition traîne.
La 3G survivra-t-elle à SFR ?
Concernant la 3G, la fermeture est prévue dans deux ans. Or, SFR pourrait avoir changé de mains d’ici là, si le rachat est autorisé. Bouygues Telecom, Free et Orange ont signé le 6 juin un protocole d’accord avec Altice France pour racheter l’opérateur, sur la base d’une valeur d’entreprise (dette comprise) de 20,35 milliards d’euros.
Autrement dit, la 3G pourrait survivre à SFR, en théorie.
L’Autorité de la concurrence, qui a prévu au moins 18 mois d’instruction, ne rendra pas sa décision avant fin 2027.
Les trois repreneurs se partageraient les clients, et le sort du réseau et des antennes de SFR fait partie des gros chantiers du rachat. Si l’opération est autorisée, les repreneurs prévoient ensuite une transition de 30 mois, pilotée par une structure qu’ils détiendraient à trois. La coupure de la 3G, prévue fin 2028, tomberait donc en plein partage de SFR.
Faut-il changer de téléphone ?
Côté abonnés, rien ne change pour les smartphones 5G ni pour les modèles 4G compatibles VoLTE, la technologie qui fait passer les appels par la 4G. Les smartphones 3G et certains modèles 4G sans VoLTE devront en revanche être remplacés d’ici fin 2028 pour continuer à téléphoner sur le réseau SFR.
