articles.title: Barracuda links cloud breach to ARTEX AI-powered cyberattack
articles.text:
Hackers who breached the cloud environment of network and email security company Barracuda earlier this month used a stolen cloud access key and the ARTEX AI penetration testing framework.
The company says the attacker accessed approximately 10 of its cloud accounts over a 44-hour period between November 1 and 2.
The attacker's presence was discovered on November 4, and Barracuda's investigation determined that the open-source AI pentesting framework ARTEX was used for this "machine-speed intrusion."
The company explains that the attacker leveraged a cloud access key provided to a third-party vendor for the duration of a previous project.
"We did not retire the key when the vendor — a company working in AI — finished that work. That is on us," Barracuda says.
The security company believes the attacker stole the key from the unnamed third-party AI vendor in October. It confirmed that the key was stored in a configuration file in the vendor's GitHub repository.
The attacker used credentials they found in one system to move through Barracuda’s data analytics environment, source-code repositories, and Kubernetes clusters.
Based on the attacker's commands targeting cryptocurrency-related secrets, including private keys, Ethereum keystore files, and seed phrases, Barracuda believes the attack was financially motivated.
However, the company does not rule out that this activity might have been a diversion from the attacker’s true motive.
The threat actor attempted to establish persistence by deploying a container that mounted the host’s file system, including credentials stored on it.
A separate attempt to create a new cloud administrator identity was blocked.
Barracuda says the attack used machine-style labels, certain probing methods, and built-in hunting routines that matched what is found in ARTEX.
The firm noted that the attack was very similar to a recent incident at cloud hosting provider Railway, which also involved credential chaining and the apparent use of ARTEX.
According to the cybersecurity company, the attacker reached a system that stores customer integration credentials for Barracuda XDR; however, it found no evidence that those were accessed or stolen.
Because of the uncertainty surrounding this scenario, Barracuda asked potentially affected Managed XDR Cloud or Monitored Endpoint customers to revoke and recreate their integration credentials.
Barracuda assures customers who did not receive direct communications about this incident that they need to take no action.

articles.title: La casa familiar de Amancio Ortega: un dúplex con vistas al mar en uno de los barrios más cotizados de A Coruña
articles.text:
Amancio Ortega podría vivir prácticamente en cualquier lugar del mundo gracias a la fortuna que ha conseguido con Inditex, pero ha preferido quedarse en A Coruña. El empresario, que cumplió 90 años en marzo de 2026, lleva décadas manteniendo una vida discreta en la ciudad gallega, cerca de su hija Marta Ortega y alejado de la exposición pública. ¿Y dónde vive exactamente? En un dúplex con grandes ventanales y vistas al mar, situado en una de las zonas más cotizadas de la ciudad.
Como recoge la revista Semana en su información sobre la vivienda familiar, el inmueble se encuentra en el centro de A Coruña, cerca de la Rúa Real y del paseo marítimo. Se trata de un entorno en el que conviven edificios históricos de finales del siglo XIX con construcciones del XX, muchas de ellas con las características galerías acristaladas que forman parte de la imagen de la ciudad. De hecho, el arquitecto Faustino Domínguez fue uno de los nombres vinculados al desarrollo de esta zona, donde el puerto y la arquitectura tradicional comparten protagonismo.
El dúplex de Amancio Ortega y las otras propiedades que tiene en Galicia
La ubicación de la vivienda también permite llegar caminando a lugares como la plaza de María Pita, los Cantones o la Ciudad Vieja. A todo esto debemos sumar la cercanía del Real Club Náutico de A Coruña, un lugar muy relacionado con la familia Ortega. Fue allí donde Marta Ortega celebró su fiesta preboda con Carlos Torretta en 2018, mientras que su padre ha mantenido durante años una estrecha relación con la ciudad en la que comenzó su trayectoria empresarial.
Sin embargo, el dúplex no es la única propiedad familiar en Galicia. Amancio Ortega también cuenta con el Pazo de Drozo, situado en el municipio de Cambre, a pocos kilómetros de A Coruña. Esta residencia señorial, rodeada de un entorno más tranquilo y apartado de la ciudad, ha sido escenario de algunos de los acontecimientos más importantes de la familia. Allí se casó con Flora Pérez en 2001 y también celebró su boda Marta Ortega con el jinete Sergio Álvarez Moya en 2012.
El Pazo de Drozo conserva elementos propios de las antiguas casas señoriales gallegas, desde su planta rectangular de dos alturas hasta los escudos heráldicos y las construcciones auxiliares. En su interior también dispone de una pequeña capilla, un espacio que ha tenido especial importancia en las celebraciones familiares. Por otro lado, la afición de los Ortega por la hípica está muy relacionada con Casas Novas, el centro ecuestre que el empresario impulsó en Arteixo hace más de dos décadas y que acoge el Concurso de Saltos Internacional de A Coruña.
Y es que, aunque Amancio Ortega mantiene un perfil bastante discreto, su patrimonio está entre los mayores del planeta. En noviembre de 2026, Forbes valoró su fortuna en 125.200 millones de euros, una riqueza ligada a Inditex y a sus inversiones inmobiliarias. Todo comenzó en 1975, cuando abrió la primera tienda Zara en A Coruña, concretamente en la calle Juan Flórez, muy cerca de la ciudad en la que continúa residiendo.

articles.title: African investors are building their exits
articles.text:
Over the past month, we spoke to four Africa-focused investors who run very different funds. Yet the same ideas came up in almost every conversation.
Enza Capital just launched a fund dedicated to artificial intelligence (AI) startups. DPI Venture Capital closed a $112 million fintech fund backed almost entirely by financial institutions, with 93% of the money coming from Africa. That is more than the $107 million raised in 2025 by all six African venture funds that reached a close.
Five35 Ventures, a gender-lens fund that invests with a focus on women, sold its stake in Complete Farmer, a Ghanaian agritech company, for 3.5 times its invested capital. Kuramo Foundation is training 22 new fund managers to invest in Nigeria’s small businesses through the Wholesale Impact Investment Fund’s SME Fund Accelerator.
Taken together, these conversations show investors working to return money to their limited partners (LPs). Earlier this year, investors told us exits do not happen on their own. Over the past four weeks, some showed us how they are making them happen.
They are also raising from limited partners (LPs) that rarely put money into venture funds, such as banks and individual angels, at a time when fund managers are struggling to raise at all. They are narrowing their focus to a single sector or founder type while looking for deals beyond Africa’s usual startup hubs.
Here are the four lessons that founders and new fund managers can take from them.
Investors are building the exits themselves
In March, Five35 sold its entire stake in Complete Farmer to another investor for 3.5 times what it paid, an annual return of 38% over four years. Hema Vallabh, Five35’s founding partner, said the timing was partly about the fund itself: Five35 is a first-time fund still raising money, and it needed to show its backers it could return cash.
Enza Capital is helping build a market for selling shares with other investors; it helped launch Clearflow Markets, which makes it easier to buy and sell shares in private companies. “We cannot wait for this market to appear before we invest,” said Mike Mompi, Enza’s managing partner. Enza has already sold its full stake in Quro Medical, a South African health tech company, to what Mompi described as the country’s largest listed hospital group.
DPI is drawing on its parent firm’s track record. Development Partners International has taken companies public on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange and the Egyptian Exchange and sold others to buyers in the Middle East. Ashley Lewis, who runs DPI Venture Capital, said its startups can learn directly from how those deals were done.
Kuramo is teaching exits before it invests. Its 12-week programme for new fund managers includes classes on exit strategy, taught by people who have done exits. Ijeoma Madueke of the Kuramo Foundation said the timing helps: managers who have not yet invested can let their exit plan shape their strategy from the start.
New kinds of LPs are investing into funds
For years, African venture funds have relied on development finance institutions (DFIs), the government-backed lenders that invest in private companies in developing countries. As money for venture funds has dried up, the funds we spoke to found it elsewhere.
DPI raised its $112 million almost entirely from banks and financial services firms, and 93% of it came from Africa. Egyptian banks backed the fund from its launch in 2022, with Banque Misr as the anchor and the National Bank of Egypt and Banque du Caire as strategic investors, and the investors DPI brought in kept to the same profile. Nclude, Lewis said, “is a good case for successful pathways to capital from unique sources.”
Five35 started with women Vallabh already knew, like executives who had made money and invested in property, stocks or startups but had never put money into a venture fund. Through the 35 Club, she took cheques of $35,000 and up and raised the fund’s first $1 million. That money paid for Five35’s first investments and gave it a record, which helped it win the Mastercard Foundation Africa Growth Fund as its anchor investor in December 2025.
Kuramo is building a local pool of capital. The Nigeria Wholesale Impact Investment Fund (WIIF), which Kuramo Capital Management runs for the Impact Investors Foundation, is working toward a $100 million first close. In June 2025, Nigeria’s Federal Ministry of Finance said the government would commit $50 million. The fund is now talking to Nigerian pension funds and local DFIs.
Other funds show the same pattern. In August, Ventures Platform closed its second fund at $84 million, above its $75 million target. Alongside DFIs such as IFC and EBRD, its backers include the Ashesi University Foundation and Standard Bank. AHL Venture Partners, which we spoke to in the first half of the year, has raised $45.5 million for its credit fund from family offices and family foundations.
Investors are choosing narrow focus areas
Mompi described the pattern simply. Funds start by investing in everything, then narrow their focus as the market matures. A focused fund, he said, finds better companies and helps them more.
Enza, expectedly, is the clearest case. After seven years of general tech investing, it launched a fund only for AI startups and companies that use AI. By Enza’s count, AI took about 60% of global venture money in 2025 and just over 5% in Africa. In November, the fund reached a first close of about $21 million, 35% of its $60 million target.
Five35 invests only through a gender lens: companies co-led by women, companies with many women on staff, and companies that mostly serve women. Complete Farmer has a male founder, but when Five35 invested, 55% to 60% of its customers were women.
DPI’s Nclude Fund backs fintechs and companies with a financial product built in. Lewis’s example is Nawy, an Egyptian property platform that also offers mortgages. Companies with no financial product, such as deep tech or space tech, would be very hard for the fund to back, she said.
Kuramo chose managers with narrow plans too. Its 22 managers include two focused on the creative economy, one built entirely on Islamic finance, and one that ties healthcare funding to results. The main question Madueke asked each of them was why they were the right person to run their fund.
Money is reaching markets outside the usual hubs
Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt and South Africa, often called the Big Four, still take most of Africa’s startup funding. In January, they got between 80% and 85% of total funding in 2025. Three of the four investors are also putting money elsewhere.
Five35 invests in the Big Four, but Vallabh is also excited about Ghana, Senegal and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Its best result so far, Complete Farmer, is Ghanaian.
DPI’s fund began in Egypt and can now put up to 30% of its money anywhere in Africa or the Middle East. Its two newest companies are Kera, a health AI business in Senegal and Côte d’Ivoire, and Accord Partners, which launched in Saudi Arabia.
Kuramo picked managers from all six of Nigeria’s geopolitical zones. A lot of capital stays in Lagos, Madueke said, so the programme looked for managers in parts of the country that money has not traditionally reached.
Madica, a pre-seed programme backed by Flourish Ventures, made a similar bet in September, when it made its first investments in Algeria and Cameroon as part of five new deals worth up to $200,000 each. Its portfolio now has 18 companies in 10 African markets. In October, Flourish gave Madica another $6 million to run for three more years and back 25 to 30 more startups.
What founders should take from this
The investors we spoke to were clear about what makes a founder stand out now. AI has made prototypes cheap to build, Mompi said, so a working demo no longer sets anyone apart. Knowing the market better than anyone else and having something competitors cannot easily copy are what make founders stand out: data no one else holds, existing routes to customers, or a product people use every day at work.
Founders should also watch their margins and their cash. Many companies got into trouble between 2020 and 2022, Mompi said, by chasing big transaction numbers while ignoring what each transaction earned. For founders outside fintech, a financial product can open doors. DPI wants to see one built into a business before it invests, whether that business sells homes, health services or cars.
What new fund managers should take from this
For new fund managers, the lesson starts with a track record, and small sums can build one. Five35 raised its first $1 million in cheques of $35,000 and up from women who had never backed a venture fund. That money paid for its first investments, and the results helped it win the Mastercard Foundation Africa Growth Fund as an anchor investor.
Managers also need to focus on what they are best placed to run. Madueke asked every manager in Kuramo’s programme why they were the right person for their fund, and the programme teaches exit strategy before any of them invests. Investors will expect managers to be ready, Madueke said, with documents in order, a clear thesis and a team in place. Without these, a fund will not make it into an investor’s pipeline.

articles.title: Intel sued by shareholders who claim it hid PC sales slump before 29% stock crash
articles.text:
What just happened? It's not just Nvidia being sued by its shareholders over claims it withheld important information. Intel is facing a proposed class-action lawsuit over allegations it hid the severity of the decline in PC sales, which the plaintiffs say caused the company's stock to crash almost 29% in one day.
The complaint, filed in federal court in San Jose on November 13, names Intel, CEO Lip-Bu Tan, and CFO David Zinsner as defendants. Michigan's City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System is leading the case, seeking unspecified damages.
Shareholders allege Intel took too long to disclose how weakening PC sales and a buildup of unsold inventory would hurt revenue. They argue those problems outweighed the benefits Team Blue was receiving from data center construction and the AI boom.
The suit specifically accuses Intel of making "materially false and/or misleading" statements that suggested demand was improving. Investors say October's results undermined those assurances, revealing the extent of the PC slowdown after they had bought shares at allegedly inflated prices. The complaint covers purchases between July 23 and October 29.
Despite third-quarter earnings beating expectations and data center revenue jumping almost 80%, Intel's outlook disappointed investors. On October 29, the company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, below Wall Street's roughly $17 billion estimate, and warned of a prolonged PC slowdown. Shares plunged 28.6% the following day, wiping out around $140 billion in market value and making it Intel's worst trading day since 1974.
The lawsuit highlights Intel's PC business revenue falling 9% year-over-year, or about $800 million, to $8.1 billion in the third quarter. Its main accusation is that Intel failed to give shareholders a timely and accurate picture of that deterioration.
Shareholders also say Intel had a reason to hide its problems: it sold $23 billion worth of shares at $95 each in August.
Intel expects PC shipments to drop around 12% this year and another 10% in 2027. AI data centers continue to buy up huge amounts of memory, pushing PC prices higher and putting buyers off. Intel doesn't expect that situation to improve until memory supply and prices normalize, but when that will happen is anyone's guess.
There had already been warnings about consumer pricing getting worse. September brought reports of another planned 10% Intel CPU price increase, with the company reportedly prioritizing more profitable server processors at its factories.
The case follows the shareholder lawsuit against Nvidia and Jensen Huang over his relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Both cases allege investors lost money after information they say should have been disclosed earlier became public.

articles.title: Uno Platform 7.0 Adds WebGPU Backend, Apple TV and Reactor Support, and Retires Native Rendering
articles.text:
The Uno Platform team released Uno Platform 7.0, which unifies rendering on SkiaSharp 4 with an experimental WebGPU backend, adds Apple TV as a target platform and supports .NET 11 from day zero. The release also brings third-party .NET MAUI controls and Microsoft.UI.Reactor library to every target, and removes native rendering and Mac Catalyst.
Uno Platform is an open-source framework for building .NET applications with C# and WinUI XAML for Windows, Android, iOS, macOS, Linux and WebAssembly. The team describes 7.0 as its largest release, with 5,219 commits and 704 closed issues since 6.7. According to the team’s benchmarks, 7.0 is about 2x faster at the median and 5x smaller than 6.7, with some operations, such as brush creation, up to 38x faster. These figures come from the vendor and the workloads were not published in detail.
All targets now render through one pluggable pipeline. SkiaSharp 4 is the default, and Uno Platform is a co-maintainer of the library alongside the .NET team at Microsoft. On Android, Windows and Linux, Skia now renders through Vulkan by default. The WebGPU backend, available on all desktop, mobile and WebAssembly targets, is enabled by adding WebGpu to UnoFeatures and registering the backend on the host builder. It uses wgpu-native outside the browser and the browser’s own WebGPU support on WebAssembly. The team measured up to a 50% frame-rate improvement depending on the scene, and says a WebGPU-only app drops about 6 MB of uncompressed native code from WebAssembly builds. A new WebGpuCanvasElement lets applications issue their own WebGPU commands inside the UI.
Through .NET MAUI Embedding, controls from vendors such as Syncfusion, Telerik, Infragistics, DevExpress and Esri previously ran only on iOS, Android, macOS and Windows. They now work on every Uno Platform target, including the web and Linux. In the other direction, existing .NET MAUI apps can reach the browser and Linux through Uno Platform’s .NET MAUI handlers.
Microsoft.UI.Reactor, Microsoft’s declarative C# framework for WinUI with hooks such as UseState and no XAML, now runs on desktop, browser, Android and iOS. It is enabled with the Reactor UnoFeature, is in preview, and can coexist with existing XAML pages in the same visual tree. Apple TV support is added through the net10.0-tvos target framework, targets tvOS 15 and later, renders through Metal and uses the Siri Remote for focus navigation. .NET 11 is supported on every head, for example through dotnet new unoapp -tfm net11.0, while .NET 10 remains the long-term support option.
RichTextBlock and RichEditBox are now available on every platform, closing an issue opened in 2018. WinUI alignment continues with ItemsRepeater and ItemsView ported from current WinUI sources, LinedFlowLayout, the TitleBar control, multiple windows on iPad and Lottie rendering through Composition. Smaller additions include built-in input validation through INotifyDataErrorInfo, TalkBack, VoiceOver and AT-SPI screen-reader support, and the uno-devserver app command for launching and inspecting running apps from scripts and CI.
The breaking changes are:
- Native rendering is retired, although native views such as maps and video players can still be embedded.
- Uno.Sdk single-project apps are the only supported project format, with the UNOB0029 and UNOB0022 diagnostics for older projects.
- Mac Catalyst is removed, and macOS apps use the net10.0-desktop head.
- Apps target net10.0 by default, and the Windows head uses Windows App SDK 2.4. Minimum versions are iOS and tvOS 15.0, Android API 24 and Windows 10 19041.
- Libraries built against 6.x are binary-incompatible and must be rebuilt, and DependencyObject is now a single class without DependencyObjectStore.
Most apps upgrade by changing the Uno.Sdk version in global.json, following the migration guide. The team released Uno Platform Studio 3.3 alongside it.
The release follows Uno Platform 6.7 in September, which added Android TV, Android Auto and Wear OS targets, semantic styles shared by the Material and Simple themes, and damage-region repainting on Skia renderers. It also removed the WPF targets.

articles.title: Jordan Belfort’s new AI voice startup, Tone, wants to sell like the 'Wolf of Wall Street' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Years ago, as questions mounted about WeWork’s soaring valuation, I sat down with co-founder Adam Neumann. We were negotiating a stage interview, and he asked to meet me twice in the weeks leading up to it, once at a WeWork in San Francisco and again at his office in New York.
I knew full well that the numbers that SoftBank in particular had assigned to WeWork made little sense, but I came away understanding why investors wanted to throw in their lot with him.
It’s similarly easy to understand why people are enchanted by Jordan Belfort, the self-proclaimed “Wolf of Wall Street.” Belfort famously pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont, the Long Island brokerage where salespeople pushed penny stocks in pump-and-dump schemes while Belfort acquired a Southampton mansion, a 167-foot yacht, and at least one helicopter. (He destroyed the latter two while high on quaaludes and cocaine, as depicted in Martin Scorsese’s famous adaptation of Belfort’s autobiography, “The Wolf of Wall Street.”)
You might think someone who spent 22 months in prison and was ordered to pay $110.4 million in restitution to 1,513 victims wouldn’t get another shake. The victims ultimately received “far less” than they were owed, TMZ reported in July, noting that Belfort completed his court-ordered restitution obligations in late April of this year.
But Belfort, whose energy has a galvanizing quality, keeps resurfacing, including in recent years as a Miami-based sales consultant and one-time host of crypto workshops at his Miami Beach home. (A New York Times reporter attended a weekend workshop several years ago where the price of admission was one bitcoin or its equivalent value at the time of $40,000.)
Now he is moving into the intersection of what he knows best — sales — and the hottest trend on the planet, AI, building out a voice-based AI platform. The secret sauce is that it imbues its voices with the kind of tonality that wins deals, he says, for example, by phrasing declarative statements as questions (which “builds engagement”) and even whispering at times (which “implies scarcity of information”).
Belfort says the platform, called Tone, is already being used by companies that have more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Now, in a move that could also help expand its training data, Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and authors who want to turn their books into “expressive AI-generated narration.” Users can select from Tone’s AI voices or, as a voice-cloning feature rolls out, create a clone of their own voice.
It’s easy to argue the market is already saturated with AI voice startups and technologies, and Tone comes with added risk: Belfort’s co-founder in the business is longtime investor Shervin Pishevar, who has a controversial past of his own. We also can’t independently verify that the technology works as described (neither co-founder is an engineer).
But if my time with Neumann taught me anything, it’s that doubts about the numbers rarely get in the way of a good pitch. When Belfort looks for investors to back him in this new venture, finding believers won’t be too hard.
Here is part of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
What have you built?
It’s a very unique way of going about building a voice, and it stems from a system of influence and persuasion I’ve been teaching since the late 1980s. It’s not just what you say, but how you say it. When you’re not in person, body language collapses into tonality. There are about 15 very powerful tonalities that people use all the time. The phrase I invented for this was “goal-oriented communication.” If I’m trying to be perceived as an expert, I apply tonality strategically.
Is this effectively trained on you?
It started that way. As a non-engineer, I went to first principles: How would I teach a human to do this? One tonality at a time. I have 30 years of super high-quality data , and I started teaching the model. It was a breakthrough moment, because it not only sounded exactly like me, it had nailed the tonality. Then I taught it a second one, and then how to link them. The key to all of this is data. Even the littlest bit of corrupt data dramatically negates the progress you’ve made.
How did you and Shervin Pishevar come together?
Shervin and I have been personal friends for a long time, and we were out for dinner one night. I had been pitched by an AI company that said it had an AI that could do selling. I listened to it. It was awful. But it put the idea in my head. I thought I was just going to teach models how to sell, but I couldn’t find a voice that was good enough. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we built our own.
Who are your customers, and how do they use it?
We have law firms and health insurance companies. We do a lot in polling and automobiles. It will take you through an entire health insurance sale. It asks qualifying questions, like what type of insurance you want, your budget, your ages. Then it chooses a plan and explains the features and benefits. Our latency is like 600 milliseconds. If the payment is too high, it’ll say it can bring the payment down and explain how to raise your deductible. If you don’t like the plan, it swaps you to a different one. It does literally the whole entire sale.
How does the AI handle a sales call that goes off script?
It never says, “That’s a great question,” unless it really is. I hate that. It’s so ingratiating. In any sale there’s a happy path, how we’d want the perfect conversation to go, and every last word can be mapped out. But people have questions and concerns, and they take you off the straight line. So the trick is a model that can carry that perfect conversation, handle anything thrown at it, answer elegantly and return to the straight line, without breaking rapport and without hallucinating — or, as a salesperson, lying. We’ve trained the model to do that.
Have you generated any revenue from Tone yet? Have you raised funding for it?
Revenue, probably about a million bucks — $700,000, maybe. We’ve raised friends and family and seed, about $10 million.
I want to address the elephant in the room. You have a fraud conviction. Pishevar has faced misconduct allegations that he denies. Why should a bank or a hospital or a consumer brand trust this product coming from the two of you?
All I can say for myself is that I did make mistakes. It was a very, very long time ago, and I’ve spent the last 20-plus years teaching people all over the world. I’ve been hired by companies all over the world to teach sales and persuasion. If some companies don’t want to work with us, that’s their decision. But I think there would be more than enough that would see the value of what we created.
What close rate does Tone have versus a typical sales force?
I still don’t think it’s quite as good as a top producer. A top producer in the field would outdo it call for call. I think that will change in the next six months to a year. To make a model respond this quickly, you’re not using frontier models. We’re using our own very small, very light models, so they don’t have quite as much intelligence. I think it will significantly outperform a mediocre closer.
Where is it used most effectively? Low-dollar sales opportunities? I’d think the more money someone is spending, the more human contact they’d demand.
I don’t think it’s about replacing humans. What I see most with customers is that they simply don’t have the human capital available. They could get a lot more leads than they have people to call, or they need coverage at different times of day or in different languages. I think there’s always going to be a need for great human salespeople. I really believe that.
You’re competing with ElevenLabs and Cartesia and a lot of other voice AI companies. Tone is your edge?
I don’t think sounding human is really what this is about. They’ll all sound human in six months or a year. It’s the application of tonality that makes us different: the intelligence behind when it chooses a certain tonality. We have a patent on it. ElevenLabs is a great company, and Cartesia as well, but those voices didn’t work for us.
The FCC ruled in 2024 that AI voices fall under robocall rules under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. How does outbound sales calling work?
We only call opt-in. You’re not going to use AI to cold-call people. We would not allow that. You’d get sued by every TCPA lawyer in the world. It’s either opted-in leads or existing customers. The exception is polling, where there’s an exemption that lets you call private homes without opt-in.
How do you verify consent and prevent impersonation in voice cloning?
We could launch the cloning tomorrow. We didn’t. If you create a clone in our system, you speak into the computer, so we know who is creating it, and that person signs a consent. If someone wants to upload audio, which we don’t recommend, you’d have to match a live voiceprint in real time.
Who created the technology? You’re not an engineer, and Pishevar isn’t, either. I saw a name on the patent, Jordan Anthony Metzner.
No. Our VP of engineering is Ben Sussman. He’s a brilliant engineer. I’m the judge and the jury and the executioner of what sounds perfect. I’ll prototype something in the most obscene way, and my engineers rebuild it from scratch.
Do you charge per minute, or based on the outcomes customers see?
A combination. For streaming, it’s per minute. The content platform will be monthly subscriptions. And we have some clients where the bulk of our money is made through success.
Is this an independent company or something that belongs inside a larger AI company?
If the right offer came up, and it was substantial enough, and I thought it made sense, who wouldn’t entertain a conversation? But right now my plan is to raise a significant amount. I don’t think we need to own data centers, but we need enough reserve compute. I wouldn’t think I’d be selling it anytime soon, but who knows what the future brings.
Paramount+ released a documentary about you this summer. Did you watch it?
I didn’t. Believe it or not, I don’t watch or read anything about me, good or bad. I never read a comment. When you’re well-known, you have to live by who you are inside. I go by my own internal compass.

articles.title: How Duco transforms financial data automation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Duco transforms financial data automation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Financial institutions face a critical challenge: processing massive volumes of data with speed, accuracy, and compliance while operating under some of the world’s strictest regulatory frameworks. Duco is the agentic Operations platform for financial services, serving tier-one banks and other financial institutions. It processes 20 billion transactions monthly for 200+ clients, including 7 of the top 20 banks and 10 of the top 20 asset managers. To keep pace as data processing demands grew, Duco evolved from traditional machine learning models to the agentic AI capabilities of Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. In this post, we share how Duco rebuilt its agentic AI stack on these services, cutting deployment time and onboarding costs while keeping each bank’s data isolated.
The challenge: Scaling intelligence in a regulated environment
Duco’s platform empowers teams to automate mission-critical data processes using AI and no-code models, handling everything from data extraction to downstream publication. It already used traditional machine learning models for predictive labeling and pattern recognition, helping banks consolidate and automate over 20,000 processes.
However, these classical machine learning approaches had inherent limitations. They required extensive historical data for training, struggled with novel scenarios, and demanded significant customization for each new use case. Most critically, they couldn’t adapt quickly to the diverse, constantly evolving data formats and business rules that characterize modern financial operations.
        “The classical prediction models worked to an extent, but they weren’t agile or flexible enough. Traditional machine learning models can only amplify what they’ve already learned — they can’t help with the next step or find new problems.”
— Rob Gates, Chief Architect and Innovation Officer, Duco
The solution: Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore
Duco made a strategic decision to adopt Amazon Bedrock for managed access to foundation models, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to run agents at scale. This was more than a technology upgrade. It was a fundamental shift in how its system could understand, reason about, and act on financial data.
About Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore
Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers a choice of high-performing foundation models from leading AI companies through a single API, along with a broad set of capabilities to build generative AI applications with security, privacy, and responsible AI. Learn more about Amazon Bedrock.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale. Build with any open source framework and any model. Connect agents to your tools and data with authentication and access controls built in. Monitor and improve agents in production with tracing and evaluation. AgentCore handles the infrastructure so you focus on agent logic, not backend plumbing, and you get enterprise security and reliability without giving up open source flexibility.
Learn more on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore product page.
Why Amazon Bedrock?
Several factors made Amazon Bedrock the ideal choice for Duco’s regulated financial services industry (FSI) environment:
- Security and compliance first: With Amazon Bedrock, customer data stays within the AWS environment, and it is not used to train models. With private endpoints in its virtual private cloud (VPC), Duco can connect to internal systems while keeping them completely isolated, which matters for sensitive financial data processing.
- Model flexibility: Access to leading foundation models from the Amazon Nova 2 family, Anthropic, OpenAI, Cohere, Meta, and Mistral AI through a single API means Duco can choose the right model for each task. Duco can switch between models by changing a configuration parameter.
- Built for financial services: Amazon Bedrock provides the robust governance controls and compliance frameworks that financial services require, avoiding infrastructure complexity while maintaining the security standards tier-one banks demand.
Choosing AgentCore as the runtime
Duco’s existing agent infrastructure was built on LangChain and LangGraph, both of which were already in production. When evaluating runtime options for its agentic workloads, AgentCore emerged as the clear choice for three key reasons:
- Compatibility with existing primitives: AgentCore is fully compatible with Duco’s existing LangChain and LangGraph code, so most existing code continued to work without modification.
- Managed runtime: Instead of Duco running its own agent infrastructure, AgentCore provides a fully managed runtime, reducing operational overhead for the engineering team.
- Regulated environment suitability: AgentCore met the stringent requirements of deploying in regulated financial services environments, with built-in security and compliance controls.
Multi-tenant architecture: Isolation by design
Duco’s platform operates as a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) offering with strict tenant isolation (figure 1). This is a non-negotiable requirement for regulated institutions. The architecture reflects this at every layer, from the underlying cloud infrastructure right up to the AI agent runtime.
Infrastructure layer
- Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) clusters with namespace-per-tenant isolation and network segregation help maintain workload separation at the Kubernetes layer.
- Per-tenant dedicated AWS services: every tenant receives a dedicated Amazon Aurora MySQL database, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) storage bucket, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption keys, Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) messaging stack, Amazon ElastiCache layer, and Amazon Cognito user pool. Zero shared data infrastructure across clients.
- Per-tenant autoscaling helps minimize the impact of one client’s compute-intensive workload on another tenant’s performance.
Security and access control
Isolation is enforced through identity as well as infrastructure, with every hop between the user and their data authenticated (figure 2):
- Tenant-scoped authentication: every request carries a JSON Web Token (JWT) issued by the tenant’s dedicated Cognito user pool, validated by the inbound authorizer of the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, before agent logic runs.
- Gateway-mediated tool access: agents reach tools only through the tenant’s dedicated AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which passes calls through to the tenant’s container-based Model Context Protocol (MCP) services running in Amazon EKS.
- End-to-end user identity: the user’s identity is passed through to downstream services, and each MCP server validates both the agent’s and the user’s identity against the tenant’s Cognito user pool, so every tool call is authorized as the calling user, made by a trusted agent.
- Private networking: tenants share a VPC and Amazon EKS cluster, segregated by namespace and network policy, with private endpoints keeping traffic to Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore on the AWS network. Each tenant’s AgentCore runtime runs in VPC network mode, with network interfaces in the private subnets, so its outbound traffic enters the VPC and is governed by security groups.
Agent layer
The isolation principle extends fully into the agent architecture:
- One AgentCore runtime and Gateway per tenant: each tenant is served by a dedicated runtime and Gateway, configured against that tenant’s own Cognito user pool and Amazon EKS namespace. Combined with the built-in session isolation of AgentCore, this means there is no shared memory, context, or tooling between clients. Each bank’s unique schemas, naming conventions, and institutional knowledge remain completely isolated from other tenants.
- Per-tenant MCP servers: each tenant has its own set of MCP servers providing service-specific capabilities, dynamically discovered at boot time.
The architecture helps maintain a model where each agent only has access to one bank’s data, context, and reasoning, facilitating real isolation of context across banks.
Multi-model strategy
Rather than committing to a single foundation model, Duco uses the right model for each job, assigning each role in its agent design to the model best suited to it. This approach delivers both quality and cost efficiency by matching the right model capability to each specific workload:
| Model | Primary role | Use cases | 
| Anthropic Claude Opus | Planning agent | For complex reasoning and understanding, formulating up front plans for other agents to execute on | 
| Anthropic Claude Sonnet | Main reasoning & complex decision-making | Exception investigation, reconciliation logic, rule interpretation | 
| Anthropic Claude Haiku | Lightweight tool routing decisions | Fast routing choices, low-latency classification, cost-efficient first-pass triage | 
| Amazon Nova 2 Pro | Tool output summarization | Condensing MCP tool responses, generating readable summaries for analysts | 
This multi-model approach is architecturally designed to allow model swapping without disrupting the stack, which is critical in a landscape where model capabilities evolve rapidly.
Solving context bloat: The MCP skills architecture
One of Duco’s most significant technical innovations addresses a challenge familiar to anyone building production agent systems: context window management.
The problem
With 300–400 tools exposed per tenant through AgentCore Gateway (which fronts a separate MCP server for each underlying Duco service), approximately 200,000 tokens of tool descriptions were loaded into context before work began. This caused context overloading: response quality degraded as conversations lengthened, and the model lost the thread of earlier reasoning. The team emphasized that a feeling an agent is becoming less capable isn’t enough evidence on its own. Evaluations must be run before engineering decisions are made.
The solution: On-demand skills loading
Duco created a skills architecture using MCP resource types to move tool descriptions out of the static context and load them only when needed:
- skill:// resources — on-demand tool descriptions loaded only when a skill is required.
- system:// resources — dynamic system prompt sections composed at runtime, keeping the base system prompt lean.
- ui:// resources — UI-specific resources, isolated from operational tooling.
Three new meta-tools, implemented in Duco’s agent harness, replaced the bloated tool description payload:
- load_skill — fetches skill descriptions on demand, only when the agent determines a skill is needed.
- find_tool — locates relevant tools without loading all schemas into context.
- invoke_tool — executes the selected tool once identified.
The results
- 90% context reduction: Main context reduced from 200,000 tokens to approximately 20,000 tokens by moving tool descriptions out of static context and limiting the size of tool responses.
- Prompt caching preserved: the static prompt prefix (system prompt plus the three meta-tools) stays small and stable, and skills load into the conversation rather than the tool list, so loading a skill does not invalidate the cache.
- Measurably improved agent response quality: validated through a rigorous evaluation framework.
- Zero infrastructure changes required: same underlying models, same tools, and same tasks, with measurably better outcomes.
MCP tool discovery: Deploy a service, gain a capability
A key architectural decision was implementing MCP tool discovery at boot time. When a new service is deployed, its MCP server is registered as a target on the tenant’s AgentCore Gateway as part of the deployment. When an agent boots, the harness builds a registry of every tool the Gateway exposes and shares just the tool names. The agent then uses find_tool and invoke_tool to discover the details and invoke tools on demand. As a result, the agent automatically gains that capability with no redeployment or agent reconfiguration required. Access control is enforced by the underlying services themselves: because the user’s identity is passed through the Gateway, each tool call succeeds only if that user is permitted to perform the action.
This provides operational agility: the platform team can ship new capabilities to agents by deploying a new microservice, without touching the agent configuration or requiring downtime. For a platform that serves 200+ clients with diverse and evolving operational needs, this dynamic capability model is a significant competitive advantage.
Deploying agents at scale
Duco implemented Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore to power two critical workflows that previously required extensive manual effort:
1. Intelligent onboarding
Previously, onboarding new reconciliation processes was a manual, time-intensive exercise requiring significant professional services resources. Banks would take years to migrate thousands of processes, moving at a pace of roughly one per week.
With Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore, Duco can now:
- Automatically understand diverse file formats and data structures across legacy and modern systems.
- Translate legacy configurations from existing systems into structured Duco processes.
- Parse complex spreadsheet macros written decades ago that no one fully understands.
- Deploy new reconciliations 10× faster than before.
One global bank experienced a 70% decrease in onboarding costs for new reconciliations and achieved an increase of over 20% in straight-through processing through better match rates and allocation rules.
2. AI-driven exception investigation
Financial institutions run thousands of quality gates between systems, generating countless exceptions daily. Traditionally, armies of analysts manually investigate each break to determine if it’s worth worrying about, already being investigated, or represents a new risk.
Duco’s agents now handle the “first mile” of investigation:
- Triage new breaks as they arrive, grouping related exceptions that share a likely root cause.
- Check context, such as whether a break is already known, already being worked, or a timing difference expected to clear.
- Investigate by pulling evidence from source data and systems to trace the root cause of each inconsistency, whether a data quality issue, a missing or late record, a mapping or reference data problem, or a genuine mismatch, and explain why it happened.
- Recommend a decision-ready case: the likely cause, a proposed resolution such as an adjustment, a rule change, or an escalation, the alternatives considered, and the supporting evidence.
- Route each case to the right analyst, who reviews the evidence and makes the final call, with every decision recorded in the audit trail.
This agentic approach excels because financial workflows involve highly variable paths through information, exactly the kind of complex, context-heavy reasoning that foundation models handle well.
Operating in a regulated environment
Deploying AI agents in financial services requires more than technical capability. It demands rigorous compliance, auditability, and risk management. Duco’s implementation on Amazon Bedrock addresses these requirements through four core principles:
- Comprehensive observability: Every agent decision is logged in a complete audit trail. Reviewers can trace each decision to check it against regulatory requirements.
- Human-in-the-loop controls: High-risk actions require explicit authorization, with clear escalation pathways for complex scenarios that exceed agent confidence thresholds.
- Fail-safe architecture: Systems default to client protection over operational efficiency, supporting safety even when agents encounter edge cases or unexpected data.
- Regulatory alignment: The platform supports workloads subject to SOC 2 and DORA requirements, with data residency controls per institution.
Results that matter
Duco’s adoption of Amazon Bedrock has delivered measurable, auditable business impact across client deployments:
| 10× Faster reconciliation deployments | 70% Reduction in onboarding costs | 20%+ Increase in straight-through processing | 1000s Hours saved in manual investigation | 
Perhaps most importantly, Duco now has a foundation for rapid innovation. Building new agentic capabilities no longer requires extensive machine learning engineering, so the team can focus on solving business problems rather than managing infrastructure.
Roadmap: The future of human–agent collaboration
Duco’s architecture is designed not to replace workers, but to elevate them. The platform envisions a clear progression in human roles as agentic capabilities mature:
Task Worker → Investigator → Decision Maker
Rather than humans performing repetitive tasks, the future sees operations teams orchestrating multiple agents in parallel with humans making final approval decisions based on agent-prepared analysis. The architecture is designed to support agent-to-agent communication, including cross-firm scenarios where agents at different financial institutions could coordinate.
Conclusion
For regulated financial institutions, Duco’s architecture shows that agentic AI isn’t only viable. It’s already delivering at production scale. Duco rebuilt its agentic AI stack on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, combining strict per-tenant isolation, the right model for each job, and an MCP skills architecture that cut context overhead by 90%. The results include reconciliation deployments 10× faster and, for one global bank, onboarding costs down 70% and straight-through processing up by over 20%. To build a similar multi-tenant setup, start with the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide, then read Building multi-tenant agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore on the AWS Machine Learning Blog. For the operating model behind this work, see Duco’s Agentic Operations: a new operating model for post-trade.

articles.title: Barracuda Hacked Amid Surge in Artex-Powered Cyberattacks
articles.text:
The Artex agentic AI penetration testing framework has become a common tool in Chinese threat actors’ arsenal, and Barracuda is one of its victims.
Published on GitHub in July 2026, Artex relies on a planner to formulate an objective and create tasks based on it, and on agents to perform those tasks, while the platform itself records the progress, findings, and assets.
It reportedly used DeepSeek v4.1-flash as the initial model, but can use other LLMs as well, and GLM-5.3 and Grok 4.6 were observed in certain instances. Overall, however, its users mainly rely on Chinese models, which are more permissive compared to US-made ones.
Artex was designed for security testing, but threat actors have been using it as part of in-the-wild intrusions since at least August, and its occurrence in real-world attacks has increased significantly during the past several weeks.
“The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale,” the FBI warns in a new alert (PDF).
Mentioning the framework’s use in attacks on South Korean financial firms and ConnectWise, the FBI warns of the risks Artex poses: faster attacks through automation, exploitation of neglected peripheral devices, and the ability to find and exploit supply chain attack vectors.
The framework’s developer removed their GitHub repository in October, but Artex continues to proliferate through other channels. In early November, Censys was seeing roughly 1,500 hosts running exposed Artex consoles.
In October, Artex was used by Chinese espionage group Vapor Panda in a campaign targeting over 200 organizations in 14 countries, including “foreign ministries, a European presidency, and US pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, and nuclear organizations,” SentinelOne reports.
Storm-0940 is another Chinese state-sponsored group using Artex, but evidence shows that financially motivated threat actors such as Storm-3358 have also adopted the framework, Cisco’s Talos notes.
Post-exploitation, the threat actors were seen abusing compromised credentials and keys, escalating privileges, deploying persistence, moving laterally, and stealing credentials and data.
“Observed impacts range from access to cloud secrets and mailbox data to the use of compromised applications to reach connected environments,” Talos says.
Amazon describes similar observations, noting that one of the most prominent Artex campaigns was focused on large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, while another targeted cryptocurrency exchanges.
Barracuda, which fell victim to an Artex-powered intrusion, published similar findings: hackers used an exposed valid cloud access key to map its reach, then reused discovered secrets to access more systems and exfiltrate more credentials and secrets.
“In all, the attacker touched about 10 cloud accounts in roughly 44 hours. The work was methodical and tireless. The probe names, the other indicators we collected, the order in which the attacker worked through our systems, and its built-in routines for hunting credentials and wallets all match Artex,” Barracuda explains.
The attack unfolded between November 1 and November 2, targeted sensitive material across secret stores, configurations, Kubernetes service accounts, and server metadata services, and left a backdoor behind in a Kubernetes cluster.
On some servers, the attackers gained shell access and used it to search for Ethereum keystore files, seed phrase files, extended private keys, and other wallet-related information.
The attack, Barracuda says, was similar to the October intrusion at cloud application hosting platform Railway. Furthermore, it fits the previously reported wave of intrusions at dozens of AI developer platforms.
Barracuda has not attributed the attack, noting that Artex is used by many groups.
Amazon’s analysis of two Artex-powered campaigns revealed that the attackers relied on long-known techniques, but operated at far greater speeds courtesy of AI.
“The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software. Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense,” Amazon says.
“The reported Artex activity shows that autonomous attackers don’t need a zero-day. They can find exposed services, exploit authorization gaps, and keep adapting while defenders are still triaging alerts and approving a response. When every defensive action has to wait for a person, the attacker controls the pace. Defenders need to move from identifying exposure to verified protection at machine speed,” Miggo Security co-founder and CEO Daniel Shechter said.
Related: Is AI Making Us Worse at Cybersecurity?
Related: OpenAI Unveils Daybreak Red Team, Defense Factory Security Tools
Related: Notion Customer Data Compromised in Fireworks AI Hack
Related: Google Widens Gemini 4 Carbon Access After AI Agents Verify Signal Code

O Edge 70 Pro de 512 GB está saindo por R$ 3.869 no Pix no Magazine Luiza. O celular da Motorola, com câmeras de 50 MP e bateria de longa duração, recebe desconto de 36% sobre o preço original de R$ 5.999 durante a Black November 2026, o menor valor entre os principais varejistas.
Todas as câmeras do Edge 70 Pro, lançamento recente da Motorola, são de 50 MP: há uma wide com OIS e uma ultrawide, que captam belas cenas ao ar livre, telefoto periscópica com zoom óptico de 3,5x para aproximações, e frontal que tira ótimas selfies. articles.title: Neural Rendering Could Keep Xbox Project Helix Affordable
articles.text:
Monday, November 16th 2026
Neural Rendering Could Keep Xbox Project Helix Affordable
For the 25th anniversary of Xbox, celebrating one of its longest-running projects, Microsoft announced that it sees great potential in new technologies that could lower hardware costs while enhancing visual fidelity. According to Jason Ronald, Xbox VP for next-generation technologies, neural rendering could be one of those technologies that significantly boosts visual fidelity. This would allow the compute requirements to remain within the limits of what a console can support, rather than needing a full workstation, and fit within a home entertainment form factor. Not only would raw compute be lower, but actual memory demand would also be reduced, as neural rendering tends to be more efficient, which is particularly useful when memory is in short supply.
Jason Ronald, Xbox Vice President of Next GenerationThis is a big reason why we're really focused on advancements like neural rendering, because it's an entirely new way to generate a frame without requiring more computational horsepower, additional memory, and things like that.
Neural rendering employs AI to enhance lighting, shadows, and material details using information from the game engine. This technology acts as a final rendering stage, building on the original frame, geometry, textures, and lighting data. This method enables developers to incorporate more realistic lighting and material effects without having to explicitly model and render all the additional details. AMD will power Xbox Project Helix, which suggests we can expect more AI cores embedded in the semi-custom SoCs that power Xbox, featuring next-generation RDNA 5 / UDNA graphics IP.
Sources:
				Xbox, 				via VideoCardz			
	
	
	
		
	
		
17 Comments on Neural Rendering Could Keep Xbox Project Helix Affordable

www.nybooks.com/articles/2019/10/24/zadie-smith-in-defense-of-fiction/

It takes the output frame and runs it through an image to image AI model.
You can literally use DLSS 5 in comfyui, no motion vectors needed.
Ultimately it has some fundamental issues right now like being screen space only, influencing the art style, and it destroys details in brights and darks.
The screen space part is why you see the constantly color shifting as the camera moves around.
Hard to say how fast these issues will be solved. Nvidia recently increased performance but a chunk of that was due to lowering the model size. Making the effect not just screen space will massively increase performance requirements. The other issues are going to be hard to address as well. DLSS upscaling is able to be a more transparent effect because it has a very limited scope. DLSS 5 on the otherhand doesn't. It runs into the same issue other image gen models do.
What I can say is if this starts getting used en mass without resolving these issues, it will hurt in the industry in the long run. Everything will look more similar and there'd be even more artifacts added into the picture. It's always AAA games implementing these things as well. Probably why indies have overwhelming been the source of good games for a long while now, outside of a few outliers.

And that the NR stage would be used in place of path-tracing at home to get a similar effect but cheaper. As it is now, NR doesn't match path-tracing in performance or look for a game. Hopefully it does someday.

Basically in order to get a generationally better output without making a $2-3000 console they'll leverage neural rendering and make a 1000-1500 console. (depending on where the component apocalypse is when it releases)

(The tiktok generation loves this stuff and that's probably the demographic they are going for so I get it)
The whole argument here is either consoles do the standard brute force approach and require another (die shrunk) 300mm^2 GPU with ~12-16GB of RAM (or more) which would immediately set a $750-1000 price floor, or maybe they go with a 150-200mm^2 GPU with 8-12GB of RAM that is built around Neural Rendering (and upscaling and frame generation) to "fake" better graphics that comes in at a floor of $500-750 instead.
