articles.title: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future
articles.text:
Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades.
Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round.
Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago.
For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it.
Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow.
Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors.
Recently, she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before.
Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA?
A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain.
A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before.
If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner.
Q: What’s an example of that in practice ?
A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity.
In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication.
Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today.
Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms?
A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned.
As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing.
For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with Coherent and Lumentum.
Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly.
Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else?
A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing.
If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.”
That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them.
Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen?
A: It goes back to relationships. When you decide that you’re going to push a line hard to increase volume, you have to have the relationships. You have to know their processes in detail. You have to know their people in detail, and they have to trust you. Only then are you in a position to ask them for special favors, because you can do it surgically, and your ask is credible and reasonable.
And when you’re successful together, they’re happy, you’re happy, and the appreciation for the partnership deepens. We all appreciate those that make us successful.
Q: How do you prioritize resources across the supply chain?
A: You need to first understand what the most critical components are, and protect and prioritize production around them. We need wafers like we need air. And the critical component is the TSMC chip. As it comes out of assembly every week, we decide what factory gets what chip.
Every week, we look at factory performance. If a particular factory yield is low, if their time of ownership is not at the level we want, they don’t get more chips that week.
We keep track of every chip, from the identification number on the die all the way to the customer invoice. If you want to be our supplier, you have to support that traceability process. With that process, we took the time it takes from chip out at TSMC to system out at Foxconn and Wistron from five to two weeks when supply and demand requires it.
Think of the supply chain as a large circulatory system with pathways everywhere — and when you need to accelerate any branch of it, you have the power to do that. We have the capability to do that. It’s empowering and exciting.
Q: What’s an example of a time things didn’t go as planned? How did you, the team and your partners find a way forward?
A: We were getting ready to go to volume production with Foxconn and Wistron for the compute board of NVIDIA GB200. The last step in the process was a test managed by an automated handler — a completely new approach for us, developed to meet the demands of high-volume throughput for these complicated products. During the initial ramp, the throughput was significantly below plan.
The operations director of Taiwan manufacturing made the call that to protect the product and shipments, he needed to disable the entire process and return to manual test loading. Our manufacturers backed him without question and brought in the necessary manpower to meet the immediate needs, literally hundreds of operators. That kept production moving, but would not solve the throughput requirement of full production.
As with any operations problem, the root cause had many elements to it: test tray assembly, test tray design, automation hardware design, automation control software, product yield. From all viewpoints, it was a difficult problem to resolve quickly.
That’s when we executed the NVIDIA swarm. Teams from NVIDIA design engineering, operations industrial, and product and test engineering, as well as from Foxconn automation engineering, flooded the line with talent to redesign and reactivate the line before the scale ramp hit.
This is not an unusual occurrence when there is a problem in operations. All teams at NVIDIA are street fighters — action-oriented, and know no organizational boundaries. We say that “the mission is the boss,” but we also live “the mission is the boss.”
Q: What makes this work so exciting for you?
A: Operations is a very empowering place to be at NVIDIA. Our team is designing and implementing changes to the supply chain constantly to meet the strong demand of our new products. The challenges are understandably high, but we’re always given the resources we need to be successful. The only thing between our goals and our success is our own creativity. That is exhilarating.

articles.title: Após décadas de atrasos, avião espacial pode finalmente estrear em 2027
articles.text:
O avião espacial Dream Chaser, desenvolvido pela empresa estadunidense Sierra Space, superou etapa importante antes de sua primeira missão orbital. A Administração Federal de Aviação dos Estados Unidos (FAA, na sigla em inglês) autorizou o retorno da nave à Terra, abrindo caminho para o voo inaugural, previsto para a primavera de 2027 no Hemisfério Norte.
A aprovação permite que a espaçonave pouse na antiga pista de aterrissagem dos ônibus espaciais, no Centro Espacial Kennedy, na Flórida (EUA), ou na Base da Força Espacial de Vandenberg, na Califórnia (EUA). A missão inicial não será tripulada e servirá como teste em órbita terrestre.
A Sierra Space, responsável pelo desenvolvimento do veículo, agradeceu à FAA pela colaboração e pelo apoio à inovação comercial no setor espacial. A agência concluiu que as operações previstas não devem provocar impactos ambientais significativos.
Dream Chaser terá pouso semelhante ao de um avião
- Com aproximadamente nove metros de comprimento, o Dream Chaser foi projetado para ser reutilizável. Diferentemente das cápsulas espaciais tradicionais, que normalmente retornam à Terra com auxílio de paraquedas, o veículo tem asas e foi desenvolvido para pousar horizontalmente em uma pista convencional;
- O projeto está em desenvolvimento há mais de duas décadas. Embora tenha realizado testes de queda a partir de aeronaves, o Dream Chaser ainda não chegou ao espaço;
- A nave foi inicialmente considerada pela NASA para transportar astronautas de e para a Estação Espacial Internacional (ISS, na sigla em inglês). Em 2014, porém, a agência escolheu a Boeing e a SpaceX para prestar esse serviço, com as espaçonaves Starliner e Crew Dragon, respectivamente;
- No ano seguinte, a então responsável pelo projeto, Sierra Nevada Corporation, apresentou versão de carga do avião espacial. Em 2016, a NASA selecionou a empresa para realizar pelo menos seis missões não tripuladas de abastecimento da estação orbital;
- O cronograma, entretanto, sofreu sucessivos atrasos. O Dream Chaser deveria inicialmente viajar a bordo do foguete Atlas V, da United Launch Alliance (ULA), mas acabou transferido para o Vulcan Centaur, sucessor do lançador;
- A nave estava prevista para participar da segunda missão do Vulcan, mas não ficou pronta a tempo. Em outubro de 2024, o foguete realizou o voo sem o avião espacial.
Leia mais:
- Falta pouco! Espaçonave da NASA chega a um dia-luz de distância da Terra esta semana
- Captura inédita da Starship mostra até onde a SpaceX chegou – e o que ainda falta resolver
- Elon Musk revela planos para versão do Starship ainda maior
Primeiro voo será um teste em órbita
Agora, a Sierra Space trabalha com a primavera estadunidense de 2027 como previsão para a primeira decolagem do Dream Chaser. A missão será um voo de demonstração livre em órbita terrestre, sem passageiros.
A empresa também busca oportunidades para utilizar o veículo em diferentes tipos de contratos, incluindo missões para a NASA, as Forças Armadas dos Estados Unidos e companhias privadas.
Entre as possibilidades estão operações relacionadas a futuras estações espaciais comerciais. A Sierra Space, por exemplo, integra o consórcio responsável pelo desenvolvimento da Orbital Reef, estação privada planejada para operar em órbita.
A autorização da FAA representa mais um avanço para o projeto, mas o Dream Chaser ainda precisará demonstrar que consegue completar uma missão espacial com segurança. Depois de tantos adiamentos, o voo previsto para 2027 será teste decisivo para o futuro do avião espacial.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Google enciende las alarmas: la IA podría lanzar ciberataques sin ayuda humana
articles.text:
Uno de los peores miedos de los especialistas en seguridad está a punto de volverse realidad. Google advirtió que los ciberataques totalmente automatizados con IA llegarían en poco tiempo, por lo que es necesario prepararse. La compañía dijo que los hackers están empezando a usar sistemas de IA capaces de identificar vulnerabilidades, desarrollar exploits y comprometer sistemas de forma remota y sin ayuda humana.
Según una nueva investigación del Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), varios actores maliciosos han comenzado a desplegar marcos de trabajo agénticos. Estos sistemas compuestos por varios agentes de IA pueden trabajar y colaborar entre sí para ejecutar las distintas fases de un ataque. Entre las herramientas descubiertas por el grupo de seguridad se encuentran ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI y HexStrike AI.
Si bien esta no es la primera vez en que Google advierte sobre la ola de ciberataques con IA, los hallazgos del GTIG van más lejos. Los hackeos autónomos se han incrementado en los últimos meses y el ejemplo más evidente fue lo que ocurrió con Hugging Face. Si hacemos memoria, un grupo de agentes de OpenAI escapó de su entorno seguro y vulneró los sistemas de seguridad de la startup, un hecho que se replicó después en una oficina de gobierno en Australia.
¿Qué son los ciberataques automatizados con IA?
Desde hace décadas, un ciberataque siempre requería la participación de una o más personas. Los atacantes deben buscar vulnerabilidades, analizarlas, desarrollar un método de explotación, obtener acceso al sistema y moverse dentro de la infraestructura comprometida. Esto involucra diversas habilidades que van desde la programación hasta la ingeniería social.
Tras la llegada de modelos como Claude Fable y GPT-6 Astra, los hackers han buscado automatizar este proceso. La clave de todo está en los agentes, a los que pueden asignarse tareas específicas para llevar a cabo cada una de las fases del ataque con supervisión mínima o incluso inexistente. A diferencia de un humano, estos agentes de IA no duermen y pueden intentar vulnerar sistemas cientos o miles de veces hasta lograr su cometido.
Google menciona que los nuevos sistemas automatizados son efectivos con vulnerabilidades poco complejas y sistemas conectados a internet que no se han actualizado. Esto último es evidente en los hackeos a los sistemas de refrigeración de supermercados y bancos de sangre en Europa, en donde los atacantes aprovecharon un componente desactualizado que permitió explotar una vulnerabilidad.
Así funcionan los nuevos marcos de ataque que usan los hackers
De acuerdo con el GTIG, algunos de los frameworks que utilizan los hackers operan como una cadena automatizada. Primero analizan actualizaciones de software y comparan versiones antiguas y nuevas del código para detectar las partes que se corrigieron. A partir de ahí, la IA intentará deducir la vulnerabilidad, crear un exploit y ejecutarlo automáticamente contra posibles objetivos.
Los investigadores de Google encontraron evidencia de un sistema denominado exploit_agent, el cual se alojaba en un servidor expuesto y realizaba el proceso sin ayuda humana. El marco integraba varios modelos de IA y podía llevar a cabo análisis de código, generar exploits para comprometer sistemas y ejecutar tareas como instalar webshells o realizar reconocimiento interno.
El informe del GTIG señala que el peligro de estos sistemas radica en que reduce el tiempo de reacción para los equipos de seguridad. Si una vulnerabilidad puede analizarse y explotarse automáticamente apenas se publica un parche, algunas empresas no alcanzarían a actualizar sus sistemas para impedir el hackeo. Google advierte que los ataques con agentes de IA se incrementarán en los próximos meses, pudiendo operar sin participación humana en un futuro no muy lejano.

articles.title: Hacker gets Doom running on a USB flash drive's built-in LCD, played by copying files — hacker dumps firmware from chip with scrubbed markings through an open debug port, then gets the game running with AI help
articles.text:
Hacker gets Doom running on a USB flash drive's built-in LCD, played by copying files — hacker dumps firmware from chip with scrubbed markings through an open debug port, then gets the game running with AI help
Key presses turn into bursts of reads and writes to play the game.
Doom now runs on a USB flash drive’s built-in LCD and is played by copying files to and from it, as hardware hacker Aaron Christophel showed in a teardown video. The marking on the drive’s display chip had been removed, but an open debug port let him extract its firmware, which enabled identification. He was then able to use AI to reverse-engineer the hardware and get the game running on the drive’s screen.
The off-the-shelf drive, the MOVESPEED MSSU10, has USB-A on one end and USB-C on the other, and the 128GB model, the smallest capacity in the range, cost him about 50 euros. Its screen normally shows status data such as transfer speed, how full the drive is, and its temperature.
The main flash controller is the Silicon Motion SM2320G, one we have reviewed in portable SSDs like the Kingston XS2000 and Lexar SL660 Blaze, with a separate C*Core CCM4101 microcontroller — which has 2MB of flash and a small amount of RAM to itself — for the 428 x 142 color LCD. The NAND carries SanDisk markings. All of this is fairly standard portable SSD hardware, aside from the display.
The drive’s metal body uses heavily glued plastic end pieces but, past that, the display lifts off first and unplugs. The board slides out after the USB-C end cap is removed, in this case with minor cosmetic damage inflicted. The display chip’s marking is scrubbed, most likely with a laser, by the hacker’s reckoning, which can hinder identification and tinkering. Luckily, a probe on the debug pads, ground, and a 3.3V pin connected on the first try, and memory was immediately readable.
The bootloader returned a version string dated 2023, followed by the full firmware, which helped greatly with identification. He says the chip is marketed as one for security — for fingerprint readers and access control, for example — but no related features were found to be enabled for this drive. He also discovered that, although the data sheet and stock firmware declare a 200 MHz operating clock frequency, it measured 40.2 MHz. This is unexplained.
One critical issue is immediately apparent: how do you play on a drive with no buttons? The display chip has no USB connection of its own and, from the connected PC or host, it only sees the storage controller’s activity, which it uses to gauge transfer speed. The primary storage controller has read and write counters, and the chip pulls these every 50 ms over I2C. Christophel says this is far easier than relying on a single physical button, as he did on a previous power bank mod.
The solution, then, is a PC script, doomctl.py, which turns key presses into small, timed transfers in each direction. The commands are simply encoded as transfer rates, at five levels per direction, and each read/write pair can map to a certain button combination. Arrow keys are for movement and turning, Space or Ctrl for firing and opening doors, and M for the menu, keeping it simple. Ordinary copying, without the script, can still steer, but the control scheme is much nicer.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Performance is…well, not really playable at about 13 frames per second, although the game logic runs at Doom’s normal 35 ticks per second. This is why he names the chip’s clock as the biggest potential performance gain. The game itself is built on DMC100-DOOM, Artur Bieniek’s port for very small microcontrollers. Only the first map, E1M1, fits in the chip’s flash, and no sound is produced as the drive lacks a buzzer. Christophel did play the level end to end, noting the low resolution.
AI did the heavy lifting: the reverse engineering as well as the port, and Christophel said, “I would not be able to do such a thing in a few hours.”
The open-source project, with its code and prebuilt firmware published, is likely to draw attention and may spawn similar hacks. The tools required are relatively minimal, mainly a debug probe, and he does suggest backing up the stock firmware before trying. For his own unit, he put it back together to use as a normal drive, but one that can still play Doom, if so desired.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
articles.text:
Sponsored
Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
While we’re used to predictable technology, AI challenges that assumption. Therefore, the goal must be bounded, observable, and controllable AI.
Provided byUL Solutions
In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.
For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.
AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.
We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.
Where traditional definitions of trust fall short
Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.
Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.
With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.
Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.
Building trust that scales
It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.
Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.
The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.
Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:
- What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution.
- Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds.
- Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step.
- Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows.
- Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle.
The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

articles.title: United Airlines system outage disrupts departures just days after the big ground stop
articles.text:
Less than a week after an issue with air traffic control communications and radar caused the FAA to halt takeoffs nationwide, United Airlines departing flights are being disrupted by an outage. At 6:13PM ET, United said the problem has been fixed:
United Airlines system outage disrupts departures just days after the big ground stop
Is everything down right now?
Is everything down right now?
Earlier today we experienced a technology-related issue that impacted some departing flights. The issue has been resolved. Please check the latest status of your flight at united.com or the United app.
The outage is also coming after last week’s global Microsoft Outlook shutdown, and the great-bank-outage-that-wasn’t earlier Monday afternoon. According to posts on social media, a number of people onboard the planes have heard from their pilots that a systemwide IT outage for United has caused problems with a weight and balance calculator that has stopped them from getting clearance to take off.
United tweeted earlier that “We are troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights. There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.”
Update, November 16th: Added note that United says the problem has been resolved.

articles.title: Apple change d'avis sur l'iPhone Duo : la reconnaissance faciale arrive
articles.text:
L’iPhone Duo est un excellent smartphone, mais un de ses défauts par rapport à l’iPhone 18 Pro est sa technologie de déverrouillage biométrique.
Puisque les capteurs infrarouges nécessaires à la reconnaissance faciale 3D prennent trop de place et devraient être présents en double (sous l’écran externe et sous l’écran interne) pour être efficaces, Apple a remplacé Face ID par Touch ID avec son premier smartphone pliant. Un capteur d’empreintes est accessible sur la bordure droite, sans oublier l’option « Déverrouiller avec l’Apple Watch » qui permet aux porteurs d’une montre connectée d’aller plus vite.
Le 16 novembre 2026, Apple annonce un changement majeur pour son iPhone Duo : la bêta 2 d’iOS 27.3, la future mise à jour qui sera disponible pour tous en décembre, ajoute la reconnaissance faciale à l’iPhone Duo.
Déverrouiller avec son visage sans Face ID : le changement de philosophie inattendu d’Apple
L’annonce d’Apple risque d’en surprendre plus d’un : aucun iPhone n’a jamais fait cohabiter deux technologies de déverrouillage biométriques jusqu’à aujourd’hui. Apple est une des rares entreprises qui assume de décider ce qui est mieux pour ses utilisateurs, alors que tous ses concurrents sous Android proposent à la fois un capteur d’empreinte et une technologie de reconnaissance faciale, généralement 2D, moins sécurisée que Face ID.
Avec iOS 27.3, Apple va tester de la reconnaissance faciale 2D, sans la modélisation infrarouge de Face ID, sur un iPhone. Le système, qui s’appelle « Unlock with front caméra » (Déverrouiller avec la caméra frontale) en anglais, se distingue de Face ID sur plusieurs aspects :
- La reconnaissance faciale de l’iPhone Duo n’est disponible que lorsque l’iPhone est fermé. Il utilise la caméra frontale de l’écran de couverture.
- Apple prévient que la technologie est moins sécurisée que Touch ID ou Face ID, mais estime avoir fait de son mieux pour proposer la reconnaissance faciale 2D la plus sûre du marché. Les données du visage sont enregistrés dans la Secure Exclave, rien n’est collecté en clair.
- La reconnaissance faciale de l’iPhone Duo est un réglage optionnel : Apple ne recommande pas à tout le monde de l’activer. L’idée est que les personnes qui veulent vraiment retrouver une expérience semblable à Face ID puissent le faire.
- Toutes les 45 minutes au départ, la reconnaissance faciale se désactivera. Il faudra utiliser Touch ID pour relancer la reconnaissance faciale pour 45 minutes supplémentaires (et chaque appui sur Touch ID pendant l’utilisation relancera les 45 minutes). Apple indique que ce délai peut évoluer d’ici le lancement final : tout dépendra du retour des utilisateurs.
- Puisque la sécurité est moins bonne que Touch ID, la reconnaissance faciale ne permettra pas d’afficher les mots de passe ou de payer avec Apple Pay. Touch ID reste la technologie principale.
- Sans infrarouge, la reconnaissance faciale de l’iPhone Duo ne marchera pas dans le noir complet. Ce n’est pas une surprise : seul Face ID permet ça.
Malgré de nombreuses limites, la reconnaissance faciale de l’iPhone Duo va permettre de consulter ses messages avec l’iPhone sur un bureau sans avoir à le déverrouiller à chaque fois. L’iPhone Duo est le second appareil Apple, après l’écran domotique HomeView, à utiliser un algorithme de reconnaissance faciale 2D différent de Face ID. Les iPad et Mac y auront-ils droit un jour ? Pour l’instant, Apple ne parle que de l’iPhone Duo.
Pourquoi prendre cette décision maintenant ? On peut imaginer que la reconnaissance faciale 2D est testée depuis de longs mois chez Apple, mais que la marque ne voulait pas en faire une caractéristique de lancement pour éviter la comparaison avec Face ID. Apple ne dit rien sur ce qui l’a motivé à développer cette fonction.
Deux autres nouveautés pour l’iPhone Duo dans iOS 27.3
En plus de la reconnaissance faciale, iOS 27.3 déploiera deux autres nouveautés sur iPhone Duo :
- Un nouveau réglage permettra de mettre le téléphone en veille en le fermant (ce n’est pas possible aujourd’hui, l’app passe du grand écran au petit).
- La fonction Accès facile (Reachability) fait son grand retour pour décaler l’écran vers la droite ou vers la gauche quand le téléphone est fermé, afin de rendre son utilisation à une main possible.
Apple en profite pour mettre à jour le nombre d’applications compatibles avec l’iPhone Duo : il y a désormais 200 000 logiciels adaptés au SDK de l’iPhone Duo, contre 100 000 une semaine plus tôt. De quoi faire taire les principales critiques sur le produit ?

articles.title: Pourquoi il ne faut plus jamais appuyer sur « Mettre à jour plus tard » : Google repère une IA pirate qui transforme chaque correctif en attaque — Frandroid
articles.text:
J’ai un collègue, dont je tais le nom, qui me conseillait d’attendre 2 à 3 jours avant de lancer une mise à jour, car cela laisse le temps de détecter d’éventuels bugs, incompatibilités ou problèmes. C’est une approche de gestion du risque : on accepte un petit risque de sécurité pendant quelques jours pour réduire le risque d’interruption ou de régression. C’est sans doute ce que vous faites avec une mise à jour iOS ou Windows. Mais, c’est peut-être désormais une mauvaise pratique.
En informatique, chaque correctif de sécurité est aussi un aveu involontaire : en colmatant une brèche, un éditeur indique publiquement où elle se trouvait. Des attaquants confient désormais l’analyse de ces mises à jour à une machine infatigable, et plusieurs sites français en ont déjà fait les frais.
Sur un serveur de préproduction mal sécurisé, les chercheurs de Google ont découvert « exploit_agent », un programme autonome qui orchestre plusieurs grands modèles de langage pour rédiger et exécuter des cyberattaques sans intervention humaine. Selon la firme, il s’agit de la première chaîne d’intrusion entièrement automatisée jamais observée en conditions réelles.
Cette révélation figure dans le dernier rapport AI Threat Tracker du Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), publié le 16 novembre avec Mandiant, sa filiale spécialisée dans la réponse aux incidents. Deux mois plus tôt, les mêmes analystes assuraient n’avoir encore croisé aucun agent de ce type dans la nature.
Le mode opératoire glace le sang par sa simplicité : exploit_agent scrute en permanence le code d’applications web populaires avant et après la publication d’un correctif, isole la vulnérabilité réparée, écrit le programme d’attaque (l’exploit) puis passe à l’offensive.
D’après Google, les cibles touchées étaient principalement des sites français issus des médias, du divertissement et de l’éducation, sans attribution formelle, même si des commentaires en russe apparaissent dans la configuration de l’outil.
Du 19 au 30 novembre, le Plaud Note Pro passe à 149 € au lieu de 189 € ! Il enregistre vos réunions, les transcrit et les synthétise pour vous, il suffit d’appuyer sur un bouton. Les Plaud Note, NotePin et NotePin S sont aussi à -20 %. Bref, c’est le moment d’arrêter de perdre du temps au travail !
Les failles déjà corrigées deviennent la cible prioritaire
Pendant des années, les experts redoutaient surtout de voir l’IA dénicher des failles « zero-day », ces brèches totalement inconnues des éditeurs et dépourvues de parade. Le rapport documente un virage bien plus pragmatique vers les failles « n-day » : des vulnérabilités déjà publiques et corrigées, mais pas encore installées par tous les administrateurs.
John Hultquist, analyste en chef du GTIG, résume ce basculement sans détour, jugeant « bien plus facile de décortiquer un correctif que de chasser un zero-day » à l’aide de ces modèles. Concrètement, la fenêtre de tir entre l’annonce d’un correctif et les premières vagues d’attaques s’effondre.
Après la publication de deux failles dans le logiciel de gestion d’impression PaperCut, des chercheurs ont ainsi généré des exploits fonctionnels avec des LLM en moins de 24 heures, et une campagne réelle frappait des centaines d’organisations quatre jours plus tard. Dans l’un des incidents observés, les intrus ont décroché les droits d’administrateur de domaine, soit les clés maîtresses de tout le réseau, en quelques minutes.
Gardons toutefois la tête froide : ces agents privilégient la vitesse brute au détriment de la furtivité et laissent des traces très visibles, faciles à détecter selon le GTIG lui-même. Sur deux récentes failles PHP, les preuves de concept générées par IA étaient même souvent défaillantes, saturant les sondes des équipes de défense plus qu’elles ne compromettaient les serveurs.
Le contexte commercial incite aussi à un minimum de recul. Google accompagne son rapport du lancement de Google AI Threat Defense, une suite commerciale combinant Gemini, la plateforme Wiz et l’outil de réparation automatique CodeMender, avec cet argument : « défendre à vitesse humaine contre des menaces à vitesse machine n’est pas réaliste ». Le constat technique est indiscutable, mais l’arbitre vend aussi le remède — sans en dévoiler ni le tarif ni le calendrier.
En première ligne figurent toutes les structures qui laissent traîner leurs mises à jour : sites WordPress chargés d’extensions, PME dépourvues d’équipe cybersécurité ou collectivités locales. Le rapport cite d’ailleurs explicitement Spectra, une extension WordPress très répandue, parmi les cibles passées au crible par exploit_agent.
Pour le grand public, le danger est indirect mais bien réel : ce sont les comptes et données personnelles des lecteurs ou clients qui dorment dans les bases de ces sites. On regrettera en revanche que Google reste muet sur le nombre exact de victimes, le taux de réussite réel de l’agent ou le nom des modèles d’IA détournés.
L’étude pointe enfin l’essor du « LLMjacking », le piratage de clés d’accès à des IA payantes pour consommer de la puissance de calcul aux frais des entreprises, avec des factures frauduleuses dépassant parfois 100 000 dollars en une seule journée.
Les réflexes pour réduire la casse
La meilleure parade reste aussi la moins spectaculaire : comprimer au maximum le délai entre la sortie d’un correctif et son déploiement, puisque c’est précisément cette fenêtre que les agents exploitent.
Le reste repose sur quelques mesures d’hygiène numérique rappelées par Mandiant :
- Automatiser les correctifs : activer les mises à jour automatiques de son CMS (comme WordPress) et de ses extensions, tout en supprimant celles qui ne servent plus ;
- Protéger ses clés d’API : ne jamais exposer de clé d’accès à un modèle d’IA dans un dépôt de code public et fixer des plafonds de dépenses stricts chez son fournisseur ;
- Cloisonner les accès : remplacer les mots de passe permanents par des jetons temporaires et restreindre au strict nécessaire les droits de chaque compte ;
- Surveiller les connexions légitimes : traquer les comportements inhabituels sur son réseau, car ces agents opèrent souvent avec de vrais identifiants dérobés.
Le pirate infatigable décrit par Google n’a au fond rien inventé : il lit simplement les notes de version beaucoup plus vite que les humains.
Le vrai bouleversement, c’est cette contraction brutale du calendrier, où le délai entre un correctif et une attaque passe de plusieurs semaines à quelques jours.

articles.title: Apple prépare ses lunettes connectées, mais un obstacle bien connu pourrait tout retarder
articles.text:
Apple miserait sur Siri et les applications de l’iPhone pour donner un intérêt à ses premières lunettes connectées. Mais les difficultés de développement du logiciel pourraient encore bousculer leur lancement, toujours envisagé pour 2027.
Une belle monture ne suffira pas. Pour nous convaincre de porter ses lunettes toute la journée, Apple devra leur donner autre chose à faire que prendre des photos et diffuser de la musique. Son meilleur argument pourrait se trouver dans notre poche : les applications de l’iPhone. Encore faut-il que Siri sache les utiliser correctement, sans nous obliger à reprendre le téléphone au milieu d’une demande, et que Siri AI soit un jour disponible dans l’Union européenne.
Les applications de votre iPhone, sans sortir votre iPhone
Selon les informations de Mark Gurman pour Bloomberg, Apple viserait une présentation à la WWDC de juin 2027, puis une commercialisation avant la fin de l’année. Le matériel serait largement arrêté, mais le logiciel et l’intelligence artificielle prendraient du retard. Un nouveau décalage resterait donc possible.
Ces premières lunettes, connues sous le nom de code N50, ne proposeraient pas d’affichage en réalité augmentée. Siri servirait d’interface, avec des caméras pour comprendre l’environnement. Identifier un bâtiment, traduire un panneau ou obtenir un itinéraire figureraient parmi les usages envisagés.
Le projet irait surtout chercher sa valeur dans les applications : réserver une table, commander une voiture ou acheter des billets de cinéma à la voix. Les développeurs n’auraient pas à concevoir de logiciels spécifiques aux lunettes. Ils devraient rendre les fonctions de leurs applications iPhone accessibles à Siri, le téléphone associé se chargeant d’une partie du travail. Un iPhone récent resterait nécessaire, sans compatibilité Android prévue.
Siri doit convaincre avant les lunettes
Cette stratégie prolonge l’ouverture de Siri AI aux applications tierces amorcée avec la bêta d’iOS 27.3. L’assistant ne reçoit pas pour autant les clés de chaque application : les développeurs doivent eux-mêmes exposer les actions qu’il pourra effectuer.
Pour Apple, l’intérêt serait de s’appuyer sur un écosystème existant plutôt que de demander aux éditeurs de repartir de zéro. Pour l’utilisateur, la promesse se jugera beaucoup plus simplement : la réservation a-t-elle abouti, ou faut-il sortir son téléphone pour terminer ? De là passera l’adoption ou non d’un format sans interface tactile.
Il reste une autre inconnue pour les fans français de la marque. Siri AI demeure indisponible dans l’Union européenne sur iPhone et iPad. Cela ne permet pas de préjuger de la situation en 2027, mais ajoute une condition au lancement chez nous : des lunettes dépendantes de l’iPhone auront besoin d’un assistant plus puissant et malin, encore faut-il qu'il soit accessible sous nos latitudes.

articles.title: Microsoft says months-old bug caused global Microsoft 365 outage
articles.text:
Microsoft says a software bug introduced in July caused last week's worldwide Microsoft 365 outage, triggering a cascading failure that left more than 80% of its networking gateway servers unresponsive.
The nearly 24-hour outage on November 12 disrupted Microsoft 365 services worldwide, including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams, and Copilot, leaving users unable to access their email and causing significant delays in message delivery.
In a preliminary post-incident report shared in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center, the company said the outage was caused by three problems: a previously undetected software bug, increased traffic after a Microsoft Teams failover, and reduced server capacity.
The incident began at 11:20 AM ET on Thursday, November 12, and continued until 11:10 AM ET the following day, when Microsoft confirmed that services were full restored.
According to Microsoft, the software bug was introduced in July through an update developed for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers.
While the update had been deployed for more than three months without issues, it contained a bug that could overwhelm servers under certain traffic conditions, causing them to stop responding.
Microsoft says its tests of the update did not detect the bug as it used less powerful testing hardware than the production servers.
"Our normal load testing did not detect the latent issue because the traffic mix and SKUs used in our labs," Microsoft explained in its preliminary report.
"The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores."
The bug was eventually triggered after Microsoft Teams automatically switched to the networking infrastructure used by Exchange Online approximately 15 hours before the outage, increasing traffic on those servers.
Microsoft Teams also experienced a separate outage earlier that day, but it is unclear whether the two incidents are related.
To make matters worse, Microsoft says nearly 14% of the gateway's server capacity was already offline due to an unrelated issue. While the infrastructure had sufficient capacity to handle the reduction, the combination of increased traffic and reduced capacity triggered the software bug.
As servers stopped responding, Microsoft's systems redirected users to other available servers, which also became overwhelmed by the additional traffic and failed as well.
"In less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet and rendered them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive," explained Microsoft.
Microsoft says safeguards designed to prevent problems from spreading between regions also failed to contain the cascading outages, allowing the disruption to spread worldwide.
While other Microsoft 365 services, like Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint, could switch to alternative infrastructure and recover earlier, Exchange Online could not make the same switch, leaving users unable to access their mailboxes.
Microsoft says recovery was difficult because restarting affected servers caused them to be quickly overwhelmed again by backed-up traffic.
After identifying the bug, Microsoft engineers developed a fix and deployed it across affected servers, allowing services to stabilize throughout Friday.
Microsoft confirmed that active customer impact had ended by 11:10 AM ET on November 13.
The company says it has since increased capacity, improved monitoring, and added safeguards to prevent traffic redirection from triggering similar cascading failures.
In a separate statement on X, Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, apologized for the disruption.
"We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations," Lamanna said.
Microsoft says its investigation is continuing, with a final post-incident report expected later this week.

articles.title: “Si hoy fuera el último día de mi vida, ¿querría hacer lo que estoy a punto de hacer?”: Steve Jobs, fundador de Apple
articles.text:
Una de las frases que dejó en 2005 Steve Jobs en su discurso de graduación en la Universidad de Stanford fue una pregunta que convirtió en un método personal para revisar sus decisiones: “Si hoy fuera el último día de mi vida, ¿querría hacer lo que estoy a punto de hacer?”.
El fundador de Apple explicó que la repetición de esa respuesta negativa durante varios días era una señal de que debía modificar algo. El discurso, pronunciado ante graduados, incluyó tres relatos personales sobre los “puntos” que se unen con el tiempo, el amor y la pérdida, y la muerte.
En esta última parte, Jobs vinculó una experiencia médica con una idea que atravesó su vida: la conciencia de que el tiempo es limitado puede ayudar a distinguir entre las expectativas ajenas y las decisiones propias.
Por qué Steve Jobs se hacía la misma pregunta cada día
Jobs contó que, cuando tenía 17 años, leyó una cita que lo marcó: “Si vives cada día como si fuera el último, es muy probable que algún día hagas lo correcto”. A partir de entonces, dijo, integró una rutina frente al espejo.
Durante 33 años, se preguntó cada mañana si elegiría hacer lo que tenía por delante si ese fuera el último día de su vida. La respuesta no era una fórmula para tomar decisiones inmediatas.
Su criterio estaba en la persistencia: “Siempre que la respuesta ha sido ‘no’ durante varios días seguidos, he sabido que tenía que cambiar algo”. La frase planteaba una revisión sostenida del rumbo, más que una invitación a reaccionar ante cada jornada difícil.
Qué lugar ocupaba la muerte en sus decisiones
El fundador de Apple sostuvo que recordar la propia mortalidad fue la herramienta más útil que encontró para tomar decisiones importantes. Según explicó, frente a la muerte pierden peso factores como “las expectativas externas, el orgullo” y “el temor a la vergüenza o al fracaso”.
Para Jobs, ese ejercicio permitía concentrarse en aquello que consideraba esencial. “Recordar que vas a morir es la mejor manera que conozco para evitar la trampa de pensar que tienes algo que perder”. La idea no consistía en negar el riesgo, sino en cuestionar la parálisis que puede surgir ante el fracaso o la opinión de otros.
Cuál momento atravesó Steve Jobs que le hizo repensar la muerte
Jobs relató que, aproximadamente un año antes de hablar en Stanford, un estudio realizado a las 7:30 de la mañana detectó un tumor en el páncreas. Los médicos le indicaron que podía tratarse de una forma incurable de cáncer y le dieron una expectativa de vida de entre tres y seis meses.
Su médico le sugirió volver a casa y “poner en orden” sus asuntos. Jobs tradujo esa expresión médica en tareas concretas: hablar con sus hijos sobre temas que pensaba abordar durante la década siguiente, resolver cuestiones familiares y despedirse. “Significa prepararte para morir”, resumió ante los graduados.
Ese mismo día, el empresario se sometió a una biopsia. El procedimiento incluyó el uso de un endoscopio que pasó por la garganta, el estómago y los intestinos hasta llegar al páncreas, donde los médicos extrajeron células del tumor con una aguja.
Su esposa le contó después que los especialistas lloraron al analizar la muestra, porque se trataba de una forma poco frecuente de cáncer pancreático que podía tratarse con cirugía.
Jobs fue operado y dijo que estaba bien. “Es lo más cerca que he estado de la muerte”, aunque expresó su deseo de que esa situación no volviera a repetirse durante décadas.
Qué mensaje dejó a quienes comenzaban una nueva etapa en su vida
Tras describir esa experiencia, Jobs dijo que nadie desea morir, incluso quienes creen en una vida después de la muerte. Aun así, definió a la muerte como “el destino que todos compartimos” y como un agente de cambio que desplaza lo viejo para dejar lugar a lo nuevo.
El cierre de su discurso recuperó una frase de The Whole Earth Catalog, publicación creada por Stewart Brand que Jobs definió como una referencia para su generación.
En la contraportada de su última edición aparecía el mensaje “Seguid hambrientos. Seguid alocados”. Jobs lo adoptó como una despedida para los estudiantes, junto con otra advertencia: “El tiempo es limitado, no lo pierdan viviendo la vida de otra persona”.

articles.title: Alpine Linux Users Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw
articles.text:
A recently disclosed vulnerability in OpenSSH lets an unauthenticated attacker log into accounts that should have no usable password. The issue, named *sshole and tracked as CVE-2026-123158, affects Linux systems running OpenSSH with the musl C library and which don't use PAM. Security researchers now report that attackers are exploiting it in the wild.
The flaw comes from the way OpenSSH checks passwords when musl handles the underlying crypt() call. On an affected system, a password longer than 256 bytes causes musl to return an error value. That value is an asterisk, the same character Linux uses in /etc/shadow to mark an account as having no password. OpenSSH then treats the returned asterisk as a match and permits the login.
The conditions to exploit the vulnerability are however quite narrow. The server must run OpenSSH before version 10.6p2, be built against the musl library rather than glibc, and operate without PAM. It must also have at least one account with a SHA-256 or SHA-512 password hash and another account marked with an asterisk in its shadow entry. When those conditions are met, any password between 257 and 1,024 characters can authenticate against the passwordless account.
Alpine Linux is the most prominent distribution affected, as it uses musl and its default OpenSSH configuration does not enable PAM. Other musl-based environments, including OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto, may also be affected where the same configuration applies. Systems using glibc, PAM, Dropbear or OpenBSD are not affected.
"Accounts that should never take a password at all (root, your key-only deploy user, ldap users, the default user on alpine's aws and azure images) take any password longer than 256 characters."
Ozgun Kultekin, *sshole
Ozgun Kultekin, a security researcher at Wakefield, published the technical explanation on the *sshole site. Kultekin traces the problem to two musl changes made in 2012: the first replaced the NULL error return from crypt() with an asterisk, and the second added a 256-byte limit to SHA-512 password hashing, so longer inputs caused an error. Together, the changes produced a value that could be mistaken for a password hash.
The OpenSSH side of the problem dates from a 2016 fix for CVE-2016-6210, which was a timing attack that could reveal whether a username existed. To make responses take a similar amount of time for valid and invalid users, OpenSSH borrowed the salt from another account and hashed the supplied password anyway. That workaround also applied to real accounts whose shadow entry contained an asterisk.
Kultekin writes that the issue remained unnoticed for roughly a decade because the vulnerable combination was uncommon in testing. OpenSSH is tested on OpenBSD and glibc-based systems, while many Linux distributions route authentication through PAM, which does not call crypt() for asterisk entries in the same way. Kultekin says the bug was found after building OpenSSH in several configurations and testing about 17,600 unusual login attempts.
"On alpine's official aws and azure images that's the default `alpine` user, and it has passwordless `doas`. so it's root"
Ozgun Kultekin, *sshole
On Alpine's official AWS and Azure images, the default alpine user is marked as passwordless and can use doas without a password. This means that an attacker who reaches that account can therefore obtain root privileges. Dan Goodin reports for Ars Technica that the issue can give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts within seconds on affected systems.
OpenSSH 10.6p2 contains a fix. Operators who cannot update immediately can disable password authentication by setting PasswordAuthentication no in the SSH server configuration and restarting sshd. Kultekin also advises checking authentication logs for evidence that an account with no password accepted a password. The project has published a detection and background repository.
The vulnerability is being actively exploited. Goodin notes that GreyNoise reported that honeypots in Southeast Asia had been attacked by a group it is tracking known as GT10, which reportedly deploys a backdoor which supports shell commands, reconnaissance and persistence. Goodin reports that watchTowr linked the activity to botnets and cryptocurrency operations, while Previdian recorded 20 exploitation attempts from 13 IP addresses in nine countries. The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added CVE-2026-123158 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 9 November, according to Hackread.
Red Hat has said that its products are not affected because they do not meet the required combination of musl and no PAM. Amazon has likewise marked Amazon Linux 2 and Amazon Linux 2023 as not affected. That does not remove the risk for teams running Alpine-based containers, embedded devices or custom musl builds. Administrators should look for SSH servers built against musl, check whether PAM is disabled, review shadow entries for asterisk-locked accounts, apply OpenSSH 10.6p2 and restart the service.
The vulnerability was publicly disclosed on 5 November and exploitation reports followed within days. For organisations with internet-facing SSH services, the immediate action to take is fairly straightforward: update OpenSSH, restart it, and remove password authentication where it is not needed.

articles.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
articles.text:
AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
- Date:
- November 14, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.
- Share:
More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.
Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.
The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.
AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss
The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.
Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.
Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.
Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.
The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.
"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."
Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict
Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.
Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.
For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.
Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.
"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."
The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening
Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.
But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.
The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.
At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.
"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."
The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.
How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns
Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.
The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.
The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.
This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.
"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."
Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.
"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."
From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments
The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.
Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.
Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.
These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.
For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.
Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.
Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?
Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.
Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.
Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.
"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Ziad Obermeyer, Alexander Schubert, James Ross, Sendhil Mullainathan, Markus Lingman. An ECG biomarker for sudden cardiac death discovered with deep learning. Nature, 2026; 655 (8121): 210 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10674-6

articles.title: Après l'iPhone Duo, Apple aurait un nouveau cheval de bataille qui va rythmer son année 2027
articles.text:
Apple préparerait l’annonce de ses premières lunettes connectées pour sa WWDC de juin 2027, le grand-messe des développeurs qui a souvent été le théâtre d’annonces de nouveaux produits (le dernier en date étant le Vision Pro en 2023). Les lorgnettes se limiteraient à des caméras, des micros, des haut-parleurs et Siri, sans affichage de réalité augmentée, pour affronter les Ray-Ban de Meta sur leur propre terrain. Avec une commercialisation prévue pour la fin de l’année 2027, les lunettes dépendraient d’un iPhone récent dans la poche pour à peu près tout.
Siri aux commandes, l’iPhone à la manœuvre
Les prototypes, connus en interne sous le nom de code N50, seraient légèrement plus fins que les Ray-Ban Meta de deuxième génération, avec des verres ovales et des caméras affleurantes. Les unités de test embarqueraient une version allégée de visionOS, animée par une puce dérivée de celles de l’Apple Watch. Un chargeur magnétique de la taille d’un Tic Tac, fixé à la branche gauche, permettrait de les recharger sans les quitter.
Les montures n’embarqueraient aucune application. Les développeurs ouvriraient leurs services existants à Siri via App Intents, directement depuis l’iPhone apparié, et l’assistant exécuterait les demandes à la voix. Réserver une table, commander un VTC ou un café : les scénarios à l’étude s’appuieraient sur des applications déjà en place comme Uber, OpenTable ou Starbucks.
Il faudra en contrepartie un iPhone récent apparié en permanence, et les possesseurs d’un smartphone Android resteront à la porte. Les lunettes conserveraient un filet d’autonomie en Wi-Fi, de quoi poursuivre l’écoute quand le téléphone s’éloigne, sans jamais devenir un appareil indépendant.
Un calendrier suspendu à Siri qui questionne, surtout en Europe
La partie matérielle serait pratiquement figée, au terme de travaux entamés au début de la décennie. Le logiciel accuse en revanche un retard susceptible de faire glisser la date de sortie. Le nouveau Siri dopé à l’IA, qui porte l’essentiel du produit, n’a ouvert sa préversion aux développeurs que le 3 novembre, dans les betas d’iOS 27.3. Ses capacités s’étendront aux applications d’Apple en décembre, puis aux applications tierces au printemps 2027.
Le projet a déjà glissé une fois : visé pour fin 2026, le dévoilement aurait été repoussé cet été à la WWDC 2027, le temps de trancher la place de la caméra et le discours sur la vie privée. En face, plus de sept millions de Ray-Ban connectées se sont écoulées l’an dernier, vendues autour de 329 euros. L’agenda 2027 d’Apple s’annonce chargé, entre les 20 ans de l’iPhone et la suite de l’iPhone Duo lancé cet automne. Des AirPods équipés de caméras resteraient d’ailleurs programmés pour fin 2027, avec des fonctions qui recoupent en partie celles des lunettes.
Apple vient par ailleurs d’ouvrir les ventes de son écran connecté HomeView dans sept pays, en excluant l’Union européenne. « HomeView n’est pas disponible à la vente dans l’Union européenne, car Siri AI est actuellement indisponible sur iOS dans l’UE », justifie la page d’annonce. Les lunettes reposeraient sur la même mécanique, un appareil jumelé à un iPhone dont Siri AI pilote les applications. Ce Siri nouvelle génération manque justement à l’appel sur les iPhone européens depuis son lancement en septembre, Apple et la Commission se renvoyant la responsabilité au nom du DMA, sans calendrier de déblocage.

articles.title: Una comunidad permite durante años el uso de una salida de humos y lo prohíbe tras el cambio de propietario la reforma del local: el Supremo anula el acuerdo por ir contra sus propios actos
articles.text:
Que una comunidad de propietarios permita durante años utilizar una instalación y después decida prohibirla puede acabar siendo un problema, especialmente cuando el dueño de un local ya ha invertido dinero en reformarlo. Justo eso es lo que ocurrió en un edificio de Madrid, donde los vecinos exigieron retirar una chimenea de salida de humos que llevaba instalada desde 1990. Sin embargo, el Tribunal Supremo terminó dando la razón a la empresa propietaria del local al considerar que la comunidad había actuado contra sus propios actos.
Como recoge NoticiasTrabajo en su información sobre el conflicto, la instalación había sido autorizada inicialmente a un inquilino con carácter personal y temporal, pero siguió utilizándose cuando este abandonó el local. De hecho, otro arrendatario la empleó al menos desde 2002 sin que la comunidad exigiera retirarla. La situación cambió cuando una empresa compró el establecimiento en 2016 para abrir un restaurante y comunicó su proyecto de reforma a la presidenta y al administrador, que incluso visitaron las obras. ¿Y qué ocurrió? Nadie se opuso al uso de la chimenea y las únicas preocupaciones que trasladaron estaban relacionadas con el ruido.
El Supremo considera que la comunidad actuó contra sus propios actos
Una vez terminada la reforma, llegó el conflicto. En marzo de 2017, la comunidad aprobó un acuerdo para prohibir el uso de la salida de humos y exigir el desmontaje de la chimenea, pese a que había conocido las obras y permitido que finalizaran. La propietaria acudió a los tribunales y perdió en primera instancia, pero la Audiencia Provincial de Madrid anuló el acuerdo al entender que los vecinos habían generado una situación de confianza que después contradijeron. La comunidad recurrió de nuevo y el caso terminó en el Tribunal Supremo.
Aquí entra en juego el artículo 7.1 del Código Civil, que establece que los derechos deben ejercerse conforme a las exigencias de la buena fe. En su sentencia 103/2026, de 29 de enero, el Supremo explica que la comunidad no podía ignorar su comportamiento anterior, especialmente después de permitir durante más de 14 años el uso de la instalación y conocer las reformas del nuevo propietario sin plantear ninguna objeción a la chimenea.
A todo esto debemos sumar que los artículos 7 y 17 de la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal regulan las actuaciones sobre elementos comunes y los acuerdos necesarios para modificarlos. Sin embargo, esas facultades también tienen límites, como ha ocurrido en este caso. El Supremo consideró que la comunidad había esperado a que concluyeran las obras y se realizara la inversión para prohibir algo que llevaba años tolerando. Por eso, desestimó su recurso y confirmó la nulidad del acuerdo, al entender que vulneraba la buena fe y la doctrina de los actos propios.

articles.title: Missão falha e Amazon Leo perde 40 satélites • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Missão falha e Amazon Leo perde 40 satélites
Falha interrompeu sequência de 20 anos sem lançamentos malsucedidos da ULA. Missão terminou cerca de dez minutos após a decolagem.
Um foguete Vulcan, da United Launch Alliance (ULA), falhou neste domingo (15/11) durante uma missão que levaria 40 satélites do Amazon Leo à orbita. O problema ocorreu cerca de dez minutos após a decolagem, em Cabo Canaveral, na Flórida, e resultou na perda de toda a carga.
Segundo a Reuters, esta é a primeira missão malsucedida nos 20 anos de história da ULA, joint venture formada por Boeing e Lockheed Martin. O voo também inauguraria um pacote de 38 lançamentos contratados pela Amazon para ampliar a constelação de internet via satélite.
Além da banda larga, a Amazon também tem ampliado sua constelação de satélites para dar suporte ao Direct-to-Device, que deve concorrer com o famoso plano da Starlink. A falha pesa sobre os planos da Amazon para dar sequência a esse crescimento, que colocou 398 satélites em órbita em 14 lançamentos desde 2025, pouco mais de 10% do objetivo da companhia.
Diferentemente da SpaceX, que utiliza seus próprios foguetes para lançar os satélites da Starlink, a Amazon depende de contratos com diferentes fornecedores para levar sua constelação ao espaço. A Starlink já reúne mais de 11 mil satélites em órbita e atende milhões de clientes ao redor do mundo.
Cerca de dez minutos após a decolagem do foguete na Estação da Força Espacial de Cabo Canaveral, a ULA confirmou que o veículo havia sofrido uma “anomalia” e não conseguiria colocar os satélites em órbita, diz um comunicado publicado pela empresa na rede social X.
De acordo com a Reuters, o problema parece ter ocorrido logo depois da separação entre o primeiro e o segundo estágio do Vulcan. Era no estágio superior que estavam os satélites da Amazon. A causa da falha ainda não foi identificada.
No post, a ULA afirmou que começou a analisar os dados coletados durante o voo. A Amazon também se manifestou após a perda da missão, dizendo que “há risco em qualquer lançamento” especialmente “para missões inaugurais como a LV-01”. A companhia, controlada por Andy Jassy, reafirmou o compromisso de longo prazo com ULA.
A perda da missão quebra uma sequência mantida desde a criação da United Launch Alliance, em 2006, criada com a união dos programas Delta, da Boeing, e Atlas, da Lockheed Martin. A missão com os satélites da Amazon, porém, foi apenas o quinto voo do foguete Vulcan, que estreou em 2024, e o primeiro em nove meses. Ele ficou esse período em solo sob investigações de problemas técnicos pela ULA.
Um deles envolvia os propulsores sólidos laterais, que apresentaram falhas nos dois voos anteriores do foguete. Em outra frente estão os motores BE-4, da Blue Origin, que também teve um foguete que explodiu em maio, poucos dias antes de uma missão que também levaria satélites do Amazon Leo.
Segundo uma fonte ouvida pela agência, a Blue Origin já participa da investigação da falha deste domingo. Até agora, porém, não há indicação de que os motores BE-4 tenham sido responsáveis pelo acidente.
A investigação sobre o Vulcan pode manter o foguete fora de operação por meses, segundo a Reuters, restringindo ainda mais a oferta no mercado após falhas recentes na SpaceX.
