articles.title: Telegram Widgets Hit by RCE Demos, Malware Warning Days After Launch
articles.text:
Kaspersky has warned that a vulnerability in Telegram’s newly launched widgets may have been exploited in the wild to deliver the WebRAT malware. The warning came shortly after researchers showed what they described as remote code execution through the new feature.
In a November 13 post on its Russian-language Telegram channel, the security firm said it had observed malicious activity that it suspects is tied to the flaw. According to the company, exploitation took place when users visited certain Telegram channels.
Kaspersky said the activity results in a PowerShell script running without the user’s knowledge. The script fetches and launches WebRAT, a piece of malware also known as Salat Stealer.
WebRAT is a Rust-based trojan that gives attackers control of the infected system. It can also steal cryptocurrency wallet and Telegram account data.
Kaspersky did not share technical details on the exploitation, or say how many users were targeted. Its main recommendation was “do not launch widgets in Telegram until a fix is released.”
Telegram CEO Pavel Durov promoted the widgets feature on X on November 10, saying that any message on the platform can now become an app.
A day later, researchers at V12 posted a video on X with the caption “Any telegram message can now become RCE.” The video showed an interaction with a bot causing the Calculator app to open on an Android phone.
Telegram replied the same day, saying the Android issue “was fixed yesterday, and the fix was deployed to all users earlier today.”
V12 later published a second video, saying it had another RCE exploit that worked against the supposedly patched Telegram client for Windows. In the researchers’ view, letting QuickJS, a JavaScript engine, run inside messages without a sandbox creates a large attack surface.
Durov has dismissed the reports. “No one could be hacked just by receiving a message,” he wrote on X on November 13.
According to Durov, an attack required the user to first start a third-party service, and that scenario has since been fully patched on the server side. He challenged skeptics to hack his own account.
SecurityWeek has reached out to Telegram for comment and will update this article if the company responds.

articles.title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing.
OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI.
The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic, which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat.
The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user.
Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions.
Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers.
With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI.
Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organization is also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release.
At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits.
Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations.
Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work.
Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged.
In previous coverage, John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisade Research, told TechCrunch that it’s important to see this data in order to assess whether a model was trained to perform well on a “shutdown resistance benchmark.”
In OpenAI’s first pilot, the AI lab is providing Apollo with access to only the information required to assess whether the models engage in subversion attempts. This includes “relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints.”
The scope of access will be limited to “only the agreed claims and only for the specific models and time periods agreed for the assessment,” Apollo says. OpenAI still reserves the right to withhold certain information within that scope if it deems it necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks, or IP protection. The company agreed not to withhold information simply because it is unfavorable.
Apollo also won’t get access to all OpenAI staffers, instead being limited to “only authorized staff,” which are participants that the AI lab selects, though Apollo can suggest certain individuals. Crucially, if an OpenAI employee outside this group raises confidential information within the scope of Apollo’s research, the firm cannot follow up and will need to cease communication and route follow-up through OpenAI.
That condition is significant. It comes in the wake of OpenAI firing three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential information with safety evaluation firm METR — which performed the Hugging Face incident post-mortem alongside independent AI safety research group Redwood.
Buck Shlegeris, CEO of Redwood, said in a post on Monday that the agreements announced don’t meet the bar of granting third parties “employee-like access,” saying it’s “disappointing but not surprising.”
OpenAI said that they'd have embedded evaluations with employee-like access; the agreements announced today obviously don't meet that bar.
This is disappointing but not surprising.
Maybe future agreements will be better. https://t.co/kmDbg1Dqav
— Buck Shlegeris (@bshlgrs) November 16, 2026
The pilot will also be limited in how much researchers can disclose. While Apollo will be allowed to publish independent conclusions of its findings, OpenAI will be able to limit evidence available to substantiate them publicly, which could make it hard for outsiders to independently assess the findings. Apollo has pushed back against this limitation, saying it believes researchers should be allowed to disclose the findings of the evaluation “to an appropriate outside audience even if the developer was trying to prevent the disclosure of unfavorable findings.”
That said, while the public cannot see the full supporting evidence, OpenAI says its Safety and Security Committee, which oversees safety on behalf of the OpenAI Foundation’s board, will get to review unredacted assessment reports and can communicate privately with evaluators.
While OpenAI is not granting all of Apollo’s conditions for a truly independent evaluation, the firm says the pilot is “an ambitious first step towards deeper access and disclosure rights,” and that it is working toward running full embedded evaluations with multiple AI developers in the future.
This article has been updated to include pilots with METR, Goodfire, and Transluce, as well as with information from OpenAI and comment from Redwood.

articles.title: Developer creates a 100% valid ZIP file that doubles as a BIOS-bootable operating system — hiding BIOS boot flags inside uncompressed files and turning file headers into CPU instructions
articles.text:
Developer creates a 100% valid ZIP file that doubles as a BIOS-bootable operating system — hiding BIOS boot flags inside uncompressed files and turning file headers into CPU instructions
The original definition of "hacking" was making hardware and software do something it wasn't supposed to.
Hacking stories these days mostly involve someone using an army of AI agents to find vulnerabilities in networks and software that were carefully hidden in plain sight. Today, for a change, we have a story about hacking in its original meaning — twisting computing artifacts into purposes not in their design spec. David Oberhollenzer, aka Goliath, a greybeard in spirit if not in shade, crafted a 100% valid ZIP file that's simultaneously an archive, BIOS-bootable, and a Multiboot-compatible OS image.
You can unpack the ZIP file just like any other, boot it using Linux's GRUB, QEMU, or any other Multiboot-compatible loader (even if imaged to different media), or alternatively, perform the finest party trick: image-write it to a floppy and boot from it directly from BIOS on any compatible PC, without modification.
Much like me, that sequence of words may be triggering a head-tilt reminiscent of a confused puppy, so we'll explain. The first thing you need to know is that unlike most file types, the metadata (in this case, file directory) of a ZIP is actually at the end of the archive. Up to that point, the data is comprised of every compressed file in sequence.
The file packs all have a predictable structure: "PK" followed by bytes 03 04, metadata (including name), some extra/comment fields, and then the file's contents. Notably, any file can be stored uncompressed, and Goliath made use of that for the very first file, called ZIPHEAD.COM — remember, this is the start of the ZIP archive.
Goliath said that it was "easy" to make the ZIP file a valid Multiboot system image. A valid image only needs to contain bytes 0x1BADB002 in the first 8 KiB, followed by some flags and a checksum. It was trivial to place that datum in ZIPHEAD's data, along with the location of where the bootloader lies.
Grub or QEMU don't care about anything else in the image, as once they have the initialization information, from that point it's the bootloader's problem. The actual bootloader, predictably, is in ZIPHEAD's uncompressed data, and the image will happily boot directly, or, say, from a floppy.
Making the same exact archive bootable via a standard PC BIOS took a little more work and some clever shenanigans. Making a disk bootable is simple enough: the BIOS reads the first exact 512 bytes of the disk's contents, and if they end with bytes 0x55AA, then it's bootable, and the BIOS starts executing whatever code is the first byte.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Placing 0x55AA precisely at position 510 of the ZIP, already in ZIPHEAD's contents, is once again simple, and won't corrupt the Multiboot image, as if you'll recall, the Multiboot spec is flexible with data locations. But you may wonder: once the BIOS runs code in sequence starting from the ZIP's first byte, then ZIPHEAD's header ("PK" + 0x0304, plus all metadata) surely is garbage for practical purposes, and not proper code? Well, yes, but actually no.
The first four bytes represent CPU instructions that don't write anything to memory, so they're harmless, other than a push-to-stack. The next few belong to ZIPHEAD's metadata, and Goliath massaged those values to represent instructions that would either be innocuous or perform operations he could use, namely using the modification time bytes as instructions to jump further down the data.
Sounds simple, but the actual process of choosing bytes that represent (1) non-crashy CPU instructions, (2) useful code for setting up the boot process, and (3) still represent a valid file header in a ZIP archive is far trickier than the above. Do go and check out the full blog post if you want all the details.
Download the Tom's Hardware app for up-to-the-minute updates on iOS and Android. Also follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
articles.text:
Before Clavicular and other manosphere streamers were introducing young guys to the concept of breaking their facial bones to become more attractive, there was an older generation of creators building massive followings with content focused on chemical biohacking. Were it not for steroid-obsessed influencers like Anthony “Tony Huge” Hughes launching YouTube channels over a decade ago, looksmaxxing might not have become such a prominent part of the digital media landscape in 2026. These creators became internet famous by presenting themselves as peak male specimens. But their larger-than-life online personas often concealed the truth about how sinister and toxic this kind of influencing can really be.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
Hughes is the gravitational center of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death — Hulu’s new three-part docuseries from director Stacey Lee. The series is both a deep dive into Hughes’ strange life and a fascinating exploration of how perilous the creator economy can be in the age of manosphere and looksmaxxing influencers. Through Hughes’ ever-expanding orbit of creators, Lee is able to highlight how lonely, impressionable men are all too easily radicalized by what they see and post online. And it makes clear that all these men are trapped in a deadly psychological prison of their own making.
Get Huge takes some time to touch on Hughes’ former life as a bankruptcy lawyer and supplement salesman who was investigated by the FDA for hawking unapproved performance-enhancing drugs. But most of the series takes place in Pattaya, Thailand, where Hughes spends his days producing content showcasing his extravagant life of nonstop partying and injecting substances that swell his muscles to huge proportions. Hughes takes pride in his image as a man with access to a harem of women, and the fact that his money gives him power over many of the people around him. He presents himself as the ruler of a small kingdom — and his entire brand is built on the idea that he can show people how to become more like him.
The men caught in Hughes’ aspirational fantasy aren’t just stateside fans who’ll never reach his muscle-y heights. He is also marketing himself to other established bodybuilding influencers who might be interested in joining his inner circle by following him to Thailand. These include a menagerie of biohacking / manosphere influencers who became vital parts of Hughes’ operation over the years. Leo Longevity (legal name Laith Abdallah Algaz), Elon Muscular (his legal name isn’t revealed), and Connor Murphy all built sizable social media presences of their own. But they were each compelled to move to Pattaya and join Hughes’ entourage by a powerful desire to feel connected to something larger and more fulfilling than their individual followings.
As Get Huge features clips of Hughes’ videos — the bulk of which are now only featured on Rumble and X following multiple account bans on YouTube and TikTok — you can see that he’s trying to sell his audience on his highly specific way of life. Hughes’ own videos make it seem like he’s living his dream surrounded by people who revere him. But with each interview, Get Huge makes it clear that for all of his posturing, Hughes has been living in something of a nightmare — one where many of his disciples have died under mysterious circumstances.
As these men explain why they were drawn to Hughes, you get the sense that looksmaxxing culture is a direct response to the widespread disaffection that followed the last decade of interconnected societal shifts, from the #MeToo movement to Donald Trump’s presidencies. Hughes seems very much like an entrepreneur profiting from men’s loneliness by convincing them that their lives would be better if they were part of his community. As Get Huge first maps out Hughes’ friendships, they all appear to be anchored by an odd, sometimes envious, but genuine kind of intimacy. But as the documentary digs deeper into its subjects’ lives, it becomes hard to see them as anything but emotionally stunted men who perform cartoonish masculinity for one another in ways that are psychologically unhealthy and, at times, physically dangerous.
Part of what makes Get Huge such an unsettling watch is how relatively calm and collected Hughes and the other interviewees are as they begin to discuss how many people in their circle have died in recent years. Hughes and Murphy grow closer as friends following Algaz’s death in 2023, but they seem to bond by making Algaz the butt of the joke in content produced after his death. Simply by letting these men speak frankly about their social dynamics, Get Huge reveals the manosphere as a space in which connections built on mogging and the objectification of women can quickly deteriorate into infighting and petty jealousy. Elon Muscular readily speculates that Murphy might have had something to do with Algaz’s death because Murphy openly jokes about it. And the entire situation becomes that much stranger and more grim when Get Huge reveals that Murphy drowned shortly after the series initially wrapped filming.
Though the deaths in Hughes’ circle bring a dark whodunit energy to Get Huge, the documentary emphasizes how much peril comes as a part of existing in the looksmaxxing space. Rather than trying to solve the mystery of how Algaz died, the docuseries presents his story as a cautionary tale. He’s an object lesson in how this lifestyle can warp a person’s perception of reality in a way that ultimately cuts them off from the kind of help they really need.
What might be most disturbing about Get Huge is the way it ends. The series follows Hughes to a youth bodybuilding event where he talks up his less-than-legal products to a new group of boys — some as young as 13. To keep his momentum going, Hughes has to appeal to a new, younger audience that doesn’t understand how everything about looksmaxxing is a performance. Though the docuseries gives you the distinct impression that people like Murphy and Algaz felt a true belonging with Hughes, its closing shots call into question how genuine any of his connections with other bodybuilders really are. By juxtaposing the deaths of Hughes’ adult acolytes with his focus on turning children into fans, Get Huge paints a clear picture of how the manosphere’s promise of emotional connection often ends in a twisted kind of exploitation. And that extractive energy feels foundational to a culture that runs on people turning every aspect of their lives into content.
All three episodes of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death are now streaming on Hulu and Disney Plus.

articles.title: The Download: testing tech promises and searching for cognitive immortality
articles.text:
The Download: testing tech promises and searching for cognitive immortality
Plus: Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia CEO.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Are we there yet? Six technologies that promised to change the world
How do you measure progress towards the future? In the Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review, our series “Are we there yet?” examines how far six potentially transformative technologies have come after years of promises.
We spoke to experts, researchers and engineers to find out what’s holding them back, then scored each on a progress meter from zero to ten.  Find out how we rated each of these technologies—and how close they are to delivering on their promise.
Nuclear-powered spaceships
Exercise in a pill
Interspecies communication
Solid-state batteries
Cleaning up PFAS
Eliminating traffic deaths
Subscribe now to get every issue of our print magazine as soon as it lands.
Inside the quest for cognitive immortality
Could technology keep your brain going beyond death? Far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to make it happen, from gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud. MIT Technology Review’s latest Roundtables event explores these ideas and how close they might be to reality.
Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado for this subscriber-only discussion tomorrow.
Tune in live on Tuesday, November 17 at 5:00 p.m. GMT / 12:00 p.m. EST / 9:00 a.m. PST.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia CEO
He’s discussed with confidants the possibility of returning. (FT $)
+ Elon Musk has joined 165,000 signatories calling for his recall. (Guardian)
+ The Treasury Secretary wants them to hire an outsider. (Axios)
+ Megaspeed says the alleged China spy left the company last year. (BBC)
+ Trump plans to name Nvidia an AI “national champion.” (WSJ $)
+ Nvidia privately said it can track chips to China. (MIT Technology Review)
2 SpaceX has caught a rocket returning from orbit for the first time
The feat brings fully reusable rockets closer to reality. (Guardian)
+ The feat shows what audacious engineering can achieve. (Atlantic $)
+ Meanwhile, Ukraine says SpaceX is lying about Starshield speed restrictions. (Reuters $)
3 The US and allies have agreed to guard AI supply chains from China
Ten countries will collaborate to secure critical technologies. (FT $)
+ Chinese AI stocks have plunged on export control fears. (Information $)
+ Nvidia privately said it can track chips to China. (MIT Technology Review)
4 The US flight shutdown exposed weaknesses in air traffic technology
Officials blamed the disruption on a faulty router installation. (Reuters $)
+ It was a terrible week of outages. (WP $)
5 The first in-body CRISPR treatment is set to reach patients next year
The treatment could gain FDA approval as early as March. (Nature)
+ CRISPR has created female clones of male mice. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Congress plans to make data centers pay billions more for power
A proposed bill would shift grid costs onto tech companies. (NYT $)
+ Utilities also want tech giants to pay more for power. (Bloomberg $)
+ Is data center hatred all about electricity? (MIT Technology Review)
7 Apple plans to launch its first smart glasses next year
It’s betting on Siri to give the specs an edge. (Verge)
8 Bill Gates has made billions from climate-polluting landfills
His investment in a landfill operator is worth $29 billion. (ProPublica)
9 A new AI device turns everyday objects into needy virtual pets
The tiny gadgets aim to encourage healthier everyday habits. (Wired $)
10 Scientists made monkeys watch Minions to study their brains
Their findings challenge traditional vision models. (404 Media)
Quote of the day
“If our hopes for the future are pinned on any one individual being trustworthy, then we're pretty screwed.”
—Helen Toner, former OpenAI board member, tells The Verge that AI needs stronger governance than trusting tech executives to do the right thing.
One more thing
How AI and Wikipedia have sent vulnerable languages into a doom spiral
When Kenneth Wehr started managing the Greenlandic-language version of Wikipedia, he discovered that almost every article had been written by people who didn’t speak the language.
A growing number of them had been copy-pasted into Wikipedia from machine translators—and were riddled with elementary mistakes. This is beginning to cause a wicked problem.
AI systems, from Google Translate to ChatGPT, learn new languages by scraping text from Wikipedia. This could push the most vulnerable languages on Earth toward the precipice.
Read the full story on what happens when AI gets trained on junk pages.
—Jacob Judah
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ Adelaide Zoo is celebrating its first cassowary eggs in 34 years.
+ Photos fill the frame at the Epson Pano awards, which celebrate panoramic photography.
+ Indonesia has called an early halt to the world's largest deforestation project, saving up to 4 million acres.
+ After over a month on the loose in Yellowstone, a little dog called Luna has been reunited with her owners.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 16, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 16, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Monday, November 16, 2026.
From Ola Electric making a major change to its retailing business, to India and US-based semiconductor company Bharat Semi raising $24 million in seed funding to develop programmable smart sensors, here are the latest developments across sectors.
Featured Stories
Ola Electric hands the keys to dealers. What led to this shift in gears?
On November 1, Ola Electric stopped taking orders at its own outlets. Most of them will be shut by December, as Ola moves away from the direct-to-consumer model that defined the company and turns to a dealer-led business.
Ola has recorded this in its investor presentation filed with the NSE and BSE on November 12 under Regulation 30 of the SEBI Listing Regulations. The document covers the unaudited standalone and consolidated results for the second quarter and half-year ended September 30, 2026.
In its Q2 FY27 shareholders' letter, dated November 12, the company calls the move towards a dealer-led model a "reset". What prompted this 'reset'?
Latest News
Oister Global launches Rs 600 Cr deeptech fund
Oister Global, an India-focused multi-strategy private markets asset manager, has announced the launch of a Rs 600 crore deeptech fund to back revenue generating Indian startups.
The Oister Deep Tech Fund aims to raise Rs 400 crore with a Rs 200 crore greenshoe, taking the potential corpus to Rs 600 crore.
A statement from Oister Global said this deeptech fund will build a concentrated portfolio of 8 to 10 mature companies in the frontier tech ecosystem. The fund will focus in sectors such as space technology, defence and aerospace, semiconductors and electronics, quantum technologies, advanced mobility, advanced materials and energy storage.
Funding News
Bharat Semi raises $24M to develop AI-enabled sensors
India- and US-based semiconductor company Bharat Semi has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop programmable smart sensors for Physical AI, where machines use artificial intelligence to perceive and act in the real world.
The round was led by Info Edge, the internet group behind Naukri; South Park Commons, a founder community and early-stage investor; and IndusBridge Ventures, which backs deeptech sector.
Micromax, an electronics group; Valour Capital, a deeptech investor; New York-based venture syndicate Gaingels and angel investors Mukul Agarwal and Kartik Iyer also participated.
Other News
Equity Intelligence invests Rs 2.5 crore in 90+ My Tuition App to launch Future+ Foundery
Equity Intelligence, the investment firm led by Porinju Veliyath, has invested Rs 2.5 crore in 90+ My Tuition App, owned by Daskalos Virtual Academy, at a Rs 50 crore valuation. The funds will launch Future+ Foundery, a separate brand offering school-integrated future-skills programmes. Its 15 learning areas include artificial intelligence, space technology, entrepreneurship, digital marketing, defence careers and leadership.
Students begin with a Discovery Programme, then progress through Foundation, Advanced Learning and Real Industry Learning, each a one-year pathway. Proceeds will fund curriculum, school partnerships, technology and national expansion through a Future+ Integrated School Network, while Daskalos develops an AI Teacher Programme.
Arborum Labs raises pre-seed funding to build world models for complex networks
Bengaluru-based Arborum Labs has raised an undisclosed pre-seed round co-led by Speciale Invest and Ideaspring Capital to build AI world models for complex infrastructure networks. Other participants include BCG's Neeraj Aggarwal and Pranay Mehrotra and Sriram Rajamani, while ARTPARK and FSID are also supporters.
Founded by IISc's Himanshu Tyagi and former BCG AI leader Pooja Rajdev, the startup models how power and telecom systems behave, supporting forecasting, trading, battery optimisation and outage detection. It already works with several Indian networks. The funds will accelerate development and expansion in India and the US, with a public version planned within a year.
Brighter Mind Category III AIF crosses Rs 50 crore in investor commitments
Brighter Mind Asset Management has crossed Rs 50 crore in investor commitments for its Category III AIF, Brighter Mind Inevitable Fortune Fund, launched in April 2025. The long-only fund focuses on listed Indian equities and the pre-IPO space, and uses no derivatives.
Its investment approach rests on a proprietary 3M framework: Megatrend, Management and Margin of Safety. Led by founder, managing director and CEO CA Rajeev Ranjan and co-founder and CIO Manoj Bandre, the firm says the milestone reflects investor trust. It plans to stay disciplined in portfolio construction and remain committed to high-conviction, research-driven value investing as the fund grows.
mistEO raises Rs 18 crore seed round led by MGF-Kavachh to scale climate risk intelligence
Thiruvananthapuram-based climate intelligence company mistEO has raised Rs 18 crore in a seed round led by MGF-Kavachh, with Seafund and others participating. Announced at Huddle Global 2026, the funds will scale its Climate Decision Intelligence platform for banks, insurers and agri-value chains across India and Asia, deepen its forecasting models and grow its team.
The platform fuses physics-based weather modelling with AI, using satellite, radar and sensor data to show how weather affects specific farms, assets or loans. Its Indra model forecasts at 3 km spatial resolution. mistEO already works with NABARD, UNDP, the Indian Air Force and Australian livestock farmers.
Consint.ai and Pramana HealthTech partner to drive connected health ecosystem across Asia-Pacific
Consint.ai, an Indian deep-tech company building foundational health AI models with IndiaAI Mission support, has signed a strategic partnership with Pramana HealthTech to explore opportunities across Asia-Pacific. The collaboration combines Consint.ai's generative and agentic AI capabilities with Pramana's ecosystem orchestration approach, aiming to connect financial, administrative, operational and clinical processes across payers, providers, pharmacies and laboratories.
It will examine six areas, including financing models, claims and payer coordination, programme economics and outcome-based models, aligned with Pramana's Financial Orchestration for Healthcare Sustainability domain. Both firms intend to engage regional stakeholders, focusing on claims intelligence, financial integrity and process automation across programmes.""
Arborum Labs raises pre-seed round co-led by Speciale Invest and Ideaspring Capital
Arborum Labs, a Bengaluru-based AI startup building world models for complex networks, has raised an undisclosed pre-seed round co-led by Speciale Invest and Ideaspring Capital. Backers include BCG's Neeraj Aggarwal and Pranay Mehrotra, Sriram Rajamani, ARTPARK and early supporter FSID.
Co-founded by IISc's Himanshu Tyagi and former BCG generative AI leader Pooja Rajdev, the company's models learn how infrastructure components interact, helping operators simulate scenarios. In power, they support forecasting, trading and battery optimisation; in telecom, they detect impending outages. Arborum already works with several nationwide Indian networks and will use the funds to expand in India and the US.
Zoho Desk marks 10 years from Tenkasi and unveils Blended Agents for customer service
Zoho Desk, built in Tenkasi, Tamil Nadu, marks 10 years serving more than 125,000 businesses across 155 countries, growing roughly 35% annually between 2017 and 2025. To mark the anniversary, Zoho has launched Blended Agents, powered by Zia Agents, which retrieve information, execute tasks across connected applications and hand over to humans when judgement is needed.
Businesses can build and deploy AI agents at no extra cost, paying only for LLM usage. The release also adds Automation Studio, a customisable Workstation and WhatsApp calling and payments. Zoho's Tenkasi campus houses around 1,100 employees, about half of them local.
Uber partners with Mahindra Last Mile Mobility to support 5,000 electric autos
Uber has signed a memorandum of understanding with Mahindra Last Mile Mobility to support the adoption of 5,000 electric three-wheelers over the next 12 months. The EV Auto Advantage programme will offer drivers financing, trade-in incentives and support, focusing on markets where electric vehicle penetration remains low.
Announced in Mumbai on the sidelines of Earthshot Week, the partnership aims to make electric mobility a better economic choice for drivers. Uber also showcased Connected Journeys, a feature rolling out progressively from Delhi that combines autos or two-wheelers with metro travel in a single journey plan, with route options, timings and pricing visible in the app.
Medi Assist appoints Aruna Vaidyanathan as Chief Growth and Culture Officer
Medi Assist Healthcare Services has appointed Aruna Vaidyanathan, formerly Global Head of Growth Marketing at TCS, as Chief Growth and Culture Officer, reporting to CEO Satish Gidugu. She will build a unified go-to-market engine across its three businesses: Medi Assist Insurance TPA, India's largest third party administrator; its technology platforms; and Mayfair We Care, which administers international health benefits across 185 countries.
Her remit covers brand, market messaging and stakeholder communications, with each business given its own identity under one brand. She will also build a single culture across teams brought together through acquisitions and countries. She began her career as a business journalist.
Visage Lines launches rE, a recovery brand built around 10-minute daily resets
Visage Lines Personal Care, parent company of Bombay Shaving Company, has launched rE, a recovery brand built around 10-minute daily resets. The range has 14 products across three categories: Reset, Rewind and Recover, including a massage gun, foam roller, eye massager and calf sleeve.
Short routines target areas, such as three minutes for the neck and shoulders, five for the lower back and seven for the scalp and eyes. Routines were developed with orthopaedic surgeon Dr Manan Vora and physiotherapist Dr Yamini Burkule. The brand is pursuing partnerships with marathons, gyms and workplaces, and is available online from 16 November.
Quest Global acquires Tests Assured to strengthen wearables engineering and testing
Quest Global Engineering Services has acquired Tests Assured, a San Jose-based company specialising in quality assurance and technology-enabled testing for immersive products, smart devices and wearables. Founded in 2018, Tests Assured brings expertise in AR/VR/XR and smart-glasses testing, biometric validation, human-interaction modelling and computer-vision data collection, along with a strong presence among global wearable-device companies.
The acquisition aims to strengthen Quest Global's ability to deliver engineering solutions for wearables in the high-tech consumer space and support customers across the product lifecycle. The two companies will also pursue new opportunities in the hi-tech and semiconductor industries.
Recode Studios reports 24% revenue growth in H1 FY27
Beauty and personal care brand Recode Studios reported a 24% year-on-year growth in revenue from operations to Rs 45.82 crore for the first half of FY27, compared with Rs 36.91 crore in the corresponding period last year. Profit after tax increased 27% to Rs 4.92 crore, while EBITDA rose 9% to Rs 6.45 crore. The company attributed the performance to deeper market penetration and an expanding omnichannel distribution network.
Recode has expanded its retail presence to 25 franchise outlets, two company-owned stores and seven premium kiosks across more than 20 cities. It has also increased its portfolio to over 400 SKUs. The company expects to deliver more than 50% growth in FY27.
Scalar Field records $60 million in trading activity through AI agents
Y Combinator-backed fintech startup Scalar Field has recorded $60 million in cumulative trading activity through its AI trading agents, approximately four months after launching the platform in July 2026. The figure includes both simulated and live trading activity. The platform enables investors to develop trading strategies, test them against historical market data and deploy them through supported accounts.
Its AI capabilities assist with research and strategy development, while a separate execution system applies user-defined rules and monitors positions. Ramakant Yadav, Co-founder of Scalar Field, said the platform enables investors to translate market ideas into testable strategies without requiring dedicated research and engineering teams. The startup's next priority is improving transparency and helping users understand their agents' trading decisions.
Pensionbazaar partners Zypp Electric to offer NPS to gig workers
Pensionbazaar, a brand under Paisabazaar, has partnered with electric mobility platform Zypp Electric to offer National Pension System (NPS) solutions to its gig delivery partners. Zypp operates a fleet of more than 30,000 electric vehicles across eight cities and has impacted over 2.8 lakh gig workers. Under the partnership, eligible delivery partners can enrol in NPS through a digital, consent-based process and make contributions using UPI, net banking or cards.
Zypp aims to bring 60-70% of eligible delivery partners into the pension ecosystem within the first six to 12 months. The initiative seeks to address the limited access gig workers have to formal retirement benefits and encourage long-term savings through flexible contributions.
Fireflies.ai expands platform with AI teammate Fred
Fireflies.ai has expanded its product portfolio with the launch of Fred, an AI teammate designed to help organisations manage tasks across workplace applications. The platform brings together meeting notes, email, Slack, scheduling, screen recording and enterprise search. The company said Fred completed nearly 100 million tasks over the past six months, while usage beyond meeting notes grew 140%.
The expanded offering includes AI-powered meeting preparation, voice typing, email assistance, scheduling and voice agents. Fireflies also introduced Fireflies Fly, a hardware device designed to capture notes from phone calls and in-person conversations. The platform connects with over 240 tools. Fireflies said its new experience would roll out progressively, with paid plans starting at $10 per user per month.
Embark launches location analytics tool for GCC expansion in India
Embark has launched a Location Analytics Tool to help global companies identify suitable cities and micro-markets for establishing Global Capability Centres (GCCs) in India. The platform evaluates locations across seven parameters and more than 35 sub-parameters, covering talent availability, real estate, regulatory conditions, connectivity, infrastructure and liveability.
Companies can customise criteria based on their sector, proposed workforce and business functions. The tool also provides insights into peer GCCs, role-level talent availability and office rental costs. According to Embark, its database draws on research covering approximately 2,100 GCCs in India. The platform aims to simplify location selection, which traditionally involves extensive consultant-led studies, and enable companies to make faster, data-backed expansion decisions.
Kotak Mahindra Bank, NSRCEL onboard 90 women entrepreneurs under startup programme
Kotak Mahindra Bank, through its CSR initiative Kotak BizLabs, has onboarded 90 women entrepreneurs for the sixth cohort of its Women Startup Program (WSP 6), implemented in partnership with NSRCEL at IIM Bangalore. The seven-month hybrid incubation programme, running from September 2026 to April 2027, will help founders strengthen business models, improve customer acquisition, build brands and prepare for fundraising.
The programme is aimed at women founders who have developed a minimum viable product and begun engaging with customers or generating revenue. It combines online sessions with workshops, bootcamps and exhibitions. The initiative also provides mentorship, market access and investor-readiness support to help women-led businesses build sustainable enterprises.
Unstop launches AI bootcamp for students
Unstop has launched a Student AI Bootcamp, sponsored by Amazon Web Services (AWS), to provide students with opportunities to understand and explore artificial intelligence. The initiative aims to bridge the gap between classroom learning and practical exposure to emerging technologies.
Through its platform, Unstop will help students discover and participate in programmes focused on AI and its applications across sectors such as banking, healthcare, education and manufacturing.
NIELIT Hyderabad trains over 200 students in quantum technology
More than 200 students from nine educational institutions participated in a three-day workshop on quantum communications and applications in quantum technology organised by NIELIT Hyderabad under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.
Conducted from November 11 to 13 in partnership with QClairvoyance Quantum Labs, the workshop covered quantum mechanics, entanglement, quantum algorithms, quantum key distribution and post-quantum cryptography.
(This article will be updated with the latest news throughout the day.)

articles.title: Google selects 10 startups for inaugural Africa Applied AI Lab cohort - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Google has selected 10 startups for the first cohort of its Google Africa Applied AI Lab, which gives founders early access to Google AI models, technical mentorship and links to venture capital.
Based at the Accra AI Community Centre (AICC) in Ghana, the Google Africa Applied AI Lab is managed by the Google AI Futures Fund alongside Google Research. It aims to support founders from across the continent interested in using the latest AI research to address real-world, uniquely African challenges – and, in turn, “build Africa’s first generation of AI-native unicorn startups”.
Google received thousands of entries from startups across more than 45 African countries, and has now selected 10 to take part in the inaugural cohort.
Three of the selected startups are from Nigeria – Intron, which builds speech recognition that understands African accents and code-switching; Termii, which provides customer verification and messaging for financial services; and Vendy, which lets businesses run storefronts and take payments inside WhatsApp.
Uganda’s Crane AI Labs builds offline AI tools for health workers and schools on affordable phones; Kenya’s Satlyt turns satellites into computing nodes that process data in orbit; and Senegal’s Tolbi combines satellite imagery with voice guidance to help smallholder farmers.
The cohort also includes four pan-African startups. AethexAI provides AI voice agents for banks, telcos and call centres; Agrails builds AI-powered insurance infrastructure for farmers, gig workers and small borrowers; Smile ID uses computer vision for identity verification; and Viamo brings generative AI to feature phone users through voice calls in local languages.
Over the coming weeks, the startups will work with Google engineers, researchers and product leaders, building with models such as Gemini and Gemma. They will also get go-to-market support from the lab’s VC partners – 4DX Ventures, Norrsken22, Novastar Ventures and Ventures Platform.
The programme ends with a demo day at the Accra AI Community Centre in December.

articles.title: Affaire Jensen Huang : une « cellule de crise » pousse pour le retour du patron de Nvidia
articles.text:
L’affaire Jensen Huang n’est toujours pas terminée : après sa démission il y a quelques jours, certains de ses proches et des salariés de Nvidia travailleraient d’arrache-pied pour convaincre le conseil d’administration de l’entreprise de le réintégrer. Une « cellule de crise » se serait même formée autour de l’homme d’affaires, rapporte le Financial Times.
Les soutiens de Jensen Huang veulent son retour à la tête de Nvidia
Une source du média américain a expliqué qu’une cellule de crise serait en train de se créer et elle serait composée de patrons d’entreprises de la tech dans la Silicon Valley. Tous voudraient faire pression sur le conseil d’administration afin de le convaincre de nommer à nouveau Jensen Huang à la tête de l’entreprise. Ces alliés tenteraient même d’obtenir le soutien de la Maison Blanche ; tous disent l’adorer.
Un site Internet s’est même monté en quelques jours, avec une lettre ouverte déjà signée par plus de 158 000 personnes. Parmi les signataires, des dizaines de milliers d’actionnaires de Nvidia, et des gros noms comme celui d’Elon Musk, dirigeant de SpaceX et de Tesla, ou encore celui de Tim Sweeney, dirigeant d’Epic Games. On compte aussi beaucoup d’employés de Nvidia qui réclament le retour de leur ancien reponsable.
Selon plusieurs sources du Financial Times, Huang aurait évoqué un possible retour auprès de ses proches. Il soutiendrait même les efforts de cette cellule de crise. Bien que pour le moment, l’enquête indépendante sur les relations intimes de Huang avec des employées est toujours en cours. Depuis, c’est la directrice financière de Nvidia Colette Kress qui a repris les rênes de la société en intérim, en attendant qu’un nouveau dirigeant soit recruté.
Jensen Huang : un patron très populaire, et qui a rapporté beaucoup d’argent à ses actionnaires
Nvidia a été fondée en avril 1993, notamment par Jensen Huang, qui était auparavant designer de microprocesseurs chez AMD. Depuis le premier jour, il était à la tête de Nvidia et durant ces décennies, il s’est bâti une très solide réputation, tant auprès de ses salariés qu’auprès de ses partenaires. Ce qui explique la mobilisation pour sa réintégration à la tête de Nvidia.
D’un autre côté, ses soutiens ont aussi un intérêt économique. En un mois, l’action de Nvidia en bourse a perdu 25% : un quart de la valeur des actions s’est envolée. Pour beaucoup, sans Jensen Huang, l’action de Nvidia vaut beaucoup moins. Comme l’a rapporté BFM Bourse, c’est ce qu’exprimait par exemple l’analyste Dan Ives : « Nvidia sans Jensen Huang vaut 25% à 30% de moins en bourse. » Les soutiens de Huang sont également convaincus d’autre chose : il est le seul homme capable de faire remonter la pente en bourse de Nvidia.

articles.title: Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing
Enterprise teams are building multi-agent systems, and when early implementations fall short, the cause is rarely the model. Multi-agent coordination is a distributed systems problem, and many teams taking it on haven’t yet built distributed systems instincts.
The numbers are consistent across sources: ~88% of AI pilots never reach production. Stanford HAI demonstrated that two models can perform worse collaborating than either alone when coordination overhead exceeds the benefit. The pattern is clear: teams are adding complexity faster than they build understanding. Ten steps that are each 95 percent reliable deliver only 59.9 percent end-to-end reliability, and 20 steps deliver 35.8 percent. This illustrative model assumes a strictly sequential chain with no retries, but the direction holds: each dependent handoff multiplies risk.
In this post, you learn how to decide whether a use case needs multiple agents, choose a coordination pattern, and spot costly anti-patterns early. You also see how takt time, safety boundaries, edge data, and shift cycles shape the architecture.
Multi-agent coordination patterns
Coordination patterns fall into two tiers, based on who controls the flow. In Tier 1, you define the path.
In Tier 2, the model chooses the path at runtime. That flexibility handles work whose steps you can’t define in advance, at a higher cost in tokens, latency, and debugging. The practical default is to start with Tier 1 and move a task to Tier 2 only when its subtasks emerge during the work.
Tier 1: Patterns (deterministic control flow)
1.1 Sequential Pipeline: Orchestration patterns that implement linear execution where each node’s output feeds into the next node (A -> B -> C) supporting ordered processing with predictable execution timing
In the following diagram, input flows to agent A (extract), then agent B (transform), then agent C (validate), and then output. The user defines that order at build time, and nothing is decided at runtime. As a result, the pipeline is straightforward to debug and test, and its cost is predictable. Typical fits include document processing, extract, transform, and load (ETL) chains, and warranty-claim triage.
1.2 Conditional Workflow: Logic-based edges select the next node by condition, so the workflow can branch and send each case down a different path.
In the following diagram, a user request goes to agent A (write code) and then to agent B (test code). A pass/fail check sends passing work to agent D (deploy). Failing work loops back to agent A for a retry, up to a maximum of N times, and then escalates to a human. The orchestration layer enforces that cap, for example through an AWS Step Functions iteration limit, which keeps the loop from becoming the unbounded iteration anti-pattern described later in this post.
1.3 Conditional Router:
A classification step examines the input and directs it to the appropriate processing path. Only one path is executed per request. Best for intent-driven dispatch, quality-gate decisions, customer inquiry routing, and anomaly triage.
The following diagram shows a plant supervisor’s request being read by a classifier and sent to exactly one specialist. Questions about whether parts meet spec go to the Quality Agent, overdue equipment services go to the Maintenance Agent, and shift changes go to the Scheduling Agent. This decision is made at the entry point.
1.4 Parallel Workflow: A task splits into independent subtasks that run simultaneously across handlers, each on its own data. A fan-in step combines the results when all handlers complete, and a failure in one path retries only that path. Best for multi-source analysis, batch processing, and work that decomposes into independent pieces.
In the following diagram, a research orchestrator decomposes the task and dispatches it to three specialist agents that run concurrently: a financial data agent, a geopolitical agent, and a logistics agent, each analyzing its own source. A combined step waits for all three, then synthesizes the results, resolves conflicts, and ranks the findings. Latency equals the slowest single agent rather than the sum of all three.
Tier 2: Autonomous patterns (LLM-determined control flow)
In autonomous patterns, control flow is determined at runtime by the AI model itself, not predefined by developers. Agents read task state, reason about what’s needed and coordinate through shared context rather than fixed paths spanning a spectrum from structured orchestration to fully emergent behavior.
2.1 Plan-based orchestration
In plan-based orchestration, a single orchestrator agent acts as a project manager. The orchestrator maintains an explicit task plan with assignments and dependencies, sees all context while each worker receives only its slice, distributes work dynamically against the current plan, and monitors progress centrally. Key design choice is that the workers are stateless and independent. If one fails, it doesn’t contaminate others. The orchestrator retries only the failed worker, not the entire workflow.
The following diagram shows how a planner agent decomposes a task into an explicit plan and dispatches each step to a worker’s agent. Each step goes to a dedicated worker (a research agent, an analysis agent, and a report agent) that sees only its assigned slice.
2.2 Handoff pattern
Agents operate with limited, local knowledge and coordinate through peer-to-peer delegation. Each makes local decisions about when and to whom to transfer control, based on the task and the agents it knows. Control passes with state: each transfer carries validated task state, the evidence behind it, and any unresolved questions, so the receiving agent continues rather than reinterpreting a summary. A handoff that moves only through the conversation is not a handoff.
In the following diagram, a customer service agent transfers control, together with its context, to either a technical support agent or a billing agent, and technical support can hand off further to a senior engineer. Each agent knows only the small set of peers it can transfer to.
2.3 Conversation-driven pattern
In conversation-driven patterns (also known as group chat patterns), all agents participate in a shared conversation where orchestration emerges through turn-taking rather than explicit plans or structured handoffs. This mirrors human team collaboration where everyone can see the discussion and contribute when appropriate.
In the following diagram, an agent-selection mechanism decides whose turn it is, and agents A, B, and C each add to one shared conversation, where every turn is a message plus a tool call. The selection mechanism sets the turn-taking, and state lives implicitly in the conversation history.
Control flow characteristics:
- Visibility: Broadcast all agents observe all messages in the shared conversation.
- Decision making: Next speaker selected based on conversation context, not predetermined plans.
- State management: Implicit in the conversation history.
- Turn-taking: Determined by selection mechanisms (round-robin, AI-driven) 
         
  - Round-robin. Agents take turns in a fixed, repeating order until a termination condition is met, which keeps it predictable.
  - AI-driven. A model selects the next speaker from the conversation context rather than a fixed order.
2.4 Debate/consensus
Multiple agents independently evaluate the same input, and their conclusions are reconciled by majority, by a judge agent, or by escalation when they disagree. Unlike a conversation-driven pattern, the agents do not see each other’s reasoning before committing to a position, which is what makes disagreement informative rather than socially convergent.
Use it sparingly. Debate is the most expensive pattern here, and on perceptual tasks it buys latency rather than accuracy (see the quality-inspection case in anti-pattern 3 that follows). Reserve it for high-stakes, low-volume decisions where being wrong costs more than deliberating.
Hybrid approaches
In practice, most production systems combine several patterns based on task decomposition:
- Use workflow patterns for predictable, well-understood components.
- Apply autonomous patterns where flexibility and adaptation are essential.
- Implement task management patterns (termination, delegation) consistently across all orchestration types.
- Design hierarchical compositions where complex agents internally use different patterns at different layers.
The governing principle: pattern-to-task alignment. Match the orchestration approach to each task’s inherent characteristics and your system’s reliability requirements rather than forcing everything through a single pattern.
Anti-patterns that burn budget
Each of the following five anti-patterns looks reasonable at design time, and each surfaces later as an inflated token cost, a missed takt-time window, or a decision that has quietly drifted out of sync with the plant floor.
1. God agent
One agent owns overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) analysis, programmable logic controller (PLC) diagnostics, and maintenance behind a single prompt with 15 or more tools. Tool selection degrades as tools grow, and failures become hard to attribute.
The fix: Bounded agents of five tools or fewer, such as an OEE analyst, a fault diagnostician, and a maintenance drafter.
2. Unbounded iteration
The agent loops on “try again” with no hard stop. A four-agent system can burn a significantly higher number of tokens before a single retry, and no one call trips an alarm. Retries multiply coordination failures rather than fixing them.
The fix: Hard iteration ceiling in code, per-agent token ceiling, budget alarm wired to an automatic stop. Infrastructure enforces limits. The model will not stop itself.
3. Natural-language contracts
Agents hand each other free-text prose with no schema. Interpretation hardens at every hop: “could indicate wear” becomes “confirmed wear” becomes a maintenance order. The drift happens between agents, where tracing is thinnest.
4. Premature multi-agent
Multi-agent where one agent with tool groups would do. Each agent adds a coordination tax that is not linear, and the gains flatten around four. Most “specialists” are one model in different costumes.
The fix: Needs at least two different models, different tool access, concurrent execution, and real interdependency. Fewer than two, and one agent with action groups does it.
The test: can one agent handle the phases by switching tools? Then it is not a multi-agent problem.
5. Unguarded customer contact
The agent triggers real-world actions (email, service visits, machine parameters) with no approval step. Hallucinations cross into the physical world, irreversible actions compound, and liability escalates from a refund to product liability.
The fix: Defense in depth: recommendation → Amazon Bedrock Guardrails → schema validation → business rules → human approval → execution.
Every point where agent output reaches a customer, or a safety system is a trust boundary.
Choosing an architecture
With the patterns and anti-patterns in view, the architecture choice comes down to a short sequence of questions.
- Does the task require action beyond text generation? Treat a direct model call as the baseline and add orchestration only for a measured reason. Summarizing documents or generating code from a specification rarely supplies one.
- Is the solution path known in advance? If you can write down what happens in what order, you don’t have a “how many agents” decision at all. Your real choice is simpler: a single agent that calls tools, or a Tier 1 workflow.
- Does the work require genuinely distinct expertise? Separate domains with established handoffs justify specialized agents. A single domain belongs to one agent, no matter how many tools it needs.
- Does the solution emerge only through exploration? When the action sequence is known and can run as an act-and-validate loop, it belongs to a single agent, even one that plans its steps dynamically. Tier 2 earns its added cost, latency, and debugging burden only when the subtasks themselves are discovered in the course of the work.
The following decision tree turns these four questions into a path you can follow from top to bottom.
The tree starts by asking whether the task requires actions beyond text generation. If it doesn’t, a simple model call is enough. If it does, the tree asks whether the solution is well known and can be expressed as a workflow. On the known solution side, work that benefits from specialized expertise or domain separation go to a Tier 1 multi-agent workflow (a pipeline, fan-out, or router). Everything else goes to a single agent with tools and action groups. On the unknown-solution side, only tasks that involve exploration or significant side effects go to Tier 2 for autonomous multi-agent patterns. The rest stays with a single agent. The guiding principle is to choose the simplest architecture that meets your requirements.
The following chart compares the patterns on four things: when to reach for each one, how control flows between agents, how deterministic the result is, and what it costs to build and operate. Build cost is a relative scale, not an estimate.
Tier 1 patterns score high on determinism at low to moderate build cost. Tier 2 patterns give more of the path to the model, and plan-based orchestration costs the most to build. If you can draw the control flow on a whiteboard before runtime, start with Tier 1.
Applied: Mapping patterns to manufacturing use cases
| Use Case | Pattern | Rationale | 
| Shift handoff summarization | Sequential Pipeline | Linear: raw logs → summary → report | 
| Multi-station root-cause analysis | Plan-Based Orchestrator | Dynamic: subtasks discovered during analysis | 
| Real-time quality gate | Conditional Router + Edge Agent | In-cycle: local model decides. Agent reasoning off path | 
| Predictive maintenance scheduling | Parallel Fan-Out/Fan-In | Independent models per asset class | 
| Engineering change order impact | Debate/Consensus | High stakes: adversarial review justified | 
| Supplier communication drafting | Sequential + Human Gate | Must not auto-send (see Unguarded Customer Contact) | 
| Cross-plant optimization | Plan-Based Orchestrator | Multi-source: dynamic queries. Solver does allocation | 
The manufacturing lens: Four constraints that change the calculus
Manufacturing is not a generic enterprise IT environment, and four constraints make that arithmetic unforgiving.
Constraint 1: Production-line latency = direct revenue loss
Automotive body shops, where robots weld the vehicle body together, typically run at 60 jobs per hour. Each of their over 40 stations has a 60-second takt time before the line advances. Inference latency that sits on a station’s cycle path eats into those 60 seconds, and a delay at the bottleneck station slows the whole line. Even a 2 percent throughput reduction can translate to significant annual revenue impact.
Architecture implication: budget latency at p99, not average. The tail is what stops the line. Give every agent a sub-second deterministic fallback, and match it to the risk:
- Advisory/quality-flagging: Pass the part with a flag for end-of-line review.
- Safety-critical: Containment or a deterministic stop, not continuation.
- Decide this mapping per station before deployment.
Constraint 2: Safety has physical consequences
A hallucinated chatbot causes embarrassment. A hallucinated welding parameter causes structural defects that surface in crash testing or field failure and can lead to a safety recall. Two failure modes recur:
- OT/IT boundary state desync: An agent reads the manufacturing execution system (MES) as Station 12 running Part #A, but a manual PLC override already switched it to Part #B, so it tunes parameters for the wrong part.
- Hallucinated safety boundary: A maintenance agent reasons about lockout/tagout from scratch and declares Station 7 accessible while adjacent Station 6 runs, breaking the interlock zone.
Architecture implication:
The boundary: keep the deterministic core unchanged, including PLCs, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, and the MES, and wrap an advisory layer around it.
- Agents observe, analyze, and recommend. They do not actuate.
- Safety constraints live as deterministic guardrails in an external service that agents query rather than reason about. They’re never embedded in prompts, where they can be argued away.
Validation and approval: A recommendation passes schema validation and physics simulation, checked against the OT source of truth immediately before actuation, never against OT state cached beyond one cycle. It’s then approved at a level matched to its scope:
- Level 0: Agent resolves autonomously.
- Level 1: Operator confirms with one click.
- Level 2: Engineer decides from the presented analysis.
- Level 3: Management evaluates a line-stop recommendation.
Only then does a validated command interface pass permitted commands to deterministic control. The large language model (LLM) proposes. The physics engine and the human operator dispose.
Constraint 3: Data lives at the edge
A single stamping press generates 50+ GB/day of sensor data whose value decays in milliseconds. Shipping it to the cloud costs more in bandwidth than compute, and by the time the cloud answers, the press has moved on.
Architecture implication: hybrid edge-cloud is the practical default, and the Constraint 2 boundary holds at the edge too.
- Edge (AWS IoT Greengrass): sub-takt anomaly detection, threshold monitoring, and stop-or-continue signals at the source: the edge agent recommends, the PLC acts.
- Cloud: What the edge can’t do: cross-shift analytics, trend correlation across plants, and model retraining on fleet data. The edge distills and transmits only what matters.
Constraint 4: Shift-aligned agent lifecycle
Unbounded context makes an agent drift as stale observations crowd out current reality. A full reset loses continuity between shifts. Manufacturing already solves this for humans with structured shift handoffs, and agents need the same discipline.
Architecture implication: Bound agent memory to the shift cycle.
- Initialize: Shift context, including the crew roster, production targets, and the prior shift handoff.
- Accumulate: Working memory within the shift window only.
- Hand off: Emit a shift-end summary of open issues, flagged anomalies, and recommendations that seed the next crew, mirroring the human ritual without unbounded context growth.
Building on AWS
The following managed services map to the concerns raised earlier in this post. Each row names the mechanism, not just the service.
| Need | Service | Mechanism | 
| Runtime | AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Where agents run, their control flow is determined or model determined. Bring Strands, LangGraph, or CrewAI. | 
| Shift-bounded memory | AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Managed short-term and long-term context, so the shift-scoped memory from Constraint 4 is configuration rather than custom state plumbing. | 
| Typed handoffs | AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Converts APIs and AWS Lambda functions into Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools with validated schemas, so handoffs carry typed fields rather than prose. | 
| Agent permissions | AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | A unique, verifiable identity for each agent with fine-grained access control. It’s the enforcement point for which agent can reach which system, and on whose behalf. | 
| Tracing between agents | AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Spans and traces across runtime, memory, gateway, and tools, through Amazon CloudWatch Transaction Search and AWS Distro for Open Telemetry (ADOT). Handoffs are the least observable part of a multi-agent system and where untyped contracts fail silently. | 
| Human approval surface | AWS Quick | Where the escalation tiers land. AWS Quick Automate runs approval workflows with one-click approval in Slack, and its action connectors can invoke Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agents. | 
| Tiered model selection | Amazon Bedrock | One API across model families, so cost tiering is configuration: a small model for a router’s classification and a stronger one for an orchestrator synthesis. | 
Conclusion
Multi-agent systems change how automotive manufacturers orchestrate intelligence at scale, but only when built on the right foundations.
The patterns and anti-patterns here come from real deployments where poor architecture shows up as runaway token costs, takt-time violations, and, at worst, physical safety risks. The economics at plant scale are unforgiving, because token volume grows with every agent, robot, and shift. Tiered model selection, context compression, and edge-cloud distribution are the main levers for delivering the same value at a fraction of that cost.
The recommendation here is to start with Tier 1 patterns, prove value, and then expand. Most manufacturing use cases, such as shift handoff summarization, quality-gate decisions, and predictive maintenance, are well served by deterministic workflows. Reserve autonomous orchestration for genuinely open-ended problems where dynamic subtask discovery justifies the added cost, latency, and debugging complexity.

articles.title: Starship : pourquoi la récupération du second étage change tout
articles.text:
Ça y est, Starship a réussi ce que personne n’avait jamais fait : la récupération d’un second étage de fusée. Un exploit qui rapproche un peu plus SpaceX de la fusée entièrement réutilisable.
Ce n’était pourtant pas gagné. Car à l’origine, l’objectif de ce 15e vol test était de rattraper à la fois le booster et le second étage. Mais le Super Heavy a rencontré un problème lors de son retour, et finalement terminé sa mission dans le golfe du Mexique. Mais le « Ship », lui, a poursuivi sa route afin de déployer 26 satellites Starlink V3 avant d’entamer une longue série d’orbites autour de la Terre. Puis le moment tant attendu est arrivé.
Première mondiale
Après 22 heures de vol, le second étage a entamé sa manœuvre de désorbitation avant de survoler le Mexique pour rejoindre Starbase, au Texas. Après sa descente, il s’est redressé au dernier moment, puis s’est glissé sans encombre dans les gigantesques bras mécaniques de la tour de lancement. « Félicitations à une équipe incroyable chez SpaceX », a réagi Elon Musk. Le patron de la NASA, Jared Isaacman, a lui aussi salué l’exploit. De quoi presque faire oublier l’échec de Super Heavy.
Car depuis 10 ans, l’entreprise sait effectivement récupérer le propulseur de sa fusée Falcon 9, qui vient se poser sur une barge dans l’océan pour être réutilisé. Mais c’est une première pour un second étage, qui filait à plus de 27 000 kilomètres par heure en orbite. D’autant que sa marge d’erreur est minuscule : il ne tient sur les bras de la tour que par deux petits ergots d’une trentaine de centimètres.
2027 sera déterminante
À terme, SpaceX pourra inspecter, remettre en état et relancer les deux étages de sa fusée, ce qui lui offre une marge de manœuvre inédite pour augmenter la cadence et réduire les coûts. Des éléments essentiels pour concrétiser les projets d'Elon Musk.
À noter, tout de même, que cette capture est une preuve de concept qui ne mènera pas encore à une réutilisation rapide. Car il va aussi falloir peaufiner le bouclier thermique, qui devra être en mesure de résister à la rentrée atmosphérique vol après vol.
Cap sur la suite. Et on se dirige vers une autre étape déterminante, car le vol 16 pourrait décoller depuis la Floride, Starbase seule ne suffisant pas à absorber la hausse des lancements prévue. SpaceX espère aussi réaliser l’an prochain un ravitaillement en orbite : deux Starship lancés coup sur coup, amarrés l’un à l’autre, avec un transfert de carburant.
Sans cette manœuvre, la fusée ne pourrait pas quitter l’orbite basse de la Terre, alors qu’elle doit poser les astronautes de la NASA à la surface lunaire dans deux ans.
Sources : The New York Times, Ars Technica

articles.title: Fini les excès de vitesse, Tesla met à jour son FSD pour l'Europe
articles.text:
Déjà chez plusieurs de nos voisins, mais toujours pas en France, le Tesla FSD gagne du terrain en Europe. Ces pays ont repris l’homologation de la RDW, l’autorité néerlandaise des véhicules, comme dernièrement la Finlande qui l’a fait le 10 novembre.
Un peu plus tôt dans le mois, le 3 novembre, la RDW a validé une première série de changements : le logiciel change officiellement de nom et devient « Tesla Assisted Driving » (Tesla Conduite Assistée en France et en Belgique). Surtout, la marge que le conducteur peut régler au-dessus de la limite de vitesse passe de +50 % à +10 %. Sur une route à 80 km/h, la voiture pouvait ainsi se mettre à 120 km/h si elle jugeait l’environnement propice ou le flux de la circulation semblable. Dans cet exemple, elle plafonnera désormais à 88 km/h. À noter que cette marge revient à 0 % à chaque démarrage. Il faut la régler de nouveau à chaque trajet.
Ces réglages sont déjà dans les modèles de Tesla compatibles. Le 12 novembre, le site spécialisé Not a Tesla App a repéré une mise à jour qui a installé ses nouveaux réglages.
Les mains sur le volant au-delà de 130 km/h
Ce lundi 16 novembre, la RDW a validé une deuxième série de retouches. Au-delà de 130 km/h, le conducteur devra garder les mains sur le volant. Le système l’avertira aussi plus tôt s’il est inattentif pendant que le logiciel est en marche.
Pour régler une vitesse plus haute que celle proposée par le système, il faudra confirmer avec la molette, et si la voiture roule ensuite au-dessus de la limite, le panneau de vitesse clignotera en rouge à l’écran. Ce type d’exigence n’est pas nouveau puisque la Lettonie avait déjà obtenu des corrections avant d’autoriser le FSD en octobre.
Avec ces changements, Tesla remplit les deux conditions de l’Allemagne. Berlin s’était dit prêt à soutenir le FSD s’il était limité à +10 % et renommé. Selon Not a Tesla App, la France et la Suède s’inquiétaient elles aussi des vitesses que le système pouvait atteindre au-dessus des limites. De quoi les rassurer et les amener à voter pour l’homologation généralisée ? Pour mémoire, les pays de l’Union doivent voter pour autoriser ou non le système dans toute l’UE, France comprise, au mois de décembre.

articles.title: Ohne Jailbreak: So kommt Windows 11 aufs iPhone Duo
articles.text:
Im Sommer 2024 hatte Entwickler und Youtuber NT-Dev mit Tiny 11 Core eine abgespeckte Windows-11-Version auf ein iPhone 15 Pro gebracht. Dabei griff NT-Dev auf den offiziell in Apples App-Store verfügbaren Emulator UTM SE zurück.
Windows 11 läuft auf dem iPhone Duo
Ganz ohne Emulator kommt derweil WindowsiOS aus, ein von Google-Entwickler Ammaar Reshi entwickeltes Projekt. Reshi ist es jetzt gelungen, eine ARM-Version von Windows 11 lokal auf Apples neuem Falthandy iPhone Duo zum Laufen zu bringen. Ein Jailbreak war dafür nicht notwendig, wie techspot.com schreibt.
WindowsiOS übersetzt demnach den ARM-Code von Windows 11 in ARM-Code, den der A20-Pro-Chip direkt ausführen kann. Denn beide Plattformen nutzen denselben Befehlssatz. Unter die Arme gegriffen hat Reshi dabei Googles aktuelles KI-Modell Gemini 4 Carbon, wie der Entwickler auf X schreibt.
Dort demonstriert er auch, wie Windows 11 auf dem iPhone Duo funktioniert. Im Video läuft das Ganze recht flott und anscheinend ohne nervige Unterbrechungen. Zum Vergleich: Tiny 11 benötigte allein zum Booten satte 20 Minuten und lief auch danach eher im Schneckentempo.
35 Hintergrunddienste abgeschaltet
Ein Vorteil von Reshis Windows-11-Version ist, dass sie auf dem iPhone Duo nur 4,5 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher benötigt. Dafür mussten mehr als 35 im Hintergrund laufende Dienste wie der Windows Defender weichen.
Das iPhone Duo lässt sich halb aufgeklappt zum Mini-Laptop mit Touch-Tastatur umfunktionieren. Ganz aufgeklappt, öffnet sich Windows auf der gesamten Display-Oberfläche des Foldables.
WindowsiOS: Quellcode auf GitHub
Wer Windows 11 auf das iPhone Duo bringen will, findet den Quellcode des WindowsiOS-Projekts auf GitHub zum Download. Laut techspot.com sind dafür aber Xcode sowie ein eigenes Windows-11-Arm-Image notwendig.
Zudem muss das Gerät bei jedem Startvorgang mit einem Debugger verbunden sein, um den ausführbaren Speicher freizuschalten. Und genau hier liegt auch ein mögliches Problem. Denn dabei handelt es sich um einen inoffiziellen Workaround, den Apple mit einem künftigen iOS-Update unterbinden könnte.
