articles.title: MTN in talks to acquire Telkom four years after failed deal
articles.text:
MTN, Africa’s largest mobile network operator, has returned to the negotiating table to acquire Telkom, South African telecommunications provider Telkom, four years after its previous attempt collapsed.
This time, the telecommunications group is contemplating an all-cash acquisition, with an option for Telkom shareholders to receive MTN shares.
In separate cautionary announcements on Monday, the two companies confirmed that they had entered discussions that could result in MTN acquiring Telkom’s entire issued share capital. Telkom said the discussions followed an approach from MTN.
The proposed acquisition could reshape South Africa’s telecommunications market, bringing two major operators under one roof and giving MTN access to Telkom’s mobile and fibre infrastructure. But the transaction comes with a higher valuation, a powerful state shareholder and potentially difficult regulatory hurdles.
“It is currently contemplated that the consideration will be settled in cash, with an alternative for Telkom shareholders to receive MTN shares,” MTN said in its announcement. The group added that the terms of any transaction, including the form of consideration, remained subject to negotiation.
Telkom’s statement confirmed that the proposed transaction would involve its entire issued share capital, but cautioned that the discussions were still at an early stage. The company said there was no certainty that the transaction would be concluded.
The renewed approach revives a pursuit that dates back more than a decade. MTN and Telkom previously entered formal acquisition discussions in July 2022, but those negotiations collapsed three months later after the parties failed to agree on exclusivity.
At the time, Telkom was also considering a competing proposal from Rain, South Africa’s data-only mobile operator, which wanted to merge with the state-linked telecommunications operator. MTN subsequently withdrew from negotiations because Telkom could not provide assurances that it would negotiate exclusively with the group.
The talks had not progressed to due diligence, and MTN had not submitted a binding offer, Telkom said in October 2022. Rain’s proposed transaction also failed to materialise.
The economics of a potential acquisition have since changed considerably. When the two companies entered discussions in 2022, Telkom was valued at R17.1 billion ($1 billion). Its shares closed at R62 ($3.66) on Friday, giving the company a market capitalisation of R31.7 billion ($1.9 billion).
That is almost double its valuation during the previous negotiations, although it does not represent an agreed acquisition price. MTN has yet to disclose a proposed offer value.
Telkom also presents a different strategic proposition from the business MTN pursued four years ago. Its mobile operation has gained market share while Openserve, Telkom’s wholesale fibre business, has become South Africa’s second-largest fibre network operator by homes passed, with more than 1.5 million homes within reach of its network. .
For MTN, acquiring Telkom would provide an opportunity to expand its mobile subscriber base while gaining access to an established fibre network and enterprise connectivity business. It would also advance the group’s long-standing argument that South Africa’s telecommunications market needs consolidation to support investment and competition.
MTN Group CEO Ralph Mupita has previously argued that the market should consolidate into two or, at most, three major mobile operators. However, he has also acknowledged that any transaction would require regulatory openness, political support and commercial agreement between the parties.
The ownership structure of Telkom makes the political dimension particularly important. The South African government holds 40.5% of the company, while the Government Employees Pension Fund, through the Public Investment Corporation (PIC), owns another 11.1%.
Together, the two public-sector shareholders control 51.6% of Telkom, making their positions important to any transaction involving the company. The interests of the state and public-sector pension beneficiaries will therefore be central to negotiations over a potential sale.
Competition approval is another significant hurdle. Combining MTN and Telkom would remove an established mobile network operator from the market as an independent competitor, potentially strengthening the position of an enlarged MTN against Vodacom, a pan-African mobile network operator .
The Competition Commission and the Independent Communications Authority of South Africa (Icasa) would have to consider the implications for market concentration, spectrum allocation, infrastructure access and competition. Any approval could come with conditions designed to protect smaller operators and ensure fair access to essential telecommunications infrastructure.
The renewed discussions come a day before Telkom publishes its interim results for the six months ended September 30, 2026, as the telecommunications industry gathers in Cape Town for Africa Tech Festival.

articles.title: How MoEngage built agentic customer engagement on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How MoEngage built agentic customer engagement on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
This post was co-written with Ashwin Srinivasan, Nishan Das and Karthik Baile from MoEngage.
A marketing or product team member planning a weekend flash sale often opens three tools before writing a single line of copy. First they open the analytics dashboard to see what worked last time, then the content library to find the right tone, and then the campaign builder to build the campaign itself. Repeat that across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp, and much of a marketing team’s week goes to navigating tools instead of making decisions.
The MoEngage Model Context Protocol (MCP) Connector gives an MCP-compatible assistant, such as Claude or ChatGPT, secure, tenant-scoped access to a brand’s segments, campaign history, and content library.
This capability points to a broader shift in software platforms. Beyond a user interface for business users and an API for engineering teams, a third layer is emerging, where a user describes an outcome in plain language and an agent carries out the steps across the platform. For a customer engagement platform, that means a capability already exposed as an API can become a tool an agent calls, and a campaign that once moved across several tools can move through one conversation instead.
MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use across channels including push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and Rich Communication Services (RCS), set out to build this layer. MoEngage built Merlin AI, a set of artificial intelligence (AI) agents that work with live platform data. Marketing and product teams can now draft, analyze, and adjust campaigns from a single conversation, while agents decide what to send each customer. One customer, Glance, saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates as a result.
MoEngage treated this as an architecture problem. The question was how to give agents secure, tenant-scoped access to live data without rebuilding hundreds of existing APIs. In this post, we walk through how MoEngage solved it with Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale with any framework or model. The post covers the four agent modes in Merlin AI, how MoEngage exposed its existing APIs as MCP tools, and how the architecture keeps each tenant’s data isolated. It closes with the results MoEngage customers have seen and the pattern other software providers can reuse.
Solution overview: Four agent modes in Merlin AI
Merlin AI runs four kinds of agents. All four share the same foundation: foundation models in Amazon Bedrock for reasoning and generation, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for hosting, and MCP for standardized access to data. Across all four modes, Merlin AI uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, tool-call planning, and content generation. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock.
Embedded agents in Merlin AI Studio
Merlin AI Studio places purpose-built agents at the exact point in the workflow where marketing and product teams do that piece of work:
- Copywriter generates personalized push and transactional copy that stays consistent with the brand voice.
- Designer produces a marketing banner or image from a text description.
- Segment Assist turns a plain-language audience description into the correct set of attributes and filters. For example, a marketing or product team member can ask for users who abandoned a cart in the last 2 hours.
- Jinja Assist converts natural-language requests into working Jinja and Liquid markup for dynamic content.
- In-app Template Builder creates responsive, accessible HTML templates for in-app messages, including gamified formats, lead-capture pop-ups, and surveys.
- Flow Assist turns a high-level idea into a ready-to-deploy customer journey. Behind the scenes, a sequence of specialized steps interprets the request, proposes paths, builds the flow structure, refines it with historical data, and packages it for deployment.
Conversational agents
Conversational agents work across campaigns, analytics, segments, and flows. A user can ask a question in plain language and the agent calls the right tools to answer it or act on it. The Campaign Insights Agent, embedded on the analytics page, delegates to specialized sub-agents. One sub-agent runs analysis across several metrics at once. A second diagnoses why a metric is underperforming, and a third compares performance across time periods or segments. A final step formats the findings into a clear answer.
Custom agents
Custom agents let lifecycle and customer relationship management (CRM) teams design agents that run continuously on MoEngage data and tools, inside rules the product and marketing team defines. Every agent shows its work through an activity log of the data it pulled, the decisions it made, the channels it touched, and the content it sent. Teams can run an agent with full autonomy or require human review before anything executes.
Decisioning agents
Decisioning agents act for each individual customer. Each agent decides what to say, when, how often, and on which channel, and it learns from every outcome. Product and marketing teams set the content, goals, and guardrails, and the agents handle the rest, with visibility into every decision. Offer Decisioning selects the best offer on web and app surfaces. Campaign Decisioning delivers 1:1 decisions across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp. Together with workflow agents, this puts both halves of agentic marketing in one system.
Architecture overview
The architecture has four layers. Each layer has a single responsibility and can change without affecting the others.
- Clients. Merlin AI agents inside the MoEngage product, and external MCP clients such as Claude and ChatGPT, through the MoEngage MCP Connector, connect to the MoEngage MCP server. Clients that support MCP can connect.
- MCP server on AgentCore runtime. MoEngage hosts its MCP server on AgentCore runtime. The server exposes MoEngage platform capabilities as MCP tools. It does not run its own model. Reasoning happens in the agent that calls it.
- MoEngage platform APIs. The MCP server calls the same OpenAPI 3.0-compatible APIs that MoEngage customers already use. These APIs enforce existing permissions and data residency rules.
- Foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. Agents use foundation models in Amazon Bedrock to plan tool calls, generate content, and summarize results. For model availability by Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
In a typical request, a user signs in to MoEngage and asks a question. The client sends the request with the user’s existing JSON Web Token (JWT). AgentCore runtime validates the token and starts an isolated session for that user. The agent asks a model in Amazon Bedrock which tools to call. The MCP server calls the MoEngage APIs with the user’s tenant context and returns the results. The agent then composes the answer.
The following diagram shows how these components connect.
Turning existing APIs into MCP tools
MoEngage opens its platform to agents through an MCP server and agent-callable APIs. Its platform APIs for campaigns, analytics, segments, content, and flows were already OpenAPI 3.0-compatible, so MoEngage used the FastMCP framework to generate MCP tools from those specifications. Each operation becomes a tool with a structured schema, a description, and parameter validation.
The following simplified example shows the pattern:
The tools fall into five groups:
- Campaign tools create, edit, schedule, and send campaigns across channels.
- Analytics tools query delivery funnels, click-through rates, conversions, and cohort performance.
- Segmentation tools list, inspect, and create segments from behavioral and attribute filters.
- Content tools manage content blocks, templates, and dynamic content rules.
- Flow tools inspect, pause, or modify automation journeys.
The tools come from the specifications, so they stay in sync with the APIs. When a team updates a specification, the tool definitions update with it.
Keeping tenants isolated and identity out of the model’s reach
A multi-tenant system cannot let a model decide whose data it is reading. MoEngage made three design choices to help prevent that. First, the MCP server reuses the existing authentication model, accepting the same JWT-based authentication that MoEngage APIs already use, and AgentCore runtime validates each token before a request reaches the server. Second, workspace and user context travel in request headers that AgentCore runtime forwards to the server rather than as tool arguments, so the model does not see these values and cannot change them. Third, AgentCore runtime runs each user session in its own isolated environment, so one user’s conversation cannot read another’s session state.
On top of this, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content safety and personally identifiable information (PII) filters to agent responses. A backend-for-frontend layer then validates the structure of generated content before the MoEngage interface renders it.
Give users control over agents. Users set guardrails on what each agent can do, review every action in its activity log, and choose between autonomous and human-reviewed execution.
Why MoEngage chose AgentCore runtime
AgentCore runtime provides the production capabilities that a multi-tenant MCP server needs, and each one addresses a specific requirement of MoEngage’s workload. AgentCore runtime scales sessions as demand changes, so MoEngage does not plan capacity for traffic bursts across its customer workspaces. Each session runs in its own isolated environment by default, which keeps one brand’s conversation and data separate from another’s. The built-in JWT authorizer validates tokens against MoEngage’s existing identity provider, so the MCP server uses the same authentication model as the APIs.
Hosting on AgentCore runtime is also framework-agnostic. MoEngage can change models or agent frameworks without touching the MCP server, which matters as the agent layer evolves. Built-in metrics, logs, and traces through Amazon CloudWatch give MoEngage engineers visibility into every session. Together, these capabilities let the team focus on agent logic and marketing intelligence rather than hosting infrastructure.
Inference through Amazon Bedrock gave MoEngage two more benefits. Merlin AI agents run on Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock, and MoEngage moves between these versions through the same Amazon Bedrock API. MoEngage also pays per token instead of operating GPU infrastructure. Amazon Bedrock does not use customer prompts or responses to train foundation models, which matters for a system that processes customer engagement data at scale.
One campaign, one conversation
The following example shows how a user builds a campaign without leaving the conversation.
- Ask for the draft. The user types:
Draft a weekend flash sale push for our high-value segment, using the same tone as our best-performing December campaign. The agent calls the analytics tools to find the top December campaign, the segmentation tools to confirm the high-value segment, and the content tools to pull the brand voice. It returns a draft with several copy variants.
- Check what underperformed. The user asks:
Which push notifications last month had below 2% click-through rate (CTR), and what do they have in common? The Campaign Insights Agent compares those campaigns and reports the shared pattern, such as send time or audience overlap.
- Adjust the journey. The user asks:
Show me the drop-off at step 3 of our onboarding flow, and pause the SMS branch if it’s below 5% conversion. The agent reads the flow state through the flow tools and pauses the branch after the user confirms. This is the human-review mode in practice.
Each step uses the same tools that power the MoEngage interface. The user does not open a separate dashboard.
Results
Merlin AI agents on this architecture have been in production for more than 6 months. One customer, Glance, reached campaign go-live 50% faster and saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates. With Merlin AI Copywriter, Glance teams also produce about three times more content variants per campaign.
Across the platform, MoEngage reports a 60–70% reduction in manual effort by marketing and product teams for channel, timing, and frequency decisions, and a 20–30% improvement in conversion rates from goal-based decisioning. Managed, pay-per-token inference in Amazon Bedrock reduced AI infrastructure costs by more than 50% compared with self-hosted models.
AgentCore feature availability varies by AWS Region. For supported Regions, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation.
Conclusion
MoEngage made its platform agent-ready without rebuilding it. Existing OpenAPI specifications became MCP tools. AgentCore runtime provided hosting, authentication, and session isolation. Foundation models in Amazon Bedrock provided reasoning and generation. The result is a platform where marketing and product teams move from question to action in one conversation, where MoEngage engineers spend their time on marketing intelligence rather than infrastructure, and where agents handle workflows for the team and decisions for every customer while users stay in control.
The same pattern applies to other software providers with a mature API surface. Start from your existing specifications, keep identity outside the model, and let a managed runtime handle the production concerns.
To build your own MCP server on the same foundation, start with the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and follow the AgentCore runtime guide to host it. To choose a foundation model for your agents and review the security and data-handling controls, see the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. To generate MCP tools from your existing OpenAPI specifications, review the FastMCP documentation. To see Merlin AI in action, visit MoEngage Merlin AI. To plan a similar architecture, contact your AWS account team or Solutions Architect.

articles.title: Telus pulls out of two government-backed AI data centres in Vancouver | BetaKit
articles.text:
Telus has pulled out of two AI data centre projects in Vancouver that former CEO Darren Entwistle announced alongside federal AI minister Evan Solomon just six months ago.
The news: Daily Hive reported on Saturday that the Canadian telecommunications giant is no longer partnered with local real estate developer Westbank on the AI data centre projects. When reached for comment, Westbank confirmed to BetaKit that Telus is no longer a partner on the two Vancouver projects. It did say, however, that it’s proceeding with the projects as planned and that a new partnership will be announced in the coming months.
When reached for comment, Solomon’s office deferred to Telus about its decision, but said Canada remains committed to building secure, sovereign computing capacity; Telus did not respond by press time.
From the source: According to an anonymous source quoted by The Globe and Mail, a lack of local support caused Telus to reconsider the project. Hundreds of people protested the data centre projects over the summer, and the sites are still awaiting municipal decisions, including rezoning and an upcoming city motion that could impose stricter requirements on data centre owners. The Globe’s source noted that the level of opposition in Vancouver would have made it challenging to proceed, but that Telus is still open to opportunities at these sites in the future.
The context: The Telus data centres were announced in May and were among the first to advance under the enabling large-scale sovereign AI data centres initiative, a federal program announced earlier this year designed to build domestic AI compute infrastructure and reduce reliance on foreign-owned systems. The proposed facilities included a 100,000-square-foot, repurposed facility in the Mount Pleasant neighbourhood, as well as a 400,000-square-foot development adjacent to Vancouver’s BC Place stadium.
Telus’ withdrawal from the project comes as the telecom giant is also facing mounting debt and is working to rejig its non-telecom sectors of the business. Its stock has fallen nearly 25 percent year-to-date.
Final thought: The recent federal budget pledged to enable Canadian AI companies to access 500 megawatts of sovereign AI compute as foreign hyperscalers like Meta, Anthropic, and Microsoft buy up space in Canadian data centres. As building up sovereign compute capacity continues to be a government priority, a Westbank spokesperson said the firm has already chosen its new partners, who are Canadian and “will meet sovereignty requirements.”
Feature image courtesy Telus.

articles.title: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing
articles.text:
Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors.
Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction.
In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware.
The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob, IBM, IQM, Pasqal, Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces.
Beating the Bottleneck
Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. It also means that supercomputing centers can add new quantum processors to their existing scheduling and resource-management workflows without developing bespoke QPU-specific solutions.
For quantum computing to advance science, it needs to be used by scientists. Now scientists can run quantum-classical applications developed with platforms such as NVIDIA CUDA-Q with Slurm coordinating access to all the processing they need.
Slurm 26.11 will be available later this month.
Orchestrating Resources in an Open Quantum-GPU Platform
The Slurm expansion adds a community-developed orchestration layer to NVIDIA’s open platform for quantum-GPU supercomputing, which centers around the CUDA-Q open platform for hybrid quantum-classical computing. At SC26, new releases expand all aspects of the platform:
CUDA-Q QEC allows researchers developing quantum error correction to rapidly prototype and test new ideas, including with a new decoder server. A new TCBP-JOBS decoder is 13,000x faster than the industry standard.
CUDA-Q gets an expanded layer of fault-tolerant primitives that application builders can use to realistically compile their ideas. Fermilab has already used CUDA-Q to perform studies in three weeks that would normally have taken five months.
CUDA-Q Algorithms provides reusable components for builders of quantum applications, including new capabilities in helping design the loading data into quantum circuits and tools specifically for chemistry and materials applications
CUDA-Q Pulse gives quantum hardware builders a layer for shaping the ‘pulses’ needed to control qubits on a QPU, including tools to GPU accelerate their generation.
The quantum ecosystem around the world is continuing to build with this platform. Quantum Motion integrated its QUICHE chemistry framework with CUDA-Q. Altera and Oxford Quantum Circuits designed an FPGA-based controller connecting qubit control and readout to GPUs through NVQLink.
At supercomputing scale, QunaSys used cuQuantum and 1,024 NVIDIA Hopper GPUs on ABCI-Q to simulate more than 300 million quantum operations, reaching chemical accuracy for a four-hydrogen-atom model. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER to simulate 104 qubits under realistic noise, testing fault-tolerant designs before they’re built.
Learn more about NVIDIA quantum computing technologies.

articles.title: Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’
articles.text:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. “I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer,” Altman said today. “I think the home tinkering is great.”
Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’
Altman suggested we all ‘share this memory’ and said, ‘I think the home tinkering is great.’
The comments were made onstage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday.
Altman’s remarks on RAM stirred up controversy last month. In an appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, Altman said that it’s “quite terrible” for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers. He later followed up on those comments in posts on X earlier this month, saying, “i want you to have so much ram” and saying the original remarks had been “taken out of context.”
AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from phones to game consoles. Altman commented on supply chain issues, saying OpenAI has “been constrained by different things at different times,” like memory, rack assembly, data center capacity, or “some random component.”
Onstage today, Altman went on to say that “a few years ago we started saying the world needs to build a lot more memory supply chain in particular.” He acknowledged how RAM prices have soared over recent months, saying:
“The world did not build out that much, and now we have seen DRAM prices — I don’t know exactly, but maybe they went up 5x, 7x, something like that. I think it would be much better if the world just had a lot of memory. That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by is that, if we’re going to be in this memory supply shortage, then in some sense — whether or not we’ll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference — the optimal thing would be, can we share this memory and have it working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply. Maybe it’s not the reason to make the decision but that’s what I was trying to say.”
Altman also commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO, saying he “doesn’t know enough” to say if Huang should be reinstated.

articles.title: Cybercabs aus Deutschland: Tesla will Werk in Grünheide für 3 Milliarden Euro ausbauen
articles.text:
Cybercabs aus Deutschland: Tesla will Werk in Grünheide für 3 Milliarden Euro ausbauen
Der US-Elektroautobauer Tesla will drei Milliarden Euro für den Ausbau des Werks in Grünheide bei Berlin ausgeben. Damit soll zunächst ein neues Produktionsgebäude errichtet werden, teilte das Unternehmen von Elon Musk mit. In dem Gebäude soll es später möglich sein, bis zu einer Million Cybercabs zu produzieren. Diese sollen als Robotaxi fahrerlos Menschen befördern.
„Damit schaffen wir die Grundlage für die weltweit technologisch fortschrittlichste Tesla-Fabrik hier in Grünheide“, hieß es von dem US-Autobauer. Tesla sucht den Angaben zufolge im Zuge des Ausbaus mehrere Hundert neue Mitarbeiter in den Bereichen Bau und Fertigungsplanung.
Baubeginn in Grünheide für erste Hälfte 2027 geplant
Tesla nannte auch einen Zeitplan: Der Baubeginn sei für das erste Halbjahr 2027 geplant, Produktionsbeginn für das Jahr 2029. Ein Genehmigungsantrag für das Gebäude soll noch dieses Jahr eingereicht werden. Er beruhe auf einem Antrag von 2023 für das Gesamtvorhaben, hieß es.
Die drei Milliarden Euro seien neben dem Bau des neuen Produktionsgebäudes auch für Nebengebäude und etwa eine weitere Abwasserbehandlungsanlage vorgesehen.
Zuletzt zog die Tesla-Nachfrage wieder an
Tesla hatte die Ausbaupläne auch während eines Absatzeinbruchs nicht aufgegeben, aber zunächst auf Eis gelegt und von einer besseren Marktlage abhängig gemacht. Zuletzt zog die Nachfrage wieder an, und Tesla stellte gegen den Trend Beschäftigte ein. Die Fabrik bei Berlin, die im März 2022 öffnete, hatte nach Angaben von Tesla im Oktober 12.600 Beschäftigte. Zwischenzeitlich war die Zahl unter 11.000 Mitarbeiter gesunken.
Das Unternehmen hatte zuletzt angekündigt, die Produktion auf dann 7.500 Fahrzeuge pro Woche steigern zu wollen. Das entspricht rund 375.000 Fahrzeugen im Jahr. Außerdem sollte die Batteriezellfertigung in Grünheide ausgebaut werden. In den vergangenen Monaten seien bereits 2.000 Mitarbeiter zusätzlich eingestellt worden, hieß es von einer Sprecherin.
~ Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: The Sound of Smarter Farming - EE Times
articles.text:
It was amid the stillness of the Covid-19 lockdowns that Conrad Young, founder and CEO of Chirrup.ai, realized that birdsong would make an excellent proxy for biodiversity. Birds have always acted as sentinels for changes in the environment, and as he told EE Times, “Birdsong is a pretty powerful and visceral way of understanding what’s going on in the environment but is also scientifically valid and benchmarkable.”
In March 2022, as the pandemic ended, Young launched Chirrup.ai to monitor birdsong and track farmland diversity. The first task was to deploy acoustic sensors and establish a baseline of bird activity that could provide a reference point against future recordings and reveal whether biodiversity was improving, declining, or remaining stable over time. Earlier trials used audiomoths—low-cost, acoustic loggers that record birdsong—but Chirrup.ai has now developed smart acoustic sensors.
The sensor pairs a MEMS analog microphone with a 24-bit digital audio codec, a 240-MHz processor with Bluetooth, and a high-speed 4G LTE modem. A multi-constellation GNSS receiver supporting GPS, GLONASS, and Galileo provides geolocation and timestamping for the acoustic data. The device is powered by a rechargeable lithium-polymer battery.
Chirrup.ai’s technology has already measured biodiversity on more than 300 farms in eight European countries. In the U.K., these include sites on the Greenwich Peninsula in London, broiler farms in Lincolnshire, and pig farms in Norfolk. To record birdsong in the field, multiple devices are placed at least 200 meters apart at the edges of woodland and open land populated by birds but away from roosting sites, footpaths, and roads. Birdsong is recorded for two to three weeks with devices then sent back to Chirrup.ai, where the recordings are converted to spectrograms and analyzed to identify the species and assess biodiversity.
As Young pointed out, farmers do not require instant answers when assessing biodiversity but instead want to understand how nature is changing year on year. “We need a large enough period of sampling, so we’ve got a good representative picture of what’s there, and then we’ll provide an annual snapshot,” he said.
Chirrup.ai technology director Paul Nebel agreed and added that remote analysis of data is preferable to using edge AI right now. “With edge processing, we would need a bigger battery and probably a solar cell, which would make the device way more expensive,” he said.
Sensor aside, identifying bird species from recordings is critical, and Chirrup.ai has developed machine-learning (ML) algorithms to detect subtle nuances in recordings, such as one species mimicking another, and remove background noise. The firm also uses ML platform BirdNET, which is trained on species worldwide.
“Birds are very individual: Some use the same songs day in and day out, but others do not and are very complicated,” Nebel said. “Many have songs to raise an alarm, for waking up, for saying hi to their mates, and for courting. Some birds pretend to be other birds; others even pretend to be mobile phones. We also see birds that have different accents from one country to another, even from county to county.”
These remarkable complexities make human oversight critical, and Chirrup.ai has been working with ornithologists and ecologists who have reviewed thousands of hours of recordings, comparing their judgements against ML predictions, and setting appropriate confidence thresholds. “We need to keep checking that the machine learning doesn’t drift off and remains reflective of what humans hear,” Nebel said.
Chirrup.ai has also developed algorithms that generate a biodiversity index based on its bird species data as well as local environment conditions, such as hedgerow health, land management practices, satellite data on habitats, and species position in the food chain. Work is underway to include other bioindicators, such as weather data, to contextualize changes from season to season, and the firm is also considering extending bioacoustic sensing beyond birdsong. “There are also so many nascent datasets that are becoming available as well as birdsong—we could look at insects, mammals, even the livestock,” Young said.
One firm already working with insects and, very recently, livestock is AgriSound (U.K.). Founded in 2020 by CEO Casey Woodward, the government-funded startup set out to monitor pollinating insects to help growers improve crop pollination and provide insights into biodiversity for farming and land management. Woodward and colleagues developed a solar-powered acoustic sensor, Polly, that monitors honeybee and bumblebee activity in glasshouses, polytunnels, and open fields by detecting wingbeat frequencies.
The sensor combines a MEMS microphone and acoustic sensor array to capture the insect wingbeat sounds, alongside temperature, humidity, and ambient-light sensors to monitor environmental conditions.
An onboard processor runs ML algorithms to analyze the discrete Hertz range of the wingbeat frequency and distinguish bee activity from background noise. The resulting pollinator data packets are transmitted to the cloud via 4G cellular connectivity for visualization and interpretation, typically on an hourly basis, and a Bluetooth module enables firmware updates.
So while Chirrup.ai, with its emphasis on biodiversity insights, currently prioritizes battery life and cost by analyzing recordings remotely, AgriSound processes signals locally to deliver swift results on insect activity. “We are trying to help farmers who want results quickly,” Woodward said. “For example, the almond flowering season may only be 10 days, so growers will want to take recommended interventions pretty quickly.”
Like Chirrup.ai, AgriSound has spent some time developing and training ML algorithms to recognize, in this case, different pollinators. Woodward and colleagues have built an extensive library comprising thousands of hours of insect sounds, recorded under a controlled environment. Here, individual bees have been encouraged to fly toward a flower and collect pollen and nectar while their acoustic signatures are recorded. “Bees are very smart and difficult to incentivize to do what you want,” Woodward laughed.
The sensor has been deployed by U.K. retailer Marks&Spencer to provide insights into pollinator densities and can be found in strawberry, sugar beet, and other farms across the nation. Woodward highlighted how his company’s work in glasshouses has helped to reduce the amount of misshapen fruit. AgriSound’s tech has also reached almond orchards in Spain and Portugal, blueberry crops in the U.S., and avocado farms in South Africa—and is now being extended to livestock. In recent U.K. projects, Woodward and colleagues have worked with veterinary-led sustainable livestock production group Raft Solutions and egg producer Noble Foods to monitor the welfare of laying hens.
“With Raft, we’ve been listening for changes in the gut contractions [of cattle] and how these affect methane emissions from the herds,” Woodward said. “This can take time, as you need a veterinarian to collect the sounds with a stethoscope … but with the hens, we just put our non-invasive sensors into the sheds to record data.”
Pest control
Beyond birds, bees, and bovine, the next acoustic sensing frontier is, arguably, the smaller insect pests that infest crops and devastate yields—think beetles, termites, stem borers, and more. U.K.-based BugBug—launched by Cornell entomologist Emily Bick, director of Indonesian PT Gunung Madu sugarcane plantation Jadey Huray, and University of Wisconsin–Madison researcher and ML engineer Laurence Still—is tackling this problem head on.
Laurence Still, BugBug’s CTO, highlighted how a few years ago, Gunung Madu switched from burning fields before harvesting to the more sustainable method of green cane harvesting—that is, harvesting sugarcane without first burning the crop. “[The plantation] went from 5% crop loss to 50% crop loss due to insects over the course of a year,” Still said. “Burning resets the insect population back to zero, but without this, insect numbers were compounded and compounded.”
To tackle the problem, the colleagues decided to use piezoelectric contact microphones to detect insect vibration frequencies, connecting these to Raspberry Pi processors and clipping them onto plant stems to detect the vibrations caused by the chewing and tapping of feeding insects.
“We record the sound of the damage being done to the plant by the insect,” Still said. “A lot of biological acoustic sensing detects sounds transferred through air, but we’re listening to [vibrations] being transmitted through the plant. These travel very well through hard materials, so we can pick up very, very small signals.”
Trials on tobacco-plant-feeding hornworms, Colorado potato beetles, and European corn borers revealed distinct differences in the feeding patterns, frequency, and amplitude—and low background noise. Following initial success, the BugBug team, led by systems integration engineer Callum Hockey, has since redesigned its device, sticking with the piezo-sensors but switching the Raspberry Pi processor for a custom sound card and embedded electronics. This latest design decreases the form factor, cuts power consumption, and enables field operation with a smaller solar panel.
Recorded data is converted into spectrograms and analyzed using custom ML algorithms. Unlike birdsong and bees, the sounds of insects feeding internally cannot readily be identified and labeled, so BugBug’s ML approach relies heavily on unsupervised learning. Like their peers at Chirrup.ai and AgriSound, Still and colleagues have collected thousands of hours of recordings. These are combined with contextual information, such as insect location on the plant, and plant location, to label populations of sounds rather than individual events. By comparing these datasets, the ML algorithms learn to distinguish insect activity from background noise and identify patterns associated with particular pests. Some processing takes place locally while the Wi-Fi-enabled sensor also transmits data to the cloud for further analysis. However, BugBug is also exploring lightweight ML models that could run on the device in the future.
Still and colleagues have characterized the sounds of more than 25 insect species, amassing data on sugarcane, sweetcorn, oilseed rape, grapevine, coconuts, potatoes, and tomatoes. The sensors can also detect the distinctive feeding sounds of piercing-sucking insects, including aphids and scale insects—the scourge of sugarcane. It’s early days, but the company is investigating if acoustic monitoring can detect the first flight of these insects, just after they emerge from larvae, to give growers an early warning of pest activity.
“Our idea is to put the sensors in the field at the start of the season and build up a picture of insect activity over time,” Still said. “So you see no insects, no insects, no insects, and then you start to see your signal rising—and that’s the time to act. Identifying the optimal time to treat a crop is our goal—timing is absolutely critical.”
Practical proliferation
BugBug is undoubtedly breaking new acoustic sensing ground by using AI to uncover data that was previously inaccessible to humans. “We’re doing something [with AI] that wouldn’t have been possible five years ago, before some of the newer advances in unsupervised learning,” Still said. The company is currently working with leading agrochemical companies to solve practical problems. “You might have a company that has developed a biopesticide but needs to know if it is stopping insects feeding, killing them, and how quickly,” he said. “That’s hard if you can’t see the insect as it’s inside the plant … but with our sensors, you could monitor feeding activity before pesticide and post-pesticide.”
BugBug, AgriSound, and Chirrup.ai are not alone in their development of acoustic sensors and AI to eavesdrop on the environment. In Sri Lanka, Permia Sensing is combining satellite, drone, and bioacoustic data with AI to monitor red palm weevil activity in palm trees. Meanwhile, Biofonic (U.K.) uses below-earth acoustic sensors and ML to gather soil data for sustainable crop management.
Altogether, these companies point to a growing shift toward bioacoustic sensing and AI-driven analysis to check in on nature. Indeed, Young highlighted how the “amalgamation” and AI analysis of so much sound data with myriad databases, combined with years of work with growers, is truly helping agri-industry balance commercial production with ecology.
Woodward concurred. “The beauty of acoustic sensors is that they make the invisible visible,” he said. “To some extent, pest damage can be monitored by looking at bites on a leaf, but you can’t necessarily quantify the number of beneficial insects in a field or poor pollination. I see acoustic sensing as a statistically rich and powerful means of data collection, which in many cases is super-affordable.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s China Dilemma: Sell Chips or Lose Influence?- EE Times
articles.text:
On Nov. 12, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO after 33 years at the helm. The resignation followed a series of reports about his relationships with different women, including Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. officials reportedly assessed as a Chinese intelligence asset, and an independent investigation by Nvidia’s board into the national security concerns.
I don’t want to write about the personal side of the story; I can only say I feel sorry for all the individuals and families involved. For the purpose of this article, the more interesting question is the one Jensen championed for years: Should American tech companies sell their technology to China, with or without restrictions, and in doing so try to control how China advances? Or should they keep it out of China’s hands altogether? I’m spending this week in Silicon Valley, and the question has come up in many of my conversations here.
It is a strategic question, almost a philosophical one, and the question will continue to bother us even with Jensen’s departure.
The gift
To a large extent, this is not a new question. This summer, Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey brought Homer back to the big screen, and with it the most famous gift in history: the wooden horse that Odysseus left at the gates of Troy.
As the reader may remember, after a 10-year siege failed to break Troy’s walls, the Greeks followed Odysseus’s plan: They built a wooden horse, hid soldiers inside, and pretended to sail home. The Trojans were told the horse was an offering to Athena that would make their city invulnerable, in effect a symbol of the war’s end.
In my view, there are similarities between the Trojan horse and the current case: In both instances, one side gives something to the other, positioned as a gift that will benefit the receiving side, but with an ultimate goal of maintaining control. 
True, unlike the Trojan horse, nothing here was free: China has paid good money, often at a premium, for every Nvidia chip it bought. But in the current state of affairs, even the readiness to sell those chips can be considered a gift. 
In fact, Jensen was the most articulate advocate of that bet. The spy story is now old news, but it illustrated his openness to “sleeping with the enemy,” at least in the strategic and figurative sense. Moreover, he didn’t consider China an enemy at all. In September 2025, he told the BBC’s Faisal Islam:
“President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win, and President Xi wants China to win, and it’s possible for both of them too. And the reason for that is because it’s not a zero-sum game. The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game.”
He never changed his mind. In a Bloomberg interview with Emily Chang, filmed weeks before the story broke, he called the U.S. restrictions a mistake that is “hard to unwind,” and was explicit about China:
“I’ve been very clear that even though we compete against China, they’re not our enemies. If we care deeply about the safety of the world with respect to artificial intelligence, then of course we must open dialogues, we must work with them in every possible way.”
His case was not only idealistic. As in the Trojan horse case, he argued that if China would run its AI workloads on his technology, that would give the U.S. more control. As he told CNN’s Fareed Zakaria in July 2025, America’s AI leadership depends on making the American tech stack available worldwide, “so that amazing developers, including the ones in China, are able to build on American tech stack.” In contrast, export controls that limited his ability to sell those chips would represent a failure that only accelerates Chinese development. (Granted, he never argued for selling China everything: The U.S. should have “the first, the most, and the best,” and China the second-best.)
Laocoön in Beijing
One Trojan priest, Laocoön, warned the Trojans, in Virgil’s famous words, to beware of Greeks bearing gifts. They ignored him and pulled the horse in themselves.
Beijing, this time, sided with Laocoön and refused two horses: The first was the H20, a cut-down chip Nvidia designed for China to stay within U.S. export control rules, which China’s cyberspace regulator questioned in July 2025 over alleged “backdoor” risks. And even after Washington opened the door to Nvidia to sell H200s, a far more powerful chip from an earlier Nvidia generation, Beijing reportedly told companies to pause orders and limited purchases to special circumstances. By the time of the Bloomberg interview, Jensen described the market as “completely blocked from us today.”
Ironically, Beijing did so on Jensen’s own logic. He had dismissed the security concern by arguing, as he told the BBC, that “any military is smart enough to build their military on top of their own indigenous technology.” His reason, as he explained on CNN, was that American technology “could, of course, be limited at any time,” which is precisely the switch Washington hoped to hold. In my reading, Beijing simply applied that argument to its entire AI sector.
Necessity is the mother of invention
To Jensen’s very point, as China could not rely on unlimited access to Nvidia chips, they started developing their own internal alternatives across the full stack: In models, DeepSeek shocked the industry in early 2025 with frontier-class results trained on export-compliant, lower-bandwidth H800 chips. In chips, Huawei has built its own accelerators. In manufacturing, SMIC has kept stretching how small a feature it can print with older DUV equipment. And finally, China is reportedly trying to circumvent ASML altogether, with a prototype EUV machine in Shenzhen that it hopes will produce chips by 2028, though 2030 is seen as more realistic.
Much of this is costly and may lag the West for years. But it is exactly the independence the controls were meant to prevent, and exactly what Jensen warned about.
A horse with no Greeks inside
In parallel, Chinese demand for Nvidia compute didn’t disappear, and Chinese buyers allegedly managed to smuggle Nvidia chips through intermediary countries. The Justice Department has brought a string of smuggling cases, including one involving at least $160 million of H100 and H200 chips. From the U.S. perspective, this is giving the horse, but without Greeks inside, without keeping any control: China gets the horse, and America gets none of the leverage or visibility. Nvidia may still book the revenue, but the strategic leverage is gone.
The Singaporean company Megaspeed, whose former executive is at the center of the affair, shows how blurry this can get. According to the New York Times, its Malaysian subsidiary received roughly $2 billion of Nvidia hardware in a year, raising questions about where it was deployed and who used it. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing, Nvidia says it found no evidence of diversion, and Singapore’s police say investigations are ongoing. Paperwork doesn’t settle much either: In the quarter ending July 2025, Singapore accounted for 22% of Nvidia’s revenue by billing location, mostly for products shipped elsewhere, until Nvidia stopped reporting it separately.
The U.S. is now trying to stop these empty horses, or chips without control, from making their way to China, for example, with on-chip location verification, which Senator Cotton’s Chip Security Act would require.
The remote horse
The hardest part of the Trojan plan was getting the horse inside the city. But compute doesn’t need that: AI “horses” don’t need to sit on a country’s territory to be used. A GPU in Malaysia or Virginia can serve a lab in Shanghai without crossing a border.
Interestingly, this cuts both ways. For Washington, a horse that stays outside the walls can be watched and, if needed, switched off. For Beijing, it delivers the benefits without letting the horse in, and without slowing the domestic chip industry it is keen to protect.
The catch is that a remote horse only gives America control if it knows who is riding it. Physics can help where paperwork fails: Tens of thousands of GPUs imply tens of megawatts of power and cooling, and U.S. officials reportedly noticed a mismatch between Megaspeed’s chip imports and its disclosed data center capacity.
Not surprisingly, remote access is currently being legally contested, and the House has already passed a Remote Access Security Act to bring it under export controls. This, alongside the Chip Security Act already mentioned above, could address much of the problem.
The horse has left the barn
Some people argue that for Nvidia chips the debate is already irrelevant: Beijing has closed its gates, Huawei is filling the gap, and some leakage has happened anyway. To use another equestrian image, the horse may have left the barn.
I’m not sure this is the case and, be that as it may, the same question applies, with even higher stakes, to other layers of the stack, above all the tools that make chips. ASML already cannot sell its most advanced DUV tools to China; China’s share of ASML’s sales fell to 14% in the second quarter of 2026, from 19% in the first, and a proposed MATCH Act would push the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions. Sell, and keep China dependent on Western tools with some visibility into its fabs? Or don’t sell, and maybe delay China, while accelerating the domestic toolmakers trying to replace ASML?
Hold your horses
As we said already, Jensen was the most vocal supporter of the “sell and control” camp.
It is clear that with Jensen gone, more players are weighing in. On Capitol Hill, the scandal has revived the push for the restrictions he spent years fighting. Ryan Fedasiuk, whose research at Georgetown University documented China’s military reliance on Nvidia chips, calls Jensen’s dependency argument “seductive” and urges Congress to pass the Chip Security, Remote Access Security, and MATCH acts.
As if we didn’t have enough drama, this week Trump is set to meet Xi (and Putin), and Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, reports earnings on Nov. 17, her first chance to signal whether the China stance changes.
Needless to say, there is no clean answer. Selling may keep China on the American stack, but only if the offer is accepted, visible, and can be switched off. Not selling may delay China for a while, but it accelerates exactly the independence Washington fears. But the current status, where the horse is refused at the gate but slips in through the side door, may be the worst of both.
Whether one agreed with it or not, Jensen’s answer was clear and consistent, and his departure removes its strongest advocate. But the question itself, sell and try to control, or don’t sell and maybe delay, will outlive this scandal, this CEO, and probably this administration.
Moshe Zalcberg‘s views are his own and do not represent the organizations he works for.

								November 16th, 2026 - 
								By: Technical Paper Link
								
							
Researchers at Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD), A*STAR, and National University of Singapore (NUS) published “Self-Supervised Attention-Based Virtual Metrology for CMP MRR Prediction.”
Excerpt
“In this paper, we propose Global Regression Pretraining (GREP), a self-supervised, attention-based framework for CMP* MRR prediction. GREP learns temporal representations from unlabeled sensor signals through global proxy-target regression, followed by supervised fine-tuning for MRR estimation. The framework is evaluated against a feature-engineered supervised baseline under three conditions: limited labeled data, sensor noise, and temporal process drift. “
*chemical mechanical planarization
