articles.title: Novo Nordisk modernizes manufacturing process documents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Novo Nordisk modernizes manufacturing process documents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Novo Nordisk (Novo) is one of the world’s leading global pharmaceutical companies, manufacturing medicines for chronic diseases such as diabetes and obesity, and delivering them to patients across many countries. Behind every product lies a manufacturing network that adheres to strict quality requirements. Every quality-relevant process step must be described, controlled, and validated through formal documentation. Keeping this documentation current and accurate is a core responsibility of the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area, a responsibility that spans a large and diverse portfolio of controlled documents, including standard operating procedures, work instructions, forms, and training materials, across the global organization.
Managing this portfolio presents significant challenges. Document updates are frequent, driven by regulatory changes, process improvements, equipment modifications, and audit findings. Each update demands careful review, structured approval workflows, and timely communication to all affected stakeholders. With thousands of active documents spread across multiple divisions, departments, and product programs, tracking which documents are due for revision, pending approval, or require immediate attention becomes increasingly complex. Much of this oversight currently relies on manual processes and fragmented tracking methods such as spreadsheets or disconnected systems. These methods are time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to scale. The result is a risk of outdated documentation remaining in circulation, delayed updates, and critical gaps in compliance visibility.
Beyond document management, there is a deeper knowledge challenge. Valuable manufacturing knowledge is distributed across many controlled documents, versions, sites, and product programs. Finding the right answer at the right time often depends on experienced individuals knowing where to look. This dependency on tribal knowledge creates bottlenecks that slow down decision-making and, ultimately, impact how quickly life-saving medicines reach patients.
To address these challenges, the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area has embarked on developing an intelligent support system powered by agentic AI, deployed on AWS. The goal is to reduce lead times, improve documentation visibility, and make critical manufacturing knowledge more accessible, ultimately helping the organization move faster and serve more patients around the world. This post dives deep into the architecture and the key design decisions made to meet the high standards of accuracy and traceability required in a regulated pharmaceutical environment. The solution helped subject-matter experts (SMEs) complete work that used to take hours or days in minutes.
We also describe an AI process-intelligence assistant that can answer complex process questions with grounded, cited responses. The solution is built around a GraphRAG architecture, combining a knowledge graph with hybrid search to retrieve the most relevant and contextually accurate information. AI agents, built on a managed agent framework, coordinate the retrieval and response process end-to-end. A guided mode helps clarify ambiguous questions before a search is initiated, helping make responses more precise and defensible.
The challenge
Teams supporting manufacturing repeatedly answer variations of the same question: what does the process require, for this site, this product, and this equipment? Answering well requires four things at once:
- The right document out of a large corpus.
- The right version and lifecycle state (approved and effective, not draft or obsolete).
- The right scope (it actually applies to the site, product generation, and equipment).
- The relationships (which documents reference which, and what a change would impact).
Conventional keyword search returns documents, not answers, with no concept of scope, version, or relationship. A plain vector-based Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system improves recall on natural-language questions but still struggles with exact identifiers (document numbers, equipment codes), with multi-hop relationship questions, and (most importantly for a regulated domain) with identifying when relevant content is not available. The team needed a system that treats structure and relationships as first-class, stays grounded in approved sources, and clarifies instead of guessing.
Solution overview
The assistant is built on a GraphRAG architecture: a knowledge graph in Amazon Neptune captures structure and relationships, and a hybrid search index in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless provides semantic and exact-match recall over document contents. The two stores are deliberately kept separate and bridged at query time rather than combined into a single engine. This is a common production GraphRAG pattern.
The reasoning layer runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore was chosen for its managed agent runtime with built-in session isolation, native tool orchestration, and integrated AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and observability. This removes undifferentiated infrastructure work so the team could focus on the domain logic. The agent runtimes are built with the Strands Agents SDK and powered by Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. Documents are processed through an ingestion pipeline that uses Amazon Bedrock Data Automation for multimodal parsing, orchestrated with AWS Step Functions and AWS Lambda. The stack is defined as infrastructure as code with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK).
At a high level, a question flows through the system like this:
- The query agent receives the question and, in guided mode, determines whether the scope is clear enough to answer well.
- If it is ambiguous, the agent asks a short, graph-grounded clarifying question (for example, which site or product generation applies) before searching.
- After scope is clear, hybrid search retrieves candidate passages, the graph expands from those results to add structure and relationships, and a reranking step sharpens precision.
- The agent composes an answer grounded in and cited to approved source documents, and is explicit when content is not available.
Architecture
A two-layer taxonomy: Structure plus domain detail
The graph is organized around two complementary layers, which is what lets the assistant take into account where a document sits and what it is about.
High-level taxonomy: The process tree. The organization’s official process framework is modeled as a hierarchy of process nodes (roughly three levels, parent to child). Each controlled document is attached to the lowest applicable process level, so each onboarded document has a known place. This lets the assistant scope a question to a process area before retrieving anything, and automatically categorize newly ingested documents.
Low-level taxonomy: Domain entities. SMEs define the entities that make an answer correct or incorrect in manufacturing: sites, product generations, equipment, process steps, and similar attributes. These are modeled as first-class graph nodes linked to the documents that describe them, using a small set of unified relationship types rather than an ever-growing list of edge names.
Modeling both layers is what distinguishes a genuine GraphRAG system from two databases side by side. The document number on an OpenSearch passage is also a node in the graph, so a search hit is an immediate entry point into the graph’s structure with no fuzzy re-matching required. This chunk-to-graph bridge is a key design choice in the retrieval path.
Why a fixed, curated taxonomy (and why this is best practice)
Early GraphRAG work favored open-ended extraction, letting a language model discover entities with no fixed schema. This approach is powerful for open-ended sensemaking over sprawling text, but it is noisy, hard to maintain, and difficult to audit. Over the past couple of years, the consensus has shifted toward ontology-guided extraction using a predefined, domain-specific schema to guide the model, which improves accuracy and reliability for specialized corpora.
For regulated pharmaceutical manufacturing this is not a compromise, but the right default. The domain already has a real ontology, curated by experts, and a fixed schema with a human-in-the-loop promotion process for new entities supports the auditability the team needed in a regulated pharmaceutical environment. The design aligns with where much of the field has moved since early open-schema approaches, while making design decisions easier to explain to quality and audit stakeholders.
Retrieval: Hybrid search, graph expansion, and reranking
Each store covers the other’s blind spot:
- OpenSearch provides recall – Hybrid search combines dense vector similarity (Amazon Titan Text Embeddings) with lexical BM25 matching, fused with reciprocal rank fusion. Vector search captures meaning. And lexical matching catches the exact tokens that matter here: document numbers, equipment codes, and multilingual terminology.
- Neptune provides structure – Given the entities and documents search surfaced, the graph answers “what is connected, how, and how far”: neighboring documents, references, position in the hierarchy, and impact of a change, which is exactly what vector-only retrieval cannot do.
A common pattern is vector finds the seeds, the graph expands from them, and the reverse for relationship-first questions. A reranking stage (a cross-encoder through Amazon Bedrock Rerank) sits after fusion: it reads the question and each candidate passage together and reorders them, adding a precision pass on top of the cheaper recall stage before anything reaches the model.
Guided mode: Clarify before you retrieve
A distinctive part of the assistant is how it handles ambiguity. A question like “which samples are taken on the granulator?” has several correct answers depending on product generation, site, equipment, and batch size. Answering immediately risks a confident, wrong, out-of-scope response, which is the worst outcome in a regulated setting.
Guided mode inverts the usual RAG order: instead of retrieving first, the agent narrows scope through clarification first, then searches. This follows recent research on clarifying ambiguous questions before retrieval and on using a knowledge graph to supply the clarification options rather than letting the model invent them. It uses two classes of scope:
- A small, near-universal set of attributes (such as site and product generation) is asked directly and consistently for process-specific questions.
- Everything deeper: which equipment, which batch size, and attributes added over time. This is all derived from the graph at query time. A scope-resolution step matches the user’s term against real graph nodes, filters by what is already known, and, if more than one candidate remains, offers the attribute that genuinely distinguishes them, using only values that exist in the graph.
This keeps clarification options grounded in real data (designed to help reduce the risk of hallucinated options) and it scales: when experts add a new distinguishing attribute to the taxonomy, the assistant surfaces it automatically, without requiring changes to prompts or code.
Grounding and trust in a regulated environment
Accuracy here is defined narrowly and enforced deliberately:
- Explicit indexed state – A document can exist in the graph with metadata, relationships, and place in the hierarchy before its contents are searchable. A deterministic flag tracks whether a document’s content is indexed, so the assistant can distinguish between “I have this document’s contents” and “I only have its metadata,” rather than inferring availability from empty search results.
- Approved sources by default – Answers rely on approved and effective documents and the latest applicable version, unless the user explicitly asks for drafts or historical revisions.
- Anti-hallucination rules – Clarification options and cited claims are designed to come from actual tool results rather than the model’s own knowledge.
- Stated limitations – When retrieved material is missing or ambiguous, the assistant says so rather than filling the gap and flags when SME, quality, or regulatory review is needed.
An automated evaluation harness checks responses against these criteria: relevant-source selection, valid document status, latest applicable version, scope compliance, citation accuracy, and faithful preservation of requirement strength (must, should, or may) so behavior can be measured as the system evolves.
An intelligent search engine over a vault of millions of documents
The wider vault this solution sits on top of holds on the order of four million documents. At that scale, the problem is not a shortage of information but the near-impossibility of finding the exactly right, in-scope, current answer by hand. Traditional enterprise search returns long lists ranked by keyword overlap and leaves the hard work to the person asking. This includes deciding which result applies, which version is effective, and how documents relate.
This solution turns the vault into an intelligent, answer-first search engine, and the two-layer taxonomy is what makes that tractable at scale:
- The graph is the full map and the index is the searchable subset. Each onboarded document across all registered domains is placed in the graph with its metadata, relationships, and hierarchy position. This means the assistant can reason about where a document sits and how it connects, even for the millions whose contents are not yet indexed. Full-text contents are indexed for onboarded domains, added incrementally, and the assistant is explicit about which is which.
- Scope narrows the search space before retrieval. Because guided mode resolves site, product generation, process area, and equipment up front, a question is filtered to the small slice of the vault that can answer it. The system searches the few documents in scope, not millions. This helps keep answers precise as the corpus grows.
- Hybrid search plus graph expansion goes beyond keyword ranking, surfacing related documents, references, and hierarchy a ranked list would never reveal, and returning a grounded, cited answer (not ten blue links) while saying when content is unavailable.
The design is intended to scale with the vault rather than degrade as it grows: the larger and more interconnected the documentation, the more value the graph and scoping add.
Outcomes
Depending on the type of task an SME is doing (searching for an answer, updating a document, or adapting one for a new context), work that used to take hours or days is reduced to minutes. Beyond raw time saved, the solution changes what is practical to do at all:
- Navigate the group’s process landscape – Users can move across all three levels of the process taxonomy, spanning roughly four million documents and their many subprocesses through a single assistant that acts as both a search engine and a guide over the documentation, the process, and the organizational maps.
- Consolidate structured and unstructured data – Metadata, process hierarchy, and document contents are unified into one searchable knowledge graph, so information that used to live in separate systems can be queried together.
- Understand relationships between entities and documents – The graph helps users ask how documents, processes, equipment, sites, and products connect, including multi-hop questions that manual search cannot answer.
- Trace and validate references end to end – The solution can map a document’s full chain of references and flag where a document points at out-of-date or superseded material, surfacing integrity issues across the corpus rather than one document at a time.
- Extend to further AI and agentic capabilities – The same grounded foundation opens the door to capabilities like document generation, revision with impact analysis, and other agentic workflows reusing the same graph, retrieval, and guardrails rather than starting from scratch.
Just as important in a regulated setting, the assistant’s design to clarify scope and flag missing or ambiguous content helps reduce the risk of confident, out-of-scope answers, where the real cost of a mistake lies.
A collaborative delivery model
The Novo Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area collaborated with AWS to build this solution, with subject-matter experts and data and AI engineers working closely throughout. The taxonomy that makes the assistant accurate comes directly from the group’s domain experts. The retrieval and agent architecture was designed and iterated with AWS.
Building a prototype was key to getting the solution to go live. Rather than debating capabilities in the abstract, the team put a working system in front of subject-matter experts early. They tested it against real questions and used what they learned to sharpen the taxonomy, the retrieval path, and the guided-mode behavior. The prototype turned an ambitious idea into something people could try, critique, and trust. It also de-risked the architecture decisions before any broader rollout.
Conclusion
By combining a curated knowledge graph, hybrid search, and a clarify-before-retrieve agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the Novo Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area built a process-intelligence assistant that is fast where speed helps and grounded where accuracy matters. The design applies current GraphRAG patterns to regulated manufacturing: ontology-guided extraction, a bridged two-store retrieval path, graph-grounded disambiguation, and reranking. This turns a large documentation landscape into grounded, cited answers with room to extend to new domains.
To get started building your own agentic AI solution, explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for managed agent runtime, tool orchestration, and observability at scale. The agent runtimes in this post were built with the Strands Agents SDK, an open source, framework agnostic toolkit you can use with your own retrieval stack. For GraphRAG reference architectures using Amazon Neptune and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, visit the AWS Architecture Center.

articles.title: Google found hackers using autonomous AI agents to turn security patches into exploits
articles.text:
Google found hackers using autonomous AI agents to turn security patches into exploits
Google’s Threat Intelligence Group says attackers are using autonomous AI agents to reverse-engineer security patches, generate exploits, and attempt to execute them without human approval.
In a report published Monday, Google and Mandiant describe the first cases their researchers have identified of attackers using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation.
The framework uses an orchestrator to coordinate specialized agents, share context, and invoke tools through interfaces such as MCP. The agents apply familiar coding workflows to offensive security, identifying vulnerabilities, generating exploit candidates, and testing them against targets.
Inside the exploit pipeline
Google found a publicly exposed staging server running a multi-agent framework called exploit_agent alongside stolen victim data and scripts used after a successful intrusion. The framework connected several frontier and locally hosted language models to automate patch diffing, turning potential vulnerabilities into exploit code that it could then attempt to execute.
The server also contained scripts for reconnaissance, brute-force attacks, installing webshells, and removing those left by competing attackers. Google found evidence that the operators were interested in French media, entertainment, and education websites, and that the framework had examined access controls in the Spectra WordPress plugin.
What’s changed is that agents can now do much of that work themselves.
Patch diffing is nothing new. Attackers have been comparing code before and after security patches for years to figure out what was fixed and how to exploit it. What’s changed is that agents can now do much of that work themselves.
Google didn’t identify which models handled individual tasks or disclose how often the generated exploits succeeded. And while the server contained stolen data, researchers couldn’t determine whether exploit_agent obtained it.
Agent harnesses go offensive
Google also found attackers using open-source offensive frameworks built around orchestration patterns familiar from coding agents.
CAIRN coordinates specialized agents through a shared blackboard and an observe-orient-decide-act loop, using the results of each task to determine what happens next. Google observed the framework in intrusions targeting U.S. aerospace organizations.
Other frameworks take different approaches. CyberStrikeAI uses a Go backend to orchestrate commercial and open-weight models across more than 100 security tools, YAML attack recipes, and custom scripts. HexStrike AI exposes more than 150 offensive security tools through MCP, with specialized agents handling reconnaissance, exploitation and binary analysis.
Faster than patch cycles
Publicly available vulnerability information is also reaching attackers faster, leaving defenders less time to deploy fixes.
After two PaperCut vulnerabilities were exploited as zero-days in August, security researchers and Huntress developed working exploits with LLM assistance within a day of disclosure.
The attacker moved from initial access to domain administrator within minutes.
GreyNoise documented a campaign four days after the initial disclosure in which an attacker likely used language models to develop exploits, build target lists, and attack hundreds of organizations. The attacker moved from initial access to domain administrator within minutes.
Two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, presented a similar risk when patched code and a proof-of-concept video became public ahead of the official October 21 release.
Hundreds of purported exploits appeared online after the patches shipped, although many didn’t work and were likely generated with LLM assistance. Security teams then had to determine which exploits posed a real threat and which were simply nonfunctional code.
Velocity over stealth
These frameworks are still relatively easy to detect. Google found that they generate substantial network traffic and leave behind recognizable signatures and code artifacts. Researchers noted that attackers “currently trade stealth for velocity.”
The agents also hallucinate technical details and nonexistent targets, sometimes derailing attacks or exposing operators.
For application security teams, the concern is how quickly attackers can move from a published patch to a working exploit.

articles.title: AI is reshaping the creator economy: trust will decide who wins it
articles.text:
AI is reshaping the creator economy: trust will decide who wins it
Building creator trust in the age of AI
There’s always been a balancing act between creators and creator platforms over profit, value, and ownership. Now, AI tools are upsetting that balance and reshaping commercial dynamics, while raising new concerns about transparency and control.
As creators compete for engagement against low-effort AI “slop,” they must also navigate opaque monetization policies and inconsistent enforcement. These pressures are rapidly increasing the friction between creators and the platforms they rely on.
At the same time, as more platforms and revenue streams emerge, creators have greater choice about where to build an audience.
President of Tipalti.
As the terms creators operate under keep changing, creators are pushing for more control. They want their voices to be heard, their work protected, and the value they generate recognized.
For platforms, this raises the stakes for attracting and retaining top creators. Trust is becoming a competitive differentiator, and the platforms that recognize this are protecting their creators and paying them reliably in the age of AI.
The creator economy’s ongoing transparency issue
Today, high-volume, low-effort AI-generated content has become an inescapable part of the online experience. But for creators, lax moderation of that content can directly impact earnings by creating an uneven playing field and increasing competition for engagement and views.
Not only must creators compete with AI-generated content, but concerns are also mounting that their work is being used to train the models producing it, without their consent or compensation. Trust is eroding as a result, and inaction risks alienating the very people whose work underpins the success of digital platforms.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
These challenges are becoming increasingly evident. Recently, a US court approved a $1.5 billion settlement relating to Anthropic’s use of pirated books to train its AI models. While the case represents a clarification for rights holders, smaller creators and artists often lack the resources required to pursue litigation in the first place.
Concerns have also been raised about YouTube reportedly using AI to alter creators’ videos without their consent. Even where there is no evidence of financial loss, the incident highlights a potential broader imbalance in the relationship if platforms can make unilateral changes to creators’ work without meaningful consultation.
Creators rely on platforms to distribute, monetize, and govern their work fairly. But platforms need creators too. Their business models depend on compelling content that attracts and retains audiences. It’s a mutual dependency that makes listening to and responding to creators’ concerns a strategic imperative.
Creator trust is intrinsically linked with income reliability
Questions about trust extend beyond how content is used to how creators earn a living. In just a few decades, the creator economy has evolved from a relatively informal ecosystem into a multibillion-dollar global industry. The decisions made by the platforms shaping this industry now directly affect how millions of creators build their careers and earn income.
Even before AI, changes to recommendation algorithms, monetization models, and advertising guidelines meant creators had to become accustomed to their earnings changing overnight. These realities have encouraged them to move away from relying on individual platforms for predictable income and monetizing their content and brands across multiple platforms and revenue streams instead.
Whether they earn through commission-based selling on ecommerce platforms, livestreaming, brand sponsorships, or content views, creators’ incomes are becoming increasingly fragmented. While this diversification reduces their dependence on any single platform, it also creates greater complexity for the businesses responsible for managing and paying them.
Across the industry, poor payout experiences are already damaging creator relationships. Tipalti’s recent global payments research revealed that 26% of businesses lost contributors because of payment-related issues in the past 12 months, with creators accounting for 36% of those losses. Payment friction can directly affect a platform’s ability to retain the people generating its content.
Failing to address these pain points creates a commercial risk, particularly when creators have more options than ever to build and monetize their audiences. If a platform is frustrating to work with or fails to provide reliable payouts and transparent breakdowns of earnings, creators can move to a competitor that offers a better customer experience.
The foundations of creator trust
To keep creators engaged and earn their trust, platforms must address two priorities: protecting creators' work and paying them reliably and transparently.
First, creators need confidence that their interests are protected and that they remain in control of their work. Platforms must acknowledge the issues posed by AI, introduce safeguards for creators’ content, and ensure that any resulting benefits are shared fairly.
Second, platforms must offer a transparent and reliable payout experience. At the end of each payment cycle, creators should receive a clear breakdown of how their payout was calculated, including the factors responsible for any monthly variations. They should feel confident that the economic value they create is recognized and that they will be paid accurately and on time.
Both priorities carry more weight as creator economies grow worldwide, presenting new opportunities for global partnerships. New markets often bring inconsistent standards for content protection and payments, and incompatible financial infrastructure can bottleneck growth.
To compete for creators in these regions, platforms need protections that hold up regardless of where a creator is based, and payout infrastructure capable of supporting an expanding range of currencies, payment methods, and regional requirements.
The next stage of the creator economy
AI is changing what creators make, how platforms distribute it, and how value gets created. But the fundamental relationship hasn’t changed: creators need platforms to reach audiences, and platforms need creators to keep those audiences coming back.
As that relationship becomes more complex, trust will matter more, not less. Creators need to know their work is protected, their earnings are transparent, and they’ll be paid accurately and on time, no matter where they are. These aren't minor priorities. They show whether a platform actually values its creators, or just profits from them.
In the age of AI, trust won’t just shape the creator economy. It will shape who succeeds in it.

articles.title: Uber Data Breach Impacts 150,000 People
articles.text:
Uber is notifying roughly 150,000 drivers that their personal information was stolen in a data breach involving a third-party services provider.
The company learned of the incident on October 9 and immediately severed its data connections with the provider and launched an investigation.
On October 13, the investigation determined that the hackers used compromised service provider credentials on October 7 to access data Uber had shared with the provider.
According to Uber, the hackers accessed images of driver’s licenses and personal information such as names, addresses, dates of birth, driver’s license numbers, and government-issued ID numbers.
The company says that the data was stored in an environment created and managed by Uber’s Cloud Security team. While alerts were enabled, none were triggered because the threat actor used valid credentials.
“The service provider’s compromised credentials did not provide access to other Uber systems. The investigation remains ongoing,” the company said.
Uber has filed data breach notifications with multiple US states, including California, Iowa, Massachusetts, South Carolina, Texas, and Vermont, and reportedly notified the Texas Attorney General’s Office that a total of 149,346 people were affected.
Uber is providing the potentially affected individuals with free credit monitoring and fraud assistance services.
Uber did not identify the service provider in its breach notifications, but a company spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch that the incident involved Fireworks AI, a cloud platform for running and fine-tuning open source AI models.
Fireworks initially said it had found no evidence that customer personal information, models or datasets had been accessed. However, in a November 9 update, the company acknowledged that the breach also affected account and billing information, as well as some customer datasets and incomplete models.
SecurityWeek has emailed Uber for additional information on the data breach and will update this article if the company responds.

articles.title: Minister Solomon says Canada’s national AI literacy training will go live next month | BetaKit
articles.text:
Canada’s national AI literacy program will roll out nationwide next month, according to federal AI Minister Evan Solomon.
The news: Solomon broke the news in an as-yet unaired episode of The BetaKit Podcast, telling BetaKit editor-in-chief Douglas Soltys that the much-anticipated literacy program would be available to all Canadians this December. Solomon did not elaborate on what the rollout would look like, or offer specific dates as to when in December to expect the launch, but did say the nationwide programming would take participants about 90 minutes to complete.
From the source: “In December, you’ll see the national literacy program roll out for every single Canadian. This one is for every Canadian—my mom; anybody—and it’s 90 minutes,” Solomon said.
The context: Launching AI literacy training for the general public would be the third and final program delivered as part of Ottawa’s larger National AI Literacy Initiative, which Solomon unveiled in September. Under that framework, the federal government launched a three-hour training course for post-secondary students, as well as an Essentials for Educators course for teachers. It has previously stated that those courses would reach as many as one million students and 50,000 educators.
The $13-million initiative was first outlined in Canada’s National AI Strategy. The government tapped the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute (Amii) to lead development of the program’s curriculum and its delivery to Canadians.
Final thought: Programming is intended to help learners gain the skills to “more confidently and responsibly” use AI. Solomon’s ministry previously said that training will focus on developing the skills needed to assess AI-generated content, identify misinformation, bias, or privacy concerns, and to provide “practical learning opportunities.” These training initiatives have been central to Ottawa’s efforts to increase AI adoption and trust among Canadians, given that some studies indicate Canada lags behind when it comes to both categories.

articles.title: Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
articles.text:
Constellation Energy – America’s largest operator of nuclear power plants – does not share Wall Street’s concerns that the Democrats will slow down data center development. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Joe Dominguez was, for lack of a better word, unbothered as he addressed the blue wave.
Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
They may have a point.
They may have a point.
“I do think we’ve seen a bit of an overreaction in the market to the election results based upon fear that Democrats won’t let data centers get built,” Dominguez said.
Many of the Democrats who seized control of the House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections ran on anti-data-center campaigns, which triggered a historic $2.5 trillion sell-off in AI-adjacent stocks that reached well beyond tech to the energy, construction, and materials sectors.
Up until a few years ago, many of Constellation’s nuclear power plants were in severe financial distress and in danger of shutting down early. But the data center development boom and its enormous demand for electricity have dramatically reversed the nuclear industry’s fate.
Now, Constellation and other companies like it are signing major deals with Big Tech companies to provide power to data centers. Microsoft, for instance, signed a deal with Constellation to fund the revival of a nuclear plant at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania. (Three Mile Island is the site of what the Nuclear Regulatory Commission refers to as the “most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power plant operating history.”)
Constellation also signed major contracts in the third quarter to provide power to Amazon and Google data centers, Dominguez said.
Nuclear energy has had bipartisan support for years. The US Department of Energy classifies nuclear as a “clean” energy source because the act of operating a nuclear reactor does not directly produce carbon emissions. This makes nuclear an appealing investment to Big Tech companies that have to balance aggressive data center development with the ambitious climate goals they set long before the AI race took off. Still, nuclear energy has its issues. One of the biggest is nuclear waste, which the US government has not figured out how to dispose of at scale.
Big Nuclear and Big Tech also tout these deals as good for the economy and job creation.
“The market scare that people got last week was not lost on Democrats,” Dominguez said on the call. “They do not want to be the reason that the economy takes a nosedive by halting data center development.”
Of course, Constellation’s future is essentially staked on the data center buildout, and Dominguez’s job is to convince investors they have nothing to worry about.
In this instance, however, Dominguez really does seem genuinely unconcerned by the new Democratic majority in the federal government. It could be that he understands that, yes, while the Democrats won the midterms on promises of data center regulation and the blue wave included many new Democratic governors, data centers aren’t necessarily a strictly partisan issue. Some Democrats have opposed harsh measures like moratoriums — though on the flip slide, Constellation may also have to deal with challenges from the other side of the aisle.
In Virginia, some of the state lawmakers who have been the most vocal about data centers are actually Republican. Virginia Sen. Richard Stuart, a conservative Republican, has aggressively pursued data center regulation. Last month, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, denied Stuart’s request for a special session to address a concerning new report from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality on the state’s groundwater supply, which has become strained amid rampant data center growth.
For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
The fight against data centers so far has been highly fragmented and hyperlocal, but that could change soon. The Trump administration loves data centers, and the federal government is working on wresting some control over data center development away from the states. But even then, Democrats and Republicans at the federal level tend to view data centers as an inevitable part of the future that needs some guardrails rather than out-of-control corporate growth infringing on the average American’s quality of life.
Just look at the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was co-sponsored by two Democrats. The Senate is expected to vote on a passage of a sweeping bill which is being marketed as a way to speed up the permitting process for new power plants and transmission lines and connect new data centers to the grid faster. New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, one of the Democrats backing the bill, has touted its inclusion of provisions designed to protect utility customers from rising rates due to data centers, ensuring Big Tech pays its fair share of costs. Researchers at Columbia University SIPA’s Center on Global Energy Policy called the bill’s protections “mixed,” noting they do not account for wholesale capacity and energy prices, a “principal way” data center electricity demand can lead to higher household bills.
Senate Democrats are sharply divided on the bill, which critics say will fast-track data center projects at the expense of public input and environmental oversight and lead to a massive overbuild of energy projects that Americans will end up paying for.
On Constellation’s earnings call, Dominguez pointed out that Virginia and Illinois, states with Democratic governors already in place before the election, have seen “a great deal of data center development.”
“The bottom line is that Democrats care deeply about economic growth and they care very deeply about the many labor jobs that go with data center construction,” Dominguez said. “With labor such a key constituent for Democrats, it’s hard to imagine that we are going to halt work …There might be some differences and certainly there are going to be some local areas, I think, that are not going to want data centers.”
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns. He also has a good point. Grassroots efforts to stop local data center development have been successful and have contributed to broader opposition to data center development across the country. But data center developers can also abandon projects and go elsewhere. Until a few years ago, data centers were largely concentrated in Northern Virginia, but with the AI boom, developers have fanned out across the country in search of available power and land. A total of 38 states have welcomed them with open arms and generous tax breaks, per the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns.
Thanks to the convoluted way the US electric grid and energy markets work, Constellation’s power plants don’t even need to be located in the same state as their data center customers — the plant supplying the power just needs to be connected to the same region from which the grid is drawing power. The purchase agreement, in that sense, is symbolic: Because the data center needs more electricity than it can draw from the local grid without causing disruptions for everyone else, the data center pays for independent power providers like Constellation to supply the grid with extra electricity.
That’s why data centers and the enormous amount of electricity Big Tech says it needs to power them have been such a boon for the nuclear industry. For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
Nuclear lobbyists will tell you that’s because the NRC’s safety regulations are overly restrictive and lead to untenable upfront capital costs that make projects impossible to finance. (This has been an industry talking point since 1979, after the NRC seriously overhauled its safety standards following the partial meltdown at Three Mile Island. That site is now owned by Constellation, which has signed a 20-year deal with Microsoft.)
Both the Biden and Trump administrations have worked to support the development of nuclear power in the US by passing developer tax credits. The Trump administration has gone even further, pushing for a sweeping reform of the NRC that would make it much easier for new reactors to obtain operating licenses.
And the Department of Energy this month approved a $5 billion loan to Constellation, which the company will use to upgrade its existing nuclear fleet. Another nuclear energy company, Vistra, received a $4.2 billion loan.
It’s not totally unlike the Biden administration’s passage of the Civil Nuclear Credit Program in 2022, which planned to loan $6 billion to struggling nuclear companies in the US.
That’s not lost on Dominguez.
“Interestingly, in many respects the election had the Republicans saying a lot of the same things that the Democrats were saying,” Dominguez told investors on the call. “And I believe that the policy solutions are going to be somewhat similar.”

articles.title: NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries Give Agents the Tools to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
articles.text:
With expanded NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology.
The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems.
The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries faster than ever.
Bringing Black Holes Into Focus
Seeing a black hole takes a telescope the size of Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio dishes worldwide, generating petabytes of data that can take months to process.
With NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam, a module within the cuPhoton Toolkit, black hole observations from the Event Horizon Telescope can now be correlated orders of magnitude faster than ever. Analysis that once took over a month now takes eight minutes.
By combining global radio dishes into Earth-sized aperture, cuPhoton delivers unprecedented astronomical imaging resolution. cuPhoton successfully correlated observations of powerful black hole jets J1924 and 3C279 in the night sky — making it a reality to reconstruct a Messier 87* black hole galaxy in real time.
The entire pipeline, from data loading and processing to visualization, runs on distributed multi-GPU systems or a compact NVIDIA DGX Spark system, helping scientists study how gas spirals inward under a black hole’s powerful gravitational pull.
Steering Fusion Simulations
Sustaining plasma at millions of degrees is essential to achieving stable, continuous fusion energy. But simulating its behavior is costly: on petascale systems, a single time step can take days, with simulations running for weeks. Experiments also generate data faster than traditional pipelines can process it, often leaving scientists waiting until experiments end to analyze results.
Pacific Fusion researchers used NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module to extract insights while plasma simulations run, helping them visualize what’s happening as results emerge.
The NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module extracts insights while plasma simulations run, helping researchers understand what’s happening as results emerge. Researchers can couple the entire pipeline with an NVIDIA Nemotron-powered agent running locally on the same system, enabling interactive analysis that can help steer simulations in real time to inform fusion reactor target and chamber design.
Exploring Potential Medicines
Molecular simulations help scientists evaluate drug designs before costly laboratory experiments. NVIDIA cuPotential, built on work by researchers at Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute and D. E. Shaw Research, accelerates existing simulation software by up to 3x while improving calculation stability and accuracy. It expedites synthetic data creation for generative AI models, finding previously unknown molecular binding sites and calculating the strength of molecular interactions.
NVIDIA is working with Schrödinger and the AMBER, NAMD, GROMACS, LAMMPS and Open Molecular Software Foundation communities to bring cuPotential acceleration to molecular dynamics engines and workflows.
Cadence, Fathom Therapeutics, Topos Bio, Genesis Molecular AI and Terray Therapeutics are adopting it for drug discovery.
Accelerating Materials Research
Daviator, a collection of batched GPU kernels for the widely used Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package, is coming to NVIDIA ALCHEMI — delivering quantum-mechanical calculations up to 22x faster and at up to 75% lower cost. With Daviator, researchers building simulation models can now use GPU acceleration across atomistic systems of all sizes to generate the millions of calculations of atomic interactions needed for model training and inference, including for small systems that previously ran faster on CPUs.
At Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the NVIDIA DAQIRI networking library connects a high-speed electron microscopy detector to GPU processing, moving analysis into the experiment itself. Researchers can identify useful signals, discover previously unknown regions of interest and decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken.
The workflow supports atomic-resolution materials studies that can distinguish elements, laying the groundwork for future automated experiments.
Revealing Biology at Scale
The newly open source cuSpa accelerates cell polygon calculations, enabling developers to generate massive spatial graphs for next-generation patient and cancer models at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, with a 900x speedup compared with using CPUs.
Codeveloped with scverse, the rapids-singlecell framework accelerates single-cell analysis — and is now available in a single, agent-ready container. Using the tool, Therna Biosciences processed data 200x faster for therapeutic design. 10x Genomics integrated rapids-singlecell in its new Sentira platform, helping academic researchers, biopharma teams and foundation model builders accelerate the path from large-scale spatial data to biological insights.
And the NVIDIA GPU-accelerated HMMER library, also open source, accelerates the annotation of predicted protein sequences, supporting data preparation for biological foundation models. At Basecamp Research, benchmark searches ran up to 84x faster than with standard HMMER, reducing the time required to annotate the large biological datasets used to train the company’s therapeutic design models.
Explore NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries. Learn more in this technical blog on GPU-powered black hole reconstruction.

articles.title: How does a compass work?
articles.text:
If you’re like me, when you pick up a compass you can’t help but spin it this way and that, to see if you can trick it. It’s hard to resist experimenting with a spooky force we can’t see or feel ourselves. Yet it always turns the compass needle back towards north.
Even in today’s high-tech world, compasses are useful navigation tools. A compass works without power, unlike GPS, and in any weather and lighting conditions, as opposed to navigation using the Sun, stars or landmarks. If you know which way north is, you can determine any direction.
Like all cool phenomena, the explanation of how a compass works is not magic – it’s physics. And people have been making use of this particular aspect of physics for more than 2,000 years.
A lodestone spoon
The earliest versions of the compass were developed in ancient China. They were spoon-shaped and made of lodestones, pieces of the naturally magnetic mineral magnetite.
When allowed to rotate freely, the spoon handle would align itself with a particular direction (north–south). This was used to organise and harmonise environments, as part of a practice you might know as feng shui.
At the time, it was known that some materials were naturally magnetic – able to attract one another. However, it wasn’t clear exactly what was causing a compass to align itself north–south until 1600, when English physicist William Gilbert deduced that Earth itself acted as a giant magnet.
An invisible field
Like all magnets, Earth generates a magnetic field – an invisible region within which its magnetic forces act.
Electricity and magnetism are closely connected. Together, they form one of the fundamental interactions in physics: electromagnetism. Magnetic fields can be created by electric currents, which are the movements of charged particles; a changing magnetic field can also induce an electrical current.
Our planet spins around an axis once roughly every 24 hours, which is why we have a night and day cycle. The end points of this axis are the North Pole and the South Pole.
Beneath Earth’s surface, in the outer core, electrically conducting liquid metals circulate in convective currents. This movement generates electrical currents. Paired with Earth’s rotation around its axis, these currents maintain a global-scale magnetic field. It extends out into space like a giant, invisible bubble, known as the magnetosphere.
And it’s this global-scale magnetic field that allows a compass to work.
In modern compasses, a magnetised metal needle has replaced the lodestone spoon. That needle is mounted on a low-friction pivot so it has minimal resistance to the effects of external magnetic fields.
As a result, unless there’s a magnet directly nearby, the needle will align itself with Earth’s magnetic north–south direction.
If you’ve ever found that a compass needle didn’t perfectly align with north–south, it might be because it detected a localised magnetic field. Electrical devices such as your phone produce weak magnetic fields. These can affect a compass, causing it to deviate from Earth’s magnetic field.
Which way does a compass really point?
All magnets have two opposite points – a “north” pole and a “south” pole. If you have two magnets, opposite poles (north–south) will pull towards each other, while the same poles (south–south or north–north) will push away.
The next bit will seem a little confusing, but it’s key to understand why compasses point towards the geographic north.
Because opposites attract, the “north” arrow on a compass points towards the “south” pole of Earth’s global-scale magnetic field – the area where field lines point down into Earth’s surface. Despite it having a magnetic polarity of “south”, we call this spot the north magnetic pole because it’s located close to the geographic North Pole in the Arctic.
Earth also has a magnetic south pole, and you guessed it – it’s located near the South Pole in Antarctica, while being the “north” counterpart of Earth’s magnetic field.
Useful in more ways than one
The magnetic poles don’t align perfectly with the poles of Earth’s rotational axis. The reason for this is that Earth’s magnetic field is dynamic. The ever-changing motion of liquid metal in Earth’s outer core means the global magnetic field changes, too.
In fact, the magnetic north and south poles slowly change their locations, and the entire magnetic field has even flipped its polarity in the past, making the two switch places.
Earth’s magnetic field also acts as a protective barrier from space weather generated by our Sun: there’s a constant stream of charged particles coming our way, known as solar wind. The global magnetic field helps to shield Earth and our atmosphere.
Mars, by contrast, no longer has a strong global-scale magnetic field to act as a protective shield. Interactions with solar wind have, over time, contributed to the loss of much of Mars’ atmosphere.
So, the same invisible magnetic field that turns a compass needle also plays a much bigger role in helping to keep Earth our home.

articles.title: Après les tirs dans les lycées, le gouvernement interdit la vente de feux d'artifice, on a décortiqué le décret
articles.text:
Après des semaines de tirs de mortiers d'artifice jusque dans les salles de classe, le gouvernement a interdit par décret la vente et l'utilisation de nombreux feux d'artifice. Treize jours de diète pyrotechnique, à l'échelle du pays.
L'interdiction de vente et d'utilisation des mortiers d'artifice et d'une large gamme d'engins pyrotechniques est parue au Journal officiel le dimanche 15 novembre, avec effet immédiat. Signé la veille par le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu, le décret entend désamorcer les violences qui accompagnent la mobilisation lycéenne depuis septembre, et qui ont parfois atteint les salles de cours. Avec les fusées, batteries et pétards, la liste est longue, les exceptions peu nombreuses, et le décret que nous pu consulter mérite quelques explications.
Des mortiers d'artifice jusque dans les salles de classe
Tout est parti du lycée Saint-Exupéry de Créteil, mi-septembre. Puis le manque de professeurs, Parcoursup, et les suppressions d'options sont très vite venus s'ajouter aux revendications qui ont gagné le pays, et les étudiants ont fini par rejoindre le mouvement. Le 30 septembre, 356 lycées subissaient déjà des blocages ou des tentatives de blocage. Sauf qu'en marge des cortèges, une autre bande-son s'est installée, à base de détonations, poubelles en feu, tirs contre les forces de l'ordre. Une proviseure a même été blessée par un tir de mortier, entre autres incidents.
Le pas le plus inquiétant a été franchi à l'intérieur des établissements. À Villeurbanne, des individus encagoulés sont entrés dans le lycée Frédéric-Faÿs et ont tiré des mortiers depuis un étage. À Villefranche-sur-Saône, le lycée Claude-Bernard a fermé ses portes après l'explosion d'un engin pyrotechnique en pleine classe, devant les élèves et leur professeur. La diffusion sur les réseaux sociaux de vidéos d'affrontements est évoquée par le gouvernement pour expliquer la montée des tensions et justifier la prise de certaines décisions.
Matignon s'est d'ailleurs appuyé sur l'article 37 de la Constitution, qui lui donne la main sur tout ce qui ne relève pas de la loi, et a invoqué l'urgence. Le décret n° 2026-1047 veut prévenir les troubles graves à l'ordre public lors des blocages devant les lycées et les universités, mais aussi pendant les manifestations. Il s'applique partout en France jusqu'au 27 novembre inclus, ce qui couvre la journée de mobilisation nationale de ce mardi 17 novembre.
Feux d'artifice interdits : ce que dit (et ne dit pas) le décret
Pour comprendre ce que vise le décret, un détour par la réglementation s'impose. En France, comme partout dans l'Union européenne, les feux d'artifice sont rangés en catégories selon leur niveau de risque. La F1 regroupe les articles les plus inoffensifs. Les F2 et F3 désignent des produits plus puissants, réservés à un usage en extérieur avec des distances de sécurité qui augmentent d'une catégorie à l'autre.
C'est dans ces deux catégories, F2 et F3, que le gouvernement a établi sa liste noire de quatorze types d'articles. On y trouve les fusées, les batteries, les chandelles romaines, plusieurs familles de pétards et, surtout, les « pots à feu en mortier ». Ces tubes, conçus pour projeter une charge vers le ciel, sont au cœur des incidents de ces dernières semaines. Enfin, le texte interdit leur vente, sans distinguer la boutique du commerce en ligne.
Tout ce qui ne figure pas dans cette liste reste autorisé, à commencer par les articles F1, à très faible risque, comme les cierges magiques. La catégorie F4, qui nécessite de détenir un certificat de qualification artificier, était déjà réservée aux professionnels, donc elle n'est pas concernée par le décret pris par le gouvernement. Ces derniers peuvent d'ailleurs continuer à travailler s'ils disposent des agréments requis, tout comme les collectivités publiques. Les spectacles pyrotechniques encadrés restent possibles.
Mais il reste quelques zones grises. Le décret interdit la vente et l'usage, mais pas la détention. Donc les stocks achetés avant le 15 novembre restent hors du champ du texte. Ce dernier ne prévoit pas non plus de sanction propre. Tirer sur quelqu'un ou dans un lycée relève toutefois déjà du droit pénal, bien plus sévère. Nous verrons désormais si ces treize jours de sevrage suffiront à faire retomber la fièvre.

articles.title: « Je ressens des vertiges » : le nouveau MacBook Pro pose problème à certains utilisateurs
articles.text:
La sortie de l’iPhone Duo avait été quelque peu entachée par le fait que l’écran de certains appareils se soit brisé après seulement quelques utilisations. Apple avait réagi en expliquant que le problème se situait au niveau de la chaîne d’approvisionnement et qu’il concernait seulement « un petit nombre » d’appareils. Mais l’entreprise à la pomme semble maintenant faire face à un nouveau problème, qui concerne cette fois-ci son nouveau MacBook Pro PROLED. En effet, certains de ses utilisateurs rapportent une expérience d’utilisation peu agréable.
Certains utilisateurs de MacBook Pro PROLED pris de nausées et de vertiges
Il n’est pas ici question d’un écran qui se brise ou de touches du clavier défectueuses, mais d’une réaction de certains possesseurs de MacBook Pro PROLED face à une technologie d’affichage. Pour être précis, l’écran de ce nouvel ordinateur d’Apple utilise une gradation PWM à relativement basse fréquence, comprise entre 240 et 480 Hz selon les conditions. La perception de ce type d’affichage peut différer d’une personne à l’autre. Certains ne perçoivent aucune gêne, tandis que d’autres peuvent être pris de vertiges, de nausées, de maux de tête et d’autres symptômes peu agréables.
Certains utilisateurs de MacBook Pro PROLED ont justement ressenti ces symptômes. À tel point que certains ont été contraints de renvoyer l’appareil en magasin. Sur Reddit, un utilisateur explique : « J’adore le mien, mais il me donne tellement le vertige que je n’ai pas d’autre choix que de le retourner ». Un autre confesse : « Je suis assez naïf pour penser que je ne serais pas affecté, mais je me trompais lourdement ! J’ai le nouveau depuis deux jours et je ressens des vertiges ».
Pourquoi de tels symptômes avec le MacBook Pro PROLED et pas sur d’autres appareils ?
Il faut noter que l’iPhone 18 Pro et les iPad dotés d’un écran OLED utilisent également une gradation PWM à basse fréquence. Pourtant, peu d’utilisateurs font état de vertiges ou de nausées. Pourquoi alors serait-ce le cas sur le MacBook Pro PROLED ? La raison est simple : l’écran de l’ordinateur est plus grand et l’utilisateur y effectue bien souvent des tâches qui demandent une certaine concentration (lecture, travail, etc.). Justement, un utilisateur de Reddit explique : « Je ne pouvais littéralement pas travailler (beaucoup de lecture) sur cet ordinateur portable sans avoir la nausée et me sentir déconnecté de la réalité ».
Malheureusement, Apple n’a pas intégré dans son MacBook Pro PROLED une fonctionnalité permettant d’atténuer les effets indésirables de la gradation PWM à basse fréquence. Dans tous les cas, si vous utilisez un MacBook Pro PROLED et que vous éprouvez des sensations désagréables, ne soyez pas surpris. En revanche, une seule solution serait proposée : un retour en magasin.

articles.title: Dax Raad rebuilt his browser tool in Rust for $60. Then memory use fell 97%.
articles.text:
Dax Raad rebuilt his browser tool in Rust for $60. Then memory use fell 97%.
OpenCode developer Dax Raad says he rebuilt the project’s browser automation tool in Rust for $60, replacing the parts of Playwright and Patchright it actually used and dramatically reducing its memory footprint.
A 4.3 MB binary
The figures he posted to X on Saturday are striking. The new Rust binary is just 4.3 MB, compared with 53 to 64 MB for the previous Node version. Memory use for each OpenCode Browse connector also fell from roughly 190 MB to 5.6 MB after a few calls, a reduction of about 97%.
The new Rust binary is just 4.3 MB, compared with 53 to 64 MB for the previous Node version.
The relay that wires AI coding agents to the browser shows a similar gap, with Raad’s comparison putting the Rust implementation at 6 MB idle, or 6.6 MB once it has served calls, against 353 MB for the old Node relay after six days of running.
Replacing Playwright and Patchright
OpenCode Browse connects AI coding agents to a developer’s existing browser through a Chromium extension and an MCP server. The previous Node implementation used Playwright for browser automation and Patchright to reduce detection, but Raad rebuilt the functionality Browse needed in Rust to cut runtime overhead.
Raad rebuilt the functionality Browse needed in Rust to cut runtime overhead.
The new Rust relay communicates with the Chromium extension over WebSockets and uses the Chrome DevTools Protocol to handle browser operations, agent sessions, recordings, and network captures. It also embeds QuickJS to execute agent-supplied JavaScript without requiring the previous Node runtime.
Inside the pull request
The merged pull request confirms that Raad replaced the Node-based CLI and relay while keeping the existing Chromium extension and using the Chrome DevTools Protocol for browser operations.
The team ran two rounds of testing with about 10 regression agents against a real Chrome browser. Browse scored 85% on Stealth Bench v2, compared with 90.5% for Browser Use Cloud, although the pull request doesn’t include a score for the old Node version.
Not everything made it into the rewrite; Raad dropped time zone and locale emulation along with the download tool, which Chrome blocks for extensions. The Rust version also retains a problem from the Node implementation where a busy-looping eval can’t be stopped through the extension.
Browse still includes relay authentication, extension pairing and origin restrictions, and agents are limited to tabs they open themselves or that users explicitly share with them.
The real $60 cost
Raad says the rewrite “only cost $60” and confirmed in a reply on X that he used Claude Opus as his main coding model and DeepSeek as a subagent.
The two models helped him replace the Playwright and Patchright functionality Browse needed, although the $60 figure doesn’t include the time he spent checking, testing, and fixing the code. The challenge with Rust rewrites is finding a smaller replacement that matches the original’s functionality without creating more maintenance work.
the $60 figure doesn’t include the time he spent checking, testing, and fixing the code
The memory savings are impressive, but Raad has also taken on responsibility for code that Playwright and Patchright previously maintained. His team will also have to deal with browser updates, authentication changes and security fixes that previously came through those libraries. That’s where AI-generated technical debt can become a problem, especially when code is cheap to produce but takes considerably more work to maintain.

articles.title: Microsoft: Windows Server 2016 reaches end of support in 60 days
articles.text:
Microsoft has reminded customers again that Windows Server 2016 will stop receiving security updates after it reaches the end of support in two months.
This follows another warning issued in October, announcing the end of extended support for Windows Server 2016 and encouraging users to upgrade to Windows Server 2025.
Windows Server 2016 reached general availability on October 12, 2016, one month after its official release at Microsoft's annual Ignite conference in September of that year.
It also reached the end of mainstream support nearly 4 years ago, in January 2022, and extended support will end in roughly two months, on January 13, 2027.
On the same date, the company will also stop support for all Windows Server 2016 Essentials features, including Remote Web Access and related Essentials-specific functionality.
"On January 13, 2027, all editions of Windows Server 2016 will reach the end of extended support. The January 2027 Windows security update will be the last update provided during extended support," Microsoft said in a message center update.
"After that date, monthly security updates will continue only for Windows Server 2016 devices enrolled in Extended Security Updates (ESU)."
Windows Server 2025 upgrade
Before Windows Server 2016 stops receiving security updates, Microsoft advised IT administrators to switch to Windows Server 2025, which started rolling out to Windows Insiders in January 2024 and reached general availability in November 2024.
Admins who want to test Windows Server 2025 before deploying it across their organization can get a free 180-day trial via the Microsoft Evaluation Center.
Windows Server 2025 is the latest Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) release for Windows Server, and it will reach the end of mainstream support in November 2029, with an additional five years of extended support until November 14, 2034.
More information about Windows servicing dates is available on the Windows Lifecycle FAQ page or via the Lifecycle Policy search tool.
Last month, Microsoft announced that devices running Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro editions stopped receiving security and non-security preview updates and advised customers to upgrade to Windows 11 26H2 by installing the Windows 11 2026 Update.
On Friday, it also reminded customers that they can enroll in the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program after Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 (a stripped-down Windows 10 edition for mission-critical devices) reaches the end of mainstream support in January, until they can upgrade to Windows 11 Enterprise LTSC 2024.

articles.title: La version la plus récente de l'Amazon Echo Show 8 profite d'une remise de 41 % à l'occasion du Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
L’Echo Show 8 est un écran connecté compact conçu par Amazon, qui en a dévoilé une nouvelle version en 2025. Comme ses aînés, il combine les fonctions d’un hub domotique et d’un centre multimédia, tout en intégrant Alexa. Il est même compatible avec Alexa+, la version nouvelle génération de l’assistant vocal d’Amazon dopée à l’IA générative. Si vous attendiez le Black Friday pour craquer, sachez que vous avez bien fait : l’Echo Show 8 bénéficie actuellement d’une réduction de 41 %.
Les points essentiels de l’Echo Show 8
- Un écran tactile de 8,7 pouces
- La prise en charge des protocoles Zigbee, Matter et Thread
- La compatibilité avec Alexa+
Lancé à 199,99 euros en novembre 2025, puis affiché à 219,99 euros sur Amazon, l’Amazon Echo Show 8 est aujourd’hui disponible en promotion à 129,99 euros sur Amazon.
Du 10 au 30 novembre, le LUBA mini 2 AWD 1000 passe à 1 199 € au lieu de 1 499 €, support de lavage offert ! Vision IA tri-caméra, sans fil périmétrique, tonte des bordures, adaptation à toutes les conditions de luminosité… Bref, il a tout pour tondre à votre place !
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant l’Amazon Echo Show 8. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un écran compact au design repensé
L’Echo Show 8 est un écran connecté plutôt compact avec ses dimensions de 21 x 15 x 13 cm, pour un poids de 1 kg. On peut donc le poser sur une étagère, une table de chevet ou toute autre surface plane sans problème. Son design a par ailleurs été repensé : son nouveau support aux lignes rondes permet de surélever la dalle, et les bordures qui entourent cette dernière ont gagné en finesse. Amazon annonce d’ailleurs une surface d’affichage 15 % plus grande que celle du modèle de 2023, qui se contentait d’un écran de 8 pouces en 1 280 x 800 pixels.
En parlant de cet écran, on a face à nous une dalle tactile HD de 8,7 pouces affichant une définition de 1 340 x 800 pixels, au-dessus de laquelle une caméra de 13 mégapixels avec cadrage automatique a été installée. D’ailleurs, grâce à elle ainsi qu’à la technologie Omnisense d’Amazon, l’Echo Show 8 peut reconnaître les utilisateurs et personnaliser l’affichage. Cette technologie maison permet aussi à l’appareil de savoir si quelqu’un se trouve dans la pièce ou s’approche de l’écran, ou encore de déclencher des automatisations en fonction de la température ambiante mesurée.
Un hub complet
En plus d’être un écran qui permet de naviguer sur Internet, de consulter des recettes de cuisine ou encore de regarder des vidéos, l’Echo Show 8 fait également office de véritable hub pour la maison connectée. Il prend en charge les protocoles Zigbee, Thread et Matter et dispose d’une connectivité Wi-Fi 6E tri-bande ainsi que du Bluetooth. Vous pouvez ainsi centraliser le contrôle de nombreux objets connectés sans avoir besoin de vous équiper d’un hub supplémentaire. Il est notamment possible de jumeler et piloter des appareils compatibles avec Alexa, consulter le flux vidéo de vos caméras de surveillance ou encore gérer vos ampoules intelligentes directement depuis l’écran, ou à l’aide de commandes vocales si vous ne voulez pas vous lever.
Enfin, l’Echo Show 8 fait partie des appareils compatibles avec Alexa+, la version de l’assistant vocal d’Amazon dopée à l’intelligence artificielle générative. Alexa+ s’appuie sur plusieurs grands modèles de langage (LLM). Amazon promet un assistant capable de comprendre des requêtes complexes, d’enchaîner plusieurs tâches et de discuter de façon plus naturelle qu’auparavant. Par exemple, Alexa peut réserver une table au restaurant via TheFork et répondre à des questions assez pointues.
