articles.title: Why does your body store fat in your butt?
articles.text:
Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
Why does your body store fat in your butt? - Ellen, age 8, Cambridge, Massachusetts
Have you ever wondered why some parts of your body are firm, like your elbows, while other areas, like your butt, are squishier?
The difference is due to what scientists call fat distribution, and researchers are still trying to understand why bodies store fat in some places but not in others.
All animals have fat in their bodies, even insects. Bears even put on up to 400 pounds (180 kilograms) of additional body fat, the equivalent of 544 large cheese pizzas, to survive hibernation.
Fat is an important and constantly changing part of all bodies, including those of humans and our evolutionary ancestors.
What is fat?
Fat, also called adipose tissue, is one kind of connective tissue that helps hold your body together.
For a long time, scientists thought that adipose tissue was mainly a storage place for the extra energy your body doesn’t use from the food you eat. While fat is a great source of stored energy, it also has many other functions. There are even different kinds of fat.
Visceral fat serves as a sort of protective bubble wrap, surrounding and filling in the spaces between your internal organs. Subcutaneous fat, the layer of fat between your skin and your muscle that you can pinch, is a protective cushion and helps to keep you warm by insulating you like a coat.
Fat also produces and responds to hormones, a type of chemical messenger, to regulate how your body uses energy and to tell you when you are hungry or full.
Different kinds of fat also have different jobs. White fat is the kind of fat most people are familiar with and performs the functions mentioned above.
You may be less familiar with brown fat, which is brown because it contains a lot of mitochondria: the parts of your cells that produce the energy your body needs to perform all its functions.
Not all animals have brown fat, but humans do. Scientists know that brown fat performs a special function to heat your body when you get cold. It doesn’t store energy, like white fat does, to help your body move.
When you were a baby, you had a lot of brown fat along your torso to help keep you warm because your body wasn’t mature enough to maintain your body temperature. As you grow older, you have less brown fat. It is only located just above your collar bone and along your major deep blood vessels, like your aorta.
Why do humans store fat where we do?
Researchers don’t know enough yet about brown fat to know why it is in just a few parts of the body. It is possible that it’s near the neck and around major blood vessels to help insulate the blood and keep overall body temperature in a healthy warm range.
As for white fat, there appear to be three main factors that determine where your fat gets stored: genetics, hormones and age.
Certain genes direct fat to accumulate in the butt, while other genes tell it to collect on the torso.
Hormones like estrogen, which affects almost every system in all bodies but is typically higher in females, direct more subcutaneous fat to gather in the butt, thighs and backs of the arms. Cortisol, the stress hormone, seems to direct visceral fat to accumulate in the belly area.
But why isn’t fat evenly distributed throughout the body? Well, having a lot of fat around your elbows and knees would limit your ability to bend your arms and legs. Storing a lot of fat around your head would possibly put your brain at risk of overheating. Other parts of your body, like hips, butts, breasts and thighs, don’t have these risks – maybe that’s why we store fat there.
Why do people have fat at all?
Don’t be fooled: A lot of animals that look fat, like a hippopotamus, actually aren’t. Hippos only have around 2% body fat, the percentage of how much of your body mass comes from fat; while the average human woman has over 30% body fat.
In the rest of the animal kingdom, biologists typically only see a lot of body fat among hibernating or marine mammals. For the hibernators, the fat serves as energy storage for long, cold winters. For marine mammals like seals and whales, that extra fat is like a giant puffy coat helping to keep them warm in the cold depths of the ocean.
Humans do not hibernate, nor do we live in the ocean, so why do we have a lot more fat than all other primates and most mammals?
Anthropologists like me, who study how the human body has evolved over time, think it has to do with the lifestyle of our evolutionary ancestors who had to gather and hunt to survive. Gathering and hunting were not always reliable food sources. We think our ancestors developed the ability to put on extra fat as a food insurance policy. When food was difficult to find, they could rely on their extra fat stores to carry them through until food became available again.
Researchers are still trying to determine when this extra fat storage evolved. We have one line of evidence from small stone figures known as Gravettian statues.
These ancient statues from 25,000 to 28,000 years ago depict feminine figures who carry a lot of extra body fat. Archaeologists have found them all throughout Europe and Russia.
The way the ancient artists depicted fat on these figures matches how fat looks on bodies today. This accuracy has led researchers to believe that the makers of the Gravettian statues knew how individuals with greater body fat actually looked, meaning at least some people at this time did put on a lot of extra fat.
Europe and Russia back then were much colder than they are today, supporting the idea that our ancestors would have needed the extra fat to get through the extremely cold winters when food was harder to find.
So, the next time you poke at your butt fat, remember that fat is a really important part of our bodies, performs lots of different functions, and is likely evolutionarily ancient for us humans.
Hello, curious kids! Do you have a question you’d like an expert to answer? Ask an adult to send your question to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com. Please tell us your name, age and the city where you live.
And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.

articles.title: What Is Acoustic Micro Imaging? A Quick Guide To This Inspection Process
articles.text:
Obtaining clear images of gaps and delaminations in advanced packages.
We all know how important inspection is for advanced packaging. Not only are these processes critical for ensuring higher yield, but they’re also integral for maintaining device reliability. As the industry pushes for smaller features and tighter spacing, even the smallest defects can pose major challenges. For instance, delaminations and air gaps can be detrimental in a market that demands increasingly complex devices. Such defects will lead to electrical or mechanical failures down the road.
One technology that’s mitigating these issues is acoustic micro imaging (AMI). AMI is a high-frequency ultrasound technology, and it’s being used by the industry as an inspection method.
At the core of AMI technology is a transducer, or a device that turns energy from one form to another. It starts with a pulse of electrical energy, then converts it to mechanical energy, or a high-frequency ultrasound wave. Because ultrasound doesn’t travel through air, this allows inspectors to obtain clear images of gaps and delaminations in the device that could otherwise be difficult to see.
However, the transducers used for AMI are not all the same. Each transducer handles a specific frequency, and they’re chosen based on the sample that needs to be inspected. By moving the transducer across the sample, the inspector can generate multiple images that can then be analyzed by the AMI software. Through this analysis, the inspector can choose to accept or reject parts based on the number of defects the package is found to have.
So, how do these defects typically present themselves?
The biggest difference between ideal and defective samples is that some defective samples will have very clear air gaps. However, another common defect is thinning of the attach material on solder pads. When this material is too thin, any stress that would be put on the device could lead to delamination. An uneven solder or thermal interface material (TIM) layer may also indicate a larger problem with the build process.
With the ability to gather so much information without damaging the device, why would anyone choose to perform a destructive test to identify a defect, rather than simply use AMI inspection to check for them? One reason is for R&D purposes. Oftentimes, companies want to ensure that a process is fully developed before integrating it into their production cycle, and a destructive test can confirm proof of concept for AMI.
An example of this in action is a standard capacitor inspection. New capacitor companies will often require a destructive test to confirm the presence of voids or delaminations found by the AMI software. Once the destructive proof of concept has been completed, the company can then integrate the software into their inspection process.
There are some key differences between AMI and its transmission technology counterpart, which is more comparable to X-ray. Whereas AMI is an ultrasound technology, transmission scanning uses both a sending and receiving transducer positioned above and below the sample. Both transmission technology and X-ray create composite images, unlike AMI, which inspects layer-by-layer.
Ultrasound and X-ray are complementary technologies. There are some things AMI can do that X-ray can’t, and vice versa. For certain applications, both technologies may be recommended. For example, composite images are preferable for inspecting spherical objects like ball grid arrays.
Although AMI technology has tangible benefits, keeping up with the industry’s rapid pace is a hurdle that AMI must continually overcome. As applications become more complex, AMI software needs to quickly adapt to changing components. For instance, instead of scanning a single flip chip, AMI software could now be required to inspect multi-die stacks.
One way this mounting complexity is being addressed is through machine learning algorithms.
For example, some wafers have via patterns that look similar or identical to delamination, and humans have typically been responsible for distinguishing them. However, through advancements in machine learning, AMI software can now identify via patterns and exclude those from the defect count. As machine learning becomes more robust, it will open new doors for inspecting increasingly complicated devices.
In addition, customer requirements for higher resolution and better throughput are also driving new developments for AMI software. To meet these rising demands, Nordson Test & Inspection developed its automated SpinSAM tool that can inspect four 300mm wafers at a time.
Traditionally, acoustic microscopy systems move the transducer in a raster pattern, which is a small grid made up of individual pixels. This approach allows inspectors to collect data at every XY point, but it also requires decelerating to turn the transducer at the end of each line, thereby reducing throughput. Some acoustic microscopes address the need for better throughput by skipping lines and interpolating data points, or by using multiple transducers and stitching images together – both of which have their own drawbacks.
In contrast, SpinSAM spins the wafer to move the transducer and the wafer continuously, allowing inspectors to scan each pixel faster, allowing for better throughput without image stitching distortion.

articles.title: La caída global de Microsoft se debió a un fallo introducido por la compañía hace meses y que tumbó el 80% de sus servidores
articles.text:
La caída global de Microsoft se debió a un fallo introducido por la compañía hace meses y que tumbó el 80% de sus servidores
El incidente, que se prolongó durante más de 18 horas, afectó a millones de usuarios de algunas de las aplicaciones más populares de la tecnológica, como Outlook, Teams, Copilot, Word, Excel o Power Point
Los fallos que experimentaron el pasado jueves y viernes varios servicios de Microsoft se originaron en una sobrecarga de los servidores de la compañía. Esta sobrecarga, a su vez, vino provocada por la implementación defectuosa de una serie de actualizaciones que venía desarrollando la compañía desde hace meses. Así lo asegura la tecnológica en un comunicado difundido esta mañana, en el que también vuelve a pedir disculpas a sus clientes por las molestias causadas.
La citada actualización se empezó a ejecutar en julio y no se observaron problemas. “Durante más de tres meses, el cambio se implementó en todo el mundo sin impacto”, ha dicho esta mañana en la red X Charles Lamanna, vicepresidente ejecutivo de Copilot, Agentes y Plataforma en Microsoft. Pero unas quince horas antes de la interrupción, Teams registró un error en el uso de los servidores, lo que “aumentó la carga” y cambió los patrones de tráfico.
More details on the root cause can be found in the Microsoft 365 Admin center, and an abridged version can be found below. 
We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations. 
The incident on… https://t.co/p8mUHxDe67
— Charles Lamanna (@clamanna) November 16, 2026
Lamanna explica también que, cuando esto sucedió, casi el 14% de la capacidad de los servidores “estaba fuera de servicio debido a un problema no relacionado del día anterior”. Eso hizo que la sobrecarga tuviera un impacto más fuerte de lo normal en el sistema, que colapsó al no poder absorber un aumento súbito del tráfico de datos. “El tráfico redirigido aumentó la probabilidad de que el mismo problema ocurriera en los puntos finales restantes. Esto causó una falla en cascada de servidor a servidor”, explica Lamanna. Fue como un efecto dominó: en menos de dos horas, el problema se había extendido por todo el mundo, afectando en su punto álgido a más del 80% de los servidores que gestiona la compañía en todon el planeta.
Una vez caídos los sistemas, restaurarlos no fue sencillo. “La recuperación tomó más tiempo de lo habitual porque, a medida que los servidores regresaban al servicio, eran inmediatamente abrumados por el tráfico en espera y se volvían no responsivos nuevamente”, indica Lamanna. “Dado que el defecto principal de código era un error latente de varios meses anteriores, nuestros mecanismos normales de reversión y pruebas no pudieron revertir rápidamente el cambio”, añade.
Cuando identificaron el fallo, los ingenieros de Microsoft desarrollaron una actualización “que devolvió la ruta de código al estado previamente conocido como bueno”. Para poder aplicarla y que no volviera a colapsar todo, lo que hicieron fue ir aplicando los cambios en grupos de servidores fuera de servicio, que después se reiniciaron y pusieron en marcha. “Este proceso se aplicó cuidadosamente a grandes cantidades de infraestructura a la vez (por ejemplo, más del 50% de una región)”, indica Lamanna.
Microsoft no dio oficialmente por zanjado el problema hasta el sábado por la mañana, casi un día y medio después de iniciarse la crisis. El propio Lamanna ha dicho en X que se conocerán más detalles sobre el incidente “durante esta semana”, cuando se complete la revisión post-incidente.
Hacia las 18.30 hora peninsular española del pasado jueves día 12 de noviembre, miles de usuarios empezaron a notar que algunos servicios de Microsoft funcionaban mal. El fallo se prolongó durante más de 18 horas, afectando a millones de usuarios de al menos 70 países. En España no provocó problemas significativos en la Administración, que pudo seguir prestando sus servicios sin problemas. Otros países, como Japón, Australia o Malasia, sí tuvieron que interrumpir servicios críticos.
El servicio afectado de Microsoft 365, que incluye programas como Word, Excel o PowerPoint, cuenta con más de 450 millones de usuarios corporativos y 95 millones de clientes particulares. El programa Teams, de videoconferencias y otras funcionalidades para entornos laborales, cuenta con más de 320 millones de usuarios. La aplicación de correo electrónico Outlook también fue uno de los afectados.
Todos estos programas son desde hace años herramientas de trabajo fundamentales en muchas oficinas de todo el mundo. De ahí que la incidencia de la caída de los sistemas fuera especialemente severo en el sector privado.

articles.title: Australian retail giant Coles investigates cybersecurity incident
articles.text:
Coles Group Limited, Australia's second-largest retailer, is investigating what it described as a "cyber security incident" that has not impacted the company's stores.
Founded in 1914, Coles now employs over 115,000 people, manages a network of more than 1,800 retail outlets, and operates the Flybuys loyalty program with over nine million active members.
In a statement issued earlier today, the company said that it's now working with external experts to secure its systems and added that it has yet to find evidence that the attackers stole customer, employee, or supplier data from compromised systems.
"Coles Group Limited is currently investigating a cyber security incident. Based on the findings of our investigation to date, we have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles' systems," the retail giant said.
"Coles is working with the Australian Cyber Security Centre and will continue to engage with appropriate agencies and regulators as investigations continue. Coles is also working with global cyber security experts to contain and secure the Coles IT environment."
It also noted that customers can shop as normal, as Flybuys accounts, Coles Plus, Coles Plus Delivery or QuiteLike subscriptions, and Coles stores and online outlets have not been affected by the cyberattack.
However, it added that it is aware of Liquorland click-and-collect issues affecting a small number of customers.
While it didn't link this to the incident, the company advised customers to be suspicious of any messages requesting personal data and recommended using unique passwords.
"We advise everyone to take basic online precautions and recommend remaining vigilant to suspicious links, attempts to solicit personal information from you (including by email, phone, text, or post) and potential scam activity," it added.
"We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reusing the same password across multiple services."
Coles has not yet said when it discovered the incident or whether the attackers have made a ransom demand, and no major threat group has claimed the attack.
A Coles spokesperson was not immediately available for comment when BleepingComputer reached out for more details on the incident.

articles.title: upGrad broadens its business with new workforce advisory venture
articles.text:
upGrad broadens its business with new workforce advisory venture
upGrad launches workforce advisory business as it expands beyond skilling, aiming to help organisations navigate AI-led transformation through integrated workforce strategy and implementation.
Edtech firm upGrad has launched upGrad Next, a workforce advisory business intended to help organisations redesign how they structure, hire, reward and develop employees as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes work.
The move broadens upGrad’s corporate offering as it diversifies beyond skilling into higher education, professional courses, study-abroad services and enterprise learning. Its acquisition of Unacademy adds competitive exam preparation to its edtech portfolio, as the company, led by chairperson and co-founder Ronnie Screwvala, eyes a potential IPO.
Anandorup Ghose will lead Next as managing director, with Hrishikesh Godbole, Krishna Chaitanya and Dinkar Pawan among the initial team.
Screwvala described the launch as a response to the next phase of digital change. “The last decade, in many ways, was about the complete digital transformation of organisations. We see the next decade being about transforming the workforce to manage, and get strong returns from, the change that has already happened.”
Next will advise on organisational structure, recruitment, pay and workforce development, and help put those decisions into practice. upGrad said it will combine experienced advisers with AI and its skilling and hiring operations, with accountability for outcomes rather than consultant time billed.
Ghose, who has spent more than 24 years in HR and rewards consulting, worked as a partner at Aon and Deloitte and led the latter’s rewards consulting practice globally. He sees a gap between large technology transformation programmes and specialist products. “These demand experience and judgment. The next decade won't be won by those who adopt technology fastest, but by those who unlock human potential most effectively.”
His argument is that decisions about AI investment, job design and employee capability need to be made together. Technology adoption alone does not guarantee higher productivity.
Aon’s 2026 Human Capital Trends study found that 43% of organisations in India had deployed AI and a further 20% were piloting it, but translating investment into workforce outcomes remained difficult. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 estimated that 39% of workers’ existing skill sets would be transformed or become outdated by 2030, while 63% of employers saw skills gaps as a major barrier to business transformation.
Consulting and technology firms are also combining these capabilities. In October 2026, KPMG in India and HR technology company PeopleStrong announced an alliance pairing workforce advice with AI-enabled human capital management software for employee data and HR processes. In September, Deloitte launched an Open Model Engineering practice to help organisations build and deploy AI tools for business use, and said it would hire and train specialists to work alongside clients. Both moves highlight the growing overlap between advice and implementation.
Meanwhile, the Government programmes are expanding the skills pipeline. The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship said the Skill India Digital Hub’s SOAR programme now includes 50 AI and AI-application qualifications. By August 2026, more than 517,000 learners had enrolled and over 100,000 had been certified.

articles.title: Windows 11 sur un iPhone Duo ? Il l'a fait avec Gemini 4 Carbon, et sans jailbreak
articles.text:
Un responsable de Google a réussi à faire tourner Windows 11 sur le tout premier iPhone pliable d’Apple, avec l’aide de Gemini. Une expérience insolite qui transforme le smartphone en (presque) vrai PC miniature, au prix de quelques acrobaties techniques.
Voilà quelques années, déjà, que Microsoft a jeté l’éponge concernant Windows sur smartphone, mais il semblerait que tout le monde n’ait pas encore renoncé à l’idée. Ammaar Reshi, responsable du produit et du design chez Google AI Studio, vient de publier une vidéo sur X dans laquelle il fait fonctionner Windows 11 sur un iPhone Duo, le tout premier smartphone pliable d’Apple. Pas de jailbreak ni de PC distant pour faire tourner le système, mais un projet développé avec l’aide de Gemini 4 Carbon en seulement deux heures, à en croire son auteur.
Windows 11 et iOS, une cohabitation assez improbable
Baptisé WindowsiOS, le projet ne remplace pas iOS, mais exécute Windows 11 24H2 dans sa version ARM64 au sein d’un environnement virtuel. Pour contourner les restrictions d’Apple sur la virtualisation matérielle, il exploite un moteur de traduction binaire capable d’adapter à la volée les instructions de Windows à l’environnement d’exécution de l’iPhone Duo. Une opération facilitée par l’architecture ARM64 commune au système de Microsoft et à la puce A20 Pro du smartphone.
Ce moteur, Ammaar Reshi l’a repris de Henge, un projet open source qui avait déjà permis de faire fonctionner macOS sur iPhone, puis l’a adapté aux exigences de Windows grâce aux agents de Gemini 4 Carbon, en retravaillant la gestion de la mémoire, le démarrage du système et la prise en charge des périphériques virtuels.
L’interface a également été adaptée au format pliable de l’iPhone Duo. Entièrement ouvert, le smartphone fait office de tablette Windows sur son écran de 7,6 pouces. Replié à moitié, il se transforme en petit ordinateur portable, avec clavier et pavé tactile virtuels, sur lequel il est même possible de naviguer sur Internet grâce à Microsoft Edge.
Une prouesse, mais pas tout à fait un PC de poche
Avant d’espérer transformer son propre iPhone en PC Windows, il faudra tout de même s’armer d’un peu de patience et de solides connaissances techniques. L’installation nécessite un Mac équipé d’une puce Apple Silicon, les outils de développement d’Apple et une image de Windows 11 ARM64, tandis que chaque lancement impose de passer par un débogueur pour autoriser l’exécution du code traduit.
Ammaar Reshi revendique des performances proches d’une exécution native sur l’iPhone Duo, seul appareil sur lequel WindowsiOS a été testé jusqu’ici. Pour parvenir à ce résultat, il a dû alléger Windows 11 afin de le faire tenir dans les 4,5 Go de mémoire qui lui sont alloués, en désactivant ou supprimant plus de 35 services et composants, parmi lesquels les protections de Microsoft Defender.
Bref, il faut quand même avoir un sacré goût pour la bidouille, et les moyens de se l’offrir, pour installer sur un iPhone à 2 339 euros une version de Windows 11 dont le support vient de prendre fin, vous en conviendrez.
- Fabrication et charnière remarquables
- Format passeport très agréable
- Écran mat nano-texturé, pliure discrète

articles.title: Mercedes voudrait rendre sa Classe C électrique beaucoup plus abordable
articles.text:
Mercedes est une marque particulièrement active sur le marché des véhicules électriques. Après une première génération de modèles sous la gamme EQ, la marque à l’étoile a revu sa stratégie en déclinant les noms de modèles thermiques pour des voitures électriques. La nouvelle Classe C électrique adopte cette stratégie et devrait bientôt voir sa gamme se compléter de trois nouvelles versions, dont deux plus abordables.
Deux motorisations plus abordables prochainement
La gamme de la Mercedes Classe C électrique est actuellement composée de la Classe C 400 4Matic, version de lancement avec 489 chevaux venant de deux moteurs offrant une transmission intégrale. La batterie est une NMC de 94 kWh permettant une autonomie de 762 km en cycle WLTP.
Quelques semaines plus tard, la Mercedes Classe C 300 4Matic a rejoint le catalogue, toujours bimoteur avec quatre roues motrices, mais cette fois avec une puissance totale de 421 chevaux. Cette motorisation est associée à la batterie de 85 kWh pour 682 km d’autonomie.
Mercedes devrait ajouter à la gamme prochainement les Classe C 200 et 250, se passant de la transmission intégrale pour devenir des motorisations à propulsion et à moteur unique. Ainsi, la Mercedes Classe C électrique deviendrait plus accessible.
La Classe C électrique bientôt plus accessible ?
La Mercedes Classe C 200 devrait utiliser une batterie LFP de 64 kWh. L’autonomie devrait approcher les 600 km selon nos estimations, en s’appuyant sur l’efficience de la Classe C, le seul moteur arrière et la boîte à deux rapports pour moteur électrique de Mercedes. L’utilisation d’une batterie LFP et du moteur unique permettra de réduire drastiquement le prix de la Mercedes Classe C électrique. Une batterie LFP est 40 % moins coûteuse à produire par kWh qu’une NMC. Actuellement, la Mercedes Classe C débute au tarif de 62 999 euros. La Classe C 200 pourrait être plus proche de 50 000 euros.
De son côté, la Mercedes Classe C 250 devrait aussi utiliser un seul moteur. La puissance n’est pas encore connue à ce stade, avec une batterie de 85 kWh. L’autonomie totale devrait approcher les 700 km WLTP, une version idéale pour les grands rouleurs souhaitant maîtriser leur budget.
La recharge des Mercedes Classe C 200 et 250 devrait toujours être rapide en raison de la plateforme 800 volts, mais l’énergie récupérée en 10 minutes sera moins importante que sur les 300 et 400. En effet, plus la batterie est petite, moins le pic de charge peut être important.
Enfin, Mercedes devrait aussi lancer une Mercedes Classe C électrique plus dynamique, plus sportive. Une déclinaison AMG est au programme en 2027. Évidemment, cette version sera plus coûteuse que celles actuellement au catalogue, mais aussi plus exclusive. La Mercedes Classe C électrique devrait bientôt avoir cinq versions à son catalogue, une gamme fournie pour répondre à plusieurs usages.

articles.title: NVIDIA and Lambda Disclose First Production Co-Packaged Optics Cluster... It is FINALLY real
articles.text:
For SC26, NVIDIA and Lambda discussed their first production co-packaged optics (CPO) cluster. The industry has worked to move CPO from the lab to production for decades. Many in the industry will tell you it is a few years out, but Lambda has already deployed it in production in a cluster with over 10,000 GPUs.
NVIDIA and Lambda Disclose First Production Co-Packaged Optics Cluster
We covered NVIDIA’s co-packaged optics extensively during the company’s Hot Chips 2025 presentation. NVIDIA’s first version of the packaging is in its Quantum-X switching product, while Spectrum-X will be an updated second-generation part.
NVIDIA is using an array of 18 pluggable light sources on the front of the chassis, as shown in the photos above, to generate light en route to the switch package’s optical modules. Those light sources are pluggable, meaning they can be serviced, which was one of the key inhibitors to CPO in switches when the light source was integrated. Light sources tend to be the parts that fail in pluggable optics, so making them serviceable was an important innovation. Likewise, on the switch package side, making the connections at least somewhat serviceable helps with deployment.
Downstream, NVIDIA’s Quantum-X CPO switch pictured above has 144 MPO/MTP ports, each at 800Gbps. Something interesting is that with only 18 light sources, instead of 144x 800Gbps optical modules (or 72x dual 800G modules), there are actually fewer light sources that can fail than in a traditional switch, and it becomes easier to cool them compared to having a larger array of individual pluggable modules.
Final Words
One of the biggest benefits of the deployment is that by moving the optics to the switch package rather than the front-panel pluggables, numerous high-speed copper links do not need to drive signaling over relatively long distances from the switch chip to the front cages. As a result, CPO can significantly lower power consumption so that more GPUs can fit in the same footprint. After all, in a power-limited environment, ultimately the more power that can be used for GPUs directly impacts the revenue that can be generated per Watt of power available to the cluster.
Lambda and NVIDIA may have a short on the cluster up, but let me be clear: it exists and is running today, putting NVIDIA at the forefront of deploying CPO. I think it is actually just being announced this week as part of SC26. As a fun aside, I was at OCP Summit 2026 a few weeks ago when I heard during another vendor’s keynote that CPO was still years away from deployment. It turns out it is already deployed. We no longer have to ask if or when CPO will finally be deployed. The big question now is what the adoption curve will be.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Regensburg. Original written by Karoline Stürmer. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S. Maier, R. Spachtholz, K. Glöckl, C. M. Bustamante, S. Lingl, M. Maczejka, J. Schön, A. Riedel, K. Richter, F. J. Giessibl, F. P. Bonafé, M. A. Huber, A. Rubio, J. Repp, R. Huber. Tracking electrons at the space-time limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (8): 961 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01932-0

articles.title: Get answers from tables with tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Get answers from tables with tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports tabular search, so you can get answers from tables through agentic retrieval. When a question needs data from CSV, XLSX, or XLS files, tabular search looks up values and runs calculations across every relevant row in one or more tables or sheets. It then combines the results with facts from related documents to answer analytical questions that take several steps.
A finance team closing the quarter needs to know “Which departments must write variance commentary?” No single file has the answer. It depends on the variance policy’s threshold, the quarter-close memo’s budget revisions, and math over every department in the profit and loss (P&L) workbook.
Like this finance team, most teams keep their narratives and data in the same place. For example, a Microsoft SharePoint site holds workbooks next to policies, and an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket holds CSV exports next to PDFs. Tabular search answers questions across these files through the same AgenticRetrieveStream request you already use for documents. It runs code over the original file in an isolated sandbox, so the answer uses the whole table instead of only the rows that retrieval returns. For the finance team, one request returns the departments that must write commentary. The answer cites the policy and the memo, and the trace names the workbook the code read.
In this post, you learn how tabular search answers questions that need both table data and facts from documents, and when another tool is a better fit. You also build a knowledge base with sample finance files and use the trace to see which file the code read.
Why tables are hard for retrieval
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) returns a fixed number of passages that best match a question, which works well for prose. Tables lose information when they’re split into passages, in ways that depend on the table’s shape:
- Long tables – A table with thousands of rows spans many passages, and retrieval returns only the few that best match the question. An answer built from them uses a handful of rows, so a total, a comparison, or a threshold check can be incomplete.
- Wide tables – In a table with hundreds of columns, one row can hold more text than a passage or a search model takes in at once. As a result, values in later columns are harder to match. Long passages from wide tables can also match many unrelated questions and push more relevant passages out of the results.
Retrieval also has to match a question to the right table. Questions use business terms, such as “controllable spend,” but tables hold cost center codes, account names, and numbers. A draft and a final workbook look almost the same to search. The rule that gives the numbers meaning is often in a separate document, such as a policy.
Tabular search therefore splits the work. Retrieval only has to return one passage from the right table file, and code then reads the whole table. Because retrieval still has to find that file first, naming the file in your question helps.
Table 1 shows how plain retrieval and tabular search each handle the finance team’s question, “Which departments must write variance commentary?”
| Compared | Retrieve only | Agentic retrieval with tabular search | 
| What you get back | Passages from the policy, memo, business review, and workbook, but no complete answer | An answer naming Sales, Engineering, and Operations, with each department’s variance against its revised budget | 
| Revised variance percentages | Not available. No file stores them, so no passage can contain them | Calculated from every department row in the final workbook | 
| Sources | Each passage links to its own file, but none of them contains the answer | Citations to the finance policy and the close memo. The trace names the workbook the code read | 
Table 1: The same question with plain retrieval and with tabular search.
How tabular search works in agentic retrieval
In agentic retrieval, an agent uses retrieval to decide which documents matter and then writes the answer. Tabular search is part of that flow, so there’s nothing to turn on.
When a question needs the data in a table, the request moves through these stages:
- Retrieve – Passages come back, including passages from a table file.
- Plan – The agent uses the question and table structure to determine whether to run code over one or more retrieved tables.
- Stage – Tabular search copies the original file into an isolated sandbox with no network access.
- Compute – Model-written code runs over the whole table or sheet.
- Return – The agent gets back only what the code prints, such as totals or matching rows.
- Answer – The agent answers from the results and the passages, with citations.
Tabular search starts when retrieved passages come from a CSV, XLSX, or XLS file and the question needs a calculation across rows or a lookup of specific values.
Knowledge bases, connectors, and APIs
An AgenticRetrieveStream request can search one knowledge base or several. The Retrieve API keeps returning passages and doesn’t run code.
Tabular search works the same way whichever connector brings the files into the knowledge base, including Amazon S3, Microsoft SharePoint, Atlassian Confluence, and others.
Scope and trade-offs
Tabular search is built for questions that need calculations or lookups over the table files it retrieves. Running code adds at least one more agent turn, so answers that use table data take longer than text-only answers. Governed metrics, recurring dashboards, warehouse-scale joins, and reporting controls still belong in your business intelligence (BI) tools. Tabular search works on table files stored next to your documents, and you don’t define a schema.
Solution overview
In this solution, an Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base stores your CSV and Excel files together with related documents, such as PDF and Word files. Your application sends every question through agentic retrieval. When a question needs table data, the answer combines calculations over your tables with facts from your documents. It cites the passages it used, and the trace names the table files the code read.
In Figure 1, an Amazon S3 data source syncs these files into the knowledge base, which keeps embeddings, text, metadata, and the original files. When your application sends a question with AgenticRetrieveStream, agentic retrieval plans the work and retrieves passages from the knowledge base. If the question needs data from a table file, it sends the files to read to an isolated sandbox with no network access. There, model-written code runs over the original file and returns printed results. The answer, with citations and trace events, streams back to your application.
The worked example uses fictitious AnyCompany Retail finance files:
- Final P&L workbook (anycompany-pnl-fy2026.xlsx). It has Notes, Actuals, Budget, and Summary sheets, with one row per month, cost center, and account in the Actuals and Budget sheets.
- Draft workbook. A preliminary copy with different Q3 numbers.
- Finance variance policy (PDF). Defines controllable spend and approved budget, and sets review thresholds.
- Q3 close memo (Word). Lists approved and rejected budget revisions.
- Business review (Markdown). Explains the main variances.
These files are in the tabular-search folder of the sample-managed-knowledge-base-patterns GitHub repository. The folder also has an AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) app that deploys the resources in this post, and Python scripts that ask these questions.
Prerequisites
You need the following:
- Permissions to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, S3 buckets, and Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases.
- For the identity that calls AgenticRetrieveStream, the permissions for agentic retrieval, including bedrock:GetDocumentContent. The agent reads the original table file with the caller’s credentials.
- Amazon Bedrock in an AWS Region where tabular search is available. For Region availability, see Supported AWS Regions.
- Your own CSV, XLSX, or XLS files and related documents.
- To follow the walkthrough: Python 3.10 or later with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) version 1.43.123 or later. You can also ask questions from the knowledge base test window in the Amazon Bedrock console or with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).
The calling identity needs this policy, from the agentic retrieval documentation:
For costs, see Amazon Bedrock pricing.
Upload your files to Amazon S3
Put the table files and related documents under one prefix.
- Open the Amazon S3 console and choose Create bucket.
- Enter a globally unique bucket name (this post uses amzn-s3-demo-bucket), keep Block all public access selected, and choose Create bucket.
- Choose the bucket, choose Create folder, and enter finance.
- Open the finance folder and choose Upload.
- Choose Add files, select your table files and documents, and choose Upload.
Create the knowledge base and data source
The knowledge base needs an IAM role that Amazon Bedrock can assume. This trust policy allows only the bedrock.amazonaws.com service principal, and only for knowledge bases in your account.
Next, set up the remaining resources:
- Create a role named kb-finance-role with the trust policy.
- Attach an inline policy that allows s3:ListBucket on the bucket and s3:GetObject on its objects.
- Create a knowledge base of type MANAGED with the managed embedding model.
- Create a MANAGED_KNOWLEDGE_BASE_CONNECTOR data source for the bucket, limited to the finance/ prefix.
- Set maxFileSizeInMegaBytes above your largest file.
The inline policy for step 2 allows reads on this bucket only:
This script runs steps 3 to 5 and prints the IDs:
Sync the data source and check file types
Tabular search can start only if the knowledge base assigns the right file type, so check the file type after the first sync.
- Start an ingestion job for the data source.
- Poll the job until its status is COMPLETE.
- Review the job statistics for failed documents.
- Run a Retrieve call with your question.
- Confirm that table passages show _file_type as CSV (for CSV files) or MS_EXCEL (for XLSX and XLS files).
The first script runs steps 1 to 3:
The second script runs steps 4 and 5 so you can check the table file type before asking the question with agentic retrieval. With your own files, ask a question that pairs a rule in one of your documents with a calculation over your tables, and name both.
Ask a question across tables and documents
Send the same question through AgenticRetrieveStream. The script prints the answer, each CodeExecution status, and the files the code read.
For these files, the answer combines two workbook tables with two documents:
- From the documents. The finance policy defines controllable spend as the Contractors, Travel, Software, and Marketing Programs accounts, which leaves out salaries and facilities. The business review explains the main variances.
- From the tables. The code uses every row in the Actuals and Budget sheets, filters both to fiscal Q2 and the four accounts, and then compares cost centers.
- Answer. CC-3010 (Platform) is over by 124,559.90 US dollars, with actual spending of 394,859.90 against a budget of 270,300.00. The business review attributes the variance to contractors brought in for a data platform migration. Counting every operating expense account instead gives 133,434.05.
Read the trace
Trace events arrive in this order:
- Planning. A Planning event with status SUCCEEDED includes a codeExecution action that names the documents the code will read.
- The code step. A CodeExecution event with status IN_PROGRESS (“Running code over 1 document(s)”), then one with status SUCCEEDED. The SUCCEEDED message names each file the code read and its size.
- The answer. A second planning round and the response text precede a final result event that includes the citations. Citations point to the passages the answer used, so a table file the code read isn’t always among them.
In this example, the Planning event names only the final workbook, because the policy and the business review arrive as retrieved passages.
On longer calls, the stream repeats the IN_PROGRESS event every 10 seconds, so a read timeout doesn’t fire. A code step that can’t finish reports FAILED, and the agent usually retries or falls back.
Tabular search runs as part of response generation, which is on by default, so the script leaves generateResponse unset. If you set generateResponse to false, the agent returns retrieval results without running code. For details, see agentic retrieval.
Try more questions
Each of the following questions also pairs a document with the workbook.
Apply memo revisions to quarterly totals
This question needs a budget that exists only after the memo’s revisions:
The answer uses the revisions from the memo and the Q3 actuals and original budget from the workbook. Spending came in 49,572.40 US dollars under the revised budget, so the answer is yes, even though the same spending is over the original budget. Plain Retrieve returns memo and workbook passages, but none of them contains these figures.
Apply a policy threshold after budget revisions
Here is the full version of the finance team’s question from the introduction. It needs the policy’s threshold, the memo’s revisions, and the workbook:
The policy requires commentary when the variance exceeds 5 percent of the approved budget, which includes approved revisions, and the memo approves a Marketing increase and an Engineering cut. The answer is Sales (-6.50 percent), Engineering (+5.79 percent), and Operations (+6.20 percent). Engineering crosses the threshold only because the approved cut lowers its budget.
Continue the conversation
Tabular search also works in multi-turn conversations. Send earlier turns in messages, and it runs in whichever turn needs the table. This first question asks for a calculation from the workbook:
For the follow-up, send the first question, its answer ("role": "assistant"), and the new question in messages:
The variance is 12.40 percent over budget, so it needs written commentary. Because it exceeds 10 percent, the policy also requires review by the CFO, Nikki Wolf. Here, the first turn usually runs code over the workbook, and the second answers the policy question from the history.
For longer sessions, you can keep conversation history in an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory resource by setting memoryConfiguration on the request, instead of resending earlier turns. For details, see agentic retrieval.
Best practices for questions over tables
Word your questions with care, because retrieval picks which table the code reads. Focused questions that name their sources help retrieval pick the right table.
- Pair one rule with one table. Name the document that holds the rule, such as “as revised in the Q3 close memo.”
- Name the file when there is more than one version. For example, “use the final FY2026 P&L workbook, anycompany-pnl-fy2026.xlsx.”
- Ask for the calculation when you want one. If a summary sheet holds a figure, the agent can answer from it. Say “Calculate each department’s variance from the Actuals and Budget sheets” to compute from detail rows.
- Ask focused questions. Build larger analyses over several turns.
A few data and application choices help as well:
- Keep tables in CSV, XLSX, or XLS files. Export tables from PDF or Word documents first.
- Set the file size filter above your largest table. Files larger than maxFileSizeInMegaBytes aren’t ingested, so the code can’t read them.
- Keep Excel sheets within 200 MB. As of this writing, tabular search runs code over CSV files up to 500 MB, the ingestion limit, but over Excel sheets only up to 200 MB. You can still ingest larger Excel files, so check sheet sizes before you rely on full-table calculations.
- Use tabular search for analysis. Running code adds an agent turn, so keep plain Retrieve for quick lookups in text.
- Scope files with metadata filters. A filter under retrievalOverrides, for example on _document_title, controls which files the code can read.
- Audit with the trace. The generated code isn’t returned, by design, because it can echo cell values. The trace shows which files the code read.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete these resources in order:
- In the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Knowledge Bases, then choose finance-kb.
- Select the finance-s3 data source and choose Delete.
- Delete the finance-kb knowledge base.
- In the Amazon S3 console, select the bucket, choose Empty, and then choose Delete, unless other workloads use it.
- In the IAM console, choose Roles, select kb-finance-role, and choose Delete.
If you deployed with the AWS CDK app from the repository, run npx cdk destroy from its infra folder instead of these steps. It deletes everything the stack created.
Conclusion
The finance team members need to know “Which departments must write variance commentary?” With tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can answer that question with one agentic retrieval request that uses the workbook, the policy, and the memo together.
In this post, you learned how tabular search answers questions that need both table data and facts from documents, and when another tool is a better fit. You also built a knowledge base with sample finance files and used the trace to see which file the code read.
To get started, see Build a managed knowledge base and agentic retrieval in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide, and AgenticRetrieveStream in the Amazon Bedrock API Reference. To learn more, read Build enterprise search for agents with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base on the AWS Artificial Intelligence Blog.

articles.title: Ni Model 3 ni Semi : Tesla va produire son Cybercab dans la gigafactory de Berlin
articles.text:
L’agrandissement de la Gigafactory de Grünheide, la seule usine de Tesla en Europe, est dans les tuyaux depuis plusieurs années. Le constructeur l’avait d’ailleurs mis en pause pendant la chute de ses ventes. Une question restait sans réponse : produire quoi de plus, alors que l’usine ne fabrique que le Model Y ?
Tesla a répondu ce lundi 16 novembre, dans une annonce relayée par Reuters : 3 milliards d’euros pour un nouveau bâtiment qui pourra produire jusqu’à un million de Cybercab. Or ce robotaxi sans volant ni pédales, que Tesla s’apprête à livrer à ses premiers clients américains, n’a pas encore un avenir clair en Europe. Le constructeur américain met-il une nouvelle fois la charrue avant les bœufs ?
Un déblocage du projet
L’enveloppe couvre aussi des bâtiments annexes et une nouvelle station de traitement des eaux usées, a précisé Tesla à l’agence dpa (dépêche reprise par Handelsblatt). Tesla veut déposer sa demande de permis avant la fin de l’année, sur la base d’un dossier de 2023.
Les travaux doivent commencer au premier semestre 2027, pour une production en 2029. Ouverte en mars 2022, l’usine employait 12 600 personnes en octobre, selon Tesla. L’effectif était entre-temps tombé sous les 11 000. Un million de Cybercab par an représente presque trois fois l’objectif actuel du site pour le Model Y, fixé à 7 500 voitures par semaine, soit environ 375 000 par an.
Un million de robotaxis ? Mais pas encore d’autorisation en Europe
En Europe, l’aide à la conduite avancée de Tesla progresse pays par pays. Son FSD (Full Self-Driving), rebaptisé Tesla Assisted Driving sur le continent, est autorisé dans onze pays de l’Union. La Finlande est la dernière arrivée, le 11 novembre.
Un vote sur une homologation dans toute l’Union est attendu en décembre au plus tôt (un rejet remettrait en cause les autorisations nationales déjà accordées), et l’Allemagne plaide pour aller vite. Pourtant, ce système reste une aide à la conduite : le conducteur surveille la route et reste responsable. Le Cybercab, lui, n’a ni volant ni pédales, et relève donc d’une autre réglementation, bien plus restrictive.
Or, pour les véhicules entièrement automatisés, le droit européen ne prévoit qu’un régime de petite série, limité à des usages précis. Tesla devra donc exporter presque toute la production de Grünheide, ou compter sur un changement des règles d’ici 2029 : un sacré pari.
Tesla préfère le Cybercab à la Model 3 et au Semi
Tesla aurait pourtant pu loger dans ce bâtiment des véhicules qui se vendent déjà. Les Model 3 vendues en Europe sont produites à Shanghai, et on pouvait espérer une ligne allemande pour la berline. Une Model 3 assemblée en Allemagne aurait aussi pu viser les aides publiques que la Commission veut réserver aux voitures électriques à 70 % de contenu européen, dans son projet d’Industrial Accelerator Act présenté en mars.
Quant au Semi, le camion électrique dont Tesla a présenté la version européenne en septembre, il est assemblé dans le Nevada alors qu’il doit arriver chez les transporteurs européens en 2027.
Tesla préfère reprendre en Allemagne le pari qu’il fait au Texas, où la production du Cybercab a démarré en avril. Lors de la présentation des résultats du premier trimestre, en avril, Elon Musk, CEO de Tesla, prévenait déjà que la production du Cybercab serait « très lente » au départ, avant d’accélérer en fin d’année.
Le calendrier de Grünheide est fixé : demande de permis d’ici fin 2026, travaux au premier semestre 2027, premiers Cybercab allemands en 2029. Le premier signal tombera en décembre au plus tôt, avec le vote européen sur Tesla Assisted Driving, qui ne concerne qu’une aide à la conduite. Pour un véhicule sans volant comme le Cybercab, l’avenir est toujours incertain.
