articles.title: Accelerate Molecular Dynamics Simulations with Accurate, Flexible Primitives Using NVIDIA cuPotential | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Molecular dynamics (MD) is an indispensable tool across physics, chemistry, biology, and materials science. Owing to its arithmetic structure, particularly the parallel evaluation of many atom-pair interactions, MD codes were among the first to be ported to run on GPUs. However, as GPUs evolve, optimizing kernels and ensuring compatibility across heterogeneous hardware have become more difficult than ever for many MD engine developers.
Specifically, in simulations run with classical forcefields, the evaluation of long-range interactions under periodic boundary conditions, such as electrostatics and dispersion, remains the major computational and engineering bottleneck.
NVIDIA cuPotential, a focused library designed for molecular dynamics, addresses these challenges. By offering modular primitives with a C API, cuPotential empowers developers and users to select specific components from multiple layers of the stack to accelerate workloads (Figure 1).
cuPotential provides direct space and reciprocal space utilities such as cutoff-based interaction evaluators and charge spreading functions. This release also provides a plugin specifically for OpenMM given its popularity in the developer ecosystem as an example. The goal is seamless drop-in replacements with minimal changes to the user’s code.
This post explains how to integrate the plugin into OpenMM, evaluate accuracy against high-accuracy references, and measure simulation throughput. It also introduces two examples for developers who need control over parameter representation and updates. Finally, it briefly discusses the science and error analysis behind the new splitting and spreading methods. This rigorous attention to accuracy and energy drift in simulation allows developers to integrate and benefit from the acceleration provided by cuPotential kernels without affecting simulation results.
Building the cuPotential runtime and plugin for OpenMM
cuPotential is composed of two parts: a core methods library and a plugin for OpenMM that consumes the primitives that can be built directly in a conda environment on Linux. The following tutorial walks through building the runtime and plugin, installing the Python wheel, and running the supplied molecular dynamics sample.
Prerequisites
- Linux x86-64 with a supported NVIDIA GPU
- An installed NVIDIA driver compatible with CUDA 13.1
- Conda or Micromamba installed and initialized for your shell
- A clone of the cuPotential repository from the NVIDIA/cuPotential GitHub repo
The environment supplies the CUDA toolkit and compilers; a separate system-wide CUDA toolkit installation is not required. The GPU driver must already be installed on the host.
Step 1: Create and activate the environment
Using Conda, create and activate the environment:
conda create -y -n cupotential-build -c conda-forge \
  python=3.12 openmm=8.4.0 \
  cuda-version=13.1 cuda-toolkit=13.1 \
  cmake make gcc_linux-64=13 gxx_linux-64=13 \
  swig pip setuptools wheel numpy
conda activate cupotential-build
Alternatively, you can use Micromamba:
micromamba create -y -n cupotential-build -c conda-forge \
  python=3.12 openmm=8.4.0 \
  cuda-version=13.1 cuda-toolkit=13.1 \
  cmake make gcc_linux-64=13 gxx_linux-64=13 \
  swig pip setuptools wheel numpy
micromamba activate cupotential-build
Next, install the Python build dependencies:
python -m pip install "pybind11>=2.12" nvidia-mathdx
The cuda-toolkit package supplies the CUDA compiler and development tools. Setting cuda-version alone does not install those tools.
Step 2: Point the build helper to the active environment
In plugins/openmm/run_build, replace:
OPENMM=/opt/openmm
with:
OPENMM="${CONDA_PREFIX:?Activate the conda environment first}"
Both Conda and Micromamba set CONDA_PREFIX when an environment is activated.
Step 3: Build and install
Use the cuPotential repository root, with the environment active:
export CUDACXX="$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/nvcc"
export CUDAHOSTCXX="$CXX"
./plugins/openmm/run_build
python -m pip wheel \
  --no-deps --no-build-isolation \
  --wheel-dir plugins/openmm/dist \
  ./plugins/openmm
python -m pip install plugins/openmm/dist/*.whl
The build helper compiles the cuPotential runtime if it’s not already present, then builds the OpenMM plugin. The final installation command also installs the wheel’s declared pip CUDA dependencies.
Step 4: Verify the installation
Run the supplied sample directly:
cd plugins/openmm/samples
./solvated_systems/run
The sample evaluates DHFR (Dihydrofolate reductase), BACE (Beta-secretase 1), and ApoA1 (Apolipoprotein A1), under both NVT and NPT conditions. The DHFR and ApoA1 systems are from the OpenMM benchmark suite, while BACE is from the OpenFE benchmark set. A successful run ends with:
PASS
The samples use AMBER14/TIP3P force field, a 0.9 nm nonbonded interaction cutoff length, a 5 x 10⁻⁴ electrostatic accuracy target, and mixed precision. Its 4 fs timestep is paired with constrained hydrogen bonds, rigid water, and hydrogen mass repartitioning to 1.5 amu.
These runs measure accuracy and performance separately. For electrostatics, it compares both implementations with a double-precision reference, using twice the cutoff length for the short range part and twice the mesh resolution in each dimension for the long range part, with the Ewald splitting parameter held fixed. For truncated Lennard-Jones interactions, it uses a double-precision reference at the same cutoff, preserving the interaction model being tested.
For throughput, each implementation runs 500 warm-up steps followed by 3,000 timed steps. The cuPotential arm uses its own force and integrator, plus its barostat for NPT. The reported speedup therefore describes that integrated configuration.
Using cuPotential with OpenMM
The cuPotential OpenMM plugin provides replacements for the OpenMM nonbonded force, Langevin integrator, and Monte Carlo barostat. In your production MD simulations, the key steps to integrate cuPotential into OpenMM are:
- Replace the system’s OpenMM nonbonded force before creating the simulation context
- Use integrator and optionally barostat from cuPotential
import openmm as mm
import openmm.unit as unit
import nv_openmm_plugin as nv
temperature = 300 * unit.kelvin      # Temperature, 300 K
timestep = 0.004 * unit.picoseconds  # Timestep, 4 fs
friction_coeff = 1.0 / unit.picoseconds   # Friction coefficient in Langevin thermostat
pressure = 1.0 * unit.bar            # Pressure if using barostat for NPT
# Prepare the system using OpenMM. Replace with your system.
pdb = app.PDBFile("solvated.pdb")
forcefield = app.ForceField("amber14-all.xml", "amber14/tip3p.xml")
system = forcefield.createSystem(
    pdb.topology,
    nonbondedMethod=app.PME,
    nonbondedCutoff=0.9 * unit.nanometers,
    ewaldErrorTolerance=5e-4,
    constraints=app.HBonds,
    rigidWater=True,
    hydrogenMass=1.5 * unit.amu,
)
# replace OpenMM NonbondedForce instance with the plugin's NonbondedForce
for index, force in enumerate(system.getForces()):
    if isinstance(force, mm.NonbondedForce):
        system.addForce(nv.NonbondedForce(force))
        system.removeForce(index)
        break
# The cuPotential integrator handles center-of-mass motion removal.
for index, force in enumerate(system.getForces()):
    if isinstance(force, mm.CMMotionRemover):
        system.removeForce(index)
        break
integrator = nv.LangevinMiddleIntegrator(
    temperature,
    friction_coeff,
    timestep,
)
# Optionally, add cuPotential barostat for NPT simulations
system.addForce(nv.MonteCarloBarostat(
    pressure,           # Pressure
    temperature,        # Match the integrator temperature.
    frequency=25,       # Attempt a volume change every 25 steps.
))
# Create the simulation after configuring all forces.
simulation = app.Simulation(
    pdb.topology,
    system,
    integrator,
    mm.Platform.getPlatformByName("CUDA"),
    {"Precision": "mixed"},
)
simulation.context.setPositions(pdb.positions)
simulation.minimizeEnergy() # OpenMM 8.4 only
simulation.context.setVelocitiesToTemperature(temperature)
simulation.step(1000)
This excerpt shows that the integration changes. The complete sample includes system construction, CUDA context creation, accuracy checks, and timing. For NPT simulations, it also uses nv.MonteCarloBarostat.
The current plugin targets solvated, approximately uniform-density systems in rectangular periodic boxes, which is typical in biomolecular simulations. It accepts PME source forces; LJPME, triclinic boxes, and OpenMM particle or exception parameter offsets are not supported. Consult the plugin README before adapting an existing simulation.
Benchmarking cuPotential in OpenMM
When cuPotential is integrated into OpenMM using the built-in plugin, performance is significantly enhanced across a wide range of GPU architectures for system sizes in the range of 24,000 to 400,000 atoms, namely DHFR, TYK2 (Tyrosine Kinase 2 from OpenFE benchmarks), BACE, ApoA1, Water with 100,000 atoms, and cellulose.
Figure 2 shows a collection of speedup measures under the NPT condition for a range of GPUs. Newer generation GPUs, including NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, achieve over 3x end-to-end speedups in selected benchmarks. Other tested GPUs (NVIDIA B200, H100, A100, L40S, A10, L4 and T4) also benefit, with gains often around 2x or more. Note that the performance numbers are measured with standard, non-alchemical systems.
Improving accuracy and efficiency through new splitting and spreading methods
Ewald splitting, specifically the Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) variant, has been the de facto method for the past 30 years in the simulation field. Recently, new techniques such as the u-series, midtown splines and prolates have been proposed but not widely adopted by the simulation community given their high technical requirement and sophistication. The NVIDIA team has been collaborating with D. E. Shaw Research and the Flatiron Institute to develop a new set of C2 continuous splitting and spreading functions that are broadly applicable, highly accurate, and performant.
Figure 3 shows detailed error benchmark analyses across various grid resolutions and cutoff distances, highlighting the accuracy profile of the cuPotential approach relative to Ewald and u-series. These analyses are done with the 100K-atom water system under NPT conditions, with statistics computed over 25 frames. Ewald alpha-parameters were tuned to asymptotically reach the desired force tolerance.
Our team’s approach enables reducing the real-space cutoff and/or the reciprocal space grid-size, with no loss in accuracy (compared to the near-exact regime), defined as the L2 Force RMSE at default settings specified by OpenMM. We note up-front that the u-series was not optimized for the force error, but rather the ensemble error, and we simply chose the parameters to attain the desired force error in order to be consistent with OpenMM.
Beyond electrostatics, splitting and spreading kernels for lattice dispersion interactions through cuPotential enables highly nonpolar and membrane systems to be modelled more accurately. Conventional homogeneous analytical corrections can lead to severe simulation artifacts.
cuPotential is able to significantly improve the accuracy in the dispersion energy by several thousand fold compared to conventional methods, while maintaining comparable force errors at significantly reduced computational cost (Figure 4). The u-series is omitted because the original paper from DESRES only covered electrostatics. In practice, reducing cutoff to 6A still poses enormous challenges due to complexities introduced by NBFix as well as combining rules.
Accuracy and energy drift analysis
For long-time scale simulations, measuring energy drift is an important validation step to ensure that leakage is minimized. Although there are many potential sources of error, in addition to splitting, it’s important that the library is not the dominant cause of the drift. Compared to standard OpenMM with a smooth switching function for truncated Lennard-Jones interactions, it’s possible to measure the effect of cutoff truncation attributed to the residual in direct space under kernel splitting.
cuPotential significantly reduces drift by several hundred fold compared to default settings in PME, and far exceeds the typical requirements of the biomolecular simulation community. Figure 5 shows energy drift over the course of 10 ns for a 10,000-molecule rigid water system, with a 9 Å cutoff for cuPotential and standard OpenMM, while a 20 Å cutoff is used for converged PME. We used 2 fs timesteps and 300 K simulation temperature. For drift estimation, energy drift ΔE = E(t) – E(20ps) normalized over 60,000 degrees of freedom.
Get started accelerating MD simulations with cuPotential
NVIDIA cuPotential accelerates molecular dynamics simulations while offering modular flexibility and high numerical accuracy. To get started and learn more, visit the NVIDIA/cuPotential GitHub repo, where you’ll find additional examples, benchmarks, and code to integrate these accelerated primitives in your own MD simulations.
Acknowledgments
We thank our collaborators at D. E. Shaw Research and the Flatiron Institute’s Center for Computational Mathematics for their scientific and mathematical contributions, discussions, and guidance on the error analysis behind the new splitting and spreading methods.

articles.title: Black Friday mit KI: Findet ChatGPT wirklich die besten Schnäppchen?
articles.text:
Black Friday mit KI: Findet ChatGPT wirklich die besten Schnäppchen?
Wer in den letzten Jahren rund um den Black Friday auf Schnäppchenfang war, hat vor allem die gängigen Preisvergleichsportale wie Idealo, Günstiger und Geizhals bemüht, vielleicht noch mit einigen Preisrecherche-Tools wie Camelcamelcamel oder Keepa Preisalarme gesetzt und bestenfalls noch die Tipps in Communitys wie Mydealz verfolgt. In diesem Jahr dürfte sich das ändern. Denn immer mehr Nutzer:innen haben erkannt, dass künstliche Intelligenz nicht nur gut darin ist, das geeignete Produkt in der Beratung zu ermitteln, sondern auch nach den passenden Preisen und Angeboten fahnden kann.
Laut einer repräsentativen Umfrage des Preisvergleichsportals Idealo von Oktober 2026 sucht schon heute jede:r fünfte Verbraucher:in mithilfe von KI-Tools oder -Assistenten nach Sonderangeboten. Auch Yougov hat im Oktober die Vorlieben der deutschen Käufer:innen untersucht: Demnach wird in diesem Jahr jede:r Zweite KI für die diesjährige Angebotssuche im Vorweihnachtsgeschäft einsetzen und immerhin 42 Prozent der Nutzer:innen wollen die KI gezielt für die Recherche nach dem besten Preis verwenden.
Doch sind ChatGPT, Gemini und Co. dafür wirklich schon reif und ist das Vertrauen in die Treffsicherheit der LLMs gerechtfertigt? Unserer Erfahrung nach ist insbesondere ChatGPT schon recht gut darin, Kaufinteressent:innen im Vorfeld zu beraten, etwa „einen Saugroboter, der gut im Beseitigen von Tierhaaren ist, unter 400 Euro kostet und nicht allzu laut ist“ zu finden. Dazu wählt die KI anhand hinterlegter Eigenschaften und Daten etwas Passendes aus, berücksichtigt (mehr oder minder zuverlässige) Testergebnisse und Kundenrezensionen und zeigt die passenden Angebote einiger Händler. Hier hatten wir Anfang des Jahres in einem Selbstversuch noch einige Schwächen aufgedeckt, die inzwischen weitgehend verschwunden sind.
Dass das so ist, dafür ist vor allem das Bewusstsein der Händler und Hersteller verantwortlich. Denn – nicht nur wir predigen es regelmäßig – die Auffindbarkeit und Validität der hinterlegten Daten sorgt dafür, dass zunächst die passenden Produkte gefunden und im nächsten Schritt auch die Angebote eines bestimmten Händlers aufgelistet werden.
Nicht nur ChatGPT kann Preisrecherche vernünftig abbilden
Besonderes Augenmerk liegt hier offenbar für viele Anbieter und Service-Betreiber auf ChatGPT. Wer etwa in der Vergangenheit auf Idealo für die Preisrecherche gesetzt hat, kann seit einigen Monaten das passende Plugin mit dem OpenAI-LLM verbinden. Der eigentliche Einkauf erfolgt dann allerdings weiterhin wie gewohnt über die Händler. Die Frage, ob man sich bei der Suche also weiterhin auf eine Preissuchmaschine verlässt, ist also eigentlich falsch gestellt – die Zukunft wird auf die Preissuchmaschine innerhalb der KI hinauslaufen.
Für die Preisrecherche kann es sich aber auch lohnen, auf Google Gemini zu setzen, weil hier inzwischen mehr als 60 Millionen Preislistings angebunden sind – Google Shopping sei Dank. Durch den strukturellen Vorteil ist die Google-KI grundsätzlich gut aufgestellt im Hinblick auf Produkteigenschaften und Preisrecherche. Allerdings ist selbst für Nutzer:innen, die hierfür ein geschultes Auge haben, insbesondere in der Mobilansicht nicht immer ganz klar, welche der Angebote gesponsert sind und wie die Empfehlungen zustande kommen.
Auffällig ist auch ein anderes Problem, das auch eine Untersuchung von Shopsavvy bestätigt: Nur bei einem Teil der Preisrecherchen entspricht das gefundene Ergebnis dem von Google Shopping. Die Untersuchung kam immerhin in einem Drittel der Fälle auf Abweichungen (übrigens in beide Richtungen). Auch bei unseren Tests gibt es bei nahezu allen Konstellationen im Rahmen der KI-Preisrecherche noch Fehler zu beklagen – und das unabhängig vom eingesetzten LLM:
Nicht immer sind die Preise wirklich aktuell, was darauf hindeutet, dass hier nicht mit Echtzeitdaten gearbeitet wird. Demnach nutzt die KI unterschiedliche Datenquellen, Aktualisierungsstände und Angebote der Händler.
Defizite bei den Suchergebnissen
Defizite haben die Suchergebnisse der KI allerdings auch noch in der Aufbereitung, die offenbar in den meisten Datenquellen weniger aussagekräftig im Hinblick auf die längerfristige Preisentwicklung ist. Hinzu kommt, dass die Varianten (etwa verschiedene Farben und Größen eines Kleidungsstücks) nicht immer treffsicher ausgewiesen werden. Das war tatsächlich in der Vergangenheit auch schon bei herkömmlichen Preissuchmaschinen ein Problem.
Eine weitere Einschränkung für den Nutzen der KI in diesem Kontext ist die Gefahr, an Fakeshops zu geraten. So hat etwa das auf Markenschutz spezialisierte Unternehmen Podqi bereits in einem Test ermittelt, dass sowohl ChatGPT als auch Gemini und Perplexity teilweise Angebote auf Fakeshop-Seiten empfehlen. Dazu wurden fast 6.800 Antworten der drei KI-Systeme analysiert. In 15 Prozent der Antworten von Perplexity tauchten problematische Websites auf, bei ChatGPT waren es acht Prozent, bei Gemini vier Prozent. Als problematisch wurden dabei sowohl gefälschte Markenshops als auch Anbieter von Produktfälschungen verstanden.
Immerhin in 57 Prozent der Fälle wurden diese ausdrücklich als Einkaufsmöglichkeit empfohlen, in weiteren 34 Prozent wurden sie ohne Warnhinweis erwähnt. Auch wenn die Untersuchung sich explizit auf US-Quellen bezog, sollten Kund:innen bei von der KI empfohlenen Onlineshops vorsichtig sein. Es dürfte nämlich nur eine Frage der Zeit sein, bis auch in Deutschland ähnliche Fälle bekannt werden. Auch wenn die KI-Anbieter hier schnell tätig werden dürften, bleibt also ein Restrisiko.
Als problematisch im Zusammenhang mit den (Pre-)Black-Friday-Rabatten hat sich aber noch etwas anderes erwiesen: In vielen Fällen ließ sich eine KI wie Claude von vermeintlichen Rabatten auf den Listenpreis blenden, während der Straßenpreis schon über längere Zeit deutlich darunter lag. Erst durch gezieltes Nachfragen sah die KI den Fehler ein, fand dann bei einer Preisrecherche zwar den günstigsten Preis, benannte aber einen absolut unbekannten Händler, obwohl mehrere große Shops denselben Preis anboten.
Wie KI Beratung und Preisrecherche kombiniert
Die eigentliche Stärke der KI beim Einkaufen liegt also nicht unbedingt in der reinen Preisrecherche, sondern (noch) eher in der vorgelagerten Beratungsleistung. Hilfreich war die KI – vor allem in Form von ChatGPT – übrigens bei einigen unserer Recherchen, bei denen Vorjahresmodelle angeboten wurden, wenn diese im Laufe des Dialogs als ausreichend angesehen wurden. Das funktionierte etwa bei einem Internetproblem mit einem bestimmten Kabelmodem recht souverän.
Allerdings war noch nicht in allen Fällen die Transparenz der Angebote gegeben. Zum einen wurde nicht in jedem Fall klar, ob ein Suchergebnis gesponsert war oder es andere Anreize gab, zum anderen wurden in einigen Fällen auch andere Produktvarianten, die sich im Detail unterschieden, mit aufgeführt. Das ist etwa bei einem Fernseher, der bestimmte Features nicht hat, ärgerlich, weil man es erst auf der jeweiligen Website des Händlers erkennt – wenn überhaupt.
Widersprüchliches gab’s auch im Hinblick auf kompliziertere Preise, wie sie im Mobilfunkmarkt üblich sind: So wurden uns bei der Recherche auch die Kaufpreise von Vertragshandys angezeigt, da diese mit subventioniertem Vertrag niedriger liegen als der Kaufpreis für das Gerät.
Sinnvoll ist es daher, die KI bestimmte Informationen, die einem wenig plausibel vorkommen, noch einmal verifizieren zu lassen und dabei sowohl auf eine Websuche zu setzen als auch die jeweilige Uhrzeit und Quelle einzufordern. In einzelnen Fällen hat die KI auch Preisverläufe einfach geschätzt, sodass einzelne Ausreißer nicht mit abgebildet wurden – das sollte man ihr deshalb generell untersagen.
Blind vertrauen sollte man der KI aber vor allem auch nicht bei den Preisangaben und bei den gefundenen Händlern. Denn in einigen Fällen wurden Versandkosten unterschlagen oder das Produkt war erst deutlich verzögert lieferbar. Und einige der recherchierten Shops verwiesen auf wenig vertrauenswürdige Händler.
)) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Cómo duplicar la pantalla del celular en un Smart TV sin apps y en segundos
articles.text:
Visualizar fotos, reproducir una película almacenada en la galería o mostrar una presentación en una pantalla más grande puede hacerse sin cables, memorias USB ni transferencias de archivos.
Los teléfonos Android y los iPhone cuentan con funciones inalámbricas integradas para duplicar la pantalla en un Smart TV compatible. La herramienta cambia de nombre según el fabricante, aunque el principio es el mismo: el celular y el televisor deben compartir una red WiFi.
En Android puede aparecer como Google Cast, Miracast, Smart View, Emitir, Enviar o Pantalla inalámbrica. En los teléfonos de Apple, se llama AirPlay.
Qué se necesita para duplicar la pantalla del celular en el TV
El requisito principal es que ambos dispositivos estén conectados a la misma red WiFi. Si el teléfono utiliza una red distinta de la que tiene configurada el Smart TV, no podrá detectar la TV ni enviar la imagen. Hace falta encender el televisor y comprobar que sus opciones de conexión inalámbrica estén activadas.
Asimismo, la estabilidad de la red influye en el resultado. Una conexión de 5 GHz puede reducir las demoras al reproducir videos o compartir imágenes de alta resolución.
Cuando hay muchos dispositivos conectados al mismo WiFi, la transmisión puede sufrir cortes, pérdida de fluidez o un retraso entre lo que ocurre en el teléfono y lo que aparece en el TV.
Cómo duplicar la pantalla de un celular Android en un televisor
En la mayoría de los modelos Android, el proceso comienza en el panel de ajustes rápidos. Para abrirlo, hay que deslizar el dedo desde la parte superior de la pantalla hacia abajo. Algunos modelos requieren repetir ese movimiento para mostrar todos los accesos disponibles.
Luego se debe buscar la función destinada a compartir la pantalla. Puede llamarse Emitir, Enviar, Transmitir, Pantalla inalámbrica o Smart View. Al tocar esa opción, el celular buscará los dispositivos compatibles conectados a la red y mostrará el nombre del televisor entre las alternativas disponibles.
Una vez identificado el televisor, solo hay que tocar su nombre para iniciar el vínculo. En la primera conexión, el Smart TV puede mostrar un aviso para autorizar el acceso desde el celular. La solicitud debe aceptarse desde el control remoto o desde la pantalla del televisor.
Tras esa confirmación, la imagen del teléfono se verá en el televisor en tiempo real. El sistema permite mostrar fotografías, videos, documentos, presentaciones y páginas web. Así, el contenido almacenado en el celular llega a una pantalla más grande sin utilizar un cable HDMI ni copiar los archivos a otro dispositivo.
Cuál opción nativa tiene iPhone para duplicar pantalla
Los usuarios de iPhone disponen de AirPlay, la tecnología de Apple para reproducir contenido o reflejar la pantalla de forma inalámbrica. El sistema funciona de manera nativa con Apple TV y está disponible en varios modelos recientes de televisores inteligentes compatibles con esa tecnología.
Para iniciar la conexión, se debe abrir el Centro de Control. En los modelos más recientes, se accede al deslizar el dedo hacia abajo desde la esquina superior derecha. Allí aparece el botón “Duplicar pantalla”, identificado con el ícono de dos rectángulos superpuestos. Al pulsarlo, el teléfono mostrará los televisores disponibles en la red.
Después de seleccionar el nombre del Smart TV, el dispositivo puede solicitar un código de AirPlay que aparecerá en la pantalla del televisor. Ese número debe ingresarse en el iPhone para completar la conexión. Desde ese momento, fotos, videos, aplicaciones y documentos podrán visualizarse en el TV sin instalar aplicaciones adicionales.
Qué alternativa existe si el celular no muestra una función de duplicación
Algunos celulares no incluyen un acceso visible para duplicar la pantalla o presentan una interfaz con otro nombre. En esos casos, los dispositivos compatibles con Google Cast pueden usar la aplicación Google Home como una vía alternativa para detectar un televisor o un dispositivo de transmisión dentro de la red doméstica.
Después de elegir el dispositivo, hay que buscar la opción para enviar la pantalla del teléfono. Si el Smart TV no aparece, hay que revisar que ambos aparatos estén conectados al mismo WiFi y que las funciones de conexión inalámbrica permanezcan habilitadas. Puede ayudar apagar y encender el WiFi del celular antes de repetir la búsqueda.

articles.title: After a cyberattack, what must Nigerian banks disclose?
articles.text:
When a bank suffers a cyberattack, its customers care more about the intrusion’s technical details than about the bank. Is their money safe? Has their personal information been exposed? And what should they do to protect themselves?
In Nigeria, the answers depend partly on what happened and partly on who needs to be informed. Reporting an incident to the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) is not the same as notifying affected customers. Neither automatically requires a public announcement. But when a breach of personal data is likely to create a high risk to individuals, the law requires banks to tell those affected.
The distinction has become increasingly important as financial institutions face attacks that can expose customer information, disrupt services or compromise funds. It also raises a difficult question for regulators: how can banks be compelled to disclose incidents without turning every announcement into a threat to public confidence?
CBN figures show that Nigerian banks and their customers lost ₦134.48 billion ($100.09 million) to fraud between 2020 and 2025. The figures cover financial losses suffered by victims, not necessarily money that disappeared from the banking system, and do not distinguish cyberattacks on bank infrastructure from other forms of fraud. More recent data from the Nigerian Interbank Settlement System shows that payment fraud losses fell to ₦25.85 billion ($19.24 million) in 2025, from ₦52.26 billion ($38.90 million) the previous year.
The figures do not reveal how many cyber incidents occurred or how often customers were left unaware of compromised information. But they point to the stakes in a financial system where trust is essential to everyday transactions.
Regulators aren’t customers
Under the CBN’s 2024 Risk-Based Cybersecurity Framework, deposit money banks and payment service banks must report security incidents to the Director of Banking Supervision within 24 hours. The requirement allows the regulator to assess threats, monitor institutions, and coordinate responses. It is not a blanket instruction to announce every incident publicly.
“Banks are disclosing attacks currently to regulators, and if any bank fails to, they face sanctions from regulators,” said Festus Amede, chairman of the Committee of Chief Information Security Officers of Nigerian Financial Institutions. He did not say whether any banks have been sanctioned before for not disclosing attacks.
But a regulator and a customer need different information. The CBN may need technical details about the cyberattack, the systems affected, and the bank’s response. Customers need to know whether their accounts or personal information are at risk, and what steps they should take.
A bank can therefore report an incident to the CBN without issuing a public statement. Equally, fulfilling that supervisory obligation does not necessarily satisfy a separate duty to notify customers whose personal data has been exposed.
That second obligation comes under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023. Section 40 requires a data controller to notify the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach likely to pose a risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms. Where the breach is likely to create a high risk, affected individuals must also be notified immediately.
The distinction matters. Not every attempted intrusion exposes personal information, and not every data breach carries the same level of risk. The NDPC’s guidance identifies potential fraud, identity theft, and exposure of sensitive personal data as indicators of high risk. The assessment depends on the information involved and the likely consequences, not simply whether an incident is described as a cyberattack.
Disclosure versus panic
For banks, the challenge is deciding how to communicate while an investigation is still under way. Disclosing too little can leave customers exposed. Saying too much, too soon, can create confusion or undermine confidence before the institution has established what happened.
Gbenga Sesan, executive director of Paradigm Initiative, a pan-African organisation focused on digital inclusion and rights, argues that banks should not use the risk of panic as a reason to withhold information. They should first ensure that an incident is contained or being addressed, then explain what happened and what they are doing about it.
“They need to manage the balance between panic and disclosure,” he told TechCabal.
That balance becomes especially important when personal information is involved. A customer whose account balance remains untouched may still face risks if an attacker has obtained a phone number, email address, or other information that could be used for impersonation or phishing.
“The affected individuals need to be notified, with the bank stating which data was compromised and at the same time confirming what actions have been and will be taken,” Sesan said.
The law requires notifications to explain the likely consequences of a breach, the measures taken or proposed to address it, and how affected individuals can obtain further information. A generic assurance that customers’ funds are safe may therefore be inadequate if their personal information has been exposed.
Iyinoluwa Aboyeji, general partner and co-founder of Future Africa, sees a different danger. In a sector where confidence can determine whether customers leave their money in a bank, he worries that public disclosure could trigger withdrawals and deepen the damage caused by a cyberattack.
“Right now there is no upside except a run on the bank,” he said.
Aboyeji argues that banks should put greater emphasis on prevention and recovery, including cyber insurance that can help institutions manage the financial consequences of a cyberattack. He also warns that a system focused too heavily on punishment could discourage banks from reporting incidents.
“Punishment will make it less likely they disclose a cyberattack, not more likely,” he said.
His argument exposes a tension in the debate. Banks need incentives to report attacks promptly, but customers also need protection from institutions that might prefer to preserve their reputations rather than disclose a breach. The answer cannot be to make transparency optional. Nor should every incident, regardless of its nature or consequences, be treated as evidence of institutional failure.
The distinction regulators must make is between a bank that reports an incident, contains the threat and meets its obligations, and one that neglects basic security measures or withholds information it is legally required to provide.
Customers’ information rights
Recent incidents illustrate why the nature of a cyberattack matters. In August 2026, Zenith Bank told customers that attackers had accessed limited contact information, including email addresses and phone numbers. The bank said its core banking systems and digital channels remained secure.
In November 2026, Lendsqr disclosed attempted cyberattacks, but its chief executive, Adedeji Olowe, said the company’s defences held and no funds, customer data or accounts were compromised. Cryptocurrency platform Patricia disclosed a security breach involving Bitcoin and naira assets in 2023. Subsequent reports dated the incident to January 2022 and estimated the losses at about $2 million.
These cases are not interchangeable. An attempted cyberattack, an exposure of customer information, and a successful theft carry different consequences and may trigger different obligations. A bank can experience a serious security incident without customer data being compromised. Conversely, the absence of stolen funds does not mean customers have no reason to be concerned.
For Sesan, the problem extends beyond whether banks send notifications within the required deadlines. Regulators must establish whether institutions are identifying incidents accurately and acting on what they discover. Banks maintain internal security records, he said, which can help supervisors assess whether incidents were detected and reported.
“The notification is only a part of the measures taken to ensure transparency and ensure that action follows,” he said.
He argued that the effectiveness of the rules ultimately depends on enforcement. “The framework is only as strong as its implementation, and the latter is where we lack.”
That leaves regulators with a responsibility that extends beyond receiving reports. They must verify compliance, require corrective action, and make clear when institutions have failed to meet their obligations. Public reporting on the number and nature of incidents, compliance failures, and enforcement measures could improve accountability without exposing sensitive technical details or compromising investigations.
For customers, the practical test is simpler. They need to know whether their money or personal information is at risk, what the bank has done to contain the incident, and what steps they should take. They also need accessible support and updates if the investigation changes what is known about the breach.
The aim should not be to make every cyberattack a public spectacle. It should be to ensure that banks cannot use the fear of panic to avoid telling customers what they need to know. In a financial system built on trust, silence may protect a bank’s reputation in the short term. It can also leave the people who depend on it carrying risks they were never given the chance to manage.

articles.title: Tor Updates DoS Defenses Again as Relay Attacks Continue
articles.text:
The Tor Project has released new security fixes for its core software as a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack continues to strain the volunteer-run relays that make up its network.
Tor 0.4.9.17, announced on November 13, patches several security issues. The project singled out one fix related to how relays’ built-in DoS protections deal with IPv6.
“This release comes in rapid response to the ongoing DDoS attack on the network, which has affected most relay operators. This is not an easy problem to address, as relays across the network are being overwhelmed by a massive flood of client circuits,” Tor developer David Goulet said in the announcement.
According to the project, more defenses are under consideration, and new versions should follow shortly. Anyone running a relay has been urged to update without delay.
The latest version comes less than three weeks after Tor 0.4.9.15, which introduced three DoS protections against what the project described as a “thunderstorm” of directory requests.
Writing to relay operators at the time, Goulet noted that a single relay could be hit with hundreds of circuits per second. He cautioned that relays would remain under heavy load for as long as the attack lasted.
Reports from relay operators suggest the latest update hasn’t ended the disruption. In a forum post on November 14, one operator said two of their relays had lost HSDir status due to attacks before the update, and that another was being targeted when 0.4.9.17 was released and installed.
Roughly ten minutes after that relay was upgraded, the attack took on a new form, according to the operator. Its traffic plunged and it kept becoming unresponsive.
“Relay unresponsiveness ultimately caused loss of HSDIR. Attack ceased immediately on loss of HSDIR,” the operator wrote.
In the operator’s view, 0.4.9.17 does not do enough to shield HSDir relays, and the attacker changes techniques while an attack is underway.
The operator also warned that the attacker could be capable of deanonymizing and tracking onion services. The Tor Project has issued no such warning in its release announcements.
Related: Firefox Vulnerability Allows Tor User Fingerprinting
Related: CryptoBandits Malware Doubles as a Backdoor, Abuses Tor
Related: Tor Exit Relays Hijacked

articles.title: With Qwen4-Max, Alibaba puts the open source jacket back on the hanger
articles.text:
With Qwen4-Max, Alibaba puts the open source jacket back on the hanger
Alibaba has officially unveiled Qwen4-Max, the first model in its next-generation Qwen4 family, with a focus on complex professional tasks and autonomous AI agents.
The Chinese tech titan teased the new Qwen4 family last week, taking to X to promise improvements in coding, reasoning and real-world knowledge, while initially making Qwen4-Max available in preview through several of its products.
Now, the company has formally detailed the model’s capabilities, pitching it as an always-available “AI teammate” capable of tackling everything from software development to scientific research.
However, Alibaba appears to be keeping its most powerful model proprietary, despite the open-weight releases that have helped establish Qwen as a major force in the AI realm.
Under the hood of Qwen4-Max
In a blog post published on Monday, Alibaba revealed that Qwen4-Max is built on a new mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture comprising 2.4 trillion backbone parameters, with 71 billion activated for each token. It also includes another 328 billion parameters dedicated to a technique called “N-gram Embedding,” which helps the model process patterns in text more efficiently.
The model supports images as well as text, and comes with a one-million-token context window, allowing it to process large amounts of information in a single interaction.
Qwen4-Max is available through Alibaba’s QwenCloud platform, with API pricing starting at $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens. It can also be accessed through QwenWork, Qoder and QwenStudio, while Vercel has added Qwen4-Max to its AI Gateway, allowing developers to use the model through coding tools such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.
Alibaba claims the new architecture delivers substantial improvements over its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, particularly when performing complex tasks involving multiple tools and extended periods of autonomous execution.
On Work360, an internal benchmark developed to assess professional tasks across hundreds of specialised fields, Qwen4-Max scored 52.69 compared with 47.74 for Qwen3.8-Max. Alibaba also claims the newer model uses between 24% and 35% fewer tokens on that benchmark, depending on the reasoning effort selected.
The company reports even greater token savings on Terminal-Bench 4.0, a test of AI agents’ ability to carry out tasks in a terminal environment, where token usage fell by nearly half compared with Qwen3.8-Max.
Alibaba says those improvements, combined with lower API prices, reduced the average cost of completing a task in its Work360 evaluation by 62%, from $4.43 to $1.67.
Of course, those are Alibaba’s own results. Independent testing by Artificial Analysis offers another perspective, awarding Qwen4-Max a score of 43 on its Intelligence Index, placing it 38th among 81 models in the comparison. That puts it slightly above the median score of 41 for models in its price category, but lagging leading competitors such as Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 (65), Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon (60) and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra (57).
Artificial Analysis also calculated an average cost of $3.27 per task across its evaluations, while noting that Qwen4-Max generated 127 million output tokens, considerably more than the median of 78.6 million among comparable models.
Alibaba pulls its weight(s)
The proprietary nature of Qwen4-Max is particularly notable given Alibaba’s recent history. When the company introduced Qwen3.8-Max in August, it made an unusual commitment: for the first time, it would release the weights underlying one of its flagship Max models, allowing developers to download and run a version on their own infrastructure.
That marked a departure from Alibaba’s previous approach, with Qwen3.6-Max-Preview and Qwen3.7-Max both remaining proprietary. In hindsight, Qwen3.8-Max looks more like an exception than the beginning of a broader shift towards open weights.
The announcement followed Alibaba’s efforts to demonstrate that its models could compete with leading proprietary systems from the likes of Anthropic. As The New Stack reported at the time, the company had already been making increasingly ambitious performance claims for its Qwen family.
Qwen3.8-Max also arrived with a demonstration of autonomous software development, in which an AI coding agent worked on a project over 16 days, producing hundreds of commits and more than 100 pull requests.
However, the open-weight promise initially attracted scepticism when Alibaba announced the model release before making the files available.
“That is not a technical footnote; that is the API business model wearing an open source jacket for the launch photo.”
In reactions gathered by The New Stack, independent AI consultant Jeff Brokaw questioned the significance of advertising downloadable weights that developers could not yet obtain. He also drew parallels with Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, which had similarly been promoted as an open-weight model ahead of the files becoming available.
“That is not a technical footnote; that is the API business model wearing an open source jacket for the launch photo,” Brokaw said at the time.
Alibaba, for its part, did eventually follow through on August 12, publishing the underlying Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B weights — but there were notable strings attached. The downloadable model came under a custom licence, versus the more permissive Apache 2.0 terms Alibaba had used for various earlier Qwen releases. Businesses operating “model-as-a-service” or AI work assistant products, with combined revenue exceeding $50 million over any consecutive 12-month period, were required to obtain a separate commercial licence, although internal use was exempt under specified conditions.
The licence also required certain commercial products with more than 100 million monthly active users, or $20 million in monthly revenue, to prominently display the model’s name.
For comparison, Xiaomi released its MiMo-V2.6 models under the permissive MIT licence in September, alongside technical documentation and a public record of its reinforcement-learning training costs. The company also committed to publishing thousands of training environments and associated tools, giving outside developers a potentially deeper view of how the models were developed.
Alibaba was willing to wear the “open source jacket,” while keeping some of its most valuable capabilities behind a commercial API. And with Qwen4-Max, the company appears to be putting that jacket back on the hanger.
The released Qwen3.8-Max weights also represented a more limited version of the hosted product, lacking some of the capabilities available through Alibaba’s API, including native image input.
In other words, Alibaba was willing to wear the “open source jacket,” while keeping some of its most valuable capabilities behind a commercial API. And with Qwen4-Max, the company appears to be putting that jacket back on the hanger completely — no downloadable weights have been announced for the new model, and Alibaba has made no commitment to publish them.
On X and the accompanying blog post, Alibaba did say that the “open weights of smaller Qwen4 models will be released,” although it has yet to specify which models or when they will become available. But for Qwen4-Max itself, developers remain reliant on Alibaba’s hosted services or third-party API providers.
