articles.title: Best practices for writing Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Best practices for writing Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
With Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, you block a content category by describing it in plain language, and the guardrail applies that description to every request by meaning rather than by keyword. That same mechanism can also match more than you intend. A topic named Finance, meant to keep an assistant out of investment advice, also blocks “When does my direct deposit clear?”. Inputs close in meaning to the topic can get caught, not only the requests you intended.
When Denied Topics blocks too much or too little, the cause is usually one of four authoring patterns:
- Topics that block legitimate queries. A topic framed around a subject domain (Finance, Legal, Compensation) rather than the user’s intention can match queries semantically near that domain. This is a frequent failure mode.
- Topics that miss the requests they were written to catch. A definition built from keyword lists (“words like invest, portfolio, stock…”) misses phrasings that use other vocabulary and fires on unrelated inputs that happen to share those words.
- Examples that teach the wrong thing. Five paraphrases of one idea leave the topic’s boundaries unguarded, and examples that name specific countries, products, or companies pull those entities into the topic’s context.
- Topics that interfere with each other. Overlapping definitions compete for the same input, report matches inconsistently, and can together block inputs that neither would block alone.
The rest of this post is a practical guide to avoiding these patterns. It presents eight best practices for describing a topic precisely enough that the guardrail blocks what you mean and passes what you don’t.
The scenario: AnyCompany Bank’s customer assistant
To ground the following practices in something concrete, we use one running example throughout this post: a fictional bank we call AnyCompany Bank. AnyCompany Bank is two weeks from launching its first customer-facing AI assistant, and its first pass at the Denied Topics policy is blocking the wrong things.
Application: AnyCompany Bank’s chatbot is embedded in the AnyCompany Bank mobile and web app. It answers questions about accounts, statements, transfers, cards, and mortgages. It hands off to a human for account changes, dispute filings, and questions outside its scope.
Must-block list (from legal and compliance):
- Personalized investment recommendations (a regulatory line, because AnyCompany Bank isn’t registered as an investment adviser through this channel).
- Legal counsel or litigation guidance regarding disputes against AnyCompany Bank.
- Insider-trading advice (a specific slice of financial advice with its own regulatory weight).
- Descriptions of how to build weapons (universal safety, not domain-specific).
- Prompt injection or jailbreak attempts (a different kind of signal, because the request is trying to override the assistant’s own instructions).
- Repeating specific named competitor products in AnyCompany Bank’s outputs.
Must-pass list (the things the assistant exists to do):
- Account balance and statement questions.
- Transfer instructions, payoff quotes, escrow questions.
- Card management, fraud reports (routed to a human), lost-card replacement.
- Mortgage servicing operations, such as modifications, forbearance, and payment plans.
- General financial-literacy questions (“What is a certificate of deposit?”), phrased as education rather than personalized advice.
Against that target, AnyCompany Bank’s team first drafted four topics, all of them currently blocking legitimate queries:
Every one of these topics names a subject domain the assistant works in, rather than the intention the bank needs to refuse. Fixing this is what the rest of the post is about. The next eight sections work through the practices, most of them closing with a “Back at AnyCompany Bank” subsection that shows the fix applied to this scenario. The post then closes with the one limitation to plan for regardless of how well you follow the practices: results are not fully deterministic.
Note: Denied Topic structure in Standard tier. A topic has three parts, a name, a definition, and up to five examples, and the guardrail evaluates all three together as a single unit, not the definition alone. The name can be up to 100 characters. The definition can be up to 1,000 characters, with 100–300 as the practical sweet spot. Each example can be up to 100 characters, and a guardrail can hold up to 30 topics.
Best practice 1: Frame the topic around the user’s intention, not the subject domain
This practice sets the general frame. Best practices 2 through 4 apply it to each part of a topic in turn: the name, the definition, and the examples.
A frequent reason a topic blocks legitimate queries is that the topic describes a subject domain rather than what the user wants from the exchange. Two queries in the same domain can carry different intentions. “When does my direct deposit clear?” and “How much does an L5 engineer earn?” both concern pay, but only the second is a salary comparison. A domain-framed topic collapses those distinctions and can block queries semantically near the domain. A topic framed around the user’s intention matches only queries where that intention is present.
Intention is the framing lens. To make it operational, name the topic after the specific action or content type that expresses the intention on the surface, such as a request, a claim, or a piece of generated content. Intention tells you what to catch, and action gives you a concrete shape the guardrail can evaluate.
The guardrail evaluates both the topic name and its definition together. When either component names a domain, the topic matches too broadly. When both name an action that expresses a specific intention, the topic is precise.
Guidelines
- Identify the intention. State briefly, in your own words, what the user is trying to get from the assistant that you want to refuse, such as a personalized recommendation, a legal opinion, private contact details, or a partisan endorsement. This is the diagnostic step, and it doesn’t appear verbatim in the topic.
- Name the topic after the action that expresses that intention. Use a phrase that describes a specific action or behavior, not a broad subject area. The phrase can be an action-derived noun (Investment Recommendations, Salary Comparisons), a specific behavior noun phrase (Colleague Arguments, Passport and Visa Renewal), or a verb-ing form (Suing for Damages). See Best practice 2 for details.
- If your topic name is a category noun (Banking, Compensation, Security, Legal, Finance), the topic is domain-framed. Rename it after the action that expresses the intention you actually want to block.
- Rewrite your definition to begin with the action. Openers such as “Asking for X”, “Requests for Y”, “Statements that describe Z”, or “Generating W” express the intention through a specific action. Avoid subject-area openers such as “Related to X”, “Content about Y”, or “Anything mentioning Z”.
The next few best practices apply this idea to AnyCompany Bank’s own topics, with concrete examples. Best practice 2 renames them, and Best practice 3 tightens their definitions to match.
Best practice 2: Choose an actionable topic name
The topic name has a meaningful effect on what is matched, often greater than expected. A broad category name (Finance, Security, Legal) can lead the guardrail to associate the topic with vocabulary in that category, even when the definition attempts to narrow the scope. A specific action name (Investment Recommendations, Hacking Instructions, Suing for Damages) helps narrow the scope before the definition is read.
Guidelines
- Prefer a specific action or behavior phrase (2–5 words). Avoid single-word category labels.
- The following forms can work, as long as the phrase describes a specific action or behavior rather than a broad subject area: 
         
  - Action-noun form: an activity-derived noun as the head, such as Investment Recommendations, Hacking Instructions, or Election Fraud Claims.
  - Specific behavior noun phrase: a noun phrase that names a specific behavior, such as Colleague Arguments, Passport and Visa Renewal, or Underage Self-Statement.
  - Verb-ing form: an -ing verb followed by an object, such as Suing for Damages or Requesting Contact Details for Named Individuals. This form is useful when the action requires a verb to be clear.
- Read the name aloud and ask whether it describes something the user is doing or only a subject area the user’s query is near. If the name only names a subject area, rename it.
- Avoid names that include broad institutional labels (Government, Company, Insurance) unless the action is specifically about that institution. Institutional labels can produce unintended matches. For example, a topic named Government Documents might match queries that mention a country name plus a document, even if the query is about internal company policy.
Back at AnyCompany Bank
One of AnyCompany Bank’s first-draft topics was named Legal:
This is why “Can you help me modify my mortgage?” got blocked. Mortgages are legal instruments, so queries about them live in the semantic neighborhood of legal. Renaming solves half the problem before we even touch the definition:
The new name uses a verb-derived noun (litigation), names a second specific behavior (non-servicing legal advice), and makes clear by contrast that servicing questions, such as modifications, forbearance, and escrow, are outside the topic. The name itself now carries some of the work the definition would otherwise do alone.
AnyCompany Bank applied the same logic to the Fraud topic, renaming it to Fraud Investigation Requests. The assistant should still let customers report fraud, which gets routed to a human, but must not attempt to investigate fraud claims itself.
After these three renames, AnyCompany Bank’s topic list is:
Best practice 3: Write action-scoped definitions
The definition should describe the user’s action on a specific object, rather than the general subject of that action.
Guidelines
- Begin with the action or the content type. Open the definition with a phrase that names what the user is doing or producing. Common effective openers include: 
         
  - “Asking for…”, “Requesting…”, “Requests for…”, “Requests to…”, “Seeking…”, “Recommending…”, when the topic covers user requests for a specific action.
  - “Statements that…”, “Providing…”, “Generating…”, “Content that includes…”, when the topic covers user-produced content, disclosures, or generated output.
  - “Using X to Y”, when the topic covers a specific technique or method.
- Avoid opening with a subject-area phrase such as “Related to X”, “Content about Y”, or “Anything mentioning Z”, which is domain-framed rather than action-framed.
- Specify the objects. State what the user is asking about, using concrete items rather than broad categories, for example, “individual stocks, bonds, ETFs, or cryptocurrencies” rather than “financial products”.
- Add discriminating detail. If two topics share vocabulary (for example, both involve “customer”), give each definition a distinct feature so the guardrail can differentiate them. Definitions that share meaning cause the two topics to interfere with each other.
- Keep the definition positive. Describe what is in scope. Short trailing exclusions can help disambiguate. See Best practice 8 for cases where exclusions are harmful.
- Length isn’t the goal. Longer definitions are not necessarily better, and a longer definition can increase the topic’s sensitivity to the wording of neighboring topics.
Structural template
We recommend the following structure:
[Action or content-type opener] for [specific objects] by [qualifying constraint or purpose]. Includes [one or two sub-cases].
Back at AnyCompany Bank
AnyCompany Bank’s first-draft topic was named Finance, with a definition to match:
This is exactly why “Where can I find my payoff quote?” was blocked. Payoff is a financial term, quote concerns money, and the input is “related to” the finance domain, even though the customer’s intention, retrieving a servicing figure, has nothing to do with what AnyCompany Bank wanted to refuse.
Following Best practice 1, the team renamed the topic to Investment Recommendations and adjusted the definition’s vocabulary to match, without yet making it action-scoped:
This was still domain-framed even though the name had improved. General education (“Explain what a mutual fund is”), historical financial news (“Why did rates rise last quarter?”), and portfolio review (“Show me my holdings”) all matched. The assistant should answer all of them.
The team applied the structural template, with an action opener, specific objects, a qualifying constraint, and one or two sub-cases:
Every piece of the template serves a specific purpose. “Asking for a personalized recommendation to…” is the action opener. “Stocks, bonds, mutual funds, ETFs, or cryptocurrencies” are the specific objects. “For the user’s own investment returns” is the qualifying constraint that excludes educational and third-party discussion. The “Includes…” clause names two sub-cases: a specific-security question and an allocation-percentage question.
AnyCompany Bank applied the same template to the Litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice and Fraud Investigation Requests topics:
The team now had three named topics with action-scoped definitions.
Best practice 4: Use boundary examples, not paraphrases
Examples teach the guardrail where the boundaries of your topic are. Not every example does this equally well. Five paraphrases of the same idea teach the guardrail nothing new, while five carefully chosen examples can draw the outline of the topic with much less definition text. The examples that carry the most weight are the ones sitting near the topic’s edge, close enough to a plausible non-match that they show the guardrail where to draw the line. We call these boundary examples. A good boundary example has three properties. First, it’s inside the topic’s scope. Second, it’s close to a plausible non-match, using vocabulary or structure that resembles inputs the topic should not match. Third, it differs from your other examples in sub-case, sentence shape, and vocabulary.
Guidelines
- Use all five examples, because five varied examples are more effective than two obvious ones.
- Cover different sub-cases. If the topic covers “buy” and “sell” advice, include examples of both.
- Cover different sentence shapes. Include direct questions (What should I buy?), imperatives (Recommend a stock), and narrative statements (I’m considering putting money into…).
- Include one example that is near the boundary of the topic but still inside, a borderline version of a match.
- Don’t include country names, product names, competitor names, or company names in examples unless the topic is inherently about that specific entity. Named entities in examples create associations that cause the topic to match unrelated queries mentioning the same entity.
Back at AnyCompany Bank
The team’s first pass at examples for Investment Recommendations looked like this:
These are five ways of asking the same question. During testing, the assistant blocked “Should I buy stocks?” reliably. But it let through “Is it a good time to rotate my portfolio out of equities into bonds?”, which is exactly the kind of question the topic is supposed to catch. The paraphrases had crowded around one point in the topic, and other points were unguarded.
The rewrite spread the examples across sub-cases and sentence shapes:
These are five different sub-cases (specific stock, asset-class shift, allocation, sell timing, growth screen) and five different sentence shapes, all inside the topic. Adjacent non-matches like “Explain what an ETF is” (educational) and “Show me my portfolio report” (data retrieval) are sufficiently different from the examples that the guardrail should not match them.
The team applied the same treatment to Litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice and Fraud Investigation Requests. The original Litigation examples were all variants of “Can I sue?” The rewritten set covered lawsuit filing, formal legal opinions, class-action inquiries, damages, and rights-interpretation. The original Fraud Investigation Requests examples were all variants of “Someone stole my money, what do I do?” The rewritten set covered unauthorized-charge investigation, card-fraud tracing, transaction reversal, identity-theft adjudication, and scammer tracing. Each rewritten set covers five different sub-cases inside one topic.
At this point, AnyCompany Bank’s three topics pass every test written so far. One more problem only shows up after the assistant runs against real traffic.
Best practice 5: Anchor definitions to a specific context when needed
Some concepts are inherently ambiguous, because the same words describe both a matching and non-matching action, depending on context. In these cases, add an explicit anchor that fixes the context: an institutional setting, a stated purpose, or a dual condition of the form “only applies when both X and Y are present”.
Guidelines
- Add a physical or institutional context in which the action occurs. For a passport topic, anchor to “at an embassy or consulate” or “through an official government application process”.
- Add a purpose qualifier. For an investment-recommendation topic, anchor to “for the user’s own investment returns” so that the topic excludes educational or third-party discussion.
- Use dual conditions when a single anchor is insufficient: “Only applies when the request (1) explicitly mentions creating an advertising campaign AND (2) names personal identification data as the targeting criterion.”
- Anchors should be positive (“at X”, “for Y”) rather than “except…” or “but not…”. Positive anchors describe what the topic IS.
- Know when not to add an anchor. If the topic is already inherently narrow (a topic specifically about “insider trading”, because the phrase is unambiguous by itself), an additional anchor introduces noise. Also avoid anchoring to a proper noun that appears in many unrelated queries (“in India”, “at Amazon”). Anchor to categories (embassies, consulates) instead.
- Check whether the topic’s own name repeats the ambiguous surface phrase. A benign, educational way of asking about the same concept often reuses that exact phrase. The guardrail reads the topic name as a signal independent of the definition (see Best practice 2). A dual-condition anchor can still lose to a name built from the term it’s trying to disambiguate.
Back at AnyCompany Bank
Adding an insider-trading topic exposed the ambiguity issue. The compliance team wanted Insider Trading Advice as a distinct topic, narrower and more serious than the general Investment Recommendations catch. The first draft:
This matched the expected case: a customer asking for a trade based on private information. It also matched something the team didn’t expect: educational queries about what insider trading is, phrased as questions. “How does the SEC define insider trading?” was getting blocked, because it “asks about insider trading”.
The team added a dual anchor:
Both conditions should rule out educational queries: they fail condition 2, because they don’t describe non-public information the user personally holds. When the team tested “How does the SEC define insider trading?” against this definition, it still got blocked some of the time. The anchor was not the problem. The topic’s name was: it repeats the exact phrase the query uses. The guardrail weighs the name as a signal independent of the definition, the same effect Best practice 2 describes elsewhere. A dual-condition anchor can specify the right conditions and still lose to a name built from the term that it’s trying to disambiguate.
The team kept the anchor and renamed the topic instead:
With the rename, the educational query passed reliably, and the real examples, the ones naming a specific security and a specific piece of non-public information, still blocked.
The definition is longer than the 100–300 character target from Best practice 3, and that is deliberate. The ambiguity here justifies the extra text. The topic itself is inherently subtle, so the definition has to carry more work.
Best practice 6: Manage topic overlap and topic count
A guardrail evaluates its topics together, not one at a time. When two topics have similar meanings, they interfere with each other. It becomes difficult to predict which topic the guardrail reports as the match, and the combined effect can block legitimate inputs that neither topic alone would block. Overlap between topics is often the reason a well-written topic produces incorrect results. The problem isn’t that topic, but a neighboring topic.
Guidelines
- Review the whole topic set for overlap before deployment. Two topics with similar definitions cause interference even if neither is broken individually. For each new topic, ask whether the definition shares vocabulary or objects with an existing topic.
- Be aware that topic count influences interference. As the number of topics in a single guardrail grows, the chance of interference between topics also grows, especially when several topics share vocabulary or cover related areas. If you observe topics interfering with each other and the definitions themselves look correct, consider reducing overlap between topics or distributing topics across more than one guardrail.
- Prefer semantic diversity within a guardrail. If you have several topics on related themes (for example, three finance-adjacent topics), consider whether they belong in the same guardrail or should be separated.
- When two topics overlap, prefer to consolidate rather than split. Merging two topics whose definitions share objects and actions is safer than attempting to draw a narrow boundary between them.
- When a new use case appears, prefer to extend an existing topic’s examples rather than add a new near-duplicate topic. Adding a new topic changes how the guardrail interprets the entire topic set, but extending a topic’s examples doesn’t.
- Place semantically-similar topics apart in the list. When two topics with similar wording appear next to each other, the guardrail is more likely to attribute an input to whichever it saw most recently. Interleave the list, separating related topics with an unrelated one in between.
Back at AnyCompany Bank
Suppose, late in the process, AnyCompany Bank’s compliance team proposed adding a broader Financial Advice topic alongside the already-defined Investment Recommendations. The intuition was that the broader topic would catch requests the specific one missed. Both topics were drafted with their own definitions:
The overlap became visible when the team tested “Should I put more into my 401(k)?”. Depending on how the caller ordered the topics in the API request, either Topic A, Topic B, or both would report the match, and on some orderings the guardrail blocked the input.
AnyCompany Bank consolidated. Financial Advice was removed, and Investment Recommendations was left to carry the specific action. After the consolidation, the ordering-dependent variance disappeared. The same input produced the same verdict regardless of where topics sat in the API call, which is the primary win from removing the overlap.
The 401(k) query itself, however, was not fully resolved by consolidation alone. Because “Should I put more into my 401(k)?” shares its “Should I put more…” frame with a real trading recommendation, Investment Recommendations still matches it on the surface. This is a residual boundary case that consolidation can’t fix by itself. It’s exactly the kind of structurally-similar match that Best practice 8 warns a trailing exclusion can’t reliably override.
The team also reordered the remaining topics. The original order was:
Topics 1 and 2 both discuss securities and cover related financial actions, so adjacent placement invited attribution ambiguity for borderline inputs. The team interleaved them:
Litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice now sits between the two securities-adjacent topics. Borderline questions like “Should I trade my Example Corp shares based on rumor?” now attribute more consistently to Trading on Non-Public Information rather than flipping between Trading on Non-Public Information and Investment Recommendations.
Best practice 7: Use the right policy for the job
Denied Topics is the right tool when the rule you need to enforce is specific to your business and expressible as a short description of the content. Think of a regulatory line, a policy commitment, a legal risk, or a scope boundary, rather than a universal safety category or a fixed list of words. Guardrails offers several policies that share the same goal of blocking specific content, but each is designed for a different kind of signal. Using Denied Topics for a category that another policy handles natively tends to block too much or too little, complicates your configuration, and produces worse results. A carefully written topic for a category that Content Filter already covers is usually less effective than Content Filter for that category.
Note that enabling more than one policy in the same guardrail incurs additional cost, because each enabled policy is evaluated on every request. When you compose Denied Topics with Content Filter or Prompt Attack, plan for the combined cost.
When to use each policy
| What you are trying to catch | Right policy | Common mistake | 
| Broad safety categories (hate, insults, violence, sexual, misconduct) | Content Filter | A Denied Topics topic named Hate Speech or Violence | 
| Prompt injection, jailbreak attempts | Prompt Attack | A Denied Topics topic named Jailbreak or Instruction Override | 
| Specific words, phrases, or product names to consistently block | Word Filter | A Denied Topics topic named Blocked Terms or Competitor Names | 
| Personal identifiers (names, phone numbers, SSN, credit cards) | Sensitive Information filter | A Denied Topics topic named PII Detection | 
| Custom content categories specific to your business or policy | Denied Topics | (this is the correct use) | 
| Custom content categories that also require Content Filter-like coverage | Compose Denied Topics with Content Filter | Attempting to reproduce Content Filter functionality in Denied Topics alone | 
Back at AnyCompany Bank
Looking back at AnyCompany Bank’s must-block list (from the scenario at the start of the post), three of the six items are not really Denied Topics at all. They belong to policies that Guardrails already provides natively.
- “Descriptions of how to build weapons” is a universal safety category, not a bank-specific policy. It moves to Content Filter → VIOLENCE at HIGH strength.
- “Repeating specific named competitor products” is exact-string blocking, not semantic matching. It moves to Word Filter with the competitor names as literal entries. (AnyCompany Bank’s first-draft topic list did include a topic called Competitors for this purpose. That topic is deleted, because Denied Topics evaluates meaning and would match ordinary mentions of the competitor’s name while missing rephrasings.)
- “Prompt injection or jailbreak attempts” is a different signal entirely. The user is trying to override the assistant’s own instructions, not asking about a domain. It moves to Prompt Attack.
After this cleanup, AnyCompany Bank’s guardrail configuration composes multiple policies:
Denied Topics carries only the four bank-specific rules that no other policy can express.
Best practice 8: Avoid these anti-patterns
The following patterns cause topics to block the wrong inputs even when the rest of the definition is otherwise well written. Avoid them. Most are a specific case of guidance already given in earlier best practices, so each line that follows points back to where the full reasoning lives.
- Writing the definition as an instruction to the guardrail (“Block all content related to…”) instead of a description of the topic. See Best practice 3.
- Framing the definition mostly by what it excludes (“All content except…”) instead of what it is. See Best practice 3.
- Listing trigger words (“Questions containing words like…”) instead of describing the concept. See Best practice 1 and Best practice 3.
- Using Denied Topics to block a specific word, phrase, or entity type, such as a competitor name or a person’s name. Use Word Filter or the Sensitive Information filter instead. See Best practice 7.
- Naming countries, products, competitors, or companies in examples, unless the topic is inherently about that entity. See Best practice 4.
- Writing examples that paraphrase the definition instead of marking its boundary. See Best practice 4.
- Writing a vague definition and relying on the examples to carry the meaning. See Best practice 3 and Best practice 4.
Trailing exclusions: A caveat and a general guide
A short trailing exclusion isn’t a general-purpose fix for every false refusal. It reliably rules out queries that are categorically different from the topic, such as a different intent, a different asker, or a different type of content. It’s less reliable when a benign query is worded almost exactly like the definition’s positive language, only about a different object. In that case, the exclusion competes against wording it closely resembles, and the match often wins.
For that structurally-similar case, prefer one of these three alternatives instead:
- A dual-condition anchor that names the confusable case directly as part of the definition (see Best practice 5).
- A rename that promotes the discriminator into the topic name itself, so the gate is visible before the definition is read (see Best practice 2).
- An upstream intent-routing step that hands the ambiguous case to a specialized flow before Guardrails sees it.
A trailing exclusion remains the right first move for every other case. Reach for one of these three only when testing shows the exclusion is losing to a near-identical match.
Limitation: Results are not fully deterministic
Even a guardrail that follows every practice in this post won’t produce fully deterministic results across every possible input. Denied Topics reads meaning with a language model, and language-model evaluations carry some inherent variance. There are two forms of this variance you should plan for.
Variance when repeating the exact same request. Sending the identical input to the identical guardrail configuration two times in a row can, in rare cases, produce different results. The same characters go in, the same topic list applies, everything is the same, and yet one call blocks and the next passes. For most inputs, and for topics that follow the preceding guidance, this doesn’t happen, and the result is stable across repeated calls. The exceptions are borderline inputs, whose meaning sits close to the semantic edge of a topic. Those are the ones prone to flipping on repeat. The more precisely a topic is defined (action-scoped, specific objects, clear anchor, boundary examples), the fewer of your inputs fall in that borderline zone.
Variance when the topic list changes. The guardrail evaluates all topics together with the input on every request. Changes to the topic list, such as adding a topic, removing one, or reordering the same topics, can shift results for previously-tested inputs. An input that was blocked with one topic list might pass with a different one. This effect happens more when two topics share meaning or when a topic definition is broad. It happens less when every topic in the list has a specific, action-scoped definition and clear boundary examples. Applying the practices in this post meaningfully reduces both forms of variance.
How to plan for it
- Don’t treat a single evaluation as proof of correctness. For an input that matters, test it multiple times, and test it as part of a small representative evaluation set rather than in isolation.
- Keep an evaluation set that includes borderline cases. These are the inputs most likely to shift when you change something. Include a mix of clear-match, clear-non-match, and near-boundary cases.
- Retest after changes to the topic set. Adding a topic, renaming one, tuning a definition, or reordering the list can shift results on inputs that previously behaved as expected.
- For inputs where correctness is critical, don’t rely on Denied Topics alone. Compose it with other policies (Content Filter, Prompt Attack, Sensitive Information filter) so that no single policy is the sole line of defense on a high-stakes decision.
- Design your product so that a wrong block is recoverable. Route blocked inputs to a human when the topic is high-stakes, give the user a way to rephrase, and log blocks with reason codes so you can audit and improve the topic set over time.
Note: Every pass-or-fail claim in this post was tested end-to-end against Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (Standard tier), each query repeated multiple times to confirm the result was stable.
Key takeaways
To recap, the practices in this post come down to eight points:
- Frame every topic around the user’s intention, expressed as a specific action. Diagnose what the user is trying to get, then name the topic after the action that expresses that intention, not the subject area the query is near. Use “Investment Recommendations”, not “Finance”.
- Write the definition to describe what the topic is. Use an action or content-type opener, name the concrete objects, add a qualifying constraint, and include one or two sub-cases.
- Use up to five boundary examples. Cover different sub-cases and sentence shapes. Don’t paraphrase the definition, and avoid country, product, and competitor names.
- Anchor ambiguous topics with a context or purpose. Use institutional settings (“at an embassy”) or purpose qualifiers (“for the user’s own investment returns”). Use dual conditions when a single anchor isn’t enough.
- Manage overlap and topic count. Consolidate topics that share vocabulary, keep semantically-similar topics apart in the list, and retest after changes.
- Use the right policy for the job. Denied Topics is for custom, business-specific topics. Content Filter, Word Filter, Sensitive Information, and Prompt Attack cover the categories they were designed for.
- Avoid the seven anti-patterns. Instructions in place of descriptions, negative-only framing, keyword lists, entity capture, named entities in examples, paraphrase-only examples, and placeholder definitions all produce topics that block the wrong inputs.
- Plan for the fact that results are not fully deterministic. Keep a borderline evaluation set, retest after every change, and design the product so a wrong block is recoverable.
Conclusion
Denied Topics is a powerful policy. With it, you can describe a bespoke content category in a short natural-language definition, without training a classifier or hand-crafting regular expressions. That power depends on describing the category the way the guardrail reads it: as the user’s intention, expressed as a specific action on a specific object, not as a subject domain. Get the framing right and the rest of the practices in this post, such as naming, definition, examples, anchors, overlap management, and policy selection, fall into place naturally.
To apply this in your own application:
- Audit your existing topics. For each topic, ask whether the name describes an action or a subject area. Rename the ones that describe a subject area.
- Rewrite each definition against the template: [Action or content-type opener] for [specific objects] by [qualifying constraint or purpose]. Includes [one or two sub-cases].
- Move every non-topic signal to the right policy. Send universal safety to Content Filter, specific strings to Word Filter, identifiers to the Sensitive Information filter, and jailbreak attempts to Prompt Attack.
- Build a small evaluation set that includes both obvious matches and near-boundary non-matches drawn from your real traffic. Retest after every change to the guardrail.
To get started, visit the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails console and the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails documentation for the full policy reference and API details, including CreateGuardrail and ApplyGuardrail.

articles.title: Nubank agora é banco de fato • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Nubank agora é banco de fato
Antes exclusivamente digital, o roxinho tem aprovação do Banco Central para oficializar a denominação no país.
O Nubank agora pode ser chamado oficialmente de banco no Brasil. A empresa teve a aquisição do Banco Porto Real Investimentos S/A aprovada pelo Banco Central e passou a cumprir os requisitos que permitem a nomenclatura.
Na prática, a novidade não traz grandes mudanças para os clientes da instituição, mas serve como uma espécie de certificação de confiabilidade do BC. Agora, são três licenças vigentes para o Nubank, que já opera como Instituição Financeira e Corretora de Títulos e Valores Mobiliários por aqui.
Segundo o roxinho, o Brasil é seu maior mercado no mundo, e cerca de 31,5 milhões de pessoas passaram a acessar serviços financeiros pelo Nu. O banco também destacou sua atuação no atendimento ao cliente, com nove premiações consecutivas no Prêmio Reclame Aqui.
A definição de banco passa pela Resolução Conjunta nº 17, do Banco Central e do Conselho Monetário Nacional (CMN). O documento foi publicado em 2025 e dá conta da nomenclatura tanto para o nome empresarial quanto para o nome fantasia, além de marca e domínio de internet utilizado.
A principal vantagem para o Nu é a confiança que a novidade passa. Segundo Lívia Chanes, CEO do banco no Brasil e na América Latina, “confiança se constrói com transparência e respeito por quem escolhe o Nubank”. Ela afirma que a licença “reforça o compromisso” da instituição, sobretudo com o sistema financeiro nacional.
A empresa afirma que tem no país seu principal mercado, com R$ 45 bilhões investidos apenas em 2026. O Nubank também é filiado à Febraban desde março, além de ter alcançado a marca de segunda maior instituição financeira do Brasil em número de clientes – fica atrás apenas da Caixa, que é um banco público. A informação é de janeiro deste ano, quando o Nu passou da marca de 112 milhões de contas abertas.
O roxinho também destaca a economia dos clientes. Segundo comunicado publicado para celebrar a novidade, o banco afirma que foram economizados R$ 135,7 bilhões em tarifas e anuidade pelas contas cadastradas. Além do Brasil, o Nubank opera diretamente em países como México, Colômbia e Estados Unidos.

articles.title: IRCC can’t confirm if Start-Up Visa replacement program details will come this year
articles.text:
Nearly a year after pausing the beleaguered Start-Up Visa program, the Canadian government can’t confirm when it will release details on a proposed replacement pilot program.
The news: In December 2025, the feds suspended applications for Canada’s Start-Up Visa program, meant to be a pathway to citizenship for immigrant founders. At the time, the government said that “more information about the new pilot program for entrepreneurs will be communicated in 2026.”
But in an email to BetaKit on Friday, an IRCC spokesperson said the department is “awaiting a number of key decisions” about the pilot and is “unable to confirm” whether those details will be available before the end of the year.
From the source: While no formal announcement has yet been made about the replacement program, IRCC’s 2026-2027 Departmental Plan includes the following priority: “Creating a new high-impact Start-Up Visa pilot that will replace and address observed issues with the existing Start-Up Visa program, to better support business development and economic growth.” The program and its eligibility will focus on “elite entrepreneurs,” it says.
The context: Originally launched as a five-year pilot program in 2013, replacing the longstanding Federal Entrepreneurship Program, the Start-Up Visa program was meant to attract and retain global entrepreneurial talent to Canada. The SUV offered a direct path to permanent residency for founders hoping to move to Canada, but it was plagued by slow processing times and critics said the program’s design was vulnerable to abuse. By the end of 2025, SUV wait times had ballooned to somewhere between 10 and 35 years, before the program was suspended in anticipation of a new pilot program.
Final thought: In addition to reducing immigration levels, Prime Minister Mark Carney has committed to reducing the public sector workforce, including jobs at IRCC. Last year, IRCC announced it would cut 3,300 roles—or about 25 percent of its workforce—over three years, despite a backlog of immigration applications.
Feature image courtesy Ziyuang Wang via Unsplash.

articles.text:
Boulies cuts $90 off its EP200 ergonomic office chair for Black Friday, bringing the price down to just $219.99
Boulies proves a comfortable chair doesn't have to cost a fortune
Spending hours at a desk is much more comfortable when your chair offers proper adjustment and support. The Boulies EP200 combines a breathable mesh design with adjustable lumbar support, armrests, and headrest, making it a great option for a home office upgrade.
Best For: Home workers who want an adjustable, breathable ergonomic chair without spending a fortune on premium seating.
The Deal: The Boulies EP200 is $219.99, down from $309.99, saving you $90 (29%). There are sizable savings on Boulies' other chairs too, which you can see below. The Black Friday promotion ends November 29, 2026.
Boulies EP200 ergonomic office chair with breathable mesh construction, adjustable lumbar support, armrests, headrest, and multi-position recline. Compact design suits home offices and extended desk work, with mesh seating included.
British buyers can get the EP200 for £209.99 down from £279.99.
Read moreRead less▼
Why we recommend it
Boulies' EP200 focuses on the features that matter most when you're sitting at a desk for long periods of time. Its adjustable lumbar support helps you tailor the chair to your lower back, while the adjustable headrest and armrests offer more flexibility than a basic office chair.
The breathable mesh construction is great if you find padded chairs uncomfortable during warm weather. It also has a multi-position recline, allowing you to change your sitting position throughout the day.
In his four-and-a-half-star review, our expert Steve said the chair was "Affordable, comfortable, and ergonomic".
A year-on after reviewing it, he said: "This is still my daily driver. Unless I'm testing out another model, this is the chair I use all-day at work, which I think speaks volumes. I haven't felt any fatigue when using it, although ten hours is about my limit before I need a break. It's a firm sit. If you suffer back pains or aches, this is ideal — it may sound counter-intuitive, but a soft seat office chair is the worst choice for chronic lower back pain, since it won't support the lower back or spine."

If you work from home, spend long periods at a desk, and want adjustable lumbar support, breathable mesh, and reclining functionality without paying more than $300.
❌ Skip the Boulies EP200 chair if...
If you need a wider seat, an integrated footrest, or more extensive adjustments. The EP500 offers those features, while the OP300 adds forward seat tilt, although both cost more.

articles.title: Audible turns to AI to help users discover audiobooks | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Amazon-owned audiobook service Audible is turning to AI to help listeners find their next book. The company on Monday launched a new “audio discovery” feature that provides a brief overview of a book’s themes and a summary of what readers liked about it, as well as commentary from an Audible editor or an author, in addition to playing the narrated sample.
The overview audio itself is generated using AI, and the commentary is pulled from recordings of past Audible interviews, the company says.
The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help users decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews.
The feature follows last month’s launch of a handful of AI tools that let users engage more with the story, interact with characters, or catch up with the help of recaps. These features have come as Audible faces new competition in the audiobooks market, namely from Spotify, which introduced audiobook listening hours as part of its paid subscriptions. That service expanded last month to over 180 markets.
Audible’s new feature takes a cue from how Amazon is already using AI to help people shop: On the Amazon storefront, AI can summarize buyers’ product reviews so shoppers can get a quick sense of what people had to say, as well as the pros and cons of a particular item. In Audible’s case, it’s pulling information about what people liked about the book from publicly available reviews.
But such a feature could limit users’ exposure to negative reviews if the AI only pulls information from those that offer positive remarks. (Further testing will be needed to see if this is the case, of course.)
Audible says the overviews will also draw on other publicly available materials, like synopses and metadata.
The feature will initially be available for select English-language titles in the U.S., and will arrive alongside new personalized collections based on users’ listening taste that could help them find other books.
The company’s other recent AI features, Recaps and the interactive “Ask a Question” tool, are also now expanding to more U.S. titles, and will become more broadly available in December. These features will only be available to customers who have purchased a title or who have access to the book as part of their Audible membership, the company said.
“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend,” said Andy Tsao, Audible’s chief product and analytics officer, in a statement. “With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author. Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily,” he added.

articles.title: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing
articles.text:
This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI.
CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today.
At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do.
From SC06 to SC26
NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more.
In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research, accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films.
Today, more than 11 million developers build on CUDA across the computing stack.
Honoring the Architects of Progress
Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI:
At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics, tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on Blue Waters, one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time.
In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to train AlexNet on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system won the 2012 ImageNet competition, helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning.
That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction. Their team’s publicly released AlphaFold 2 software uses CUDA for GPU execution.
These are just a few of many examples that show how one generation’s work creates opportunities for the next. With 1,000+ NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, developers are now reshaping industries and giving machines the power to see, learn and reason — from discovering new medicines and designing next-generation factories to advancing autonomous vehicles, modeling financial markets and unlocking quantum computing — and more.
Start building with the CUDA Toolkit and visit the 20-Year CUDA Celebration Event Wall at NVIDIA’s booth at SC26.

articles.title: Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement
articles.text: In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis. In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work. In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling. What You Will Learn: How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects Register now for this free webinar!

articles.title: Pokémon a 30 ans et Apple offre des fonds d'écran gratuits pour iPhone — Frandroid
articles.text:
Pokémon fête ses 30 ans en 2026, puisque les premiers jeux sont sortis au Japon en février 1996. Apple célèbre l’anniversaire avec une page officielle qui propose quatre fonds d’écran inédits pour iPhone, repérés ce lundi 16 novembre par 9to5Mac.
Les images sont gratuites et se téléchargent depuis n’importe quel pays, sans compte ni achat. Au Japon, elles servent aussi de bonus à une carte-cadeau vendue dans les boutiques Apple.
Sans surprise, Apple a choisi Verpom (Applin en anglais) comme vedette, car ce petit Pokémon Plante Dragon, apparu en 2019 dans Pokémon Épée et Bouclier, vit à l’intérieur d’une pomme. La marque a gardé les noms anglais pour ses quatre images :
- « Applin 1 », avec plusieurs Verpom ;
- « Applin 2 », une version fleurie ;
- « Pikachu and Friends », où Pikachu, Bulbizarre, Salamèche et Carapuce sont réunis autour de pommes ;
- une déclinaison de Verpom au format de l’iPhone Duo.
Ce dernier format vise un public réduit. L’iPhone Duo, premier iPhone pliable d’Apple, s’ouvre comme un livre sur un écran de 7,6 pouces. Surtout, il est vendu à partir de 2 339 euros en France depuis le 23 octobre.
Comment installer ces fonds d’écran
- Ouvrez la page d’Apple et choisissez votre fond d’écran
- Faites un appui long sur l’image qui s’ouvre.
- Enregistrez-la dans Photos
- Sur iPhone, passez par Réglages et Fond d’écran.
Nous vous proposons également une copie de ces fonds d’écran sur notre gallerie.
Au Japon, les Apple Store deviennent des PokéStop
Les fans japonais ont droit à plus. Du 16 au 30 novembre, les 11 Apple Store du pays vendent une carte-cadeau à l’effigie de Verpom.
Pendant la même période, chaque boutique apparaît comme PokéStop dans Pokémon GO, avec un leurre actif de 10 heures à 21 heures qui peut faire apparaître des Verpom.
Ce rapprochement ne date pas d’hier : déjà en août, Tim Cook, alors CEO d’Apple, et John Ternus, qui lui a succédé, avaient reçu Pikachu et le patron de The Pokémon Company à Apple Park, le siège de l’entreprise.

articles.title: US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
articles.text:
Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions.
US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
The latest numbers are in on how much energy hyperscale data centers use and the carbon pollution they create.
The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels.
“We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, says in an email to The Verge. “I actually find that encouraging, because it means these impacts aren’t inevitable. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.”
“The same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it.”
Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025.
Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative.
Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal.
Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. “But we’ve got to figure out a way to limit the harms … Especially because those impacts are irreversible. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.”
Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the thousands of data centers in the US — with more cropping up each year.
The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes.
Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to The Verge.
Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A bipartisan bill making its way through Congress could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use.
“Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.

articles.title: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
articles.text:
Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar
I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.
The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.
“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.
When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok
The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”
For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.
But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.
Why Telesurgery Starts With Stroke
As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.
In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.
Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.
The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok
If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”
Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.
Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.
I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.
This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.
Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.
Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.
About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”
Telesurgery’s Second Act
Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.
But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.
Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok
In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.
“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.
Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.
Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.
When Surgery Depends on the Network
After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.
In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics
Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.
Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.
Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.
But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”
Where Telesurgery Could Work Best
During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.
Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.
But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.
Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics
And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.
Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.
“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt
Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.
“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”
Measures of Success
If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.
In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.
Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics
In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.
The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.
In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics
A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.
Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone.
