He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”
The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.
These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

articles.title: Can Indonesian researchers ever win a Nobel? Not without overhauling the research ecosystem
articles.text:
Will Indonesia ever win the Nobel Prize? That question probably pops into some Indonesians’ minds whenever Nobel season starts in October.
The reality is that there are no shortcuts to a Nobel. Breakthroughs recognised by the committee almost always stem from foundational work done decades earlier — often when it is impossible to foresee the practical payoffs.
Take the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded to Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth for pioneering optogenetics — a breakthrough technique that uses light to control nerve cell activity.
Read more: Bagaimana alga mengantarkan ilmuwan pada Nobel Kedokteran dan cara baru memahami otak
Interestingly, the road to optogenetics began with research that seemed to have nothing to do with medicine. Hegemann was initially investigating how the single-celled green alga Chlamydomonas swims towards light. His collaboration with Nagel eventually led to the discovery of channelrhodopsin — a light-sensitive protein that acts as an ion channel.
By 2005, Deisseroth’s team showed that channelrhodopsin could be harnessed to control neuronal firing with light. What began as a humble inquiry into pond algae laid the groundwork for optogenetics — now an indispensable tool for mapping and manipulating the brain.
This trajectory illustrates the road to the prestigious award: Nobel-worthy breakthroughs emerge from ecosystems patient enough to let basic research mature before demanding immediate benefits.
But can Indonesia’s research ecosystem nurture that kind of long game?
It all comes down to funding. Again.
The most glaring bottleneck in Indonesia’s research ecosystem is funding. The country’s R&D spending remains low, lagging far behind its ASEAN peers.
Data from the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) paint a sobering picture: in 2024, Indonesia’s total R&D expenditure stood at around US$2.8 billion — a meagre 0.23% of gross domestic product (GDP). Higher education shouldered 71.02% of that spending, while the private sector contributed a negligible 14.96%.
Neighbours tell a different story: the private sector drove 51.37% of R&D in Malaysia (2022) and roughly 74% in Thailand (2021). The lesson is structural: a nation’s scientific muscle depends not just on how much it spends, but on who funds it.
How should public research funds be accounted for?
Researchers must naturally account for every public fund they spend: explaining what they investigate, how funds are allocated and what discoveries emerge. Yet not all grant systems in Indonesia define “results” the same way — and rigid metrics can easily distort scientific work.
Take Indonesia’s 2025 Research and Community Service Guidelines. Under the Regular Fundamental Research scheme (PFR), grantees are mandated to publish at least one paper in a reputable international journal every single year.
Research benchmarks are indeed necessary. But when success hinges on short-term milestones — like annual publication quotas — scientists are almost guaranteed to play it safe, pursuing predictable findings over ambitious, high-risk discoveries.
Take Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who jointly won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work that began more than two decades earlier.
In 2005, the pair made a critical breakthrough: modifying mRNA’s nucleosides could suppress harmful inflammatory responses to synthetic mRNA. After years of funding rejections, skepticism and painstaking refinement, that fundamental discovery unlocked the mRNA vaccines and therapies that ultimately saved millions of lives during the COVID-19 pandemic.
By comparison, Japan’s Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research program, known as KAKENHI, still demands strict accountability: recipients must report on expenditure, track ongoing milestones, and submit comprehensive final evaluations.
KAKENHI explicitly urges researchers to disseminate their findings globally — via peer-reviewed journals, international partnerships, and academic conferences. Crucially, the guidelines avoid treating rigid publication targets as make-or-break funding criteria.
Lessons from Asia’s research ecosystems
In 2025, China boosted its R&D spending to roughly 2.8% of GDP. Its investment in basic research surged by 13.3% year-on-year – comfortably outstripping its 8.2% overall growth in R&D expenditure.
Meanwhile, Singapore committed S$S37 billion (around US$28.77 billion) to its Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 (RIE2030) plan. The blueprint balances market-driven applications with solid backing for open-ended fundamental science and homegrown scientific talent.
Both countries operate under distinct economic realities and strategic priorities. Yet they share a common thread: fundamental science remains an indispensable pillar of their national policy.
Boosting Indonesia’s research budget is crucial, but cash alone will not fix the system without deeper industry involvement and long-term backing for university laboratories. Accountability matters, too – but evaluation frameworks must be flexible enough to give unorthodox, exploratory ideas room to breathe.
Read more: Ribuan riset dan paten Indonesia terjebak di “jurang maut” karena tak dipakai industri
After all, scientific inquiry is inherently unpredictable. Hypotheses fall flat, experiments fail and dead ends are part of the process. A project that yields no marketable innovation within five years may still unearth foundational knowledge that sparks a breakthrough decades later.
Grant systems must therefore make room for rigorous science whose outcomes cannot be mapped in advance. Such work still demands robust evaluation – just not through the same narrow, transactional metrics applied to off-the-shelf product development.
The Nobel is a byproduct, not the destination
Indonesia does not need a glitzy roadmap to a Nobel Prize; it needs a dependable research ecosystem. That means reliable funding, smarter resource allocation, sensible evaluation metrics and real avenues for international collaboration.
Read more: Bukan (hanya) soal anggaran. Bagaimana dana riset dibelanjakan juga penting
Every nation dreams of its own Nobel laureate, and Indonesia is no exception. But the medal itself cannot be the end goal.
For Indonesia, the real debate is not a false choice between applied projects with immediate payoffs and curiosity-driven basic science. The challenge is designing an ecosystem flexible enough to nurture both, knowing full well that groundbreaking research runs on its own clock.
What matters far more is fostering a research ecosystem that empowers scientists to pursue bold, open-ended questions – even when the tangible payoffs are years or decades down the line.

articles.title: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries.
Under the interim rule, the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries.
The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others.
The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries.
“This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.”
The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions.
Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S.
The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group.
The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S.
Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect.
Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media.
The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies.
“By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.”

articles.title: Post-Training NVIDIA Nemotron to Increase Accuracy in Your Scientific Domain | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Agentic AI is reshaping scientific research and innovation. Researchers communicate complex scientific hypotheses in natural language and let autonomous agents independently plan tasks, execute simulations, evaluate results, and self-correct across multiple iterations. Scientific agents are taking on longer, more complex, and increasingly visual workflows.
Accuracy and inference efficiency matter at every step. Without verification, errors compound across the workflow, while latency and compute costs multiply with continued operation.
NVIDIA Nemotron for Science, a collection of models, datasets, tools, and recipes for accelerating agentic scientific workloads, addresses these hurdles. It includes Nemotron 3.5 Super VL—an open, customizable, multimodal model for these specialized workflows—and the NVIDIA Nemotron Litmus-Bench V2.0, an open source chemistry-reasoning dataset and benchmark that was designed to train and evaluate LLMs and agentic AI models on molecular properties. Out of the box, Nemotron delivers frontier level accuracy for scientific benchmarks (see Figure 1 below), along with the fastest time to solution for scientific coding.
An important benefit of Nemotron models is NVIDIA post-training support. You can customize models for your specific research domain to increase accuracy.
This blog provides a practical recipe for post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for scientific use cases. Starting from a raw experimental dataset, you’ll walk through how to build a custom reinforcement learning (RL) environment using NVIDIA NeMo Gym, apply RL, and measure improvement using molecular similarity scoring. NeMo Gym supplies the environment infrastructure, and NVIDIA NeMo RL supplies the post-training framework.
This guide uses drug-metabolism prediction as a practical example. Given a parent compound, the starting molecule, and its transforming enzyme, the model predicts the resulting metabolite. The examples below use records from MetxBioDB, which is a comprehensive database of experimentally confirmed biotransformation reactions.
The blog first describes direct RL, then an optional distillation step that can be used before RL when a teacher model provides useful examples.
Build the reinforcement learning environment from experimental data
The starting point is a CSV file of existing experimental records such as sequences, Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) strings, reaction conditions, and any other metadata paired with measured properties or outcomes. In this example, molecular structures are represented as SMILES strings, a text notation for describing a molecule’s atoms and bonds.
These input-output pairs are reformatted as question-answer or user/assistant prompt pairs, with the experimental ground truth serving as a verifier to score the model’s responses. This setup constitutes a basic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) environment and requires no human preference labelling: The reward signal comes directly from the data.
The fidelity of that reward signal can be tuned to the task. A simple sequence-similarity function works as a lightweight verifier, while more sophisticated tools like cheminformatics libraries, molecular simulators, or even a live autonomous lab can be a tool call and can all be wired in as the environment’s scoring layer. The richer the tool, the more precisely the model is steered toward chemically or biologically meaningful outputs.
For the metabolism example, the model receives the parent molecule and enzyme, then submits a predicted metabolite. The verifier compares the predicted and reference molecular fingerprints—numerical representations of structural features—using Tanimoto similarity. Tanimoto similarity is a metric used to measure the overlap between two sets or binary vectors and is calculated by dividing the size of their intersection by the size of their union. For the bit fingerprints used here, the score ranges from 0 to 1; higher scores indicate more similar fingerprints.
Direct RL post-training on the custom environment
With the environment in place, fine-tune the model using group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with low rank adapters (LoRA). The environment presents the model with an experimental input and asks it to reason through the problem step-by-step before submitting a predicted answer via a tool call. Each submission is scored automatically by the verifier, giving a dense reward signal that requires no further annotation. The training loop, reward server, harness, and rollout workers are fully self-contained, so the same pipeline generalizes to any domain that can return a scalar reward.
At a 16,384-token output budget on the drug-metabolism RLVR environment, supervised fine tuning (SFT) improved the accuracy of Nemotron for Science by 12% and RL post-trained lifted it a further 17%. It demonstrates that even a highly capable instruction-tuned model continues to improve meaningfully when given targeted RL feedback on a domain-specific task.
Distillation from stronger models as a “warm-start” for RL
If the base model needs a capability boost before RL training or if RL convergence is slow, a distillation step can provide significant lift. A stronger teacher model (e.g. a larger frontier model or a specialist) is run against the same environment to generate high-quality reasoning traces. A reasoning trace is high quality if the teacher model’s step-by-step logic for identifying the enzyme, predicting the reaction site, and deriving the metabolite structure leads to a SMILES that matches the ground truth metabolite. It is a low-quality reasoning trace even if the reasoning looks fluent and plausible but has some flawed logic that resulted in the wrong prediction.
The high-quality reasoning traces are used to fine-tune the student model via SFT or direct on-policy distillation, giving it a much better starting point before the RL loop begins. This is known as a “warm-start” and it typically accelerates convergence and raises the performance floor, making the subsequent RL training more efficient and more likely to find a strong policy.
Data distillation for SFT
The distillation pipeline runs Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 across the training set, scores each rollout by Tanimoto similarity (tool call) to the ground truth metabolite, and keeps only the (question, reasoning trace) pairs where the model got it right. Those become the SFT corpus for the smaller model.
In this environment 1,123 high-quality reasoning traces were filtered from 1,934 training prompts at Tanimoto threshold ≥ 0.7. Here is a distilled reasoning trace for a question-answer pair from Claude Sonnet 5.5. Note that a fixed system prompt is included with every request, which can be varied across environments. LLM requests are formatted as chat messages containing both the question and the system prompt.
MetxBioDB environment (CYP1A2 N-demethylation)
Question:
Parent compound SMILES: Cc1nn(C)c(Cl)c1C(O)=Nc1cccc2c1C(C)OC2(C)C Metabolising enzyme: CYP1A2 Reason through this biotransformation step by step, then call submit_metabolite with the predicted SMILES of the primary metabolite.
Ground truth:
Cc1[nH]nc(Cl)c1C(O)=Nc1cccc2c1C(C)OC2(C)C — Tanimoto similarity = 1.0 (exact match)
System prompt:
You are an expert computational chemist specializing in drug metabolism. Your task is to predict the SMILES string of the metabolite produced when a given parent compound is biotransformed by a specified enzyme or enzyme family. Response format: 1. Provide step-by-step scientific reasoning: a. Identify the functional groups in the parent compound relevant to the enzyme. b. Describe the enzyme's known reaction mechanism and regioselectivity. c. Identify the specific site of biotransformation and explain why. d. Describe the chemical transformation applied (e.g. hydroxylation, glucuronidation). e. State the resulting structural change to the parent SMILES. 2. Finish by calling the submit_metabolite tool with your predicted metabolite SMILES. Rules: - The SMILES passed to submit_metabolite must be valid, canonical, and represent the chemically correct metabolic product — no extra text in the argument. - Apply knowledge of the named enzyme's typical reaction mechanism (e.g. CYP450 hydroxylation/oxidation, UGT glucuronidation, SULT sulfation, MAO deamination, NAT acetylation, etc.). - If multiple enzymes are listed (semicolon-separated), use their combined or most likely reaction on the substrate.
Reasoning trace (Claude Sonnet 5.5):
a. Functional groups relevant to CYP1A2: The parent contains an N-methyl pyrazole (N–CH3 on the ring nitrogen). CYP1A2 is well known for N-demethylation of aromatic amines and N-alkyl heterocycles via alpha-carbon hydroxylation followed by hemi-aminal collapse. b. Enzyme mechanism: CYP1A2 abstracts a hydrogen from the N-methyl carbon (N–CH3 → N–CH2•), then oxygen rebound gives N–CH2OH; the hemi-aminal spontaneously collapses to the free N–H and formaldehyde. c. Site of biotransformation: The 1-methyl (N1-CH3) on the pyrazole is the primary target. The C3-methyl is on a carbon, not nitrogen, and is far less reactive. d. Chemical transformation: N-Demethylation: –N(CH3)– → –NH–, loss of CH2O. e. Structural change to SMILES: Original N-methyl: Cc1nn(C)c(Cl)c1… ← the nn(C) nitrogen loses its CH3 Product: Cc1[nH]nc(Cl)c1… ← becomes [nH]
Tool call:
submit_metabolite({"smiles": "Cc1[nH]nc(Cl)c1C(O)=Nc1cccc2c1C(C)OC2(C)C"})
Getting started with code
The recipes below are drawn from the nemo-rl and nemo-gym training modules. Each snippet is self-contained and can be adapted to a new domain by replacing the corresponding configs.
NemoGym environment registration
The following snippets register a NemoGym RLVR environment from an experimental CSV. Registering the environment takes four pieces.
1. CSV to Gym JSONL
Each CSV row becomes one JSONL row. The extra keys, ground_truth_smiles here, are passed to the server’s seed_session and verified.
import csv
import json
SYSTEM = open("system_prompt.txt").read()
TOOLS = [{
    "type": "function",
    "name": "submit_metabolite",
    "strict": True,
    "description": (
        "Submit your predicted metabolite SMILES. Returns validity and Tanimoto"
        " similarity (0-1)."
    ),
    "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "additionalProperties": False,
        "required": ["smiles"],
        "properties": {
            "smiles": {
                "type": "string",
                "description": "Predicted metabolite SMILES (no extra text).",
            }
        },
    },
}]
with open("train.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for r in csv.DictReader(
        open("metxbiodb.csv")
    ):  # columns: parent_smiles, enzyme, reaction_type, metabolite_smiles
        user = (
            f"Parent compound SMILES: {r['parent_smiles']}\nMetabolising"
            f" enzyme: {r['enzyme']}\n\nReason through this biotransformation"
            " step by step, then call submit_metabolite with the predicted"
            " SMILES of the primary metabolite."
        )
        f.write(
            json.dumps({
                "responses_create_params": {
                    "input": [
                        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
                        {"role": "user", "content": user},
                    ],
                    "tools": TOOLS,
                },
                "agent_ref": {"name": "metxbiodb_simple_agent"},
                "parent_smiles": r["parent_smiles"],
                "enzyme": r["enzyme"],
                "reaction_type": r["reaction_type"],
                "ground_truth_smiles": r["metabolite_smiles"],
            })
            + "\n"
        )
2. Resources server: resources_servers/metxbiodb/app.py
This is the only domain-specific code, and it has three parts:
- Seed_session stores the ground truth per session.
- The submit_metabolite tool endpoint scores the first submission with Morgan-fingerprint Tanimoto (radius 2, 2048 bits).
- Verify returns that score as the reward.
It also needs a pyproject.toml with rdkit. To adapt it to a new domain, replace tanimoto_similarity and the tool schema.
3. Registration yaml
metxbiodb:
  resources_servers:
    metxbiodb:
      entrypoint: app.py
      domain: knowledge
metxbiodb_simple_agent:
  responses_api_agents:
    simple_agent: 
      entrypoint: app.py    
      max_steps: 2  # submit, then one closing turn; only the first submission is scored
      resources_server: {type: resources_servers, name: metxbiodb}
      model_server:     {type: responses_api_models, name: policy_model}
      datasets:
        - {name: train,      type: example, jsonl_fpath: data/train.jsonl}
        - {name: validation, type: example, jsonl_fpath: data/validation.jsonl}
The agent name must equal agent_ref.name in the JSONL rows.
4. Wiring in the trainer config
data:
  train:      {dataset_name: NemoGymDataset, data_path: data/train.jsonl}
  validation: {data_path: data/validation.jsonl}
  default:    {dataset_name: NemoGymDataset, env_name: nemo_gym, processor: nemo_gym_data_processor,
               prompt_file: null, system_prompt_file: null}
  nemo_gym:    
    metxbiodb_simple_agent:
      datasets:
        train:      {jsonl_fpath: data/train.jsonl}
        validation: {jsonl_fpath: data/validation.jsonl}
env:    
  should_use_nemo_gym: true
  nemo_gym:
    config_paths:
      - responses_api_models/vllm_model/configs/vllm_model_for_training.yaml
      - resources_servers/metxbiodb/configs/metxbiodb.yaml
GRPO training launch
Use the following command to launch GRPO training:
# Multi-node GRPO run (16 GPUs)
python examples/nemo_gym/run_grpo_nemo_gym.py \
    --config configs/grpo_metxbiodb_super_vl.yaml \
    cluster.num_nodes=4 cluster.gpus_per_node=4 \
    grpo.max_num_steps=100
Note: grpo_metxbiodb_super_vl.yaml is the complete GRPO trainer config for the environment in this blog.
GRPO policy configuration
The following shows the policy portion of the GRPO trainer config. The full config includes rollout, reward server, and logging settings.
policy:
  model_name: nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A128-BF16
  tokenizer:
    - name: $(policy.model_name)
  chat_template_kwargs: null
  hf_config_overrides:
    num_next_predict_layers: 0
  train_micro_batch_size: 1
  logprob_batch_size: 1
  logprob_chunk_size: 2048
  max_total_sequence_length: 5120
  make_sequence_length_divisible_by: 256
  precision: bfloat16
  offload_optimizer_for_logprob: true
  optimizer:
    - name: transformer_engine.pytorch.optimizers.fused_adam.FusedAdam
      kwargs:
        lr: 1.0e-06
        weight_decay: 0.1
        betas: [0.9, 0.999]
        eps: 1.0e-08
        master_weights: true
        store_param_remainders: true
        exp_avg_dtype: torch.bfloat16
        exp_avg_sq_dtype: torch.bfloat16
  scheduler:
    - name: torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ConstantLR
      kwargs:
        factor: 1.0
        total_iters: 1000000000
    - milestones: []
  automodel_cfg:
    enabled: true
    tensor_parallel_size: 1
    context_parallel_size: 1
    expert_parallel_size: 4
    sequence_parallel: false
    activation_checkpointing: true
    cpu_offload: false
    moe_parallelizer:
      ignore_router_for_ac: true
      reshard_after_forward: true
    automodel_kwargs:
      backend:
        _target_: nemo_automodel.components.models.common.utils.BackendConfig
        attn: te
        linear: te
        rms_norm: torch_fp32
        experts: gmm
        dispatcher: hybridep
      fake_balanced_gate: false
      rope_fusion: false
      enable_hf_state_dict_adapter: true
Note: Set loss_fn.use_importance_sampling_correction=True to reduce variance between the vLLM rollout engine and the Megatron training engine. This is particularly important for mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. 
Distillation pipeline
The following snippets score teacher rollouts by Tanimoto similarity and filter traces for the SFT corpus based on the user set threshold for the scores.
The generate script and launch command look like the below:
export POLICY_API_KEY=<your-inference-api-key>
# Step 1: Generate rollouts from Claude Sonnet 5.5
python3 tools/generate_sft.py \
    --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5 \
    --split train \
    --num-repeats 8 \
    --min-reward 0.7 \
    --out-dir runs/metxbiodb_sft_distilled
# Step 2: Build OpenAI-format SFT dataset
python3 tools/build_metxbiodb_sft_messages.py \
    --in-file runs/metxbiodb_sft_distilled/generated.jsonl \
    --out-dir metxbiodb/distilled_datasets \
    --val-frac 0.05 \
    --seed 42
Where generate_sft.py is:
async def generate(row, semaphore):
    async with semaphore:
        resp = await client.responses.create(
            model=model,
            instructions=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
            input=[{"role": "user", "content": row["prompt"]}],
            tools=TOOLS,
            temperature=1.0,
        )
    predicted_smiles = None
    response_text = getattr(resp, "output_text", "") or ""
    for item in getattr(resp, "output", []):
        if (
            getattr(item, "type", None) == "function_call"
            and getattr(item, "name", None) == "submit_metabolite"
        ):
            predicted_smiles = (
                json.loads(item.arguments).get("smiles", "").strip()
            )
            break
    valid, reward = (
        tanimoto(predicted_smiles, ground_truth)
        if predicted_smiles
        else (False, 0.0)
    )
    return {
        "id": row["id"],
        "prompt": row["prompt"],
        "response": response_text,
        "predicted_smiles": predicted_smiles,
        "reward": reward,
    }
Note: Filtering at score == 1.0 (exact Tanimoto match) keeps only traces where the teacher’s reasoning was chemically logical and resulted in the exact growth truth as the final answer. For softer ground truth to introduce some variations, set a threshold (e.g., score >= 0.7) instead.
SFT trainer launch
Use the following command to launch SFT training:
# Multi-node SFT run (16 GPUs)
python examples/run_sft.py \
    --config configs/sft_metxbiodb_super_vl_lora.yaml \
    cluster.num_nodes=4 cluster.gpus_per_node=4 \
    sft.max_num_steps=55
Note: sft_metxbiodb_super_vl_lora.yaml is the complete SFT trainer config for the environment in this blog.
SFT trainer configuration
The following SFT trainer config warm-starts the student model on distilled traces before the RL loop begins:
policy:
  optimizer:
    kwargs:
      lr: 1.0e-5
      weight_decay: 0.0
  automodel_cfg:
    model_save_format: safetensors
    checkpoint:
      save_consolidated: final
    consolidation_timeout_minutes: 120
    lora_cfg:
      enabled: false
Post-training gives research teams a way to adapt Nemotron models to the tasks and experimental evidence that matter in your domain. This recipe turns experimental records into prompts and reference answers, connects model submissions to an automated verifier, and uses reinforcement learning to train against that feedback.
The central design choice is the reward: It should measure the scientific outcome you want. Teacher-model distillation offers an optional starting point, while held-out evaluation helps determine whether either training path improves performance beyond the starting model.
Together, domain-specific data, task-appropriate verification, and reproducible evaluation provide a practical foundation for developing specialized scientific agents. Start with a narrowly defined task, validate the scoring method, and expand the workflow only as the evidence supports it.
Get started by exploring NeMo Gym and NeMo RL, then use the accompanying recipe as an example to build and evaluate an environment for your own scientific task.

articles.title: AI Finds 28 Zero-Day Flaws In Physical Robotics Software
articles.text:
This article is brought to you by VicOne.
VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.
Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.
Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.
These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.
What AI changes about vulnerability discovery
Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.
When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.
Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle
VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.
Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne
The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.
- Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot
A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly.
- Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence
Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence.
- Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control
An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly.
These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.
In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.
Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne
A published patch still needs to be proven safe
AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.
An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.
Three questions can help teams respond:
- Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots.
- What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior.
- How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended.
When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.
From discovery to safer deployment
As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.
That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.
Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne
Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.
For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”
VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety. Headquartered in Tokyo, Japan, the company provides automotive and robotics organizations with software and services to identify cyber risks early, assess their potential safety impact, and protect systems in operation, helping maintain safe, reliable behavior across real-world deployments.

articles.title: Are AI Agents The New Semiconductor IP?
articles.text:
Agents are emerging as reusable design tools, but trust and use models remain challenging.
Key Takeaways:
AI agents are emerging as a new category of reusable design capability, but with a twist. Rather than providing tightly defined design blocks, agents can be used to explore different options, integrate them, and use those changes to improve designs.
At the leading edge, soft IP developers have been customizing their code for large customers for more than a decade to boost performance and/or reduce power. But that customization is typically narrow and costly, and optimizations for one design may not directly transfer to derivative chips — especially multi-die assemblies at the leading edge.
Agents, in contrast, can be used to customize different functions with little or no human intervention, and they can self-optimize for different workloads and use cases, and some agents can even adjust for aging hardware. And they can do all of this much faster than a human, even though an experienced engineering team is needed to verify those results and recommendations.
“We have in-house specialized AI agents to do different things, to do spec analysis, RTL generation for design, for formal and functional verification, and then CDC linking, and place-and-route,” said William Wang, CEO of ChipAgents. “We provide our optimized agents to a customer, and sometimes a customer builds their own AI agent. But there are some similarities with the IP business. Sometimes we’re specifically building an agent for one customer for a particular flow, which is similar to what happens in the IP business. What’s different is that we can do it in a very short amount of time. With IP, you need 10 months. Our cycle is much shorter because AI agents are very easy to customize. In some cases we can give solutions to the customer the same day.”
Those solutions still need to be verified and debugged. But the ability to sort through many different options quickly is an attractive formula, especially with rapid evolution of AI.
“I draw parallels to the early 2000s gigahertz wars, where all of a sudden everything was multicore,” said Mo Faisal, CEO of Movellus. “Now we’ve gone from,’ Everything is going to be a GPU,’ to ‘Oh, no, it’s CPUs and GPUs, and this is a one-to-one ratio.’ So effectively we’re going through the same architectural churn that we go through every 10 to 15 years.”
The business of agents
Business models still need to solidify around agents. but they also need to be flexible enough to evolve at the same pace as the technology.
“If you look at how the EDA industry has evolved, we’re not selling perpetual licenses anymore,” said Rob Knoth, senior group director of Strategy & New Ventures at Cadence. “We moved to time-based licenses many years ago. Now we see similar things as agents roll around. They’re hitting up the tool usage even more because they want to find answers quickly, and they’re trying lots of experiments. So putting together more of a consumption-based model is really good because customers know how to use that.”
This isn’t a simple transition, though. While the promise of agents is significant, their adoption in chip design will take time. In addition, security and permissions aren’t always well-defined.
“There are some things where you’d really rather sell an agent than sell the software,” said Wally Rhines, CEO of Silvaco. “People are trying to figure out if anybody in EDA is actually pricing based upon tokens rather than traditional pricing models. It doesn’t seem like anyone is, but their customers are all talking about it. I’m very much open to selling an agent that will automate [manufacturing equipment] calibration, then jump back to my store of synthetic simulated data against the physical data. We don’t get to see the physical data, but we do know how many tokens our agents consumed. It’s a way that EDA can sell a product, get the benefit, and no one ever sees the underlying data that companies want to keep proprietary.”
Divide and conquer, but with caveats
One of the big changes with the shift from generative AI to agentic AI is the need for orchestration, and this has broad business implications. Orchestration is basically a blueprint that defines how tasks are assigned, how agents access tools and data, and how that work is coordinated. But it’s especially challenging if multiple agents execute at the same time and their actions overlap.
“What’s different about traditional AI and agentic AI is the coordination of multiple agents that are working in parallel, but doing different types of work,” said Robbie Williamson, vice president of customer engineering for cloud AI at Arm. “It’s not like there’s a unique workload that we haven’t seen before. It’s more about how do you coordinate all of these at the CPU level, and have enough bandwidth, memory, etc., to do all of this at scale. Instead of an individual making a request and driving AI, we have computers that can do it much faster. The transition that we see when we talk to hyperscalers is now about what they need from the CPU. With training, that wasn’t as important because you’re just batching the job and waiting for it to come back.”
That creates a new hierarchy in the design flow. “What has happened with this multi-agent workflow is that, in an organization, you’re trying to design a chip,” said Prith Banerjee, senior vice president of innovation at Synopsys. “When they’re having a problem with the PPA, some engineers say they know exactly what changes to make to lower the power. They’ll do clock gating. But when you clock gate power, then it changes something else. It increases the area. So some area will come in — and this is exactly what happens in the real world with coordination when multiple people come together to design a system. The human manager is coordinating the activities of the human agents in the world of a multi-agent framework. We have agents for EDA tools and agents for the CAE (computer-aided engineering) tools. We have simulation with three core solvers — CFD (computational fluid dynamics), HFSS (high-frequency structure simulation) for the electromagnetics, and mechanical for the structural part. In the EDA world, we have things for the implementation, and things for sign-off. Each of these tools has sub-areas, and we have agents to do these things. But what was happening by a team of engineers coordinated by a human manager is now being done by a hierarchy of agents with that framework.”
That changes some of the dynamics in chip design in not-so-subtle ways. Soft IP is often portable across process technologies, but it typically requires optimization and validation. AI agents can automate those tasks by coordinating EDA tools and weighing alternatives, and they can work with traditional IP to optimize specific functions in the context of a larger design.
“One of the key implications of agentic workflows is disaggregation,” said Niels Faché, senior vice president for Keysight‘s Design Engineering Software business. “We believe in platforms. Now we have to see how everybody’s going to deal with that because a platform is a very sticky concept. Many of our customers invest in customizing our platform for their needs. It’s very hard to move away from it. It’s the same for Cadence and Synopsys, but we believe that ultimately customers want that flexibility. We take an open approach to this, where we accept that disaggregation is going to happen. We need to play to the strength of our simulation capability and our understanding of the application. Customers still wanting to work with us on creating their workflows will need help with orchestration, so we need to be experts in that domain, while the most sophisticated customers will do it themselves.”
That requires some fundamental changes for EDA companies. “With AI, that’s a different model where human engineers work with digital engineers or agents,” Faché said. “So now we have to redesign our products. You’ve heard about MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers where we look at a product and ask, ‘Okay, how can we modularize it to provide access to different capabilities with the proper APIs?’ All of that coding is typically done in Python. That would then allow an agent to stitch together a code-based workflow. Our job is to make sure that our customers get this MCP functionality. We also provide examples so that an agent can learn from them and say, ‘Okay, based on these examples, I understand how this works. And now I’ve got a request for a new design, and I can organize that work based on what I’ve learned.’ That’s the world we’re moving toward, and we already see that with our front-runner customers. They are already building these agentic workflows. That means we need MCP servers, and we need all the proper documentation so we can train these agents.”
What else can agents do?
How much freedom to give agents isn’t entirely clear. AI is opaque, and unlike traditional IP, it needs to be observed from the outside. This becomes more complicated as more agents are assigned to different but connected jobs.
“Orchestration is going to be a big challenge, and it will become an even bigger challenge,” said Stelios Diamantidis, chief product officer at Cognichip. “As agents become smarter, they can deliver some outcomes, and it’s been proven to work in many other spaces, as well. But putting all these agents together to drive them as a cohort toward an answer to a problem can also have some interesting challenges. We’re still working with models that generally do not understand the deep physics of the chip design problem, and that means a lot of the logic being baked into agents. But what happens when those agents begin to disagree? Are we going to have ping-pong effects and convergence issues in EDA? We’re no strangers to those effects.”
This is particularly true with multi-die assemblies. “The stack is very heterogeneous,” Diamantidis said. “You’re looking at a model that was trained with sources that generally we don’t know very much about. You have agents that have been given enough logic about a problem by enough different people that the combination of agents and models is now a fairly chaotic model. You put them all together and you get chaos times chaos.”
These challenges help explain why IP and EDA companies are working to tightly integrate agents into existing tools.
“When you look at how we’re applying agents into our data center design and operation tooling, agentic AI coupled with physics-based simulation is great at being able to integrate large amounts of disparate data, ask questions, run experiments, evaluate the output of those experiments, and then do the loop again,” said Cadence’s Knoth. “And what’s very unique about the space we operate in is that, as opposed to other industries, we don’t need a person to look at the results and say that’s right or that’s wrong. EDA has the tools that we’ve used for decades to grade the decisions. ‘That floor plan worked better. It lowered the power.’ Or, ‘That floor plan was worse. The power went up, the heating was worse.'”
Establishing a hierarchy for agents is important, but it’s not always straightforward. “So you have one agent with different sub-agents to do different things, and then we have a multi-agent solution,” said Wang. “We released a multi-agent solution last year. So for debugging, your SoC is so big that it makes it hard to optimize performance. You need multiple agents to have parallel access to different contexts to do the job. Similarly, with formal, you have multiple agents looking at doing the debugging and being able to optimize the design. Those are extremely critical. So you need multi-agent coordination. In the future, we’re going to have virtual chip companies with virtual AI engineers working together, collaborating from this agent organization, and then maybe a part of the chip companies will be virtual in the future.”
That, in turn, could accelerate the adoption of agents.
“There could be a time where we start looking at agentic workloads and try to figure out how we can model those in pre-silicon to improve IP around that, and what that means in terms of the design of the CPU itself and our CSS offerings for those building their own,” said Arm’s Williamson.
Trust and verification
The bigger question is how much autonomy chip designers will be willing to give agents.
“The cost of a mistake is $500 million at 3 or 2 nanometers,” said Ankur Gupta, executive vice president of Siemens EDA IC products. “That’s why these engines have to remain deterministic. They have to remain high-fidelity. We, of course, use reinforcement learning, unsupervised learning, and we’ve been doing that for more than a decade. But the way we measure the result of that learning capability is whether we are still delivering a trusted outcome. So that doesn’t change.”
There’s more to the trust equation than just the outcome, though. It harkens back at least a few decades to the challenge of sharing process data that chipmakers and chip companies consider to be their IP.
“All of these agent technologies and models are pretty good at understanding the language components,” said Gupta. “But the physics component is still the big challenge. And if you think about SLMs, LLMs, where are they going to get the vast amounts of data from, because the whole universe of semiconductor and electronics designs is very siloed and customers are concerned about their IP. Everybody wants on-prem, but that argument persists because you’ve got the foundry, which is not giving up anything.”
Foundries do share PDKs with end customers and EDA companies, but they tightly restrict access to them, which makes it more difficult to train AI and to share models. And because AI is opaque, it becomes even more difficult to convince people to share data.
Nevertheless, the adoption of agents continues to grow. “The analogy is to what the human engineer is doing in a company,” said Synopsys’ Banerjee. “You do not have a single engineer doing the entire design of a chip or a system. You have teams of engineers, and teams of engineers are managed by managers, by directors, by vice presidents. And you have that hierarchy because individuals are doing different things, which they are skilled at. Then the manager coordinates their work. So the early work in AI applied to EDA was to make the tools go faster, better PPA. This is what we did with our DSO.ai (design space optimization). The early work on AI was GenAI. It was generating a script. So you ask a question. ‘I am struggling with this Fusion Compiler. What setting should I use?’ And based on hundreds of questions and answers, this thing essentially is a ChatGPT targeted to this particular line of questions. So it’s an agent for RTL assistance, or whatever.”
AI agents can even be used to fine-tune existing steps in the design flow. “In general, we want to have some very commonly used workflow agents,” said ChipAgents’ Wang. “For example, when you’re building an accelerator chip, it’s very different from a CPU. So how do you do verification? Do you do more formal, less formal? It’s a very different methodology. Having that flexibility is really critical. You don’t want to build a workflow that is very rigid so people cannot customize it. The platform needs to allow you to customize for your specific chip while also being general enough.”
Conclusion
“The model brings a lot of intelligence, so the agent doesn’t have to be terribly smart,” said Cognichip’s Diamantidis. “It can be there to introduce some guardrails and add some additional skills. But right now we’re flipping it. We’re saying, ‘You know, we don’t have billions of examples of hardware, and they’re spread out in all these different silos. So we can’t get them in one place. We can train a model that’s very focused on what it does and put everything on the agent, but that makes it top-heavy, and top-heavy things tend to lose their balance. That’s one of the big challenges.”
So even though AI agents are being integrated into traditional workflows, chip design is still cautious about when and where to deploy it.
“Should agents be managing the hardware that is running all kinds of agents? The answer is yes,” said Movellus’ Faisal. “Is that going to be easy? I don’t think so, because the silicon industry that is enabling the intelligence and adopting all of that for internal tooling and even management is probably the slowest and most conservative. A $500 million silicon program failure is a big deal. There are going to be all kinds of management agents that will be needed — managing the rack, managing thermals, managing workload orchestration.”
While agentic AI won’t replace traditional IP, it could impact the design process in which that IP is used. Change is coming, but there are still a lot of challenges and unknowns ahead.
Leave a Reply

articles.title: Nextcloud Office : l'alternative libre à Microsoft Office — Frandroid
articles.text:
Vous rêvez de vous émanciper du joug de Microsoft dans votre quotidien ? Une nouvelle application devrait vous y aider. Comme l’a remarqué IT-Connect.fr, l’application Nextcloud Office est désormais disponible au téléchargement sur (presque) toutes les plateformes.
Basé sur le projet Euro-Office, le logiciel cherche à offrir une compatibilité maximale avec les fichiers issus de l’écosystème Microsoft tout en offrant une suite bureautique européenne qui met l’accent sur la souveraineté numérique.
Du 19 au 30 novembre, le Plaud Note Pro passe à 149 € au lieu de 189 € ! Il enregistre vos réunions, les transcrit et les synthétise pour vous, il suffit d’appuyer sur un bouton. Les Plaud Note, NotePin et NotePin S sont aussi à -20 %. Bref, c’est le moment d’arrêter de perdre du temps au travail !
Focus sur la compatibilité
Semblant faire fi des critiques venant de chez son concurrent Only Office et de celles émises par la Document Foundation (à l’origine de Libre Office), le collectif a donc publié une version finalisée de son outil de traitement de texte, de tableur, d’édition de PDF et de diapositives. La suite est ainsi disponible sur Windows (ARM et Intel), macOS (pour les puces Apple Silicon seulement) et Linux (en format DEB et RPM).
Le logiciel est très largement inspiré de celui de son concurrent russe, et, pour cause, une bonne partie du code a été réutilisé. Il permet évidemment de se connecter à un espace Nextcloud pour éditer des fichiers dans le cloud, mais peut aussi manipuler des fichiers en local, qu’ils soient sous des formats propriétaires (DOCX, XLSX, PPTX) ou libres (ODT, ODS, ODP).
Autrement, l’interface devrait paraître familière à quiconque a déjà utilisé un logiciel de la suite Microsoft ces dernières années. L’interface en bandeau, les différents onglets, l’arrangement des icônes, tout y est pour créer une copie libre et facile à prendre en main.
Une vague de clones
Pour celles et ceux qui ont du mal à y voir clair dans la jungle des applications de bureautique, Nextcloud Office est en fait la version « stable » des builds Euro-Office. Les deux logiciels sont basés sur OnlyOffice, qui fournit depuis des années une suite concurrente à Microsoft Office, que ce soit en ligne ou en local. D’autres clones, comme WordCraft ou Élixir Office, sont aussi apparus ces dernières semaines, aidés par le développement de l’IA.
    Pour aller plus loin
Photoshop, Premiere, InDesign : sept clones open source d’Adobe, codés avec l’aide de Claude
            
De situation de monopole quasi total sur le marché, Microsoft Office est désormais attaqué de toutes parts par des clones plus ou moins réussis et chacun avec une philosophie différente. S’il peut être compliqué d’y voir clair dans tout ça, au moins il y a désormais du choix.

articles.title: Kann es einen „Ideen-Detektor“ geben? Ein neues Tool soll das für Forschungsarbeiten prüfen
articles.text:
Anders als Pangram und weitere KI-Dektoren: Kann man erkennen, ob eine Idee von ChatGPT stammt?
Schulen, Hochschulen, Wissenschaft und Medien, sie alle befinden sich in einem Katz-und-Maus-Spiel mit künstlicher Intelligenz: Welche Hausaufgaben, Studien und Berichte stammen von einem Menschen und welche wurden von einem großen Sprachmodell verfasst? Wo wurde KI als Hilfsmittel verwendet, um Texte zu formulieren und wo war sie womöglich stärker involviert, vielleicht sogar beim Erstellen von Daten oder gar der Ideenfindung?
Während sich der Wissenschaftsbetrieb langsam damit arrangiert, dass Paper zunehmend mithilfe von KI verfasst werden, bleibt die Antwort auf die Frage nach dem Ursprung von Ideen schwierig. Texte lassen sich, mal mehr, mal weniger zuverlässig, auf KI-Formulierungen hin untersuchen. Doch kann es auch einen „Ideen-Detektor“ geben?
Forschungsidee: Was stammt vom KI-Modell und was hat sich ein Mensch überlegt?
Ja, sagen Forschende der Universität von Maryland und Google Deepmind. In einem noch nicht von unabhängigen Expertinnen und Experten geprüften Preprint stellen sie Idea Lens vor: Einen Algorithmus, der mutmaßlich erkennen kann, ob die Ideen eines Textes – und nicht nur der Text selbst – von einem Menschen oder einer Maschine stammen.
Während Prosa-Detektoren wie Pangram einen Text auf oberflächliche Merkmale wie die Auswahl der Wörter, die Satzstruktur und statistische Textmuster hin untersucht, prüft Idea Lens den Text auf seine argumentative und inhaltliche Struktur. Denn auch darin lassen sich Hinweise drauf finden, ob ein Sprachmodell zum Einsatz kam.
Idea Lens zerlegt Texte in ihre diskursive Struktur
Das Tool, das auf einer Website selbst ausprobiert werden kann, funktioniert so: Idea Lens zerlegt einen Text, etwa eine wissenschaftliche Studie, zunächst in seine Einzelteile. Für jedes Segment wird sowohl der Inhalt als auch die Funktion beschrieben: Handelt es sich bei der Passage um einen Beweis, um eine Empfehlung oder eine Beschreibung, um nur drei mögliche Funktionen zu nennen. Um die Prosa als Störfaktor auszuschließen, zum Beispiel charakteristische Formulierungen eines Autors, wird der Inhalt durch ein eigenes Sprachmodell umgeschrieben; der ursprüngliche Schreibstil und die Wortwahl verschwinden nahezu komplett. Ein netter Nebeneffekt dieser Paraphrasierung: Das Modell kann mit vielen unterschiedlichen Sprachen arbeiten.
Am Ende entsteht eine diskursive Struktur, die jedem Text innewohnt, ganz gleich ob kurze eine E-Mail oder ein 1.000-Seiten-Roman: Autorinnen und Autoren entscheiden, wie sie Inhalt und Funktion anordnen. Ein großes Sprachmodell tut das ebenfalls – nutzt dafür aber immer ähnliche Muster. Genau diese soll Idea Lens erkennen, indem es die Abfolge und Art der Argumente bewertet.
Trainingsgrundlage waren Ergebnisse des KI-Detektors Pangram
Damit es valide Aussagen treffen kann, musste Idea Lens natürlich seinerseits zunächst trainiert werden. Dazu haben die Forschenden das Modell mit rund 800.000 Texten aus verschiedenen Quellen gefüttert, die mithilfe des KI-Detektors Pangram als entweder KI-generiert oder von einem Menschen geschrieben gelabelt wurden. Dass die Analysen von Pangram nicht 100-prozentig perfekt sind, sieht das Team als Vorteil, um ein gewisses „Rauschen“ in die Trainingsdaten zu bekommen.
Getestet wurde Idea Lens schließlich an einem Korpus von Texten, von denen ein Teil aus der Zeit vor ChatGPT stammt und man relativ sicher sein kann, dass sie nicht mithilfe von KI geschrieben wurden. Gegenüber Pangram überzeugte Idea Lens vor allem bei gemischter Urheberschaft, zum einen bei Texten, die von einer KI (mit)geschrieben wurden, aber auf menschlichen Ideen beruhen: Wo herkömmliche Detektoren wie Pangram 4 dieselben Texte bis zu 92,4 Prozent als KI-generiert einstuften, sank die Rate bei Idea Lens, abhängig von der diskursiven Struktur des jeweiligen Textes, auf bis zu 7 Prozent. Soll heißen: Das Modell konnte deutlich zuverlässiger sagen, ob die Idee für einen Text von einem Menschen oder einer Maschine stammt – ein wichtiger Aspekt bei der Bewertung von wissenschaftlichen Studien.
Im zweiten Fall, nämlich bei Texten, die Menschen auf Basis einer KI-generierten Struktur verfassen, erkannte Idea Leans die KI-Herkunft in 68 Prozent der Fälle. Prosa-Detektoren kamen hier auf eine Trefferquote von unter 10 Prozent.
Der Mensch wird präzise, die KI bleibt vage
Interessant ist, welche Unterschiede Idea Lens in der diskursiven Struktur in den Texten von Mensch und Maschine fand. Demnach enthalten menschliche Texte mehr spezielle Details oder Handlungsanweisungen, welche die Kernaussage oder die Schlussfolgerung des Autors oder der Autorin unterstützen. Eine KI formuliert dagegen universeller mit austauschbaren Details. Auch benennen Menschen eher Grenzen und Hürden, während die KI Nachteile und Zielkonflikte eher unter den Tisch fallen lässt oder unterschätzt.
Trotz des innovativen Ansatzes, habe Idea Lens noch einige Schwächen, sagen unabhängige Forschende. So sei das System nicht für das immer häufiger auftretende Szenario der „Co-Autorschaft“ geeignet, bei dem Mensch und Maschine schon den Ideenprozess gemeinsam gestalten und es keine klare Unterscheidung mehr gibt. Außerdem bliebe unklar, welche Hinweise das Modell genau heranzieht und wie gewichtet, um seine Aussagen zu treffen – auf diesen Black-Box-Charakter weist das Team um Rishanth Rajendhran auch selbst hin.
Wie Rajendhran gegenüber Science sagt, sollte Idea Lens zusammen mit anderen Erkennungsinstrumenten eingesetzt werden, um den Einsatz von KI im gesamten Werk eines Forschers oder einer Forscherin zu untersuchen, und nicht nur in Einzelfällen. „Angesichts des Reputationsschadens, den solche Vorfälle mit sich bringen, ist es wichtig, dass wir vorsichtig damit umgehen“, sagt er. Die Forschenden sehen den Einsatz des Modells letztlich nicht nur darin, um Menschen der Nutzung von KI zu überführen. Sondern auch darin, dass sich Wissenschaftler und Wissenschaftlerinnen selbst bewusst machen können, welche Rolle KI in ihrer Arbeit spielt.
~~ Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: C'est le moment de changer d'ordinateur puisque le MacBook Air M5 perd 200 euros pendant le Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
Sans surprise, le MacBook Air M5 reprend la recette des modèles précédents. Preuve en est, cet écran Liquid Retina de 13,6 pouces qui commence à présenter quelques faiblesses. Ce défaut est toutefois atténué par un châssis toujours aussi réussi et une légèreté parfaite pour les déplacements. Dernier bon point : son prix puisque la Fnac le propose pour 200 euros de moins pendant le Black Friday.
Les points forts de l’Apple MacBook Air 13 M5 :
- La puissance offerte par la puce M5
- Jusqu’à 18 heures en streaming vidéo selon Apple
- Un espace de stockage doublé avec 512 Go
Grâce à cette offre de la Fnac, vous pourrez profiter de cet Apple MacBook Air M5 de 512 Go pour 1 199 euros au lieu de 1 399 euros.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant l’Apple MacBook Air 13 M5. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un manque de renouveau qui se voit
Depuis 2022, Apple adopte le même design pour ses MacBook Air. Cette version M5 ne fait pas exception à la règle. On retrouve un châssis en aluminium, une connectique limitée avec seulement deux ports USB-C et un écran qui souffle le chaud et le froid.
L’écran Liquid Retina de 13,6 pouces est toujours de la partie avec les mêmes qualités et défauts. Du côté des atouts, il y a cet affichage de 2560 x 1664 pixels et une luminosité parfaite pour l’intérieur avec un pic mesuré à 523 cd/m² lors de notre test (Apple annonce 500 cd/m²).
En ce qui concerne les couleurs, ce MacBook Air M5 remplit 94,5 % de l’espace DCI-P3, mais il pèche sur les noirs. Le LCD propose davantage du gris foncé que de véritables pixels noirs comme le ferait un écran OLED. Enfin, l’écran est toujours limité à 60 Hz et, en 2026, cela devient difficilement acceptable.
Des performances solides, et en silence
Si le design commence à sérieusement faire son temps, côté technique, c’est un sans-faute. Comme son nom l’indique, ce MacBook Air est équipé de la puce M5 qui s’accompagne de 16 Go de RAM. Cette puce est très performante et l’ordinateur ne semble jamais montrer de faiblesse même si vous effectuez beaucoup de montages vidéo. Outre ses excellentes performances, l’ordinateur ne fait aucun bruit même lors des activités les plus gourmandes.
Du côté du SSD, Apple propose un espace de stockage de 512 Go contre 256 Go précédemment. Cet espace plus important est aussi accompagné d’un gain de vitesse passant de 3,2 Go/s sur le MacBook Air M4 à environ 6,5 Go/s en lecture.
Pour l’autonomie, ce MacBook Air M5 ne se démarque pas du reste de la gamme, mais il reste très endurant. Apple annonce jusqu’à 18 heures en streaming vidéo et jusqu’à 15 heures en navigation web, avec une batterie de 53,8 Wh. C’est donc largement suffisant pour tenir une journée de travail ou de cours.
Nous avons testé l’Apple MacBook Air 13 M5 et il a obtenu la belle note de 9/10.
