articles.title: TE Connectivity at OCP Summit 2026 The Interview
articles.text:
At the 2026 OCP Global Summit, I had the chance to sit down with Brian Payne, Vice President of Product Management for the Digital Data Networks (DDN) business at TE Connectivity.
Many of our readers will know Brian from his 26 years at Dell, but he had been at TE Connectivity for about a month when we spoke. TE’s booth was built around three interconnected system-level racks, an optical interconnect rack, a sidecar power rack, and a copper IT rack, so we walked through the high-speed connectivity, the power delivery, and why TE thinks its system-level approach matters as AI infrastructure scales. We previously published a short booth tour video on STHLabs that got a surprising amount of attention, so we figured we would follow it up with the interview we did while we were there.
As always, we lightly edited this for readability.
Brian Payne and TE Connectivity at OCP
Patrick Kennedy: Brian, could you tell us a little bit about yourself?
Brian Payne: Sure. First of all, thanks. It’s great to see you again. I am vice president of product management here at TE Connectivity. I’ve got a long history in this industry. I spent 26 years at Dell.
Patrick Kennedy: Could you give us a little bit of background about TE Connectivity?
Brian Payne: TE Connectivity is a very large organization that manufactures and provides connectivity across multiple industries. But one of the most exciting things we’re doing right now is in what we call DDN, our Digital Data Networks division. We have experienced massive growth over the last three years, all building out the AI infrastructure that’s powering everything we’re doing today. It’s an exciting space to be in, with tremendous upside ahead of us.
Patrick Kennedy: As part of that, TE Connectivity is well known for its contributions to OCP.
Brian Payne: TE Connectivity has been a part of OCP since 2017, so very early days. And as you can imagine, look around us. OCP has just boomed in terms of growth. TE Connectivity is focused on power and connectivity across all domains in the AI infrastructure. We have made tremendous contributions, and there are some exciting ones we’re going to talk about today.
448G and Next-Generation Front-Panel Connectivity
Patrick Kennedy: You have some things in your hand that I think you are super excited about. Could you tell us what these are and show us a little bit?
Brian Payne: Absolutely. At TE Connectivity, we’re thinking about how we deliver power for the data center and how we connect it. With every chip innovation, more and more bandwidth is coming. How do you get that out of the compute tray, and how do you get it into the network? One of the challenges is getting to 448. There are a lot of thermal challenges and signal integrity challenges to balance, and there’s a push in the industry to find the right solution. I would say there are two competing models out there.
Patrick Kennedy: And just to be clear here, these are 3D-printed models.
Brian Payne: The reason I’ve got a 3D-printed model is that, just Monday of this week (at the October 2026 OCP Summit), in a partnership with NVIDIA and Cisco, we announced our new standard for getting to 448. That’s what I have in my hand right here. You will see that it’s a similar form factor to QSFP today. One of the things we’re trying to do is balance signal integrity, power delivery, and form factor, and not over-index on one or the other. We believe we have a winner.
When you talk about developing concepts, that’s exactly what we have here. The transceiver slides in, and we’ve got a unique way to compress it so that power delivery and signal integrity are handled separately. So our signal integrity is really, really strong. The design is also made so that, as we see the power of the transceiver escalate, we’ll be able to do cold plate liquid cooling to pull heat out of the system.
Patrick Kennedy: When you say 448G, you’re talking about the SerDes and really the per-lane communication speed.
Brian Payne: Absolutely.
Patrick Kennedy: That’s a big deal when we start talking about things like picojoules per bit, or how much power it takes to move data. But there are also a number of enabling technologies beyond USFP that you have behind us. Maybe we should start with some of the copper over here.
Copper Backplanes and Midplanes
Brian Payne: One of the huge areas of breakthrough in the industry has been copper backplane technology, and a combination of copper backplanes as well as midplanes. What we have here is an example of a midplane design, where a compute sled slides in along with power delivery. By going with this midplane design, you’re able to separate compute from GPU and then easily connect those together through the midplane. Then on the back side, we’ve got copper backplanes. In terms of an unlock for these rack-scale solutions, it is a highly technical, highly engineered solution that we have to produce in massive volumes.
TE is one of the only companies in the industry that’s able to do that. There are very few in the market, and we’re excited about that. We are focused from the chip all the way to the switch. We’ve got innovation in near-chip packaging. We’ve got innovation around optics. We’re thinking about front and back I/O connectivity and the cabling in between. We’ve got innovation and products across all of those that are being deployed today at massive scale.
Patrick Kennedy: One of the interesting things in AI deployments is just how many lanes of communication are happening in every single box in a rack. How do you make that, number one, not use too much power and not create too much heat, but then also make it reliable? I imagine that’s a lot of what TE Connectivity needs to work on.
Brian Payne: One of the things I’ve discovered, and it’s been a pleasant surprise coming into TE Connectivity, is the R&D on the front end. How do we get through the material science challenges and develop the parts necessary to unlock these massive increases in bandwidth, and then deal with all of the power that’s required to push these chips and push the data across the network?
Optics and Co-Packaged Optics
Patrick Kennedy: There are a number of technologies today focused on extending the usefulness of copper, but the next generation is really optics. I think you have a demo of that over here.
Brian Payne: The main thing I would say here is that you can go back to 10 Gigabit Ethernet, when we said the end of copper was coming, and copper is still prevalent in the industry. That being said, optics is there and solving a very, very important challenge. This is part of how we’re pathfinding and investing ahead. Earlier this year, we acquired an optics company, RAM Photonics. We’re bringing that into the product portfolio, and we’re massively investing in optics, from co-packaged optics as well as co-packaged copper, to getting the optics out of the system. So we’ve got a number of investments and new capabilities emerging to support that.
Patrick Kennedy: Folks have been talking about co-packaged optics in the industry for what feels like forever. What’s different about what’s happening today versus 10 years ago, when folks were saying, “Oh, we need co-packaged optics immediately”?
Brian Payne: I think it is the physics challenge, and how far you can route copper as we increase the number of lanes that are necessary. There is a point in time where we will have to make the pivot. I realize you could have said that 10 or 12 years ago, but it’s becoming more and more real as we face these challenges. That’s why our investment and productization are picking up in that space. But it’s not stopping our investment in copper, because copper is still the state of the art. It’s still important to deliver the outcomes our customers expect. That’s where we’ve got a dual investment.
Patrick Kennedy: One of the things you’re showing in the booth is some of the innovation around co-packaged optics, with connectors that go into the chip package so that you can service them. That was something folks didn’t know how to do even five or six years ago, and it’s a new innovation to bring co-packaged optics to the mass market and actually deploy it.
Brian Payne: When these are deployed at scale, it’s not just about getting the signal across the line. It’s about how you think about the system-level design and the operation, and what this looks like at scale. So to your point, serviceability is a critical design vector that drives innovation. That’s part of the TE approach: how do we not just get the technology working, but do it in a way that will support the massive volumes this industry is driving?
Power: The Sidecar Power Rack and Horizontal Busbar
Patrick Kennedy: This is a power shelf and a power rack. Why do we have a power rack, with racks focused on data connectivity on either side?
Brian Payne: To deliver the performance the industry is driving for, a massive amount of power is required to power the chips, and then to power the switches that connect them together. We simply don’t have the power density today to fit all of that in one rack, and that led to the innovation we see today. We’re starting to see sidecar designs like what we have here, which is a full rack of power distribution and cooling capabilities on one side.
Then on the back side, when we get around there, we’ve actually got a busbar that runs horizontally, which is unique in the industry. Nobody’s done that. We did it to solve a problem with one of our large customers, and to deliver power to the next rack, the IT rack, with the IT equipment, the compute sleds, and the switches. That’s a great example of us thinking whip to chip. How do we put together a practical solution that addresses the ever-growing thirst for more and more power?
Patrick Kennedy: One of the really interesting things there is that the density challenge is actually in the nodes, so that you can get the copper connectivity within a rack. It’s actually using power to solve a connectivity challenge. And one of the big innovations is moving that power out of the rack and figuring out how to get a lot of current back into it.
Brian Payne: Right. In this industry, we have talked about power constraints and half-full racks for years and years. We’ve talked about busbars, and none of that really took hold until the AI boom. That’s what led to the innovation where we are delivering liquid-cooled busbars that span the rack to deliver power across without having to amp up the current and the overall heat dissipation. It’s about finding that balance in power delivery, but doing it in an efficient way.
The next frontier is high voltage. We’ve got pathfinding concepts on the back side here where we’re pushing towards 800 volt. That’s what’s going to be necessary to get to a megawatt of power at the rack level. So how do we solve practically for the limitations of today, and also prepare ourselves for the future?
800V and Rack-to-Rack Power
Patrick Kennedy: One of the cool things about 800 volt is that it provides a more efficient power distribution path, which means your data center is more efficient. But there are cool things you’re doing as well. That 800 volt busbar back there has liquid cooling.
Brian Payne: Absolutely. And there are even things we can’t show you yet. Getting to 800 volt, number one, we’re thinking about how you get 800 volt all the way from the source. Every conversion has losses associated with it. So how do we bring it from the busways down into the rack, and then deliver it efficiently across the rack? To run this efficiently, liquid cooling to pull heat out is a critical element, and it’s something we’ve solved and have deployed across the industry.
Patrick Kennedy: You have another solution, which is a big, giant rack-to-rack cable. Can you tell me a little bit about that?
Brian Payne: Part of the issue is that once you get the power down to the IT equipment and you need to span multiple racks, you have to have an efficient way to get it rack to rack if a horizontal busbar isn’t the optimal choice. That’s why we’ve got prototype rack-to-rack 800 volt cables on the back of the system.
Patrick Kennedy: And that prototype is another example of how TE Connectivity is doing pathfinding with the OCP community and with customers to figure out how to solve these practical challenges.
Brian Payne: Our customer engagement starts in our customers’ data centers and in their offices, but also at places like OCP, where you can see we’re just covered up with people coming by. That inspires thought, new ideas, and future innovation. It’s super important to be a part of this community, to get those ideas in, show people what we’re thinking, and then iterate and evolve the designs going forward.
Pathfinding and Manufacturing at Scale
Patrick Kennedy: Could you give us some sense of how TE Connectivity doesn’t just make products for standards, but actually contributes to the pathfinding behind a lot of what is used in OCP?
Brian Payne: Absolutely. I’ll take power as an example. We think whip to chip. We’re one of the few, if not the only, company focused on the entire power delivery of the AI infrastructure at the AI rack. That means we see the bottlenecks before they occur, and we’re able to project ahead. The industry has the ambition to get to a megawatt of power at the rack level, and that has a lot of hard challenges. Behind us here, you’ll see some of the concepts we’re working on for how we’re going to deliver power rack to rack in the future. We get feedback on those from customers in real time, and we’re able to course correct and be ready when the industry needs us to go to full mass production.
Patrick Kennedy: I would imagine there are a bunch of steps that go into that. It starts with what problem you’re trying to solve. But then there’s also how you make something manufacturable, that you can build for a large AI data center and for an entire industry that’s really building around OCP.
Brian Payne: Everything starts with the customer. We’re partnering with the entire ecosystem, but especially the hyperscalers building out these AI data centers at a breakneck pace. The chip cycle, everything has moved faster, and we’ve got to be way ahead of where things are going: partnering, figuring out the problems they need to solve, innovating, delivering concepts, getting feedback, and continuing to iterate until we have the design the customers need.
Then that’s when we’ve got to shift to, “Oh my gosh, there are thousands of units to build to roll out in mass production.” We’ve got global manufacturing capabilities, and we’re able to rise up and produce high-quality, mass-produced parts to power the AI infrastructure we all enjoy today. TE Connectivity has a large global manufacturing footprint. We have 10 manufacturing facilities around the world, from China to Southeast Asia to North America, all focused just on the DDN business to power what’s going on in this industry.
What Is Driving TE Connectivity
Patrick Kennedy: Brian, I’ve known you for years. At the end of the day, what are the big things that are driving you?
Brian Payne: It all starts with our customers. What do they need us to do? They need us to be at the forefront of technology innovation, and they need us to be able to deliver to support their business. That means we have to be able to design high-quality products that solve the technical challenges we have. But just as important, we’ve got to be able to manufacture at scale. We’ve got that balanced investment where we can do that across power and connectivity to push the industry forward.
Patrick Kennedy: Awesome.
Final Words
A big thank you to Brian for taking the time to walk us through TE Connectivity’s booth at OCP Summit 2026. The broader theme was that AI infrastructure is no longer just a chip problem.
Getting to 448G per lane, scaling copper while preparing for co-packaged optics, and moving rack power toward 800V and the megawatt-class rack all have to work together at the system level, and then be manufactured at scale.

articles.title: Customize answers per tenant in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Customize answers per tenant in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
With retrieval instructions in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can customize answers per tenant. The same product and policy documents often serve several audiences, such as customers in different regions or internal teams, and each audience needs its own answer. You set the voice, format, retrieval guidance, and answer policy that agentic retrieval applies to each request. Before this feature, you couldn’t set the answer style, so agentic retrieval could use a different style from one request to the next. For a fixed voice or structured output, you had to turn off response generation, call a model yourself, and maintain the prompt in every application.
Now you write that guidance once, as a managed, versioned Amazon Bedrock resource, and each request references it. When you change an instruction, you can pin a version so that each application switches to the new version when you’re ready.
Take AnyCompany Smart Home, a fictitious company that sells a home controller and room sensors in three sales regions. Its customer assistant serves all three regions, and its support, field sales, and legal teams use internal assistants that they built on the same documents. AnyCompany defines each region and internal team as a tenant here, and each needs a different answer. A customer in Sales Region Central needs Spanish with day/month/year dates, and a support agent needs a short ticket note. To keep the example compact, every tenant queries one knowledge base. However, agentic retrieval can search up to five knowledge bases in a single request, and the tenant’s instruction applies to all of them.
Retrieval instructions change how the assistant answers, but they aren’t an authorization or data-isolation boundary. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to control what each tenant can retrieve. In this post, we show how to give each tenant its own answers from shared knowledge bases while keeping each tenant’s data separate. By the end, you can roll out a change to one tenant’s instruction and confirm which version answered each request.
Why tenants need their own instructions
Tenants that share documents still differ in language, date and money conventions, voice, and which policy values they can quote. A retrieval instruction has four fields for these differences:
- persona: who the assistant is, including identity, tone, and language.
- answerFormat: how the answer is structured, including how it cites sources.
- retrievalGuidance: how the agent interprets the question and what it prioritizes when it searches.
- answerPolicy: whether and how to answer, including questions outside scope.
The persona, answerFormat, and answerPolicy fields apply only when generateResponse is true, which is the default, and retrievalGuidance applies either way. For details, see Create and manage retrieval instructions. Table 1 shows how the answer to the same return question changes when the request includes the Sales Region Central instruction and names the customer’s region.
| Compared | No instruction | With the instruction and the customer’s region | 
| Answer | Every region’s return window, then a question about where the unit was bought | 45 days from delivery, in Spanish | 
| Last line | None | Source: central-returns-addendum.md | 
Table 1: The same return question with and without the Sales Region Central instruction
These patterns come up across industries. An enterprise software provider can run one assistant for many of its own customers. Each customer uploads its policies, standard operating procedures, and company values, and persona and answerPolicy give each one its own voice and rules. A regulated enterprise can put a fixed disclaimer in answerPolicy and a set citation form in answerFormat, so every answer includes both. A team that sends answers to downstream code can get strict JSON from an answerFormat, without a separate generation step. In each case, the documents are shared, and the voice, format, and policy change from caller to caller.
How retrieval instructions work
An instruction belongs to your AWS account and AWS Region, not to a knowledge base, and goes through these stages:
- Create – CreateRetrievalInstruction returns HTTP 202.
- Review – Amazon Bedrock reviews the instruction’s fields asynchronously, and you poll for the result. If the review fails, lastTransitionStatusReasons says why.
- Activate – A passing review makes the instruction ACTIVE, and DRAFT points to its current content.
- Version – CreateRetrievalInstructionVersion saves an immutable numbered version.
- Apply – A request names the instruction and, optionally, a version, which defaults to DRAFT.
- Report – The first Planning trace event includes appliedInstruction.
Scope and trade-offs
Instructions set voice, format, conventions, and policy wording. They don’t limit which documents the agent can retrieve, and they don’t choose the tenant’s own values, which come from naming the tenant in the request. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to limit what each tenant can retrieve.
Solution overview
Each tenant gets its own instruction and metadata filter. The instruction sets the voice, format, and policy of the answer, and the filter limits which documents the agent retrieves. Your backend chooses both from the authenticated tenant, so one shared knowledge base can serve every tenant. In Figure 1, your backend maps the authenticated tenant to an instruction version and a metadata filter, and adds a short tenant line to the message. Then it calls AgenticRetrieveStream on one shared managed knowledge base.
The same pattern works with a separate knowledge base for each tenant. A request can query a shared global knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base together, each with its own filter.
The example uses 32 short, fictitious AnyCompany Smart Home policy and product documents for the AnySmartProduct-5 home controller and AnySmartProduct-6 room sensors. They’re stored in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket, and each has region, audience_team, and sensitivity metadata. Each of the six tenants, three regions and three teams, has its own instruction pinned to version 1. Two restricted engineering notes belong to no tenant, so no tenant’s filter should return them.
The code is in the GitHub repo, in Python and TypeScript, and runs in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) by default. To use another AWS Region, set AWS_REGION. For the latest Region support, see Supported AWS Regions.
Prerequisites
You need the following:
- An AWS account with permissions to create retrieval instructions, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and an S3 bucket.
- One or more managed knowledge bases, with a metadata file for each document you want to filter on.
- Python 3.10 or later and a current version of the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3). Older Boto3 versions don’t include the retrieval instruction operations.
- A current version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) for control-plane commands. AgenticRetrieveStream has no CLI command, so call it through an SDK.
- Optional: an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, if you want to encrypt instructions with your own key.
Examples use Python with these two clients. Later snippets leave out the client setup and import lines.
Create a retrieval instruction for each tenant
The Sales Region Central instruction sets the language, date and money formats, and policy wording:
To create and pin each tenant’s instruction:
- Select a tenant key, such as sales-region-central, for the name and the tenant tag.
- Enter the instruction fields for that tenant.
- Send CreateRetrievalInstruction with the content and tags.
- Poll GetRetrievalInstruction until lastTransitionStatus is neither CREATING nor UPDATING.
- If the status isn’t ACTIVE, read lastTransitionStatusReasons, revise, and update.
- Create a version and record it in your release configuration.
This code runs steps 3 and 6. The repo version adds the polling for steps 4 and 5.
An update replaces the whole instruction, including the description, so resend every field you want to keep. To encrypt an instruction with your own key, set customerEncryptionKeyArn when you create it. You can’t add or change the key later. Your key policy also needs the statement in Encryption of retrieval instructions.
Keep tenant data apart with metadata filters
An instruction doesn’t limit which documents the agent retrieves. On a shared knowledge base, a Sales Region North customer’s question can return the Sales Region Central and South addenda, and even notes that no tenant should see. To keep each tenant to its own documents, add a metadata filter built from the authenticated tenant, or give the tenant its own knowledge base. A request can still query the tenant’s knowledge base alongside shared ones. Figure 2 compares the three approaches.
A metadata filter keeps one knowledge base to sync and maintain, but every document needs accurate metadata, and your backend must build the filter correctly on every request. A separate knowledge base per tenant isolates tenant data by design, but each tenant adds a knowledge base and data source to create, sync, and pay for. You can combine them: one request can query a shared knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base, each with its own filter.
With a tenant filter or a separate knowledge base, the agent retrieves only documents the tenant is entitled to, so answers don’t quote other regions’ values. An answer policy that limits the assistant to one region helps, but without a filter an answer can still quote another region’s value.
Build the filter on your server from the authenticated tenant, because Amazon Bedrock applies whatever filter the request sends:
This filter uses the equals, andAll, and orAll operators on document metadata. It isn’t per-user access filtering through userContext.
Answer policies are best effort. A line such as “Never share restricted engineering notes” can keep values out of the answer. If the notes are retrieved, though, an answer can still name the mechanism or record ID. To keep restricted content out of answers, exclude it with a metadata filter.
Answer as the tenant
For each request, your backend sends the tenant’s instruction ID and version, the tenant filter, and a tenant line. A tenant line is a short sentence, such as Customer sales region: Sales Region Central., placed before the question:
Here’s the same return question answered with three tenant instructions on one knowledge base, trimmed:
A tenant line tells the agent who is asking, which helps the answer quote that tenant’s values. It doesn’t set the tenant’s language, answer format, or date and money formats, so pair it with the tenant’s instruction. Without the instruction, a Sales Region Central answer can come back in English, without the Source: line, or in the wrong date format.
Without an instruction, a customer answer can also quote internal discount tiers from a document the tenant can retrieve. An answer policy that forbids them, like the Sales Region Central one, can keep them out, but to make sure, filter out the document that contains them. Team formats such as the ticket note aren’t guaranteed on every answer, so validate the format in any code that depends on it.
Instructions change how an answer is written. The facts still come from the documents the agent retrieves, so compute exact values such as a return deadline in your application.
Cover users who belong to a region and a team
A request can reference only one retrieval instruction. When a user belongs to both a region and a team, that instruction has to cover both. For example, a support agent in Sales Region South needs the support team’s voice and the region’s date and money formats. Table 2 compares two ways to set that up for N regions and M teams.
| Approach | Instructions to maintain | Applies the region’s formats | 
| One combined instruction for each region and team pair | N x M, plus the N region and M team instructions you already have | Yes | 
| The team’s instruction, with the region named in the tenant line | N + M | No, the team’s formats apply | 
Table 2: Two ways to cover a region and a team with one instruction
Start with the team’s instruction and a region tenant line, which keeps the count at N + M. Add a combined instruction only for pairs whose formats differ from the team’s default. Neither approach limits what the agent retrieves, so keep the tenant filter on every request. A filter also can’t remove a value from a shared document the tenant is entitled to, such as a global policy that lists every region’s dates. As of this writing, the default quota is 50 retrieval instructions per account per AWS Region, and you can request an increase. Combined instructions add up quickly, with 15 for 3 regions and 3 teams and 65 for 10 regions and 5 teams.
Scope tenant roles with instruction tags
If your application calls agentic retrieval with the same role for every tenant, IAM can’t tell tenants apart, and your code alone chooses each request’s instruction and filter. When each tenant’s requests run under that tenant’s own credentials, tag conditions add a second check on which instruction a request can apply and who can change it. Those credentials can come from a role per tenant or a role assumed with a tenant session tag.
AgenticRetrieveStream has no IAM resource. To apply an instruction, the caller needs bedrock:GetRetrievalInstruction on the instruction’s Amazon Resource Name (ARN), so that’s where the tag condition goes. These attribute-based access control (ABAC) statements from the example’s AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) app scope one tenant:
With these statements, a tenant’s applier role can apply only instructions tagged with its tenant, and its tenant admin role can manage only those instructions. The platform admin can manage any tenant’s instructions. Require both tag conditions on TagResource. With only the request-tag condition, a tenant admin can retag another tenant’s instruction into its own scope. To add a tenant, add its key to the tenantRoles context value and deploy the AWS CDK app again with the same trustedPrincipalArn. Apply permission doesn’t limit retrieval, so scope bedrock:Retrieve to each role’s knowledge bases. ListRetrievalInstructions can’t be scoped by tag, so keep instruction names free of sensitive information.
Trace each answer to a tenant and version
As Use retrieval instructions with agentic retrieval describes, the first Planning trace event includes appliedInstruction, with the ID and version of the instruction that was applied. Log it with the tenant ID:
For every event type, see the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference. To capture the applied instruction, check for the first Planning event in the loop that reads the answer:
For an audit record outside your application, use AWS CloudTrail. CloudTrail logs Agents for Amazon Bedrock Runtime operations, including AgenticRetrieveStream, as data events. A trail records data events only after you enable them. For details, see Monitor Amazon Bedrock API calls using CloudTrail.
Release instruction changes one tenant at a time
Amazon Bedrock doesn’t route traffic between versions. Keep a release configuration for each tenant, pin its version on every request, and canary, promote, or roll back by changing that pin. The trace confirms which version served each request, not whether the new version answers better, so gate each promotion on your own checks. This release configuration is from the repo’s router:
To change one tenant, update its instruction, wait for the review, create a version, and move only that tenant’s pin. For example, moving the support tenant to version 2 leaves the other five tenants on version 1:
A pin fixes the instruction, not the exact wording of each answer. During an update review, DRAFT keeps serving the previous content. A version create or a second update during the review fails with HTTP 409, so poll until the review finishes, as the retrieval instruction rollout steps describe.
More ways to use retrieval instructions
Retrieval instructions aren’t only for multi-tenant setups. The same fields work for a single application, such as an assistant that has to return JSON for downstream code or keep one voice across every answer. The repo has code for the first three.
Return structured JSON
An answerFormat can replace your own generation step:
With this answerFormat, agentic retrieval can return the JSON directly, so you don’t need a separate generation step. Validate the JSON in your code before you use it.
Serve several audiences
Give each audience its own persona and answerFormat, such as a customer answer and a ticket note, so the same knowledge bases can serve them all without mixing their formats.
Apply one instruction across knowledge bases
Several retrievers can share one instruction version:
Keep a consistent brand voice
Set identity, tone, and language once in persona, such as “Use a friendly, concise tone. Reply in the language of the question.”
Add disclaimers or citation formats
Put required lines in answerPolicy and citation forms in answerFormat, and give a realistic citation example, such as Source: central-returns-addendum.md, instead of a placeholder.
Hand off questions outside scope
Use answerPolicy to name the fallback, such as “If the documents do not answer the question, say so and give the support contact.”
Teach domain vocabulary
Use retrievalGuidance for acronyms and preferred sources, such as “Treat model numbers as exact-match terms.” Check the Planning trace events to see how the agent searched. Use filters, not guidance, to limit what it retrieves.
Best practices for writing retrieval instructions
Follow these practices when you write and roll out retrieval instructions:
- Add a tenant line to the message. It helps the answer quote the tenant’s own values.
- Bind filters to the authenticated tenant on the server. Amazon Bedrock applies whatever filter the request sends.
- Pin versions in production. Test on DRAFT, then promote by changing the pin.
- Wait for each review to finish. After a create or update, poll until the review succeeds before you create a version. A version create during a review fails with HTTP 409.
- Treat answer policies as best effort. To keep a documented fact out of answers, filter out the document that contains it.
- Validate formats your code depends on. Formats such as a ticket note aren’t guaranteed on every answer.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the retrieval instructions with the following commands. Then follow the cleanup steps in the repo README for the knowledge base, data source, S3 bucket, and roles.
Conclusion
Retrieval instructions give each tenant its own voice, answer format, date and money formats, and answer policy on shared managed knowledge bases. Pair them with metadata filters to keep tenant data apart and pinned versions to roll out changes one tenant at a time. The trace shows which version answered, and CloudTrail can record the AgenticRetrieveStream calls. Tag conditions add a check when tenants have their own credentials.
To get started, see the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference and the GitHub repo. To learn more, read Agentic retrieval for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base.

articles.title: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Leads Agentic Inference Performance on MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Agentic workloads are demanding more from inference systems. AI agents carry growing conversation histories across turns and generate a mix of reasoning, tool calls, and responses. Inference systems must support users at scale while remaining responsive.
MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 evaluates this balance between serving capacity and responsiveness using coding and enterprise workflows through API endpoints. During performance runs, generated tool calls and workflow intent are checked against reference values. Separate SWE-bench Verified evaluations assess end-to-end task-solving capability. These checks evaluate whether faster serving preserves model quality.
In MLPerf Endpoints v1.0, provisional NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 results show over 10x the throughput per kilowatt of provisioned power of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at a shared minimum end-to-end interactivity of 50 tokens per second per user.1
This post presents the benchmark results and outlines the hardware and software optimizations used in the submissions.
1MLPerf® Endpoints v1.0, Kimi K3, Standardized division, Available category, published November 9, 2026. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, 32 accelerators, result 1.0.1.kimi-k3.agentic_combined.1p, run 9: concurrency = 1,024 queries, TTFT P90 = 4,673.9 ms, system TPS = 41,414.2 tokens/sec, E2E average interactivity = 50.4 tokens/sec per user, operating power = 100.89 kW. NVIDIA GB300 NVL72, 48 accelerators, result 1.0.0.kimi-k3.agentic_combined.1, run 6: concurrency = 48 queries, TTFT P90 = 2,305.1 ms, system TPS = 2,210.4 tokens/sec, E2E average interactivity = 56.2 tokens/sec per user, operating power = 60 kW. Comparison based on throughput per kilowatt at a shared minimum E2E average interactivity of 50 tokens/sec per user. Retrieved from endpoints.mlcommons.org on November 9, 2026. GB300 results verified by MLCommons Association. For the provisional Vera Rubin results: pending MLCommons Association verification, results are subject to change pending peer review. The MLPerf name and logo are registered and unregistered trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information.
The serving demands of multi-turn agentic AI
The MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 dataset captures these workload characteristics: coding trajectories accumulate history over many turns, while enterprise workflows reuse shared instructions, tool definitions, and business rules. Figure 1 shows how context length grows across model responses during extended agentic sessions.
Vera Rubin delivers over 10x the agentic throughput per kilowatt
The submissions span Kimi K3, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Table 1 compares provisional Vera Rubin NVL72 results with verified NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 results for throughput per provisioned kilowatt at a shared minimum end-to-end (E2E) interactivity threshold and for E2E interactivity at matched query concurrency.
| Model | Throughput per provisioned kW ratio | E2E interactivity ratio | 
|---|---|---|
| Kimi K3 | 10x | 3x | 
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash | 9x | 5x | 
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 5x | 3x | 
² MLPerf® Endpoints v1.0, Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Standardized division, Available category. GB300 results published November 4, 2026; Vera Rubin results published November 9, 2026, for Kimi K3 and Qwen, and November 10, 2026, for DeepSeek. Retrieved from endpoints.mlcommons.org on November 10, 2026. Comparisons select each platform’s best TPS/kW meeting the stated minimum E2E average interactivity, or best E2E average interactivity at the stated matched concurrency. Records list: result ID; run number; concurrency (queries); TTFT P90 (ms); System TPS (tokens/sec); E2E average interactivity (tokens/sec per user); operating-point power (kW).
Kimi K3: Throughput/kW: see Footnote 1. Interactivity at matched concurrency 1,024 queries: Vera Rubin (1.0.1.kimi-k3.agentic_combined.1p; 9; 1,024; 4,673.9; 41,414.2; 50.4; 100.89); GB300 (1.0.0.kimi-k3.agentic_combined.1; 16; 1,024; 15,223.0; 13,905.8; 16.8; 60).
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Throughput/kW at minimum E2E average interactivity 280 tokens/sec per user: Vera Rubin (1.0.1.deepseek-v4_1-flash.mlperf_agentic_inference_dataset.1p; 6; 1,408; 427; 272,711.7; 294.49; 75.67), 24 GPUs; GB300 (1.0.0.deepseek-v4_1-flash.mlperf_agentic_inference_dataset.1; 1; 16; 112.8; 3,054.0; 288.65; 7.50), 4 GPUs. Interactivity at matched concurrency 1,024 queries: Vera Rubin (1.0.1.deepseek-v4_1-flash.mlperf_agentic_inference_dataset.1p; 5; 1,024; 505; 204,207.7; 307.36; 63.06), 20 GPUs; GB300 (1.0.0.deepseek-v4_1-flash.mlperf_agentic_inference_dataset.1; 8; 1,024; 4,073.5; 49,701.8; 56.65; 7.50), 4 GPUs.
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: Throughput/kW at minimum E2E average interactivity 410 tokens/sec per user: Vera Rubin (1.0.1.qwen3_6-35b-a3b.agentic_coding.1p; 8; 320; 75.2; 47,785.5; 411.9; 12.61); GB300 (1.0.0.qwen3_6-35b-a3b.agentic_coding.1; 2; 36; 65.3; 5,960.4; 531.6; 7.50). Interactivity at matched concurrency 256 queries: Vera Rubin (1.0.1.qwen3_6-35b-a3b.agentic_coding.1p; 7; 256; 65.9; 41,142.6; 501.0; 12.61); GB300 (1.0.0.qwen3_6-35b-a3b.agentic_coding.1; 7; 256; 111.7; 23,467.8; 154.5; 7.50).
Ratios are rounded as shown. GB300 results verified by MLCommons Association. Vera Rubin’s results are provisional. Pending MLCommons Association verification, results are subject to change pending peer review. The MLPerf name and logo are registered and unregistered trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information.
Figure 2 shows the tradeoff between throughput per provisioned kilowatt and E2E interactivity across at least seven concurrency levels per curve. The curves show how much throughput each system delivers at a given responsiveness requirement. The step-function plot does not interpolate between measured points to keep comparisons grounded in demonstrated performance rather than estimates.
Higher throughput per kilowatt enables organizations to run more agents simultaneously within the same power budget while meeting the same responsiveness requirement. At low concurrency, faster responses reduce inference wait times for latency-sensitive agentic tasks.
Hardware and software optimizations for agentic inference
NVIDIA Rubin GPUs combine HBM4 memory, NVIDIA Tensor Cores, and sixth-generation NVIDIA NVLink to support the demands of agentic inference. HBM4 enables rapid access to model weights and conversation state, Tensor Cores accelerate matrix operations, and NVLink supports communication across GPUs. Context-aware serving and model-specific kernels build on these capabilities to reuse prior work, independently optimize prefill and decode, and accelerate token generation—translating hardware advances into greater inference capacity and faster interactions.
Context-aware serving and model-specific optimizations improve inference performance
Agentic workloads repeatedly reuse conversation history while adding new instructions and tool results. Efficient serving must preserve reusable state, distribute requests across workers, and accommodate the different execution requirements of prompt processing and token generation. Prefix caching, state reuse, and NVIDIA Dynamo routing help reduce redundant computation and balance serving load, while disaggregated serving supports independent optimization of prefill and decode.
Figure 3 summarizes how context-aware serving and model-specific GPU execution support agentic inference.
Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B also have distinct architectures that benefit from targeted GPU execution improvements. Model-specific kernels, fusion, optimized memory access, and speculative verification reduce data movement and execution overhead. Table 2 summarizes how these serving and execution techniques work together across the three models.
| Optimization | How it improves performance | 
|---|---|
| Context reuse and routing | Reuse previously processed conversation state and distribute requests to reduce recomputation and balance worker load. Example: Qwen’s fine-grained prefix matching reuses previously processed history across turns. | 
| Prefill and decode optimization | Configure prompt processing and token generation independently through disaggregated serving, reducing contention and synchronization waits. Example: Kimi combines disaggregated serving with prefill changes that reduce GPU synchronization waits. | 
| Model-specific GPU execution | Tailor kernels, fusion, and memory access to each architecture, reducing kernel launches and data movement. Example: DeepSeek’s MegaMoE kernel uses Rubin GPU locality and matrix-multiply instructions. | 
| Speculative generation and verification | Propose multiple tokens and verify them together, reducing sequential decoding steps. Example: Qwen’s multi-token prediction pairs token proposals with Tensor Core verification. | 
More productive infrastructure for agentic AI
Agentic inference performance depends on co-design across hardware, system architecture, and serving software. The provisional MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 results show how the Vera Rubin platform brings these capabilities together to address the demands of agentic workloads and create more capacity to serve users and scale applications.
Learn more about NVIDIA training and inference performance in the companion blog post.

articles.text:
Good morning ☀️️
Welcome to another week!
We’ve been cooking up something at TechCabal, and we’re almost ready to let you in on it.
When we last asked for your feedback, some of you told us what you wanted: a better design, more interactive features, and an all-round better newsletter experience. We listened. And we’ve been busy.
In the coming weeks, we’re giving TC Daily and our other newsletters a fresh look and feel. We’re also adding a brand-new newsletter dedicated to Southern Africa, bringing you more of the stories that matter across the region.
We won’t spoil the surprise just yet, so keep your eyes peeled. There’s plenty to look forward to.
Let’s dive into today’s dispatch.
—Emmanuel
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
Capital Markets
Quickmart’s stock takes a tumble
Quickmart went public, and investors went shopping. Then some of them headed straight for the checkout.
Shares in Kenya’s second-largest supermarket chain fell 7.9% on Friday, November 13, just a day after Quickmart debuted on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE). The stock quickly changed fortunes after opening 33.3% above its initial public offering (IPO) price on Thursday.
Explain like I’m new here: Quickmart’s journey to the stock market began in 2018, when private equity firm Adenia Partners bought a majority stake in Tumaini Supermarket. Adenia acquired 51% of Quickmart the following year and merged the two chains in 2020.
The result was a retail heavyweight with 72 stores across 16 Kenyan counties, processing about five million transactions monthly. Its annual revenue grew from $37 million in 2018 to $389 million in 2025.
Adenia’s partial exit through the IPO gave investors a chance to own a slice of the supermarket business. Shares were offered at KES 7.50 ($0.058) each and opened at KES 10 ($0.077) on Thursday, November 12. Not bad for a first day at the till.
The price check: Friday’s dip suggests some investors were eager to cash in after the strong debut. The supermarket has spent years convincing Kenyans to shop there. Now it has to convince investors to stay.
Zoom out: Quickmart isn’t the first newcomer to the Nairobi Securities Exchange to lose some shine after its debut. Kenya Pipeline Company and Family Bank also enjoyed first-day rallies this year, only to stumble in their next trading sessions.
Kenya Pipeline Company closed its first trading day up 2% at KES 9.18 ($0.071), before slipping to KES 9.10 ($0.070) the next day. Family Bank had a more dramatic ride: its shares surged 44% to KES 26 ($0.20) on debut, then fell 5.2% to KES 24.65 ($0.19) in the following session.
Both stocks remained above their listing prices at Friday’s market close, so the early pullbacks weren’t disasters. A splashy debut makes headlines. But the big win for the NSE is getting investors to keep trading those shares long after the excitement fades.
Upgrade your business today
Pay with OPay is live on Fincra. Customers approve payments straight from their OPay wallet, and you get confirmation back on your site. Available now for NGN collections! Upgrade your business today with Fincra pay with OPay.
Fintech
Egypt says no to new digital lenders
Egypt’s lending market is growing fast. Its regulator’s response? Nobody else gets in. At least not yet.
Egypt’s Financial Regulatory Authority (FRA) has extended its freeze on new consumer finance and microfinance licences until October 11, 2027. The restriction covers traditional lenders and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) offering small loans. Fintech companies hoping to offer consumer loans face a separate freeze until February 25, 2027.
Explain like I’m new here: Egypt first shut the door to new lenders in October 2024, after issuing 25 licences in just two years; it gave 10 licences to microfinance providers and 15 to consumer finance companies.
The FRA wanted to slow things down and keep a closer eye on the companies already operating. Two years later, the door is now firmly shut—at least for another few months.
Here’s the funny part: Egyptians aren’t exactly borrowing less. In 2025, consumer finance volumes jumped 57% to EGP 96.3 billion ($1.8 billion), with 48 licenced companies operating in the market.
So, business is booming. But new competition will have to wait.
Why the freeze continues: The regulator cites financial stability, market needs, and service quality. It wants to ensure existing lenders are financially sound and treating borrowers properly before letting more companies in.
Zoom out: The freeze gives established lenders another year without new entrants coming through the traditional licensing route. Existing fintech lenders can continue operating, but startups waiting for a licence will have to wait longer.
Egypt wants a healthier lending market. Keeping new players out could make it harder for fresh ideas and competition to enter.
Telecoms
Vodacom wants faster 5G in South Africa
There’s 5G, and then there’s 5G Internet that does not slow down when the whole neighbourhood goes online. Vodacom, one of South Africa’s largest mobile operators, wants the latter, and it is upgrading how its network handles data.
What happened? Vodacom has commercially deployed New Radio (NR) Carrier Aggregation across its 5G network, becoming the first operator in the country to roll out the technology at scale. The technology lets the network combine multiple 5G frequency bands into a single, wider data channel. This increases the amount of information it can carry simultaneously, particularly in busy locations where many customers are competing for network capacity.
Customers with compatible devices could experience quicker downloads, smoother streaming and more reliable connections.
Vodacom is getting more out of its spectrum: In March 2022, Vodacom spent R5.38 billion ($316 million) to secure 110MHz of spectrum in ICASA’s auction, including frequencies in the 700MHz, 2600MHz and 3500MHz bands. Lower frequencies travel further and penetrate buildings more easily, while higher frequencies can carry more data but generally cover smaller areas. Carrier aggregation allows Vodacom to combine the capacity of different bands instead of treating them as separate resources.
Vodacom has not disclosed specific speed improvements or listed all compatible devices. Because the technology improves capacity rather than coverage, it will not bring 5G to places where Vodacom has yet to deploy it.
Regulation
South Africa’s gaming platforms could face new payment rules
You’re halfway through a game when you run out of coins. So you top up your wallet with real-world money or sell an item to another player. It is all part of the game until someone starts asking where the money came from and who is keeping track.
What happened? South Africa’s Financial Intelligence Centre and Reserve Bank could soon have more to say about how gaming platforms handle money. The Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the global body that sets standards for combating money laundering, has warned that gaming and gambling platforms can be used to move illicit funds through digital wallets, cross-border payments and virtual assets.
Explain like I’m new here: That warning has landed as the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) works on a new Authorisation Framework for payment services. The proposed framework would regulate businesses based on how they handle money. If users can load money onto a platform, keep it there and spend it on digital goods, regulators may want to know how the platform manages money.
The proposal could require platforms that hold this kind of in-app balance to register with the SARB. Businesses carrying out certain payment activities could also have to register with the Financial Intelligence Centre and comply with anti-money-laundering rules.
What happens next? This could mean taking a closer look at how gaming companies’ wallets, marketplaces and payment partners work. Depending on how the framework is finalised and how a platform’s services are classified, businesses could face transaction monitoring and suspicious-activity reporting requirements. This does not mean South Africa is about to ban in-game purchases or make every gaming platform a bank.

articles.title: Bußgelder drohen: Warum du nicht einfach planlos eine Ring-Kamera installieren solltest
articles.text:
Ring-Kamera und Co.: Wann du Videotürklingeln nutzen darfst – und wann nicht
Amazon und viele weitere Hersteller bieten mittlerweile eine Vielzahl von Überwachungslösungen, die die eigenen vier Wände besser absichern sollen. Wirft man einen Blick auf die Bestseller unter den „Türklingeln & Türglocken“ bei Amazon, finden sich auf den ersten drei Plätzen smarte Blink- und Ring-Kameras des Online-Riesen. Erst dahinter gibt es normale Funkklingeln, bevor auf den hinteren Plätzen wieder smarte Klingeln und Videotürspione landen.
Ring-Kamera: Warum es zu Problemen kommen kann
Da günstigere Modelle schon ab unter 50 Euro starten, ist der Kauf für viele Kund:innen kein großes Hindernis. Die Videotürklingeln versprechen im Gegenzug, den Eingangsbereich des Hauses abzusichern. Dafür nehmen sie alle Personen, die bei dir klingeln, von Kopf bis Fuß auf. Manche Modelle haben sogar noch eine zweite Kamera installiert, die den Boden filmt und so verhindern soll, dass einmal abgelegte Pakete nicht von Unbefugten unbemerkt gestohlen werden. Schließlich werden ihre Gesichter durch die Kameras aufgezeichnet, was das Aufspüren durch die Polizei erleichtern dürfte.
Wenn du eine smarte Türklingel oder einen Videotürspion installierst, solltest du aber aufpassen, dass die Polizei nicht wegen besagter Geräte bei dir klingelt. Aufgrund des Datenschutzes darf nicht einfach jeder öffentliche Bereich abgefilmt werden. Wohnst du also in naher Nachbarschaft mit anderen oder hast eine Haustür, die in Richtung Straße führt, wird das Ganze schon knifflig. Welche Vorkehrungen getroffen werden müssen, zeigen unter anderem die Landesbeauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit in NRW und die sächsische Datenschutz- und Transparenzbeauftragte.
Videotürklingel und -türspion: Was ist wirklich erlaubt?
Grundsätzlich ist es erlaubt, private Bereiche des eigenen Grundstücks per Video zu überwachen, die nur von Anwohner:innen betreten werden können. Areale wie Innenhöfe und Auffahrten, die von Paketlieferant:innen und anderen Personen prinzipiell auch betreten werden können, gelten datenschutzrechtlich allerdings als öffentlicher Raum. Sie sind deshalb strengeren Datenschutzgesetzen unterworfen.
Dazu zählt, dass die Überwachung nur auf dem eigenen Grundstück erfolgen darf und keine anderen Grundstücke, Wohnungen oder öffentlichen Straßen samt Gehweg erfasst werden dürfen. Zudem müssen Personen, die den Bereich betreten, vorab darüber informiert werden, dass eine Videoüberwachung stattfindet. Es muss ein „deutlich sichtbares, vorgelagertes Hinweisschild“ angebracht werden.
Ferner muss bei smarten Türklingeln wie der Ring-Kamera sichergestellt sein, dass sie nur „anlassbezogen“ aktiviert wird. Etwa dann, wenn jemand den Klingelknopf drückt. Eine dauerhafte Aufnahme des Bereiches ist nicht erlaubt. Die Kamera darf zudem nur den Eingangsbereich vor der Tür erfassen und muss sich nach kurzer Zeit wieder automatisch deaktivieren.
Sollten auf der Kamera dennoch Bereiche des öffentlichen Lebens zu sehen sein, müssen diese softwareseitig geschwärzt oder die Aufnahme durch physische Maßnahmen wie Blenden verhindert werden. Bei der softwareseitigen Lösung ist wichtig, dass sich die Schwärzung im Nachhinein nicht mehr rückgängig machen lässt. Zu guter Letzt sollten Aufnahmen im Idealfall nicht gespeichert werden. Allerdings bieten viele Produkte wie die Ring-Kameras eine solche Speicherung an.
Dann ist es wichtig, dass die Aufnahmen nur so lange gespeichert werden, „wie es dem vorher festgelegten Zweck erforderlich ist.“ Heißt: Soll das eigene Grundstück vor Einbrecher:innen oder Pakete vor dem Diebstahl geschützt werden, müssen die Aufnahmen gelöscht werden, sobald solche Vorfälle nicht eintreffen. In der Regel gilt dabei eine maximale Speicherdauer von 72 Stunden.
Welche Strafen drohen bei Verstößen?
Solltest du eine Ring-Kamera betreiben, die gegen die Datenschutzgesetze verstößt und das etwa von deinen verärgerten Nachbarn gemeldet werden, drohen Konsequenzen. Die unzulässige Videoüberwachung stellt laut dem Hessischen Beauftragten für Datenschutz eine Ordnungswidrigkeit dar, die nach Art. 83 Abs. 5 Buchst. a DS-GVO eine Geldstrafe nach sich ziehen kann. Die Höhe wird dabei in jedem Fall einzeln festgelegt.
Grundsätzlich können Nutzer:innen einer Ring-Kamera oder anderer smarter Türklingeln dazu aufgefordert werden, die nicht datenschutzkonform genutzten Geräte wieder zu entfernen. Sollten sie dem nicht nachkommen, kann das auch durch Zwang durchgesetzt werden. Sollten Personen, die aufgenommen wurden, auch Schadensersatz fordern, könnte das Ganze noch zivilrechtliche Konsequenzen nach sich ziehen. Etwa dann, wenn die aufgenommenen Clips im Netz geteilt werden, um auf eigene Faust nach vermeintlichen Dieb:innen oder Einbrecher:innen zu suchen.
))) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: El sistema de IA de la FAA bajo la lupa: enfrenta preguntas tras el colapso aéreo más grave desde 2023
articles.text:
La Administración Federal de Aviación (FAA) lleva años bajo presión por modernizar un sistema de control aéreo que opera con tecnología de décadas. Este año, la agencia dio uno de sus pasos más ambiciosos en esa dirección: contrató a una empresa de inteligencia artificial para rediseñar cómo se gestiona el tráfico en los cielos del país.
El resultado fue SMART, un sistema que prometía reducir demoras y cancelaciones, y que en cuestión de semanas pasó de proyecto piloto a herramienta nacional. Lo que nadie anticipaba era que su estreno a escala plena coincidiría con el peor colapso aéreo de Estados Unidos en casi cuatro años.
El viernes 13 de noviembre, la FAA ordenó la paralización total del espacio aéreo a las 3:54 p.m. hora del este.
El ground stop duró más de cuatro horas y dejó un saldo de más de 5.000 vuelos cancelados y al menos 827 desviados antes de las 7:05 p.m., según datos de Cirium citados por AP.
Qué es SMART y por qué quedó en el centro de la escena
El 10 de noviembre, la FAA extendió SMART (Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories) a los 22 centros de control de tráfico aéreo del país. Hasta ese momento, el sistema solo operaba como prueba piloto en la región de Washington D.C. desde septiembre.
SMART es una plataforma en la nube que analiza horarios de vuelo, condiciones climáticas, capacidad aeroportuaria y personal de control para anticipar congestionamientos y sugerir rutas más eficientes.
No reemplaza a los controladores humanos ni pilota aviones; sus recomendaciones pasan por revisión humana antes de aplicarse.
La coincidencia de fechas bastó para encender la especulación en redes sociales. En Politico, veteranos de la industria aérea ya habían expresado en septiembre su inquietud ante la descripción vaga que la FAA había dado del sistema. El despliegue nacional no hizo más que amplificar esas dudas.
La reacción oficial ante las dudas generadas
El secretario de Seguridad Nacional, Markwayne Mullin, confirmó que los investigadores no encontraron pruebas de un ciberataque ni de interferencia de inteligencia artificial en el incidente. Aun así, aclaró que la investigación permanecía abierta y que ninguna hipótesis estaba descartada.
El secretario de Transporte, Sean Duffy, fue más categórico respecto al sistema. “No hay forma posible de que SMART haya influido en lo que ocurrió”, afirmó durante la conferencia de prensa en la Casa Blanca, tal como recogió ABC News.
Duffy explicó que SMART provee recomendaciones a los controladores, pero no tiene conexión con los sistemas STARS ni ERAM, que son los núcleos operativos del control de tráfico aéreo.
Air Space Intelligence (ASI), la empresa desarrolladora del sistema, rechazó cualquier vínculo a través de su cuenta en X: “El actual ground stop no tiene origen ni es resultado del sistema SMART, ni de ningún producto de ASI, ni de nuestra integración con la FAA y el control de tráfico aéreo”.
Lo que dicen las primeras hipótesis sobre el origen del colapso
Duffy señaló un origen distinto al sistema de inteligencia artificial: una infraestructura de telecomunicaciones envejecida. “Tenemos un sistema de control aéreo increíblemente viejo”, declaró el secretario.
Los routers y switches de la FAA se sobrecargaron con datos hasta generar inconsistencias en la información de los radares, lo que activó los protocolos de seguridad y forzó el cierre del sistema, según informó AP.
El equipamiento digital instalado recientemente continuó operando con normalidad; los sistemas analógicos más antiguos fueron los que cedieron, que dependen de líneas de cobre.
CBS News informó que una actualización de software en el sistema privado de comunicaciones pudo haber disparado un reinicio masivo, aunque ese extremo permanece bajo investigación.
La ex controladora aérea Ruth Stilwell, experta en política aeroespacial, planteó como hipótesis que esa actualización pudo haber afectado el Voice Switching and Control System, el sistema que gestiona las comunicaciones entre pilotos y controladores.
“Sería inusual hacer una actualización de software durante el día, pero la FAA tiene una dotación de personal muy reducida”, dijo Stilwell en declaraciones a Scientific American.
Las consecuencias políticas y el debate que dejó el incidente
Duffy también convirtió el incidente en una presión directa al poder legislativo. El secretario reclamó USD 50.000 millones para renovar la infraestructura de la FAA y advirtió que, sin esa inversión, el país podría enfrentar nuevas interrupciones de este tipo.
El contrato de ASI con la agencia para el desarrollo de SMART asciende a USD 875 millones a lo largo de 12 años, un monto que contrasta con el estado del resto del sistema.
La FAA no llegó a perder totalmente el radar ni las comunicaciones durante el apagón; los vuelos médicos, de carga crítica y de fuerzas de seguridad quedaron exceptuados de la paralización, informó AP.
El viernes 13 fue el primer ground stop nacional desde enero de 2023, cuando falló el sistema NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions), y el segundo desde los ataques del 11 de septiembre de 2001.

articles.title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
articles.text:
Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows.
As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design.
The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology.
Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps.
“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”
Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery
Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale.
To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone.
That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions.
These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs.
NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries offer a growing set of optimized implementations of complex algorithms for agents to use, including those most relevant to simulation and analytics. Used together with Rubin HPC, the libraries can give agents the fastest glide path to reasoning outcomes.
And faster agent-invoked simulations mean faster feedback — shortening the loop of hypothesis, simulation and refinement, so researchers and engineers can choose next steps sooner and point lab work at the most promising candidates.
Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028.

articles.title: Microsoft Rules Out Cyberattack in Outage, Warns of Phishing Campaign
articles.text:
Microsoft says its recent Microsoft 365 outage was not caused by a cyberattack, but warns that attackers used the disruption to send phishing emails disguised as service notifications.
The November 12 outage disrupted access to Exchange Online mailboxes and Outlook. The tech giant also identified possible effects on services such as Teams, SharePoint Online and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Organizations and government agencies in several countries reported interruptions to email and other operations.
“This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents,” Microsoft said in a statement on Friday.
The company traced the failure to an earlier network capacity upgrade, with a subsequent network change exposing the problem. Microsoft said it fixed the underlying issue and was bringing services back in stages to ensure they remained stable. The Exchange Online incident, tracked as EX1550543, was marked resolved on November 13.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence said it observed a phishing campaign exploiting the disruption. The fake emails posed as Microsoft 365 service health notices and referred to EX1550543, the actual incident identifier.
In some messages detected on November 13, recipients were falsely told that emails held during the outage would be deleted within 24 hours unless they clicked a link to restore them.
The phishing emails’ subject lines began with “Outage -” followed by a six-character code. Sender display names included organization-specific wording followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.”
Microsoft identified three domains used to send the emails: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com. Recipient-specific SendGrid tracking links redirected to reallifeaccounting[.]com. Similar messages targeted organizations across several US sectors.
“The activity is consistent with credential phishing, although credential collection and malware delivery have not been confirmed,” Microsoft said.
The company subsequently reported that its security products were blocking the campaign.
Microsoft recommended that security teams examine suspicious emails and links, investigate user clicks, and review their Safe Links policies. It also advised organizations to verify service incidents directly through the Microsoft 365 admin center.

Related: Microsoft Struggles to Restore Email and Other Services in a Global Outage
