articles.title: United Airlines enfrenta pane em sistemas e afeta voos nos EUA
articles.text:
Em comunicado, a empresa afirmou que os voos que já estavam em andamento não foram afetados. As operações da United Express, que reúne companhias regionais parceiras da aérea, também permaneceram normais. Um porta-voz da United declarou que não havia indícios de ataque cibernético relacionado ao problema.
Em publicação no X, a companhia informou que suas equipes estavam trabalhando para restabelecer os sistemas o mais rápido possível. A orientação aos passageiros foi acompanhar a situação dos voos pelos canais oficiais da empresa.
Mais tarde, a companhia aérea informou que o problema foi resolvido.
Pilotos receberam orientação para aguardar nos portões
A falha chegou a interferir diretamente na rotina dos aeroportos. Uma gravação compartilhada em um aplicativo de monitoramento do tráfego aéreo registrou um piloto da United em Houston (EUA) solicitando autorização à torre de controle para permanecer no portão até que os sistemas fossem restabelecidos.
A situação evidencia como problemas tecnológicos podem afetar operações aéreas, mesmo quando não há qualquer alteração nas condições de voo das aeronaves que já estão no ar.
A Associated Press (AP) confirmou que a pane atingiu os sistemas da companhia e afetou partidas. A empresa pediu desculpas aos passageiros pelos transtornos.
Pane acontece três dias após paralisação nacional nos EUA
O novo problema surge apenas três dias depois de uma falha na infraestrutura da Administração Federal de Aviação dos Estados Unidos (FAA, na sigla em inglês) provocar paralisação nacional do tráfego aéreo.
Na sexta-feira (13), a agência determinou que aeronaves em solo não decolassem por mais de quatro horas. A medida foi adotada depois que problemas na rede de comunicação comprometeram sistemas utilizados no controle do tráfego aéreo.
O secretário de Transportes, Sean Duffy, atribuiu a ocorrência a um roteador instalado em Arkansas (EUA), que teria sobrecarregado os sistemas responsáveis por transmitir dados de radar e outras informações utilizadas pelos controladores.
Segundo a FAA, equipamentos antigos ficaram instáveis após receberem volume excessivo de dados. A investigação inicial apontou dois possíveis pontos de origem do problema: uma instalação de radar no Texas (EUA) e um centro de comunicação em Arkansas.
A agência informou que o tráfego aéreo foi retomado às 22h15 (horário de Brasília) de sexta-feira, mas a recuperação das operações das companhias levou mais tempo.
A paralisação provocou milhares de cancelamentos e atrasos. De acordo com a FAA, aproximadamente 12.462 voos foram cancelados naquele dia, embora nem todos os cancelamentos tenham sido consequência direta da ordem nacional.
Leia mais:
- Estados Unidos ampliam restrições a chips de IA e incluem o Brasil
- Retorno de Jensen Huang ao comando da Nvidia não é má ideia, diz Trump
- Governo Trump deve incluir Nvidia em grupo de campeãs nacionais de IA
Setor aéreo ainda tenta normalizar operações
A falha da United ocorreu enquanto as companhias aéreas estadunidenses ainda trabalhavam para recuperar suas operações após os problemas registrados no fim de semana.
Dados da plataforma FlightAware indicavam redução significativa nos atrasos e cancelamentos nesta segunda-feira, em comparação com o domingo (15).
A sequência de episódios também chama atenção por acontecer em meio a outras interrupções tecnológicas recentes nos Estados Unidos, incluindo problemas nos serviços da Microsoft e instabilidades relatadas por clientes de grandes bancos.
Até o momento, porém, não há evidências de causa comum entre essas ocorrências. No caso da United, a empresa informou que investigava falha tecnológica, sem indicação de ataque cibernético.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo. Original written by José Tadeu Arantes. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Xian-Peng Zhang, Chuanchang Zeng, Zhen-Biao Yang, Jose Carlos Egues, Yugui Yao. Andreev qubit readout from dynamic interference supercurrent. Physical Review B, 2026; 114 (8) DOI: 10.1103/6gkt-hghj

articles.title: Google Maps can now build trip itineraries with real-time details about each stop | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google announced on Monday that it’s rolling out new Maps features that are designed to help people plan trips and everyday tasks using AI. The company is launching the ability for Maps to create trip itineraries and find appointments for users.
The new features reflect a broader shift in how tech companies are positioning AI, which is less as a tool that just answers questions and more as an assistant that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. While many companies have released AI agents to complete these tasks, Google is working to bring that approach into a service that millions of people already use every day.
Google says users can use the navigation platform’s “Ask Maps” tool to build step-by-step trip itineraries and get real-time details about their route right when they pull up directions.
For example, you could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Google says. You’ll get a day-by-day itinerary with insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop. Once you’re happy with your itinerary, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.
When you’re ready to head out, you can use Ask Maps to reopen your itinerary or find the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll have access to real-time information, including traffic conditions, business hours, and a look at what the “vibe” is at your next stop, the company says. You could also adjust your schedule by asking Maps to do something like add a scenic viewpoint or lunch stop along your route. You can then tap any destination in your itinerary to get directions and navigate to your next stop.
Additionally, users can use Ask Maps to find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. For example, you could ask: “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will then display open slots across nearby businesses.
The new agentic calling feature arrives as tech companies continue to introduce AI agents designed to handle time-consuming tasks, such as scheduling DMV appointments and making reservations. For example, Meta’s AI agent Muse recently gained the ability to call businesses on users’ behalf.
Google also announced that you can now use Ask Maps to quickly find places on your lists by asking something like: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?”
The tech giant says the new updates are starting to roll out on Monday on Android and iOS. As part of the news, Google announced that Ask Maps is expanding to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the U.K.

articles.title: Verafin alum-led Verlo nabs $4.5 million to build AI operating system for wealth managers
articles.text:
Verlo has closed $4.5 million CAD in seed funding to reduce the administrative burden facing wealth managers using AI.
The news: The St. John’s startup, which bills itself as “the compliant AI operating system” for independent financial advisors and wealth management firms, announced the round on Monday. Toronto’s Staircase Ventures led with support from returning local backer Pelorus VC and angel investors, including founders and key executives from Canadian tech success story Verafin. The all-equity, all-primary capital financing round closed in October and brings Verlo’s total funding to $6.5 million. Verlo, which went live in March, aims to help wealth managers save time on admin work and focus more on growing their businesses without adding operational overhead. The startup plans to put this capital towards product development, adding another 10 employees to its 15-person team, and expansion in the United States.
From the source: “Verlo has the product, team, and traction to win,” Staircase Ventures founder and managing partner Janet Bannister said in a statement. “When we met Brent, we were immediately impressed by his tenacity, vision, bias for action, and understanding of the nuances of building great products in heavily regulated industries.”
The context: Verafin, which built financial crime detection software for banks and credit unions, sold to US stock exchange Nasdaq in 2020 in a massive, $2.7-billion USD ($3.8-billion CAD) cash deal. That deal was by far Atlantic Canada’s largest-ever tech exit, and still represents one of the country’s overall biggest to date. Like other Newfoundland and Labrador-based tech startups, Verlo’s Verafin connections run deep. Pretty, who launched Verlo in 2024, previously spent nearly five years leading AI workflow automation at Verafin as a product manager both pre- and post-acquisition. As founder and CEO Brett Pretty told BetaKit over email, “Working at Verafin was the best education I’ve ever gotten.” The startup’s team also features a number of other former Verafin staff with experience building software for the tightly regulated financial services industry.
Final thought: While legacy wealth management software providers are beginning to introduce AI, Pretty said in many cases, they “feel more like add-ons to existing workflows” than truly integrated, transformative tech. Verlo is betting that it can move the needle even further by ensuring all of its clients’ data is searchable to AI agents capable of helping advisors automate tasks like financial planning, portfolio reviews, client onboarding, and more.
Feature image courtesy Verlo.

articles.title: The Apple Watch Series 12 is cheaper than ever ahead of Black Friday
articles.text:
If you’re still sporting an Apple Watch that launched five or so years ago, now is a good time to upgrade. Apple’s latest smartwatch, the 42mm Apple Watch Series 12 with Wi-Fi and GPS connectivity, has dropped to a new all-time low of $329 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, beating the October Prime Day price by $20. If you prefer a larger size, the 46mm model is on sale for $379 ($70 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, which is also $20 lower than the previous best price.
The Apple Watch Series 12 is cheaper than ever ahead of Black Friday
Apple’s latest smartwatch introduces AI-powered audio features, redesigned health sensors, and faster charging.
The Series 12 stands out compared to previous models with its new AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, which are made possible by Apple’s new S11 chip. For example, the watch can alert you when it detects sounds like a doorbell, alarm, or even a baby’s cry, while other upcoming features like Live Rewind and Siri Recap lets you look back at a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of conversation and get a high-level overview of the conversations you had that day. The new chip also makes Siri more responsive, so you can get answers to questions with less waiting around.
It’s not all about AI, though. The Series 12 also features redesigned health sensors that can now track your heart rate every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, which is particularly help if you have a chronic condition and need to keep a closer eye on your heart rate. It also introduces a new readiness score to help you decide how prepared your body is for the day. Other highlights include easier navigation with simple pinch gestures, and faster charging, which helps to make up for the fact that battery life is rated at up to 24 hours on a single charge, just like the previous-generation model. In our testing, the watch went from 20 to 64 percent charge in just 20 minutes, making it relatively easy to top up while showering or getting ready for the day.

articles.title: Huawei lance une sous-marque, six ans après avoir vendu Honor — Frandroid
articles.text:
Une sous-marque, chez les fabricants chinois, sert d’habitude à vendre moins cher. Osta, la nouvelle griffe de Huawei, semble prendre le chemin inverse : son premier téléphone embarquerait 16 Go de mémoire vive, 1 To de stockage et la puce maison des modèles haut de gamme.
La dernière sous-marque du groupe, Honor, a été vendue fin 2020 pour échapper aux sanctions américaines. En relancer une, c’est assumer que Huawei a de nouveau les reins assez solides pour multiplier les gammes.
Richard Yu, président de la division grand public de Huawei, a confirmé sur Weibo, le réseau social chinois, qu’Osta (Xingmang en chinois, « lueur d’étoile ») sera présentée le 20 novembre en Chine, sur la même scène que le monospace électrique Stelato V8.
Le Black Friday est lancé sur l’univers Apple. Sur Back Market, profitez de promotions sur les iPhone, MacBook, iPad, AirPods et Apple Watch. Chaque appareil est soumis à jusqu’à 100 points de contrôle qualité et est livré avec une garantie de 12 mois. De quoi profiter de performances comparables à celles d’un produit neuf.
Le dépôt de marque couvre bien plus que les smartphones : tablettes, ordinateurs portables, montres, lunettes, écouteurs et même puces. Le premier modèle, l’Osta O1 Pro, est déjà en précommande en Chine en trois coloris.
Ses caractéristiques n’ont pas été publiées par Huawei, mais le leaker Digital Chat Station a tout détaillé : écran plat de 6,39 pouces en définition 1,5K, puce Kirin 9030S, batterie de 7 000 mAh, charge filaire de 66 W et sans fil, lecteur d’empreintes sur la tranche.
Un Pura X View avec une caméra en moins
Le format est la vraie signature de l’appareil. Son écran adopterait un ratio de 16:9,5, bien plus large que le 19,5:9 de la plupart des smartphones, avec des bordures de 1,05 mm : en main, on tient quelque chose qui ressemble davantage à un passeport qu’à une télécommande.
Huawei a inauguré cette silhouette en septembre avec le Pura X View, vendu à partir de 5 999 yuans en Chine (un peu plus de 700 euros) et jamais commercialisé en France. L’O1 Pro en reprend la diagonale, la batterie, la charge et le capteur principal de 200 Mpx de 1/1,28 pouce. Ce capteur utilise une matrice RYYB, où du jaune remplace le vert pour capter davantage de lumière, ce qui aide surtout les photos de nuit.
Les économies se voient ailleurs. L’O1 Pro se contenterait de deux caméras, le 200 Mpx et un téléobjectif périscopique de 50 Mpx (zoom optique 3,7x), là où le Pura X View ajoute un ultra grand-angle. Adieu donc les photos d’intérieur ou de groupe à bout de bras. L’écran passerait aussi d’une dalle LTPO à une dalle LTPS, une technologie moins chère qui ne sait pas descendre aussi bas en fréquence de rafraîchissement : l’écran redessine l’image même quand rien ne bouge, et la batterie le paie. En échange, la mémoire vive grimpe à 16 Go, contre 12 Go sur le Pura X View.
Le vrai pari est logiciel. Selon les fuites, Osta tournerait sous une déclinaison de HarmonyOS centrée sur l’intelligence artificielle, avec des agents intégrés au système, c’est-à-dire des assistants capables d’enchaîner des actions dans les applications à la place de l’utilisateur. Un message diffusé sur les réseaux, dont l’auteur n’est pas identifiable, évoque aussi un compagnon IA baptisé « Little Starlight ». Côté officiel, Richard Yu dit vouloir « explorer de nouvelles possibilités de l’IA », sans préciser lesquelles.

articles.title: New NoisyTCP vulnerability lets attackers crash Linux servers
articles.text:
An 11-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability, dubbed NoisyTCP, affects almost all Linux distributions and lets attackers crash systems running Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers with default configurations.
According to Hyunwoo Kim, the security researcher who discovered it, this pre-authenticated remote corruption flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-99288) stems from a NULL pointer dereference weakness in the Linux kernel's TCP networking subsystem.
Unauthenticated attackers can trigger it remotely via maliciously crafted TCP packets that exploit the timing between SYN cookie handling and socket hashing to crash the kernel and operating system on targeted servers.
However, while CVE-2026-99288 exploits cause a kernel panic and take down the host, they don't allow threat actors to alter data or gain arbitrary code execution.
Kim added that although attackers can exploit this vulnerability against any Linux system that receives TCP packets directly and runs Nginx, Apache, or an SSH server, "the race window is narrow, so triggering it against a quiet bare-metal server can take a long time."
"Due to a race condition during lockless socket lookups, recycled socket memory can be accessed before it is properly initialized and hashed. A remote attacker could exploit this issue by generating network traffic that drives socket reuse, triggering a NULL pointer dereference and kernel crash that results in a Denial of Service (DoS)," the Red Hat security team explained.
"To trigger this vulnerability, a stale ehash lookup and the freeing and reallocation of an existing request socket must proceed concurrently in different RX contexts. Packet processing has to be spread out by using the difference in receive hash between IPv4 fragments and regular TCP packets, so it can be triggered against servers that have two or more RX queues, or where RPS distributes packets across multiple CPUs," the researcher said.
While a CVE-2026-99288 patch is already available and a fix was already merged into the mainline Linux kernel two weeks ago, the researcher advised those who can't apply it or upgrade immediately to disable SYN cookies (which will unfortunately lower protection against SYN flood attacks) and serialize to a single RX queue to block the race required for successful exploitation.
In May, Kim also disclosed Dirty Frag, a Linux local privilege escalation flaw that chains RxRPC (CVE-2026-43500) and xfrm-ESP (CVE-2026-43284) page-cache write flaws to gain root access on major distributions, including Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, CentOS Stream, and Fedora.
More recently, in July, he also disclosed Januscape, a 16-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability that enables attackers to escape a virtual machine and run arbitrary code on the host.

articles.title: Il faut sauver le soldat Jensen Huang : une « war room » de la Silicon Valley veut le remettre à la tête de Nvidia
articles.text:
Jensen Huang pourrait-il s’en sortir à la tête de Nvidia, malgré les affaires qui l’ont conduit à démissionner de l’une des entreprises les plus valorisées au monde ? C’est le scénario qu’explore le Financial Times dans son édition du 15 novembre 2026, en observant de grandes manœuvres en cours dans la Silicon Valley pour le faire revenir au poste de CEO.
D’après le quotidien britannique, qui base ses informations sur un allié de Jensen Huang, une véritable « war room » est en phase de constitution pour faire pression sur le conseil d’administration et décrocher le soutien de la Maison-Blanche afin de reconfier les rênes de Nvidia à son emblématique patron.
Un soutien réel dans la Silicon Valley
Cette cellule de crise réunit des dirigeants de la Silicon Valley, d’après le Financial Times, et Jensen Huang soutiendrait la démarche. Toujours selon cet allié, « tout ce qui compte dans la tech, en dehors des laboratoires de pointe, adore Jensen ». Dès lors, l’intérim confié à Colette Kress, la directrice financière, pourrait tourner court.
En parallèle, une lettre ouverte intitulée « Stand with Jensen » demande qu’il soit réintégré le temps qu’une enquête indépendante établisse les faits. Elon Musk et Tim Sweeney, CEO d’Epic Games, l’ont signée, et elle comptait au moins 179 000 signataires ce lundi matin, dont plus de 10 000 se décrivant comme salariés actuels ou passés de Nvidia.
Mais comme le souligne Forbes, ces affiliations sont déclaratives et n’ont pas été vérifiées. Idem pour les actionnaires (plus de 94 000 recensés, dixit la pétition). Le site qui recense les soutiens admet d’ailleurs qu’il ne vérifie pas lui-même les affirmations des uns et des autres. La mention « optionnel et auto-déclaré » est d’ailleurs présente.
Cela dit, le soutien d’une partie des salariés à l’égard de Jensen Huang est réel. En lisant des commentaires internes, Wired a relevé 1 600 réactions sur le sujet, dont une partie plaide ouvertement pour le retour de l’ex-CEO. Il est difficile cependant de connaître l’ampleur du soutien, d’autant que Nvidia compte 42 000 employés dans le monde.
L’appui que reçoit Jensen Huang depuis l’éclatement de l’affaire apparaît à la mesure du lien qu’il a tissé avec l’entreprise qu’il a fondée. Pendant 33 ans, Nvidia n’a eu qu’un seul patron, devenu une figure majeure de la tech aux USA et dans le monde, transformant ce groupe en un carrefour du jeu vidéo et de l’IA, grâce aux cartes graphiques.
Le conseil d’administration n’avait désigné aucun successeur après Jensen Huang, aujourd’hui âgé de 63 ans. Et pourtant, l’intéressé a démissionné le 12 novembre 2026 dans la foulée du scandale.
Avant son départ de Nvidia, Jensen Huang a reconnu une liaison avec Alice Huang, ancienne dirigeante de la société singapourienne Megaspeed, que le renseignement américain soupçonne d’espionner pour la Chine. Le New York Times a ensuite révélé une relation avec une cadre de Nvidia qui travaillait sous ses ordres. Et depuis, une troisième liaison est apparue au grand jour.
Le conseil d’administration de Nvidia garde la main
Le lobbying en cours dont le Financial Times se fait l’écho trahit de facto l’impuissance de Jensen Huang à se maintenir à la tête de Nvidia. L’ex-CEO ne possède pas assez de pouvoirs ou d’actions pour imposer son retour au conseil d’administration, et rien ne dit par ailleurs que ses alliés auront assez de poids pour faire un contrepoids suffisant.
L’un des participants à la campagne reconnaît qu’« avoir une liaison avec une subordonnée est un motif de licenciement », et d’autres se demandent comment il pourrait réparer les dégâts sur sa réputation. Et à cela s’ajoute la crainte d’une manœuvre d’espionnage de Pékin pour obtenir des données sensibles et contourner les restrictions américaines.
Du côté de l’administration Trump, dont la « war room » espère le soutien, le secrétaire au Trésor, au moins, est loin d’être convaincu.
Dimanche 15 novembre, Scott Bessent, le secrétaire au Trésor de Donald Trump, a estimé que Nvidia devait chercher son prochain CEO en dehors de l’entreprise. Il a aussi donné 10 jours au conseil et à ses avocats pour répondre à ses questions sur le respect des restrictions d’exportation de puces vers la Chine.
Au Congrès, trois commissions de la Chambre des représentants, dont la commission spéciale sur la Chine, avaient menacé Jensen Huang d’une assignation s’il refusait de venir s’expliquer sur sa relation avec la femme soupçonnée d’espionnage. Il a accepté de témoigner à huis clos, selon le président la commission sur la Chine, rapporte Bloomberg.
Le conseil, lui, a déjà regardé hors de l’entreprise. D’après le Financial Times, il a approché Rene Haas, CEO du concepteur de puces britannique Arm.

articles.title: AI Day Seoul Brings Together Korea’s Industry Leaders, Startups and Developer Communities
articles.text:
Over two days at COEX, more than 2,000 attendees converged for AI Day Seoul, bringing together Korea’s industry leaders, startups and developer communities advancing physical AI and AI agents.
At the plenary sessions, Deepu Talla, vice president of robotics and edge AI at NVIDIA, said Korea is “punching above its weight,” with Doosan Robotics, Hyundai Motor Group, LG Electronics and SK Group — as well as startups like Real World and Luda Robotics — using NVIDIA platforms to bring general-purpose robotics into the real world.
Jonathan Cohen, vice president of applied research at NVIDIA, showed how enterprises can build agents they own and control. Breakout sessions featured speakers from Coupang Intelligent Cloud, Doosan Robotics, LG AI Research, LG Electronics, NAVER Cloud, SK Telecom and Upstage.
“It was a genuinely enjoyable time to have candid conversations,” said Hyunho Yang, research engineer for omnimodal foundation models at SK Telecom. “Seeing the passion of fellow AI developers was a real source of inspiration for me.”
The Agentic AI 10x Bootcamp Community Day brought together Pseudo Lab, Python Korea, PyTorchKR, HAERAE, Hugging Face KREW, Graph User Group, Womxn Who Code Korea, Dnol (Datayanolja) and other developer communities. Five finalists from the Hangul Day hackathon, co-hosted with Fastcampus, built agents trained on the Korean language and culture with the OpenShell runtime. The winning team, FlyGate, received an NVIDIA DGX Spark system.
More than 500 developers also took part in full-day NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute workshops and NVIDIA Certification exams in Korean. Workshops covered deploying and optimizing AI inference at scale, building end-to-end robotics workflows with the NVIDIA Isaac platform and developing secure AI agents. Certification included the new AI Model and Application Development exam.
The Physical AI Startup Connect event included pitches from 10 NVIDIA Inception startups: AIM Intelligence, Avikus, GoLe Robotics, MOVIN, Neubility, ROAI, ROBROS, TESOLLO, TwelveLabs and XYZ. The AI for Science Forum brought together the Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information, Korean universities and NVIDIA Research.
AI Day Seoul sessions will soon be available on NVIDIA On-Demand.

articles.title: The small African lab sounding the alarm on AI bioweapons
articles.text:
Out of curiosity, researchers at a small artificial intelligence lab in Accra, Ghana, removed the guardrails on their drug discovery AI model in 2024. They asked it to design toxins instead.
The model produced designs for 1,020 proteins and 5,000 small molecules. The researchers never made any of them in a lab, but software that predicts how poisonous a substance is scored all of them as likely toxic. Some of them resembled ricin, a deadly poison. The study was uploaded to the preprint server arXiv in May 2025.
“We were all shocked,” Darlington Akogo, founder of MinoHealth AI Labs, told Rest of World.
For Akogo, the results also raised a new question: If someone took designs like these to a company that makes DNA to order, would anyone stop them?
Across Africa, the need to regulate DNA synthesis providers is now echoing through the highest levels of government, Brenda Obuya, a senior official at Kenya’s Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, told Rest of World.
Akogo has traveled the world warning that AI poses an existential bioweapons threat. He discussed it on the sidelines of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund Spring Meetings held in Washington, D.C., last year. He discussed the broader risk over dinner with Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates in 2023, whom he described as “on the fence” at the time. This year, Gates has issued numerous public warnings. “A.I. has crossed the threshold that its ability to empower a bioterrorist to kill hundreds of millions, that exists today,” he said on The Ezra Klein Show in September. The study has been discussed within Interpol, showing just how far it has reached.
“I think the fact that the Ghanaian AI lab examined this and highlighted the potential for misuse shows that African institutions are contributing to … potentially to the governance [of AI],” Adam Abdullahi, a fellow at the International Biosecurity and Biosafety Initiative for Science, told Rest of World.
LLMs have become even more capable since the study came out and the barrier for entry has lowered, Ayantola Alayande, a researcher at the Global Center on AI Governance, told Rest of World. “It wouldn’t be a surprise now to see even … [lay] users generate this sort of output via chatbots.”
Dual use
Scholars have long warned about AI’s bioweapons threat, but it is only recently that AI systems have truly outperformed Ph.D.-level biologists.
In 2022, scientists at a U.S. drug company ran a similar experiment as the MinoHealth team. They built a generative machine learning software that produced designs for possible chemical weapons.
What is different with the MinoHealth Lab study, Akogo said, is the kind of AI involved. His team used a general purpose LLM trained for biology and drug discovery.
Researchers have since gotten a number of LLMs to drop their inbuilt safeguards in a process called “jailbreaking”, and generated bioweapons advice and other kinds of hazardous content. This includes Kimi, by the Chinese company Moonshot AI; Grok; Claude; and ChatGPT, said Peter Garraghan, founder of AI security company Mindgard. All it takes is persistence and creativity with language to learn how to phrase requests to the model, he told Rest of World.
“You don’t need to be a technical expert to do jailbreaking,” he said. It took his team one day to break Kimi.
SpaceXAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Moonshot did not respond to a request for comment.
The latest AI models have stronger safeguards, particularly when it comes to biological misuse requests, but even these are not foolproof, according to the AI Security Institute, a U.K. government research organization.
The danger became more real this September when Anthropic reported five cases where people tried to use its AI models in ways that could support biological weapons development. Bioweapons are now the top AI misuse risk, according to Ken McCallum, director general of MI5, the U.K.’s intelligence agency. “The misuse case to which I’d attach greatest weight – is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons,” he said.
All-in-one health AI model
When Akogo founded MinoHealth Labs in 2016, he wasn’t worried about bioweapons. Rather, he wanted to make care available to all by solving Ghana’s health worker shortage using AI.
That goal took Akogo to the edge of AI development in 2022, when his team began work on an LLM named Moremi AI. A year later, they received $149,533 from the Gates Foundation to build a foundation model that can analyze medical images for radiologists. The model would eventually process both text and images, answer medical questions, help interpret scans, and draft reports. It would also help design drugs.
The ambition is similar in scope to top Silicon Valley labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic, Leo Anthony Celi, a principal research scientist at the MIT Laboratory of Computational Physiology, told Rest of World. In October 2025, Anthropic launched Claude for Life Sciences, and this April, Open AI launched GPT-Rosalind. Both are AI tools developed to accelerate biology research and drug discovery. Investment in AI powered drug discovery reached $8.4 billion in 2025, more than double the $4.1 billion invested in 2023, according to a 2026 McKinsey report.
MinoHealth has a fraction of these resources and a 20-member team working in a modest bungalow in Accra that is the anti-thesis of Silicon Valley’s futuristic campuses.
In the early days, Akogo had sleepless nights. He worried his competitors were better funded, and had more talent. But he has since decided there is room for multiple companies working on specific use cases.
“I have a small team of extremely capable people so if that means we’re punching above our weight, I guess … it’s just more exciting,” he said.
When his team tested their model, Moremi Bio, in 2024 to see if it could be made to ignore safeguards, it took them only a few days, Akogo recalled. Few people back then knew that biology LLMs’ could have a dual purpose, so he decided to publish his findings. “To the best of our knowledge, [looking at published studies], this was the first time anyone was showing that LLMs specifically could design biological weapons,” he said.
AI models shouldn’t be able to design potential bioweapons, Abdullahi said. “The whole idea of putting guardrails is that it should never really kind of get to that stage, so to speak.”
Synthesis
Bad actors could potentially send the bioweapon designs to DNA synthesis labs to make the molecules. Although some labs screen orders for potentially toxic sequences, this process could be hacked by a malicious actor using AI, Akogo said.
In June, the heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind joined a call for U.S. lawmakers to make such checks mandatory.
Governments across Africa recognize that open-source frontier models have lowered the technical barrier to generate toxins, said Obuya from Kenya’s Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy. Cloud laboratories and AI models have created a need for regulation, she said. Intelligence agencies are setting up specialized desks to track threats at the “intersection of cyber defense and biology,” she said.
As AI design tools develop, screening must keep pace, Sandra Roy, program manager at the International Gene Synthesis Consortium, a voluntary group of nucleic acid providers, told Rest of World. They support legislation that would mandate screening across the nucleic acid supply chain, she said.
“We are also working with model developers to strengthen our ability to detect AI-designed sequences that may be engineered to evade screening, and we will keep updating our tools as the threat evolves,” she said.
AI for healthcare
Moremi Bio is currently good at a few things. For instance, it has proposed hundreds of drug candidates for diseases such as cancer, tuberculosis, and dengue. The team is now working as part of a European Union-funded consortium to develop monoclonal antibodies and diagnostics for mpox and malaria. The company is predominantly funded through sales of its AI system, Akogo said.
The promise of AI in healthcare and biology aside, Akogo continues to raise the alarm over AI risks, especially bioweapons. He believes the United Nations should set up a dedicated working group to study the risks of AI. He also suggested tighter controls over synthesis. His goal isn’t to scare people, but rather, to balance AI optimism with caution.
“I think there’s several things we can do that could limit and minimize those dangers,” he said.

articles.title: Did Canada lose its AI chip champions?
articles.text:
Last month, Toronto-founded AI chip maker Tenstorrent announced a whopping $1.5-billion USD Series E round. I say Toronto-founded because the company quietly relocated to the US in 2023 to support its fundraising and IPO goals. With over $2 billion USD in funding announced since, the move appears to have paid off.
Tenstorrent still has some 200 employees in Toronto, and hasn’t forgotten its Canadian roots. The Logic reported this week that the company has lobbied the federal government for sovereign AI contracts and funding for large-scale data centre buildouts.
Every company should be expected to make decisions in its own best interests. But Tenstorrent’s gentle tap dance back and forth across our southernmost border when it benefits them shines a light on a murky question: what makes a company Canadian?
Noting that the feds’ Buy Canadian Policy currently allows for, say, Walmart Canada, the policy wonks at The Canadian Shield Institute have argued for a revised definition in BetaKit. The think tank also recently asserted the perils of considering companies like Tenstorrent Canadian enough: “If any company, headquartered anywhere on earth, can qualify for funding because its lobbyists point to some operations here or some historic association with Canada, then economic development policy will become meaningless.”
This week, I interviewed AI Minister Evan Solomon about the federal government’s investment in Cohere. The interview will be released soon, but Tenstorrent came up. The minister said his job was to give tech companies reasons not to leave, using levers like compute, customers, and capital (i.e., why Tenstorrent said it left). But he also seemed OK with now-foreign entities continuing to hire and do business in Canada. “We want that,” he said. “They’re investing in Canadian talent.”
Successful economic development policy requires striking the tricky balance between short-term realities and long-term priorities. In the midst of Nvidia’s historic, shareholder-value-destroying self-own, it seems possible that Tenstorrent (or Untether AI or Taalas—both sold to AMD) could have been federally anointed an AI champion like Cohere had they stayed. The feds still might, but would Tenstorrent really be a sovereign selection? And if not, would it matter?
Douglas Soltys, 
Editor-in-Chief
One place for every payment your business makes.
More than 10,000 Canadian businesses use Float to issue CAD and USD corporate cards, pay bills and send money in 21 currencies, with no bank portal or second login. EFT, ACH and SEPA payments are free, and eligible bills paid by Float card earn up to 1% cashback on card spend over $25K a month.
Float Intelligence reads the GST, HST, PST and QST split off every invoice, helping finance teams close their books up to 8x faster.
Top stories from BetaKit
Real-time rail is here
After more than a decade of development and many delays, eight financial institutions, including Wealthsimple and Koho, have joined the first phase of Canada’s Real-Time Rail payments system. BetaKit sat down with Fintechs Canada executive director Adriana Vega to better understand what a successful execution of the system would look like and why it needs the as-of-yet absent Big Six banks to succeed.
Blue J takes flight
AI tax research platform Blue J raised a $176-million USD Series E round this week after more than doubling its annual recurring revenue in just over a year. Blue J CEO Ben Alarie told BetaKit the company plans to expand its agentic offerings to take more off accountants’ plates and build “Canada’s next great tech company right here from Toronto.”
Boson treasures Toronto
Well-funded US AI research lab Boson AI started quietly building a Toronto office in 2023 as a prudent “Plan B.” Now it houses around half of its 40 staff and has proven a valuable location for its compute, talent, and predictability, Boson co-founder and CEO Alex Smola told BetaKit.
Acquisitions ramp up
While Canadian venture capital activity is broadly on par with last year, disclosed exit proceeds have already more than doubled compared to 2025, according to CVCA’s Q3 report. Exit proceeds totalled $744 million CAD across 10 disclosed transactions, which is more than double the $355 million in disclosed exit value for all of 2025.
Why the feds reserved sovereign compute
The recent federal budget committed to making 500 megawatts of sovereign AI compute available for domestic companies. As smaller AI startups get crowded out by hyperscalers in the compute race, Canadian tech sees promise in the feds’ pledge to save them a seat at the table.

CIBC’s security chief on how AI is changing cybersecurity
As AI supercharges the speed and sophistication of cyber threats, CIBC is shifting toward earlier security integration and rapid vulnerability remediation while outlining how tech startups can win long-term enterprise partnerships through seamless workflow integration.
Coraltalk wants universities to stop chasing AI cheaters and start measuring learning
Backed by York University’s YSpace, EdTech startup Coraltalk is helping universities move beyond unreliable AI-cheating detectors by using conversational AI to scale individualized oral exams that evaluate students’ true reasoning and comprehension.
Fall applications are now open: hire a student with up to $5,000 in wage support
TECHNATION’s Career Ready Program, funded by the Government of Canada’s Student Work Placement Program, covers up to 50% of a student’s wage, to a maximum of $5,000, for a work term with your company. Whether you need extra hands this fall or want to meet your future hires early, it’s a simple way to add fresh tech talent and keep costs down.

articles.title: Use prompt caching with open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Use prompt caching with open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock
Many generative AI applications send the same long context with every request, and prompt caching avoids processing it again each time. That context can be a system prompt, reference documents, tool definitions, or the conversation so far. Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock can reuse it across requests, which helps reduce input costs and response latency.
Prompt caching reuses the computed state of a matching prompt prefix, so repeated context is read from cache instead of being processed again. Amazon Bedrock manages the cache for you. Depending on the model, you can use implicit caching, which works automatically, explicit caching, where you mark the reusable prefix, or both. The more context you reuse, and the more often you reuse it, the more you can save.
As with other models on Amazon Bedrock, your prompts and outputs aren’t shared with the model provider or used to train models. For more information, see Data protection in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.
Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock now support explicit prompt caching. In this post, we use both modes with an open-weight model through the Chat Completions API and show how to read cache usage from each response. We then apply implicit caching to an OpenCode coding agent session on the same API and close with best practices.
Prompt caching for open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock
When a request starts with the same content as an earlier one, Amazon Bedrock reads that prefix from cache and processes only the rest. Cache reads are billed at a lower rate than standard input, so the savings can grow each time a prefix is reused. Depending on the model, cache writes can be billed at a higher rate than standard input. See Amazon Bedrock pricing for the rates of each model.
Supported modes depend on the model and the API. For each model’s caching modes, minimum prefix length, and how long entries stay cached, see Models at a glance. The two modes compare as follows:
| Feature | Implicit caching | Explicit caching | 
| Request changes | None | On the Chat Completions API, prompt_cache_options with mode set to explicit, plus one or more prompt_cache_breakpoint markers | 
| What is cached | Eligible prefixes, selected automatically on a best-effort basis | Content up to and including each breakpoint | 
| Good fit | Prompts that already start with a stable prefix, such as conversations and agent loops | A fixed shared prefix with a changing question, or layered prefixes that you want to control | 
Implicit caching: Amazon Bedrock reuses eligible prefixes automatically, on a best-effort basis. In a conversation, each request resends the full context, so the previous request becomes the cached prefix of the next one (Figure 1). As the prompt caching guide recommends, put static content first and dynamic content last. Keeping the start of the prompt stable lets every later request reuse it. If an early part changes, as in turn 4 of Figure 1, the cache is rebuilt from that point.
Explicit caching: You mark the end of each reusable prefix with a cache breakpoint. You can add several breakpoints, up to the maximum that the model supports, to cache layers that change at different rates, as Figure 2 shows. Content up to each breakpoint is written to cache once and then read on later requests, and content after the last breakpoint is processed on each request. Check the model card for the minimum token count before a breakpoint, the maximum number of breakpoints, and the time to live (TTL), which resets with each cache hit.
With implicit caching, Amazon Bedrock can also write content to cache that later requests never reuse, such as a question that’s different each time. When the content after a shared prefix changes on every request, use explicit caching to limit cache writes to the shared prefix. Content after the last breakpoint is billed at the standard input rate. On models that charge more for cache writes, you don’t pay the higher write rate for content that’s never read back.
Solution overview
The following diagram shows how both examples in this post reach Amazon Bedrock through the same Chat Completions API endpoint.
- The Python application and the OpenCode coding agent send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint in your Region, authenticated with a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key.
- Amazon Bedrock checks the prompt cache for a matching prefix. It reads a matching prefix from cache, and writes new cacheable content to cache.
- Amazon Bedrock sends the request to the selected open-weight model and returns the response, including the cache usage fields that the following sections show you how to read.
Prerequisites
To run the samples, you need the following:
- An AWS account with access to your selected model on Amazon Bedrock. Model availability and prompt caching support vary by AWS Region, so check the model card for the Regions that your model supports.
- AWS credentials for an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity that has permission to invoke your selected model on Amazon Bedrock.
- Python 3.12 with the openai (3.26.0 or later) and aws-bedrock-token-generator (1.1.0 or later) packages.
- For the coding agent example, npm to install OpenCode 1.18.35.
Before you use a model, review its license and service terms, linked from its model card. Your use of the model is also subject to the AWS Responsible AI Policy.
Cache a product manual through the Chat Completions API
The example is a support assistant for a fictional water filter, the AnyCompany AquaPure 500. The system prompt holds a one-line instruction and the owner’s manual, which is the reusable prefix. Each request asks a different customer question.
Set up the client
The samples use the OpenAI Python SDK with the Amazon Bedrock Chat Completions endpoint. For authentication, the provide_token() function from the aws-bedrock-token-generator package turns your AWS credentials into a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key, valid for up to 12 hours. You don’t need to create or store a long-term key.
1. Create a virtual environment and install the packages:
2. Create the manual. Ours is about 4,000 tokens of Markdown. The following excerpt shows its format:
Save it as manual.md and add sections until it’s longer than the minimum prefix length on your model card. Placeholder text works, because the cache only needs an identical prefix. Keep the three sections shown, which answer the sample questions.
3. Save the following setup code as common.py in the same directory. The samples that you create next import from it.
If your model returns reasoning tokens, they count toward max_tokens. The samples set max_tokens=1024 so that short answers have room to finish.
Implicit caching
Implicit caching takes no cache controls. Put the manual in the system message and the question in the user message. Sending both as parts of one user message got no implicit cache hits. Save the following as implicit.py and run it with python implicit.py:
Verify implicit caching
Each response reports cache activity in usage.prompt_tokens_details. Figure 4 shows how to read these fields and the pattern to expect across the three calls of each sample.
In implicit mode, call 1 writes the prompt to cache. Calls 2 and 3 read the system message, with the instruction and the manual, back from cache. They also write a few tokens each, because implicit mode extends the cached prefix to cover each new question. A few tokens after the last message stay uncached on every call. This is the pattern for the first run. If you run the sample again within the TTL, every call reads from cache, and none writes.
Explicit caching
Choose explicit caching to control exactly what is cached. As Figure 4 shows, calls 2 and 3 of the implicit run each write a few tokens to cache, whereas the same calls with explicit caching write nothing. With several breakpoints, you can cache layered prefixes, such as shared instructions and tools followed by a per-customer document (Figure 2).
For explicit caching, add the following to the request:
- prompt_cache_options with mode set to explicit selects explicit mode. It’s an Amazon Bedrock request field, and the OpenAI SDK sends it through extra_body.
- prompt_cache_breakpoint on a text content part marks the end of the reusable prefix. Content up to and including that part is cached, and content after it’s processed again on every request.
Save the explicit version of the same loop as explicit.py:
Set both parts together. Explicit mode without a breakpoint caches nothing, and a breakpoint without explicit mode behaves like implicit caching. For the optional ttl field of prompt_cache_options, check the model card for supported values.
Verify explicit caching
If you run explicit.py right after implicit.py, its first call is already a cache hit. For a cold first call, add a unique first line to the system prompt, for example SYSTEM_PROMPT = f"Run ID: {uuid.uuid4()}\n" + SYSTEM_PROMPT (with import uuid at the top of explicit.py).
As the explicit bars in Figure 4 show, only the first call writes. Each repeat reads the whole prefix up to the breakpoint and writes nothing, and the question after the breakpoint makes up the uncached remainder.
Use prompt caching with the OpenCode coding agent
Coding agents resend a large, stable prefix on every step: the system prompt, tool definitions, and the conversation so far. That makes them a natural fit for implicit caching. OpenCode is an open source coding agent. It can call any Chat Completions endpoint through a custom OpenAI-compatible provider, so it can use the same Amazon Bedrock endpoint as the Python samples. Figure 5 shows the requests that OpenCode sends during one turn and which parts Amazon Bedrock reads from cache.
In one turn, OpenCode sends request 1 with its system prompt, tool definitions, and your prompt, and Amazon Bedrock writes it to cache. The model responds with a tool call, which OpenCode runs on your machine. OpenCode then sends request 2, which contains request 1 plus the tool call and its result. Amazon Bedrock reads request 1 from cache, writes only the new tail, and returns the response.
Configure OpenCode
Install OpenCode and check the version:
Next, add the following opencode.json to the root of your repository, or save it as ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json to apply it to every project. It defines a provider named bedrock that uses the OpenAI-compatible package to call the Amazon Bedrock Chat Completions endpoint:
OpenCode uses small_model for session titles, so pointing it at the same model keeps every request on a model that you’ve enabled. The provider reads its key from BEDROCK_API_KEY. Set it to a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key from provide_token(), in the virtual environment from the first example. If the key expires, run the command again to get a new one:
Confirm that OpenCode lists the model:
Verify implicit caching in a coding session
We ran a three-turn session against a small repository that holds one short Python file. Turn 1 asks for a bug review, turn 2 for a fix, and turn 3 for a short follow-up:
Replace <sessionID> with the sessionID value from the JSON output of turn 1. The opencode export <sessionID> command lists each request’s token usage: cache.read holds the cached_tokens value from Amazon Bedrock, and input holds the rest. OpenCode 1.18.35 doesn’t record cache_write_tokens for an OpenAI-compatible provider, so cache.write stays at 0.
Figure 6 shows how much of each request in the session is read from cache.
The first request processes the whole prompt, most of it the OpenCode system prompt and tool definitions, and Amazon Bedrock writes it to cache. Each later request reads everything up to the end of the previous request from cache, so only the new tail of the conversation is processed. This works with no caching configuration.
Best practices
These practices apply to any model that supports prompt caching:
- Put static content first, in both modes. Place the system prompt, tool definitions, and reference documents before content that changes, and keep them identical between requests. In explicit mode, place each breakpoint after the static content that it covers. Timestamps and request IDs belong at the end of the prompt.
- Make the prefix long enough. Prefixes that meet the minimum token count on the model card are eligible for caching.
- Confirm hits with the usage fields. Check the cache reads and writes in each response, in either mode. Across a workload, track the CacheReadInputTokenCount and CacheWriteInputTokenCount runtime metrics.
- Keep the cache warm. Steady traffic keeps a prefix cached, because the TTL resets with each hit. After an idle gap longer than the TTL, the next request writes the prefix again.
- Cache what you reuse. Savings come from cache reads, so cache content that later requests read again, especially where cache writes cost more than standard input. With cross-Region inference, expect some extra cache writes at times of high demand.
Clean up
The examples make inference calls only and create no resources in your AWS account. Cache entries expire after they go unread for the TTL. The short-term API key from provide_token() also expires on its own, and the samples never write it to disk. To clear it from your shell sooner, run unset BEDROCK_API_KEY.
To remove the local files:
1. Delete the sample directory and its Python virtual environment.
2. Delete opencode.json from your repository, or ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json if you saved it globally.
3. If you no longer need OpenCode, delete ~/.local/opt/opencode.
Conclusion
Prompt caching lets open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock reuse repeated context with little or no change to your code. In this post, implicit caching covered the support assistant and the OpenCode session with no cache settings at all. Explicit caching gave precise control with one request option and a breakpoint for each reusable layer. In every case, the usage fields on each response show what came from cache, so you can measure the benefit on your own traffic.
To get started, choose an open-weight model on Amazon Bedrock that supports prompt caching. Run the samples from this post with your own reference content, and compare the cache reads with your uncached input. The prompt caching guide covers the limits and options for each model, and the Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics let you track cache reads and writes across your applications. For questions, reach out through AWS Support or the AWS re:Post community.

articles.title: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Achieves up to 2x Blackwell Ultra Performance in MLPerf Training v6.1 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
As AI agents tackle increasingly complex workflows, reducing time-to-train is critical for rapidly iterating on both models and the agents they power. MLPerf Training v6.1 marks the debut of the NVIDIA Vera Rubin architecture, and these early results demonstrate that its CUDA software stack is already highly mature. In its first appearance, the Vera Rubin NVL72 platform delivered the fastest time to train on six of the seven benchmarks, achieving up to 2x more performance than a highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 baseline.
For the seventh benchmark, DeepSeek-V3 671B, NVIDIA captured the absolute fastest time of the round by demonstrating massive scale on a 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 cluster. This dual-platform approach deliberately showcases the strengths of both systems. While the GB300 results highlight the massive, reliable cluster scale NVIDIA is deploying today, Vera Rubin demonstrated its own exceptional scaling architecture by maintaining above 97% overall efficiency when scaling from 256 to 1,024 GPUs. Together, NVIDIA platforms hold the fastest time to train on every benchmark in v6.1.
NVIDIA platforms were also the only ones to submit results across all seven benchmarks, with Vera Rubin successfully completing the entire suite in its inaugural run. For developers, this breadth matters as much as any single top-line number. It proves that the performance gains inherited on day one span the entire modeling pipeline, comprehensively supporting everything from large-scale pretraining to the reinforcement learning post-training required for modern AI agents.
Comprehensive AI performance across all MLPerf training benchmarks
The simplest way to read this round is per benchmark: How much more performance does the new platform deliver per GPU on the same model?
| Model type | Benchmark | GPU Count | Vera Rubin NVL72 vs. optimized GB300 NVL72 | Submission ID (Vera Rubin / GB300) | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mixture-of-Experts | DeepSeek-V3 671B | 1,024 | 2x | 6.1-0116 / 6.1-0030 | 
| Mixture-of-Experts | Qwen3.5 397B GRPO (RL) | 64 | 1.4x | 6.1-0135 / 6.1-0020 | 
| Mixture-of-Experts | gpt-oss 20B | 64 | 1.6x | 6.1-0135 / 6.1-0049 | 
| Dense | Llama 2 70B LoRA | 72 | 1.5x | 6.1-0123 / 6.1-0138 | 
| Dense | Llama 3.1 8B | 72 | 1.6x | 6.1-0073 / 6.1-0138 | 
| Diffusion | FLUX.1 | 72 | 1.5x | 6.1-0124 / 6.1-0138 | 
| Recommender | DLRMv4 | 128 | 1.4x | 6.1-0129 / 6.1-0038 |

See www.mlcommons.org for more information.
The pattern is clear. The largest gain lands on the largest, most communication-heavy model. While the platform is consistently 1.4x to 1.6x faster across the rest of the suite, the generational advantage widens even further for the massive DeepSeek-V3 benchmark.
The suite covers natural language, image generation, recommendation, and reinforcement learning, so the gains hold across multiple modalities as well as across different model shapes and architectures.
DeepSeek-V3 671B: 2x per GPU on the hardest workload
DeepSeek-V3 671B is a 671-billion-parameter token-dropless Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model and the most demanding workload in the suite. Expert parallelism turns every iteration into a burst of all-to-all communication, so fabric efficiency shows up directly in time to train.
Vera Rubin NVL72 trained the benchmark in 4.14 minutes using 1,024 GPUs across 16 racks. GB300 NVL72 ran the identical 1,024-GPU configuration in 8.03 minutes, close to 2x per GPU, and the largest generational improvement in this round. Halving time to train roughly doubles how many experiments a team can run in a quarter, and experiment throughput is what moves model quality.
At a larger scale, GB300 NVL72 produced the fastest absolute result of the round: 1.38 minutes across 10,240 GPUs. That is one training job spread across 160 racks, each its own NVLink domain, and it shows the platform’s scale-out fabric holding up long after the job outgrows a single rack.
Post-training arrives, and Vera Rubin leads it
MLPerf Training v6.1 adds its first agentic LLM reinforcement learning post-training benchmark, Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO, reflecting a fundamental shift in AI development. Post-training has emerged as the critical differentiator for agentic accuracy, making the GRPO workload uniquely demanding. The continuous cycle of generating rollouts, scoring them, and updating weights pushes system architectures to their limits by forcing constant, massive weight migrations between inference and training engines.
Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved the fastest time for this new benchmark with a time of 10.44 minutes at 1,024 GPUs (6.1-0117), compared with 13.78 minutes for GB300 NVL72 (6.1-0031) at the same scale. The Vera Rubin platform also proved its flexibility by submitting on two different inference backends: NVIDIA NeMo RL with TensorRT-LLM at 10.44 minutes and with vLLM at 10.94 minutes (6.1-0118). Shipping two viable inference backends on a benchmark this new says as much about software maturity as it does about silicon.
Teaching these models to observe, reason, and act requires running each rollout in a simulated environment and executing tool calls, code, or API validations. Because driving these simulations is intensely CPU-bound, the NVIDIA Vera CPU is integral to the architecture, sustaining more than 22,500 concurrent RL environments across 256 CPUs in a single Vera CPU rack.
While the GPUs handle massive token generation and rapid weight updates, the Vera CPUs work in lockstep to simulate the environments, ensuring the accelerators are continuously fed with the rich feedback required to perfect agentic workflows.
NVLink, Quantum-X and Spectrum-X: Co-designed networking for high-efficiency AI scaling
Every result above is also a networking result. Modern AI training requires thousands of processors to act as one, a challenge NVIDIA solves by co-designing the internal rack domain and the external cluster fabric.
Inside the rack, Vera Rubin NVL72 connects 72 GPUs and 36 CPUs through a copper NVLink 6 spine. Delivering 3.6 TB/s per GPU and 260 TB/s per rack, this all-to-all domain keeps MoE expert dispatch off the critical path. Beyond the rack, the platform scales out via ConnectX-9 SuperNICs over Quantum-X800 InfiniBand or Spectrum-X Ethernet. To manage bursty MoE traffic, both fabrics use adaptive routing and congestion control to keep all-to-all communications hidden behind the compute layer.
This cohesive design translates directly to efficiency. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved above 97% scaling efficiency as it scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs (4 to 16 racks). GB300 NVL72 showcased the platform’s large-scale capabilities , extending to 10,240 GPUs to capture the fastest absolute result of the round.
Because the NVL72 architecture provides a consistent 72-GPU domain, developers see predictable performance jumps every generation without altering their operating model. Each cycle simply delivers more compute and bandwidth across the same consistent fabric.

The MLPerf name and logo are trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information.
Continuous software optimization: Unlocking faster pretraining without hardware upgrades
Vera Rubin’s results came from the NVIDIA AI software stack that customers receive: NVIDIA NeMo Framework 26.09 for the pretraining benchmarks, NVIDIA NeMo RL for the reinforcement learning benchmark, and NVIDIA PyTorch releases for FLUX.1 and DLRMv4. The optimizations are the ones described in our MLPerf Training v6.0 round.
The stack also keeps moving after a round closes. Since v6.1 submissions were finalized, we have re-run several of the benchmarks on the same hardware and configuration with a newer software build. These are unverified results rather than MLCommons submissions, and we are sharing them because they show how continuous optimizations make NVIDIA infrastructure highly productive, durable, and fungible.

Because the CUDA platform is highly programmable, customers can unlock even more performance on their own. For example, Thinking Machines Lab developed an NVFP4 training recipe and custom kernels for its Inkling 2 Small model on GB300 NVL72, using NVFP4 for forward-pass MoE GEMMs and MXFP8 for gradients. Compared with full MXFP8 training, it sped up pretraining and fine-tuning by 8% and reinforcement learning by 20%, with minimal accuracy impact.
An ecosystem that shipped on day one
Vera Rubin’s debut in MLPerf Training v6.1 proves the architecture is built for immediate global deployment. With 80 percent of all closed-division submissions running on NVIDIA platforms across 20 partner organizations, these benchmarks represent reproducible performance across clouds and OEMs rather than isolated laboratory peaks.
Systems are already generally available across various cloud infrastructure partners, complementing a multitude of AI Factory deployments around the globe. Today, Vera Rubin leads on performance per GPU across all seven workloads, while Blackwell and Blackwell Ultra maintain the scale record. Azure’s 2,560-node, 10,240-GPU GB200 NVL72 submission tied the NVIDIA 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 run to claim this round’s largest clusters.
Partners are also pushing the limits of the architecture at the node level: Firmus used AI-driven kernel generation, with automated performance testing and mathematical validation, to post the fastest GB300 8-GPU result of the round, training GPT-OSS 20B in 52.90 minutes (6.1-0091) and Llama 3.1 8B in 52.40 minutes (6.1-0094). Because these platforms share a continuously optimizing CUDA software stack, developers can expect these inaugural metrics to climb steadily higher before the next MLPerf round even begins.
As the Vera Rubin software stack matures the way the Blackwell stack did, expect these initial performance advantages to continue to unlock even greater value throughout the platform’s lifecycle.
